BY VERNON J. CHARLESWORTH.

HE author of "Ecce Homo" has endeavoured to write a Life of Christ T from the standpomt of a contemporary. Mr. Beecher, on the other hand, has "endeavoured to present scenes that occurred two thousand years ago as they would appear to modern eyes if the events had taken place in our day.'' It is, perhaps, dilfiL:ult to say whose task was the easier, or which of the two has achieved the greater success. Both works are characterised by fine touche, of genius aud poetry, and in a sense one is the complement of the other. We apply to neither the test ol' a rigid orthodoxy, but while questioning the soundness of many of the conclusions, we welcome the attempt of both writers to cr.)eLatise inLo a consistent whole the disjointed fragments of the evangelic records. "Writing in full sympathy with the Gospels as authentic historical documents, and with the 11ature and teachiugs of the great personage whom they describe," Mr . .BeeL:her has "attentively constdered whatever has beeu said, on every side, in the works of crittcal objectors," and has sought to depict the Saviour, "in his life, his social relations, his disposition, his deeds, and his doctrines." These sentences indicate the !lcope of the work to which tlie author is committed, and of which we have the first instalment in the volume before us. lt 1s not our intention to write a critical review, strictly speaking, but to glean from its ample pages a few choice extracts, which will be acceptable to those of our readers who cannot command the volume, aud at the same time indicate, in all fidelity, the points upon which we join issue with the author. We are much mistaken if many of our readers are not.induced to enrich their libraries by the addition of a book, which, beyond all his other productions, will secure for Mr. Beecher no obscure niche in the temple of fame.

The chaJ?ter on the o~erture of angels abounds with striking metaphors. m M~·· Beecher s best sty\e. "Angel_s seem as birds when n_ew-:come 1? spr!ng, ~o ha~·e flown hither and t_h1ther in songful mood, d1ppmg the1r white wrngs mto our atmosphere, Just touchin" the earth or glancing along its surface as sea-birds skim the surface "'of the sea: And yet birds are ~ar too rude and wings too burdensome to express adequately that feelmg of unlaboured angelic motion, which the narrati'l'e produces upon the imagination. Their airy and gentle co~ing would perhaps be better compared to the glow of colours flung by thG s1~n upon morning_ clouds,_ tl_iat seem to be born just where they appear. Like a_ be:1m of light stnkmg through some orifice, they shine upon Zachanas m the Temple. As the morning light finds the flowers, so fo~~~ they the i_nother of Jesus. To. the spepberds' eyes they filled the m10mght arch hke auroral beams of hght ; but not as silently, for they sarw, and more marvellously than "when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy." Mr. Beecher seeems to grow dizzy by his lofty poetising, or he would not commit himself, in sober mood, to the proposition that " traits of personal tenderness and generous love will draw the human heart to God." History warrants no such belief; indeed, it flatly contradicts it. The nnsullied purity of tl1e character of Jesus revealed human guilt as it never had been revealed before, a11d its light proving intolerable, men instead of being drawn to God, merged their prejudices in the common cry, "away with Hirn, away with Him, crucify Him, crucify Him!" Incarnate excellence does not destroy the enmity of the carnal mind. " .As asters, among plants, go all summer long unbeauLirul, their flowers hidden within, and bmst into bloom at the very end of summer and in late autumn, with the frosts upon their heads, so this aged saint (Simeon) had blossomed at the close of a long life, into this noble ecstasy of joy. In a stormy time, when outward life moves wholly agaiust one's wishes, he is truly great whose soul becomes a sanctuary in l'lhich patience dwells with hof'e. In one hour Simeon received full satisfaction for tht" yearnings of many :years." " The guide of the Magi was a light kindled in the heavens to instruct and lead those whose eyes were prepared to receive it." In deali11g wiLh those who elin inate the miraculous from the historic narrative of the appearance uf the star in the east, the author's sarcasm is most refreshing. "The disciples plucked the wheat-heads, and rul ,bing them in their hfmds, they ate the grain. But our sceptical believers take from the New Testa1uent its supernatural element,-rub out the wheat and eat the chaff." In the second chapter, Mr. Beecher deals with metaphysical questions respecting the original naLure of Christ. He sets aside the humanitarian view which regards Jesus simply as an extraordinary man; the theory of compromise which represents him as more t~an human but as less than diville; and the doctrine of the church, smce the fourth century, which attributes to Jesus a double natu~e-a human soul ~nd a divine•soul in one body,-and stands to "the simple and more philosop!:ical views of the sacred Seriptures." "We are not to look," he says, "for a glorifie~, au <on throne~ J eA~S, but for Go~, ma~ifest 1·n ~he fudi; and, in this view, the very hm1tat10ns and seemmg d1screpanc1es

in a divine life become congruous parts of the whole sublime problem. We arc to distinguish between difficulties whic:h are inherent in the nature ?f the infinite, and those which are but the imperfections of our own philosophy. In the one case, the perplexity lies in the weakne~s of our reason ; in the other, the weakness of our reasonin". Thr~ truth of the proper divinity of Christ is the marrow of the sa~red SJriptures.'' Without qualification the following propositions do not expre,s the truth respecting man as a fallen being:-" M,m'M nature and God's nar.ure do not differ in kind, but in degree of the same attributes. The identification of the divine and the human nature was one of the granri results of the Incarnation. Manhood is nearer Godhood than we have been wont to believe." It is true that " God said, let us make man in our image." But how little trace of the divine origin is there in fallen humanity? The Fall has obliterated the- fair marks of our heavenly original. The splendour of Eden's innocency is eclipsed by the black pall of sin. To accomplish human redemption God has sent forth his Son, " the express image of his person," and " He bath predesLinated us to be conformed to the image of his son." But we think our author forgets that all this points to the upbringing of redeemed humanit_v only, in resurrection, to the standard of God's lofty ideal, and by no means justifies the assertion of the identity of the divine and human no.v. It is not logical to assume an ultimate limited possibility to be a present universal f ,et. "For twelve years of childhood the only syllable of history uttered is, ' and the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with 1fis lorn, and the grace of God was upon him.' This, then, was not a divinity coming through the clouds into human life, full-orbed, triumphing with the undiminished strength of a heavenly nature over those conditions which men must bear. It was a divine child, and childhood meant latent power, undeveloped faculty, unripe organs, a being without habits, wi1 bout character, without experien,:e; a cluster of germs, a branch full of unblossomed buds, a mere sPed of manhood. Except his mother's arms, there was no circle of light aboltt his head, fo11d1_v as artists have loved r.o paint it. Nothing could be more unnatur,d than to suppose that he was a child without childhood, a full and perfect being cleft from the Almight.V, as Minerva was fabled to have come from the head of Jupittir. He was the Son of M,111-a real boy, as at·tenvards he was a most manly man. How early he came t.o himself, and felt witl1in him the motions of his Godhead, none can tell. At twelve he over- .rode the interpretations of the doctors, and, as one having auLhurity, sat in judgment upon the imperfect religion of his ancestors. TJ1is first visit to Jerusalem stands up in his childhood as Mount Tabor ris()s from the plain-the one solitary point of definite record. It is plain, from his reply to his mother, that he was conscious of the nature that was in him, and that strong impulses urged him to disclose his power. It is, therefore, very significant, and not the le,tst of the signs of divinity, • that he ruled his spirit, and dwelt at home in unrnurmuring expectation; this is in itself a wonder of divinity, if men were only wise enongh to marvel." In the chapter on "The Voice in the Wilderness," there is some clever writing on the prophetical office and the missions of the µrophets. "A prophet was more than one who foretold events. He forefelt and

all ages, has come to natures alniady prepared for the office to which the_r. were called. Tl!e morning star of a new era, John, is speedily lost m the blaze of hun who was and is the 'light of the world.' His -was_ one of those lives which are lost to themselves that they may spring up m others. He came both in grandeur and in beauty, like a summer storm, which, falling in rain, is lost in the soil, and re-appears neither as vapour nor cloud, but is transformed into flowers and fruits. John -was Christ's forerunner, as the ploughman goes before the sower. Upon the rough furrows, and not on the shorn lawn, is there hope for the see<l." The meagre records which we possess do not warrant, we think, the ass,,rtion that in John's preaching " there was no future, no great spirit land, no heaven above his world." His call to repentance was surely based upon hope as well as fear. "Flee from the wrath to come" was not the whole of his meFsage. The greatest amongst the prophets was certainly not the least evangelical. Of John's baptism, Mr. Beecher asks, "was it into the Jewish church that he baptised? Was it an initiation into a new sect? Was it Christian baptism ? " His answer is negative on each point, and he says, "It was a symbolic act, signifying that one had risen to a higher moral condition. It was declaratory or moral transition." We are not disposed to quarrel with the author's judgment of the baptism of repentance, but when he asserts that "neither John, nor afterwards Jesus, gave to the act any ecclesiastical meaning," we demand his reasons for the assertion. The very formula of Christ's baptism is against the a~sumption. If baptism is that symbolic act by which a man declares, "I forsake my sins, and rise to a better life," where is the author's consisLenc·y in pract.ising infant baptism? The inspired apostles ·always regarded Christian baptism as symbolic of incorporation with the mystiL:al body of Christ, the church. It does not indicate, merely, the rising to a higher life, but the possession of a divine life in fellowship -with the risen Christ. "We are crucified together with Christ; we are risen together with Christ," is the avo-wal of every believer by the symbolic voice of Christian baptism. The Church is the unity of sa:ved men, and immersion is the divinely appointed sign of incorporation. "A bapLism to a higher life would prolJauly be Christ's interpretation of John's baptism for himself. And he submitted to it, as one of the great multitude. The rising from lower to higher moral_ st~tes, Jesus experienced in common with the multitude." To us 1t 1s E!carce~y co11ceivable that, by a symbolic act, the Saviour made any advance m • bis moral state. We are quite contented with the belief that by this orert act he placed himself at the head of his baptised followers. The wl,ole subject is capable of a fuller discussion, but this is beside our purpose in tile present paper. . lo treating of the temptation of our Lord, Mr. Beecher 1s bold without

REMARKS ON BEECHER'S LIFE OF CHRIST. 1 liJ being irreverent. "It is not strange to us, now well instructed in the spirit of Christ's mission, that he did not enter at once 11pon his work of teaching. Midway between his prirnte life, now ended, and his pnblie ministry, about to begin, there was to be a long and silent diseipline. The three narratives of the temptation by Matthew, Mark, and Luke, lift us at once into the region of mystery. That which is important to any proper consideration of the obscure sublimity of this mystery is, that it shall be a temptation of the devil as an actual personal spirit ; that it shall be a real temptation, or one that put the faculties of Christ's soul to task, and required a resistance of his whole nature, as other temptations do of human nature. It is on this account that we have regarded the temptation as of two parts or series-the first, a personal and private conflict, runniug through forty solitary days of fasting in the wilderness; and the second, a ministerial trial, represemed b_, the symbolism of the bread, the temple, and the mountain top. Througl1 that long battle of life, in which every man is engaged, and in every mood of the struggle which men of aspiration ant.I moral sense make toward perfect holiness, there is an inspiration of comfort to be den red from the example of Christ. In places the most strange, and in the desolate way where men dwell with the wild beasts of the passions, if there be but a twilight of faith, we shall find his footsteps, and know that be has been there-is there again, Ii ving over anew in us his own struggles, and saying, with the authority of a God and t11e tenderness of a Father: 'In the world ye shall have tribulation; but be of good cheer ; I have overcome the world."' Our author thinks that by fasting and solitude our divine Lord rose at length to the vision state, and that the three temptations foreshadowed the trials to ,rbich he would be exposed through his whole career in the use of d1 vine power. The Sa.tanic challenge, "command that these stones be made bread," Mr. Beecher interprets as "the spirit of this world soliciting Jesus to employ that divine power which now began to effulge in him, for secular and physical, rather than for m<'lral and spiritual, cuds. It was, if one might so say, the whole selfish spirit of time and history pleaLiing that Jesus should work upon matter and for the flesh, rather than upun the •soul and for the spirit." Again, "Jesus was next solicited to let the spirit of admiration and praise be the genius of the new movement. 'If thou be the Sun of God, cast thyself down from hence.' This symbol, as a trial scene, contains not only an appeal to the love of praise in Jesus, but an appeal to the principle of admiration in the multitude." In the final scene "there was a tremendous temptati011 to exhibit before men his real place and authority; to appear as great as he really was; to so use his energies that men should admit him to be greater than generals, higher than kings, more glorious than temple or palace. In that mountain vision he saw the line of temptations which wuuld beat in upon the principle of self-esteem, that source and fountain of ambition among men. With men, the difficulty is to rise into eminence. With Jesus, the very reverse was true." It is quite true, as the auLhor admits, that "This view is not exhaustively sa~isfactory. Nu view is. ~hichever theory one takes in explaining the temptation, he must take 1t with its painful perplexities."

CROMWELL'S PURITANISM. 17G This was n task highly difficuH. Many of the letters had seen the light in various forms, but were so presented to the public as to repel : "too often," says Mr. Carlyle, "it is apparent that the very editor of these poor utteran?es h~d, if reading mean understanding, never read them. They stan'.1 m ~h~1r old spelling! mispunctuated, misprinted, unelucidated, umntelhg1ble-defaced with the dark incrustatiomi too well known to students of that period." This industrious, painstaking editor, however, saw much light out" of darkness on the back of darkness, thick and threefold;" and how bright that light has been for u~ who reap the harvest of an author's toilsome and persevering efforts, writers of all kinds and professions, and readers of all sorLs, have plainly seen. Perhaps the grimness of Cromwell's religious character-or we should rather say, its grim aspect, for it was not destitute of light and sweetness-had peculiar attractions ·for so rugged a mind as the editor's; and the unprosaic and vigorous piety of the Protector admirably met the tastes of a writer who has shown by his works how much he can appreciate brave conviction in past days. We are not insensible of Carlyle's theological inadequacies, but there is something in his teaching more noble even than his most ruthless unveilillg of immeasurable cant, or his strongest, and as we think unwarrantable condemnations of the present day. And we give a -warm welcome to the very cheap edition recently issued of "Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches," and wish for it a success proportioned to its uni rcrsally admitted deserts. The work must ever be regarded as au English classic, which no educated man or lad will fol to read. The letters of Cromwell, Mr. Carlyle has pointed out, are not distingui~hed by literary art-" No eloquence, elegance, not ah,ays even clearness of expression, is to be looked for in them." Cromwell had no time for such arts. Perhaps, he had bnt little disposition for them. "Superfluity, as if by a natural law of tbe case, the write1· has had to discard; whatsoever quality can be dispensed with is indifferent to him. With unwi-eldy movement, yet with a great solid step he presses through, towards his object; has marked out very decisively what tile real steps towards it are ; discriminating well the essential from the extrancou,." And again, "Crom well, emblem of the dumb English, is i11tere,ti11g- to me by the very inadequacy of his speech. Heroic insight valot1r and belief, without words-how noble is it in comparison to the aJroitcst flow of words without heroic insight." Glimpses here and there in this wonderful collection of letters are afforded us of the nature of the Protector's piety. Worthy of study are they all. In an age -when Puritanic sincerity was as greatly scoffed at and lampooned by witless worldlings, as. loyalty to the same fundamental truths is denounced to-day by the pretentious superfine criti..:ism or the "advanced" theologians, Cromwell, with true manly vigour, gave his adhesion to the cause of evangelical religion. He became, as his biographer truly says, '' the soul of the Puritan revolt;" hence the popular fancy is correct, and the general vilification of his character easily accounted for. "His words, and still more his silences," says .Mr. Carlyle, "and unconscious instincts, when you have spelt and lol"ingly deciphered these also out of his words, will in several ways re1Yard tlic study of an earnest man. An earuest,man, I apprehend, may gather

The_ earliest letter ~xtant reveals Cromwell's relip;ious earnestness. At a tun~ when the sarntly Laud was hunting down all gospel lecturers and puttrng an end to all gracious discourses, Oliver wrote from St. I ,·es l~esccching- his " very loving friend, Mr. Sto1·ie, at the sign of the Dog- Ill the Royal Exchange, London,'' to see that Dr. Wells, "a man of_ goocl1~ess and industry," probably labouring at St. Ives, should not f:nl m h~s lectureship through lack of funds-" for who goeth to warfare_ at his o_wn cost? In this letter the noble writer very faithfully declares :-" Amongst the catalogue of thos~ go?d works which your fellow-citizens and our countrymen hal'e done, tlus will not be reckoned for the least, that they have provided for _the frcding of souls. Building of hospitals provides for men's bodws; to build material temples is judged a work of piety; but they that procure spiritual food, they that build up spiritual temples, they are tl1e men truly charitable, truly pious."* An argument this every way for the proper sustentation of godly ministers and t.he augmentation of their incomes-a clear proof that whatever his faults, Oliver bad no sympathy with the heresy of those who depreciate the Christian ministry, and count the honest labourer unworthy of bis honest hire. Throughout bis life, Cromwell remained true to his early religious convictions. We see in all his letters evidences of bis unfaltering faith in the truths of the gospel ; and his earnest personal piety is to be obserred in bis correspondence with the members of his family and with his political associates. He gives us in one letter a very pleasing testimony of his conversion. We may be sure that it was in no spirit of affectation or hypocrisy that be confessed the unsatisfactoriness of his past life. "Yon know what my manner of life hath been. Oh, I lil'cd in and loved darkness, and hated light; I was a chief, the chief of sinners. This is true : I bated godliness, yet God had mercy on me. 0 the riches of bis mercy! Praise him for me;-pray for me, that he who hath begun a good work would perfect it in the day of Christ." It is n~t needful for us to interpret this confession as some have done .. There _is nu eridence that the writer had been grossly immoral, or dissolute m any \'l'ay. A man may feel himself to be the chief of sinner!:! who ~as foed a fairly moral life; sins against light and knowledg~, Vl'.arnmg a11d reproof, conscience and God, are grave enough to JUS~1fy the lowliest cunfession. Clerical writers have been only too anx10us to <lamn this man's character before conversion, and to flagellate him for an hypocrisy which they love to ascribe to him.

There is so little that is compatible with the Christian life in Lhe savage work of bloodsherl, (Dr. Norman Macleod notwithstanding,) that the frequent references to God in CromweU's letters during the Ci vii War rather grate upon the sensitive ear. And yet such allusions made by men deeply imbued with the spirit of the Old Testament, believing in Lhe "God of hosts," the "Lord strong and mighty in battle," the Lord as "a man of war," deeply persuaded that their cause was God's, and that th_ey were but instruments in his hands (as, indeed, half an eye can see) were perfectly natural. Not difficun to undersbnd are these brave Puritan warriors. We all know the oft-repeated story of the men of Naseby-the Ironsides, the Tnvincibles-who "when the roaring shot poured thit-k and hot" were "stalwart men and true ;" who in the death-grapple of physical force made their proud enemirs give way inch by inch, and triumphed over the very men who had heretofore flouted and ridiculed in their cups the psalm-singing men of Liberty. It was not a gloomy fanaticism, an unscrupulous purpose, a whinin<Y cant, that made these men mighty in the presence of foemen worthy of their steel. These were men of character, of probity and virtue, and stern piety, strong in principle, stout of heart, and unbending in the presence of temptation and wrong. Significant enough was Cromwell's description of these determined foes uf oppressions, kingly and cleric: they were men "who made some conscien, e of what they did." They were proudly con~cious of the justness of their cause, and to the God of battles they committed its issue. And Cromwell not only shared this conviction, but represented it with an intensified earnestness. After the battle of Marston Moor, he wrote: " Truly England and the church of God bath bad a great favour from the Lord, in this great victory given unto us, such as the like never was since this war began. It had all the evidences of an absolute victory obtained by the Lord's blessing upon the godly party principally." The enemy was not charged, he goes on to say, but routed; "God made them as stubble to our swords." This he writes to Colonel Valentine Walton, who had lost his son in this battle, as will appear from the following excerpt which is worth reading:- " Sir,-God hnth taken away your eldest son by a cannon-shot. It broke his leg. We were necessitnted to have it cut off, whereof he died. Sir, you know our own trials this way,* but the Lord supported me with this, that the Lord took him into the happi1,ess we nil pant for and look for. There is your precious child full of glory, never to know sin or sorrow any more. He was n g,1llant young man, exceedingly gracious. God give you his comfort. Before his death he was so full of comfort, that to Frank Russel and myself he could not express it, 'It was so great above his pain.' This he said to us, Indeed it was admirable. A little after, he said, 'one thing lay upon his spirit.' I nskctl him whnt that was? He told me it was, that God had-not su!Tcred him to be any more the executioner of His enemies. * * " * Ilut few knew him ; for he was a precious young man, fit for God. You have cause to bless tile Lord. He is a glorious saint in heaven; wherein you ought excedingly to n:joice. Let this drink up your sorrow ; seeing these are not feigned words to corn fort you, but the thing is 80 real and undoubted a truth. You may do all things by the atrength of Christ. Seek that, antl you shall easily bear your trial. Let this public mercy to the church of God make you to forget your private sorrow." * Cromwoll had only rocently lost bis son, Oliver, in conflict with lhc Il.oyalista.

Slanderous tongnes were busy in those days as afterwards, and Cromwell heard and treated them with the contempt that slander richly dcscr,es. "We desire," he says, with true lofty dignity, "to refer the m;iu~· slanders heaped upon us by false tong-urs to God,-who will, in due time, make it appear to the world that we study the glory of God, and the honour and liberty of the Parliament, for which "l'l'e unanimouslv fight, without seeking our own interests." This has in it the rin(l' of Puritanism, whic'.1 ne,cr shrank from any self-denying ordinance, ~r from any painfol self-sacrifice. Cromwell gives ample proofs, by letters and speeches, of his extreme dislike of the civil war. He professed to detest and abhor the accusation that had been made ag-ainst the Parliamentarians, that they sought to maintain their religious opinions by force. "I profess," he says, " I could never satisfy myself of the justness of this v.ar, but from the authority of the Parliament to maintain itself in its rights; and in this .cause I hope to approve myself an honest man and single-hearted." A few months after this was written, Cromwell rose from his seat in the House of Commons, and in the midst of breathless silence uttered these historic words : " It is now a time to speak, or for e,er hold the tongue. The important occasion now is no less than to save a nation out of a bleeding, nay, almost dying, condition, which the long continuance of this war bath already brought it to; so that without a more speedy, vigorous and effectual prosecution of the war-casting off all lingering proceedings like those of soldiers-offortune beyond Ilea, to spin out a war-we shall make the kingdom weary of us and bate the name of a Parliament." This speech was delivered in view of the celebrated Self-denying Ordinance, and very briskly indeed did the "great business," as Cromwell invariably called it, proceed after this new epoch in military affairs. Cromwell sits down quietly after the storming of poor Bristol, and gives to Mr. Speaker a full and detailed account of the work and of its successful issue. He thinks be must be a very atheist who cannot see that " all this is none other than the work of God." Praises were due to the gallant men: "It's their joy that they are instruments of God's glory and their country's good. It's their honour that God vouchsafes to use them. Sir, they that have been employed in this service know that faith and prayer obtained this city for you; I do not say ours only, but of the people of God with you and all England over, who have wrestled with God for a blessing in this very thing. Our desires are, that God may be glorified by the same spirit of faith by which we ask all our sufficiency, and have receiv,ed_ it." Th~re is an unusu~lly _gran_d religious force about these convrnhons; this rugged Pur1tamsm 1s heroically expressed. In the midst of those difficult, intricate Scotch negotiations, Cromwell can find but little time to write to the members of his family; but, when he does this, be manifests deep religious concern for his kith and kin. Writing from the fashionable quarter of Drury-lane-how hard to realise that this low haunt was ever fashionable !-he urges his newlywedded daughter not to forget the culture of her souL "Dear heart, press on ! let not husband, let not anything coo_l thy_ aff~ctions after Christ." On the contrary, he hopes the new relat10nsh1p will subservc her spiritual interests. "That which is best worthy of love in thy

His anxiety a little further on that his _son sh_oul_d ~ave as a wife one who had "that assurance of god: liness " 1s not ms1grnficant. The father who made " the offer of a verv great proposition" to Oliver, in the shape of his daughter to Oii vcr's son, whoever he was, seems to be a moral and fair sort of man, but of anything beyond there was no certainty in Cromwell's mind. He had, on these grounds, other preferences. Qnite at home, and exceedingly friendly with those right honourable Puritan noblemen and gentlemen, whose delight was g-reat in sustaininrr a godly and efficient ministry, Cromwell, behind none in this service t~ the state, encouraged them not a little, and poured forth his earnest and devout desires to them. To Lord Wharton he thus writes-a thanksgiving letter it is: "Wh~n we thin~ of our G?d, wh_at are we? Oh, his mercy to the whole soernty of samts,-desp1sed, Jeered saints! Let them mock on. Would we were all saints! The best of us are, God knows, poor weak saints, yet saints; if not sheep, yet lambs, and must be fed. We have daily bread, and shall have it, in spite of all enemie~. There's enough in our Father's house, and he dispenseth it. I think through these outward mercies, as we call them, faith, patience, love hope, are exercised and perfected,-yea; Christ formed, and grows to ~ perfect man within us." Here we have good Puritanie advice,-lessons learnt from such uncommonly good chaplains as Dr. Owen, and Dr. Goodwin-given to the wife of Lieut.-General Fleetwood:- " Salute your dear .rife from me. Bid her beware of a bondage spirit. Fear is the natural issue of such a spirit; the antidote is love. The voice of fear is: 'if I had done this, if I had avoided that, how well it had been with rue!' I know this hath been her vain reasoning, poor Biddy! "Love argueth in t.his wise: 'what a Christ have I ; what a Father in and through him. What a name hath my Father, merciful, gracious, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin. What a nature hath my Father: he is LOVE: free in it, unchangeable, infinite. Whnt a covenant between him and Christ, for all his seed, for every one, wherein he undertakes all, and the poor soul nothing ! The new covenant is grace-to or upon the soul; to which it (the soul) is passive and receptive; I'll do away their sin~, I'll m·ite my law, &c.; I'll put it in their hearts,-they shall never depart from me, &c.' " This commends the love of God: its Christ's dying for men without strength, for men whilst sinners, whilst enemies. And shall we seek for the root of our comforts within us,-what God hath done, what he is to us in Christ, is the root of our comfort, in thi~ is stability; in us is weakness. Acts of obedience are not perfect, and therefore yield not perfect grace. Faith as an act yields it not; but only as it <!arries us into him, who is our perfect rest and peace ; in whom we are accounted of, and received by, the Father-even ns Christ himself. This is our high calling. Rest we here, and only here." Surely, there is here much soundness in theology, and much spiritual perception likewise. Cromwell clearly had not seen the abyss of "advanced thought," now so perceptible alas ! But it was ~omething to be contented with such really substantial thought as was gi,·en the world by the Puritan chaplains afore-mentioned. And now, Oliver Cromwell is, significantly enough, "His Highness."

God to t)iis nation; approp_riat)ng [or this purpose the Psalmist's jubi- Jnnt strarns, "Su~ely salvation 1s mgh unto them that fear him; that glory may <1well m our land." " Thou hast been favourable to thy land :" "Truly I hope," says Cromwell, "this is His land. In some sense it may be given out that it is God's land; and he that hath the weakest knowledge, and the worst memory, can easily tell that we are 'a redeemed people' 'from the time' when God was first pleased to to look favourably upon us, 'to redeem us' out of the hands of Papery, in that never-to-be-forgotten Reformation, that most significant and greatest 'mercy' the nation hath felt or tasted." The preaching of the gospel without let or hindrance, he goes on to say, is a distinguishing mercy : "Who would have forethought when we were plunged into the midst of our troubles, that ever the people of God should have had liberty to worship God without fear or enemies." Indeed, it was a triumph, all the greater when contrasted with subrnquent events, and repealings, and oppressive acts against conscience, and a general state of "lrhat astronomers call" backwardation" which clearly Crom""ell could not hate foreseen. In this very speech, as in others, we have not only the fundamental creed of Puritanism, or Calvinism, (not hyper however) stated, but somewhat expounded; for the speaker was a skilled theologian, accustomed to all the ins-and-outs of the much-abused Five Points;· and a very earnest lover and supporter of a godly and instructi.e ministry. No one had a keener perception of genius in the pulpit than be. Gathering round him men who could preach, and think, and write; scholars, of whose scholarship no preacher need now be ashamed; men mighty in the Scriptures far beyond any who have come after them, as Eome of us still think, despite the current of the times; Cromwell showed how intelligently and completely he had grasped the doctrines then so ably and profitably expounded. As Carlyle tells us, in his dying hours Cromwell spoke -much of" the Covenants." "Faith in the Col'enant," made holy and true by the Mediator of the Covenant, " is my only support." This he left to his ,.ife and children "to feed upon." "All the promiees of God are in Lim; yea, and in him Amen; to the glory of God by us-by us in .Jesus Christ." Beautiful hope to die with !

W applied. In some respects it will of necessity harmonise with that which bas been generally adopted, as with regard to the substance of the doctrines maintained, and the character of the emotions intended to be excited· but in other respects-it will widely differ .from it. No variation, in fact, is n~eded in the sentiments, but in their symbolic representation and their personal application only. None need fear, therefore, any attempt being made, openly or covertly, to diminish the perspicuity end force of John Bunyan's creed. The design is not so much to give an exposition of matters of doctrine and experience as to present them in a new point of view; and of this to give a mere outline, to be filled up hereafter by such as may have more leisure and ability for the undertaking.

articles.title: The City of Destrgction
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text: THE CITY OF DESTRGCTION. Tms is an appropriate symbol of man's natural condition. It is not Bnnyan's native villnge of Elstow merely, or the town of Bedford, where he ministered and in which he was imprisoned, but the whole world. It is not spoken of a~ a city, but as the city, to intimate that it included all mankind. It is the City of Destruction, because though absorbed in its pleasure8 and pursuits, thoughtless and self-secure, it is doomed to destruction. He who would avoid its impending doom must flee from it as Lot did from Sodom. He must escape for his life, and must not even look behind him, neither stay in all the plain, lest he be consumed. Fear is the first hopeful sign in the salvation of m~ny, even when it is not guilt, but its punishment, that is feared. " Others,'' says Jude," save with fear, pulling them out of the fire." This was Bunyan's first experience in religion, and this fear may form an essential part of all first religious impressions, though in such different degrees that it may not alw1iys be perceptible. It cannot be wrong to fear the divine ,iudgments. It"is the effect which all threatenings of punishment are intended to produce. It is appealed to, moreover, as e. strong incentive to duty. There is a time in which danger and refuge absorb the whole passions and powers. "Noah, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house." This is mentioned as pertaining to his faith. There must be some faith in all fear; and the fear of divine wrath, arising from conscience and the divine word, may derive its chief value from the faith which it implies. Its propriety man-ward is the natural principle of self-preservation ; its propriety God-ward is the belief in him that is included in it. Every man is a native of the City of Destrnction; is brought up in it; is wholly intent upon its possessions and pleasures, and his first object must be, if he would escape its doom, to flee from it. To remain where he is, and what he is, is certain and eternal destruction.

articles.title: Opposition from Without
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
OPPOSITION FROM WITHOUT. A FEAUFOL apprehension of the awful consequences of sin cannot be long concealed. Efforts may be made to disguise the inward pangs, and a false cheerfulness may be assumed, but the change soon becomes obvious to all. "This," say they, "is nothing else but sorrow of heart." If it should be found to arise from such afflictions as are common to man, as from bodily infirmity, or worldly embarrassment, or the loss of friends, it will awaken general kindness and sympathy ; if suspected of having its origin in religious convictions it will excite general opposition and scorn. The ridicule of worldly companions, and the tender entreaties of endeared kindred and friends, some from mere ignorance, and others from direct enmity to that which is known to be good, are often the first trial which serious impressions ha"e to endure, and are needful to test their sincerity and power. They especially, who like Bunyan have acquired notoriety amongst the worldly-minded and profane, will have to submit to this

articles.title: Evangelist
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text: EVANGELIST. PrLGnrn seeks refuge from his distress of mind in readin" the Bible. Instead of llffording him immediate relief, it aggravates his mis~ry, and leads him to en· ont with greater vehemence, "'i\'hat must I do to be saved?" Condemnation on acconnt of sin is more easily seen in the Scriptures thA.n the way of ·salvation from sin; because mere declarations suffice for the one, and many seeming contrarieties have to be reconciled in the other. Hence the aid which those who have clearly discovered the way of life for themselves may give to nnxious enquirers. This is the office of an evangelist. Such a one met with Pilg-rirn, and after learning the cause of his distress said, " • Do yon see yonder wicket-gate?' He said, 'no.' Then said the other, ' Do you see yonder shining light?' He said' I think I do.' Then said Evangelist, 'keep that light in your eye. and go up directly thereto, so shalt thou see the gate; at which, when thou knockest. it shall be told thee what thou shalt do.' Evangelist does not profess to be able to lighten his grief, nor does he lead him to expect that it will be instantly removed. He says to him: Christ is the way. That is the gate through which you must enter. Do yon see this? 'No.' Then study the Scriptmes until you do. Do }'OU see that light? ' I think I do.' Then seek Christ by it, and go directly to him just as you are.'' Now, Pilgrim begins to see where he must flee to; before, he bad seen only where he must flee from. He bas hea.rd the,ioyful sound, .I' Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved." Evangelist here may be the gospel itself, whether heard or read, following close upon the terrors of the law.

articles.title: Opposition from Within
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
OPPOSITION FROM WITHIN. As Pilgrim left the City of Destruction for the wicket-gate, first "his wife and children began to cry after him to return;" then "his neighbours ea.me out to see him run; some mocked. others threatened, and some cried after him to return, and two resolved to fetch him back by force. The name of the one was Obstinate, and the other Pliable." No one supposes that wife, and children, and neighbours are thus to be literally forsaken by one who has _determ_ined_ to go on pilgrimage to a better country, that is a heavenly. Take Obstinate antl Pliable to be part of a Christian's own experience, a.ud especially at its commencement, antl all becomes forcible antl ~!ear. THE SLOUGH OF DESPOND. Tms follows here not from discouragements, but from self-confidence. The reason of it may he found in the anticipation of heaven, apart from the considenttion of the mem1s hy whi0h it is to be obtained. It was too earlv for Pilgrim to think much of heaven. He had just left the City of Destruction; the cries of his wife and eh ildren were still ringing in his ears; a heavy burden was still upon him; he had not yet entered through the strait gate into the narrow way; his hopes were premature, because not yet well-founded; his faith was 1rnsett\ed; in fact, Pliable was still with him. He had given Plinble to understand that nothing but happiness and glory awaited them. "There," said he, '' are crowns of glory to be given us, and garments that will make us shine like the sun in the firmament of heaven. There shall be no morG crying nor sorrow: for he that is owner of the place will wipe all tears from om eyes. There we shall he with seruphims aud cherubims; creatures that will dazzle your eyes to look on them." "The hearing of this is enough to ravish one's heart," said Pliable, "How shall we get to be sharers thereof?" "If we he trnly willing to have it," Pilgrim replied, "He (the LorJ, the Governor of the country,) will bestow it upon us freely." Nothing, observe, is said of the way to !JPaven, the sacrifices to he made, the dangers to be braved, the enemies to be o,ercome, and nothing of the slain Lamb.which makes the heaven of the redeemed, but only," be willing to have it, and it is yot:rs." "Well, my good companion," said Pliable, "glad am I to hear of these things: come on, let us mend our pace." '' I cannot go so fast as I would," said Pilgrim, " by reason of this burden that is on my hack." Just as they had ended this talk they fell into the Slough of Despond. What a change! Was this the heaven of which thay had been speaking? Instead of crnwns of glory, there is a grievous fell; instead of garments shining like the sun, there is wa.llowing in mire; instead of no more crying um· sorrow, there is sinking in despair. "Is this the happiness," said Pliable, "you have told me all this while of? :May I get out 1tgain with my life, yon shall possess the brave country alone for rue." If Pilgrim had not taken Pliable with him, he would not have fallen into that slough. He would have seen "tlrn good and substantial steps phwed there by the direction of the l11wgiver." ·why should he have fallen into the srune slough as Pliable, if the character of Pliable had not been really his own :1 It is evident that, whereas escape from the City of Destruction had first absorbed nil his thoughts, no sooner has he left its gates than by a not u11usu1tl reaction of the mind, he is absorbed in nnticipation of the city which huth fuunclations, whose builder and maker is God. As escape from misery was the chief motive then, the desire of happiness is the principal motive now. He felt some hesitation, even after the suggestions of an obstinate self-will had been overcome, some inclin,ttion while opportunity offered to have returned; and instead of remembering that the bnrdPn of guilt was still upon him, am] his main object must be to ha\'e that removed, he trierl to forgrt his load by enraptmcd imuainations 0 of the joys of hca\'ell. This plnllged him into tilt' Slo11gl, of Despo nd, where he was mudo to feel again the whole weight of tho bnrdcn thut was upon him. He was looking up to heaven, when he shoult! ha\'c been attendina to his footsteps on the cnrth. He llerclrd thus to JHl,s thrnugh this slougl~ in order by one desperate effort to get rid of his indecision, lllld to render it impossii.Jlc herenftcr to return. ( To be continued.)

P the~• have to prepare thE>m for their relationships in this world, for what ~ar be termed their n~tural du~ies. Of course, their best prepurntion for these 1s, m every aspect, their conversion to God. But they need an education and instruction to enable them to discharge the duties of the position in life which they may be cal)ed upon to occupy; and to provide for this, occasions oftentimes great anxiety and concern. " 1. Parents, in pursuance of this end, have to send their children to school. This may seem to be a trivial matter; but how frequently has the whole character of the future life of a child received its bent from the school to which he was sent. Hence the need of much wisdom in the selection. And it is of the first importance that schools should be chosen that have Christian mnsters or mistresses. It is lamentable to see how careless parents, and even Christian parents, are in this matter. For the sake of a few educational advantages, or even on the ground of convenience, they will sometimes place their children for years under the care of those who are unbelievers, and so imperil even their souls. No parent who" seeks first the kingdom of God" will fall into this mistake. Another error committed is to allow their children, at school, to read classical works full of impurity and immorality. It is sad to think that, in hundreds of our so-called best schools, more time is spent in teaching children -boys and girls-from ancient and modern writings in other languages, which -are calculated to injure them morally for life, than in instruction from the Word of God. Nay, in many, the Word of God is only beard occasionally, and then, as a matter of form, while the best energies of the scholars are devoted to the worthless (in a moral sense) productions to which we have alluded. It is claimed that the Bible must not be used too largely, lest the consciences of men -should be injured; but have Christians no conscience as to Horace and Ovid, as to Homer and Sophocles, as to the French and German Books that find most favour with tbe teachers of these languages? It is time that Christian parents took higher ground in this respect. It may be, moreover, gravely questioned whether parents are not neglecting their duty, excepting where their circumstances make it a necessity, in sending their children to boardingschools. There are cases in which this is a necessity, and with the proviso that Christians are at the bead of them, the evil is mitigated, if not abrogated. But if children can be kept at home, smely they should be kept under parental influence. God has given them into the care and keeping of their parents, and the path should be very plainly indicated before they feel justified in delegating to others the duty which has been entrusted to them. '' As to the education parents should seek for their children-it should be of such a kind as would be suitable to the positions they are likely to occupy, and especially such as would be helpful to them as the servants of God. To ke~p this aim in view, would be to glorify God in their education. So fa1: fron:i this being the case generally, parents often, on the other hand, allow their children to learn' accomplishments,' e. g., dancing, and certain kindR of music, which can only be a temptation to them in after life, qualify them for the service of the world, minister to their pride, and which must be laid aside if they are converted. It is no wonder, when we remember this, that so many young people are di'awn into the vortex of worldly gaiety to the peril of their everlasting welfare. " 2. Parents haYe to choose, or to guide in the choice of, situations in life or kinds of employment for their children. Much care and discretion are needed for this duty- care and discretion, directed by the wisdom which God

every evil rnfluence 1s concentrated. Several illustrations of this may be mentioned.· A pious and most consistent Christian received the offer of an appointment in the army for his son. It was accepted; but it was no wonder that his son lived and died an unbeliever. A Christian lady received an offer of a situation for her daughter. At the time her daughter was under deep impressions, and the influences round about her were calculated to intensify her convictions. But she was sent·to the offered place, and her impressions faded away, like the morning cloud or the early dew. Let all parents, therefore, make, even in this particular, the spiritual concerns of their children the main object. For if they seek the glory of God they may safely leave to him their temporal welfare. " One very simple rule may very much aid in this question. No child should be allowed to enter upon any calling, or situation, where sinful practices prevail ; or even where the temptation to such is very strong. More, indeed, might be said. It were unwise to allow children to enter establishments where the members are left, practically, without any moral supervision or control. 1Vho could calculate the number of young people that are irretrievably ruined annually in some of the large London establishments! This fact, together with the reasons mentioned, should make pa.rents very solicitous as to their children's position and calling in life. The great safe-guard will be found in seeking God's direction and blessing, and in remembering that the everlasting welfare of their children must, in everything, be their chief concern. " 3. Pa.rents have to decide upon the question of books and amusements for their families. " 1. Books. In the early stages of life, books play, in many instances, an important part in the fqrmation of the minds of the young. On his liCCount it is very important that they should come into contact with the best hooks; and to ensure this, much parental wisdom is required. :For it is very easy to frustrate the object proposed. If, for example, pa.rents, convinced of the pernicious character of many tales and novels, strictly forbid the reading of all tales, they will but create in the minds of their children an intense desire after them, and tempt them to procure such suJTeptitiously. " It happened to the writer once that, when young, he was sitting iu the garden iu front of the house. A carriage drove past, and a lady threw out a tract. He ran to pick it up. Its title was, "You must not read it." The effect of the prohibition was that he read it as fast as he could. So will it often be with children if you absolutely forbid the reading of novels. •· Parents should, therefore, the rather enter into their children's tastes. and select such tales for them as are made to convey sound lessons and Scriptural truth. In this way the taste will be formed aud elevated, aud they nrny be led on to read only such books as will contribute to the great purposes of their education. " It will be helpful, in this respect, to form the habit, as far as may be, of talking over with them the books they have read, and therein the opportunity is found of pointing out the defects or errors which they contain. Bad books -morally bad books-should never be allowed to fall into their hands. Such abound on every hand and iu every form, and hence the need of constant vigilance and care. Bea.ring this in mind, and guiding them to read those that may both interest and instruct, and be helpful to them in after ltfe, parents may find in books useful auxiliaries in the education of their families. " 2. Amusements. Many worldly amusements must be forbidden in every

hy the world with sin, or which might_afterward5 le1td the child into te111ptt1- t1on. Dancmg, card-play111g, and h1lhards, ,vould fall under this rlescription. 0

:Fnrther specification need not he given, for if the Christian co nscience he exercised, as enlightened by the Scriptures, the rule may e1tsily he applied. Auel there are so many Amusements which are perfectly innocent-some of which. _indeed, may he mad_e to subserve an educational purpose-that very little difficulty will lie expenenced. '' It will be at once seen, from this imperfect sketch, how vnst is the extent of parental responsibility; and how onerous is the nature of the duties thnt parenLs a.re called upon to discharge. But he who imposes both the one and the other will give all needful strength to fill the position which he !ms called t!JP.m to occupy. And how uuspeakable the recompense if he should so bless the faithful performance of their duties that, when they stand before the throne, the_v may be able to say, • Here are we, and the children whom thou didst place under our care.' The possibility and the prospect of such an issue of their labours should be a constant encouragement in their work, lightening their load, and filling their hearts with joy and praise."

i~t jiuntrs .of ~ulli.ou. C ORNWALL must surely be to high-churchmeu the Siberia of counties, and i\lullion must be the most desolate place of all that dreadful region. Methodism has taken hold upon the Cornishmen, and they cannot be cajoled into the parish church. Hence the wise priests weep in secret, and at least one priest, who is otherwise, howls in public. The Rev. E. G. Harvey, B.A., has the rnisfortune to be vicar of Mullion, a rock-bound parish in which there are two excellent well-attended Dissenting chapels. He preaches and postures with commendable perseverance, but he confesses himself to be but vox in solitudine clamantis, or, in plain Saxon, ·" a voice crying in the wilderness;" for the more he prophesies the more vacant does his church become. As any observations made in Mullion parish church would only be heard by the lion and the unicorn in the King's Arms, and Mr. Harvey's family and depend11nts, that gentleman has been at the pains to print his sermon, and " a word of remonstrance,"* for which we heartily thank him. Though not an inhabitant of Mullion, we have as much enjoyed his reverence's remarks as if we had been bred aud born on the spot. We are half inclined to make a pilgrimage to the vicar's parish, to see with our own eyes a people so benighted l\S to be unan_imous in their rejection of the religion with which the State supplies the~ at their own expense, meanwhile, as our time does not at present permit of such a Journey, we will take a inrd's-eye view of it, by the help of the vic~•s pamphle_t. . Mullion enjoys the inestimable privilege of Daily Matms, except m wmter, at fJ a.m.; but the vicar, addressing his Jla.rishioners, observes, "as there is not one of you that ever comes to this, it is impossible that you should know the nature of it." On one occasiou one of the Mullion heretics was caught alive and led to this service, but the creature was quite untameable, end utterly refused to attend a second time. " I asked the reasou,'' says the vicar, "and met with this answer, "I don't know anything about those books that you

* The Message, the Messenger, and those to whom both are sent, a sermon by Rev. E. G. Harvey.

use, and don't want to know;" the schismatic also insinuated something about the col\eets "not being prnyers from the heart.'' To what further degree of deprnvity can human nature go? Matins every morning, and nobody there but the parson! . On Sundays, at 11 a.m., there is in Mullion church, besides the Litany," the celebration of the Holy Eucharist." Concerning this Sunday service the vicar says, '' about half-a-dozen persons attend this service, with an avera<Ye of one communicant, beyond those connected with the officials." This rather small 11ttend11.nce is noL due to a want of invitation, for the vicar believes that some few absent themselves from church altogether, rather than hear him so often insist upon the cardinal duty of attending the sacrament. At Evensong, at 3 p.m., the church is attended by an average of eighteen persons, "our population numbering 700.'' These eighteen worshippers appear to have rather free and easy notions of divine worship, notions which we agree with Mr. Harvey are "neither decent nor proper." The eighteen faithful sheep, upon the whole, would seem to be rather worse than better than the 68~ who have gone astray. Their state-sent pastor says, "The public catechising at this service I was obliged to discontinue, as no children were sent to me for instruction. It is to bo regretted that those who come to this service do not attend to it better than they do. Very few attempt to join in it, scarce any kneel to pray, many sit the whole time, and some bring refreshments with them, such as apples and sweetmeats, to consume during the service.'' Other sins, both dire and horrible, lie at the door of the l\I ullion dissenters. They are undoubtedly a stiffnecked generation, u.nd like the deaf adder, they will not listen to the voice of the chu.rmer, chu.rm he never so stupidly. Thus does their parish priest rebuke them-'' For my own part, though I care not to speak of myself more than is necessary, I offered, some time ago, in addition to the preparation for the public catechisiug, to devote one afternoon in the week, or any other suitable time, to teach your children the Creed, Lord's Prayer, and the Ten Commandments; and further to instruct them in their Christian profession. Three children only, out of the whole parish, were sent to me. And is it possible with all the means of grace you have, with all the forementioned privileges neglected, with all these unperformed duties st11sing you in the face-is it possible thu.t you can, as I am told you do, raise .£:20 a year for missions for the conversion of the heathen? 0, I pray you, look at home, for true charity begins there! I think that in many instances you might take a lesson from the poor benighted heathen, whom you would ' couvert.' Look at your church-has anyone of you, during the last .five years, contributed one penny to keep it in repair? Look at your churchyard, wherein so mu.ny of your dear departed lie, where perhaps you yourselves hope one day to rest in peace; and tell me what heathen, what Jew, Turk, or infidel would he content to leu.ve the burial places of their dead in such a neglected state? 'Nflglected !' nay, yours is desecrated-turned into a. receptacle for rubbish and refuse, and polluted by the most filthy uses. 0 speak not any longer as some of you liave done, to me, of your superior 'spirituality' while such careless, irreverent, impious practices prevail." 1 This fine specimen of Christian charity is worthy of careful study. Those who do uot attend this priest's performances are worse thctn the heathen, in :his judgment. The State allows him to b0 sole lord over the purish l1urial ground, and excludes all other ministers from using it, and yet the man is in a rage with Nonconformists for not keeping in order a churchyard, from the use of which they are excluded. Is this priest insane? is not nil priesthood akin to lunu.cy? Could a humnn being reach such a height of folly if he had not Leen ordained thereunto by a bishop? Forced upon a parish to perform for it spirituu.l functions which almost every inhabitant repudiates, the vicar, instead of leaving the people alone and 011ting his tithe-pig in retirement, must needs abuse those to whom his very otiice is an

insult and an oppression. His insinuations nnd iuuendoes are of nu orde1· peculiarly irritating, but we very earnestly trust that no .\J ulliouite will ever disgrace himself by using ret_orts of a like character. A corresporident says, "Although the people of Mullion are compelled to pay for a ministry they do not appreciate, is i~ to the_ir discre~it that t_hey remember the heathen'! Tl1ey have bmlt and kept m efficient repair two mce chapels, where tht'l services are well attended. They raise annually a good sum for a branch Bible Society, and otherwise ?outrihute to the promotion and exteusio_u of religious and philanthropic obJects. If I were asked to select the Cornish parisl1 which contains, in relation to its population, the largest number of inteiligeut people, [ should turn at once to Mullion. The forefathers of the present inhabitants were so imbued with the principles of civil and religious liberty, e.nd so aggrieved at having to contribute to State parsons, whose lives and professions were une.postolic, the.t many emigrated to the United States, e.nd founded there some of the most flourishing settlements in the then far West. This spirit is inherited by the people of Mullion now, e.nd Mr. Harvey attacks the sheep of his flock in print because they heed him not. It is said, provPrbie.lly, 'it is a. foul bird the.t dirts its own nest.' Yet this is whe.t Mr. Harvey presist in doing. His life, his works, his faith, are alike unrecognised and uuapprecia.ted by those over whom the law has ordained him. In his dilapidated church and desecrated churchyard, described by himself e.s 'turned iuto a receptacle for rubbish and refuse, and polluted by the most filthy uses,' he ministers to a people who know him not. He shows how those who have the immediate benefit of his Sabbath senices, who absent themselves from the Dissenting chapels, his own peculiar people, solace themselves under his sermons with lollipops and apples. What inducement is there, from his own showing, for absentees to come to church?" Tbe same correspondent assures us that Mullion is by no means a solitary case of a state-paid priest without a people; empty churches are common enough. He very properly says, "Those who know West Cornwall are aware of such facts, and many churches which have cost hundreds of pounds to restore are little better than empty sepulchres on Sabbath days. Money is forthcoming from outside the parishes to revive and furbish up the buildings in the churchyards ; but thoughtful people exelaim, ' Behold the temple aud the priest, but where is the congregation?' I venture to assert that in- scores of Cornish parishes not half-a-dozen me.le adults regularly attend the church. The incumbents may remonstrate and print 'unspoken addresses,' yet empty pews aud unoccupied seats impeach the pulpiLs. "Tbe parish of Gunwalloe, which adjoins Mullion, he.s had subscriptions, concerts, bazaars, fetes, and festivals, by which perhaps e. thousand pounds ha,e 'been raised. This sum lavished on e. church in a desolate spot, by the melancholy ocean, for worm and mildew to de~troy ~nd def~ce. One o[ t~e latest of these resuscitations is that at S1thney, whwh pansh agam 1s m proximity to Gunwalloe. Would you be SUL"prised to find, Mr. Editor, tbat the vicar of Sithney, if he does not count school cluldren and a few ~emales, can reckon his preaching audience on his fingers. A popul_ous pe.nsh of la:ge acreage tithed to maintain a dominant sect. How long is the system wluch Ireland repudiated to burden our land? I hPar of '. disestablishme!1t,' lectures bemg delivered throughout the country; and come 1t must. ~elig1~n, reason, and common-sense demand it, and a few spoken addresses will quicken and illumine its advent." How long is the sect of the Episcopalians to ride over the heads of our churches? ls the priest with his one communicant for ever to be 9uartered upon us as e.n eccleBiastical dragoon, and for his insults to be fed with tithes and offerings? lf there be justice among our statesmen they cannot allo_w such wrongs to be perpetual: since there is justice with the Most High he ~ill not snffer them to go unpunished. To the ELerual God the Nonconformists appeal against the tyranny of that Popish church which now lords it over us. 0 Lord, how long? How long?-U. H. S.

W HEN I visited this school about twelve m?nt~s since, _the day ~:19 cold, wet; and foggy; the large school-room, with Its low pitched ce1lrng, the gas burning,* outer windows covered with the dust of ages apparently, presented such a gloomy and cheerless aspect, that my Report almost of necessity had a depressing and fault-finding tone. Happily for myself, and certainly f0r the school, my visit to day has been a perfect contrast. The day cheerful and bright, the school, notwithstanding the number in attendance, was orderly and attentive, the singing cheerful and pleasant, and all things wore a dillereut aspect. During the opening service there was quiet and decorum. I noticed, also, many more scholars using their own Bibles during the reading of the Scriptures from the platform; at prayer U1ere was silence and serious devotion, possibly this was helped by 'the late scholars not being allowed to enter during these exercises, The school soon settled down to work, and in most of the classes good order was kept, and in many there was much deep interest ancl earnest attention manifested. One feature struck me as peculi1<r; in several of the upper fenrnle classes, the teacher and scholars united in a short prayer previous to commencing the teaching; this may be useful and give a more serious tone to tlie work, but following so closely upon the prayer engaged in by the wliole school, and the adjoining classes otherwise employed, it must have heeu ditficult to conduct with prolit. The classes are numerous, but not large, scarcely any having more than nine or ten scholars, in some but four or ti ve. \Vould it not adu to the comfort, and give facilities for better te11chiug, if a sp1<ce of nine or ten inelles was left open between each of the clas;es ?t The elementary classes are taught in a separate room, and consist of very young children, almost all of whom ought to be united in two or three good infant classes, and taught by simultaneous method upon galleries. This is oue of the great wauts of the school; the other defect is ut the opposite eml, munely accommodation for the senior scholars, for although there are four gooJ clc1ss rooms, all well attended by admirnbly conu.L1cted cl,Lsses, there is neeLI of at least eight or ton more to make the school thoroughly efficieut; many of tile classes in the general school-room, especially on the female side, by tl1eir tige, numbers, and evident earnestness, o.re not only well deserving ot; but would value uuJ turn to good account, the better accommod11.tiou, It was, thereforn, very gruufying to hear tbat the prnject of getting new scl1ool-rooms w11.s uhout to be seriously entertained; and, us all greut works are so eusily uccomplist,ed through God's blessing on the spirit uuu energy of tl!e l',Lstor aud people of tho Tabernacle, it is to be hoped that in a silort time this glorious design will be carried ouq The condition of the school as a whole is very greatly improved since my last visit, and ronsidering the very l11rge number, (Llus 11fleruoou, lOU scliohtrs and 00 teachers were present, and the avemge for the quarter being uu:, scholars and 83 teachers), it is really surprisiug that such good orJer 1s maintaiued, and it bespeaks not only great elficiency on the part of the ollicers, but hearty co-operation on the part of the teuchers. It was pletlsa.nt to hear that a great number of the scholars have been • Thie has long been a great evil, but cttnnot lrn remedied, as high buildiugs havo sliut in tho Tabernacle, and taken 11way muclt light. t By so doing wo should li11ve less room, 11nd be compelled to send childreu a.way, . :I: T.llis is not 110. easy work just now, a.ud uulc:::;s 80mc generous frieu<l comes tu our aid 1t cannot be done.

in the school, finding its development iu the teachers' meeting for prnycr every Snnday morning and Thursday evening, in addition to the usual monthly meeting. The scholars also have a united prayer meeting every Sunday at 12 o'clock. besidt>s fonr special meetings dnring the month . .\ children's sen·ice is also held. both on Sunday morning and evening, nnd also on \\.ednesday eveniug; in this way the interest is kept np, and in answer to the nrnny prayers, God has given an abundant shower of blessing. On reviewing this visit, and thinking of the mighty influence for good that this noble school is exerting, one cannot but feel grateful to God, and ask e.11 our brethren in the Union to unite in prayer, that while this is the largest school in Loudon, it may he most eminent for its success, e.nd increasingly a lilessing to the district around. III.-A Lover of Order enquires whether it ought not to be a rule in all churches that persons who do not attend for six months should be withdrawn from for non-attendance? Our reply is, first, that we solemnly question the right of churches to make rules at all. The Lord Jesus is the only legislator in the church, ancl where he has not left us a command it is better to abstain from inventing one, lest we receive for doctrines the commandments of men. The genius of the gospel is freedom, and the spirit of every rightmindecl church is not law but love. At the same time, persons who forsake the assembling of themselrns together are evidently walking disorderly, unless they have some valid reason for non-attendance, ancl therefo1'e they ought to be diligently looked after by the officers of the church, and enquiry made into the cause of their alisence. If that cause should lie ira. backsliding and indifference, they should then come under discipline, and should be visited according to the excellent custom of our churches: after this comes the withdrawal, if the case be found to be incorrigible, and utterly hopeless. Where general laxness of conduct is suspected but cannot be proved, or where the exposure of a fault ~ould only gender strife and scandal, it is wise to withdraw from the offender for the unquestionable fault of non-attendance ; but in no case for that fault alone, until every means has been used. Our experience leads us to know that a large portion of the absentees are not fit subjects to be dealt with under a hard and fast rule. For instance a person reduced in circumstances, but. quite unwilling to make his circumstances known, had pawned the garments in which he was wont to appear among us. The same spirit which led him to keep his wants prirnte induced him also to worship among strangers while his raiment was_ sha~by. I do not justify the spirit, neither dare I say a hard word ag~mst lt, but a gentle rebuke and a brotherly gift soon enabled the afflicted friend to fill up his place to his own intense delight. In another instance, a member had gone to Australia and back upon a voyage as steward, and reappeared shortly after enquiry had been made; his exclusion would have greatly pained the mind of a most worthy brother, and would have been an outrage upon Christian love. .A. mother of many children had also been very ill herself for some considerable time, during "l"l"hich the family had removed, so that she could not be found, then followed an interesting event .which increased her cares, and not for some months could she again occupy her place among us. Her husband, an ungodly man, would not take the trouble to communicate her change of abode, and thus by the heartless rule suggested above she would have been excluded from the church: our knowledge of her gracious character led us to wait, and she returned to worship and to the Lord's table at the first possible moment. Many varieties of circumstances may thus render absence no sin; but surely only for sin, removal to another church, or utter failure to find out a brother's whereabouts after earnest searching, ought we to erase a name from the roll of our membership. If a sheep has strayed let us seek it; to disown it in a hurry is not the Master's method. Ours is to be the labour and the care, for we are overseers of the flock of Christ to the end that all may be presented faultless before God. One month's absence from the house of God is, in some cases, a deadly sign of a profession renounced, while in ot~ers a long absence is an affliction to be sympathised with, and not a crime to be capitally punished. I know the lovers of rule are full of arguments but houses and families under rigid rules are never happy place; to live in; life in its health and_ its disease _cannot be legislat~d for like stone and iron. The best plan 1s to deal with every_case on its own merits, without regard either to rule or precedent, lookmg_only to the great general principles of. the Word of God, an~ askrng the guidance of the Holy Spirit. There are sins enough m the wor!d without our increasing them by new commands. More quarrels m churches grow out of rules than out of anything else;_ t?e so?~er they are all burned like the Ephesian books the better, Chr~st s ~pmt leads us not into bondage. We cannot endure the letter which k11Jeth, much less that which buries men alive.
