articles.text: WHITEFIELD AT WORK. 221 effective preacher; although a sagacious observer would have discovered in the unformed character the germ of usefulness, should the heart ever come under the influence of religion. The juvenile Whitefield was a romping boy, partial to plays and amateur acting; a boy who would pilfer his mother's coin, and who was not above insulting " Old Cole," the Gloucester Dissenting minister. As a youth his days were passed in a common-place manner, until leaving school he became accustomed to the low drudgery of an inn-an occupation quite unworthy of his ancestry. Notwithstanding, from very early yeara, Whitefield entertained some shadowy notions of one day preaching the gospel, and he resolved on doing it in a much more telling and respectable manner than " Old Cole." So strange did her son's talk appear, that l\Irs. Whitefield would rebuke his chatterings and Utopian aspirations. But, there was truth in all this joking, if joking it could be called. Providence was surely opening Whitefield's way. The next scene occurs at Oxford where "the Holy Club" is in ascendancy. The young servitor, impressible by nature, readily catches the enthusiasm of those above him, and soon requires to be held hack rather than urged forw:u·d in the race after salvation by works and penance; for he afflicts his body and torments his mind with austerities not sanctioned in the Xcw Testament. These things, however, are soon over. They are eqni rnleut to a little buffeting at the entrance of the Narrow Way; and when they have passed, Whitefield compares his joy to a spring-tide orcrfiowing its banks. Now another scene opens in that wonderful career which is not to end until many thousand effective sermons have been preached in Great Britain and America. A wide circle in Gloucester is in a state of curiosity, for in the parish church, with which he has been long familiar, the quondam assistant at the Bell Inn is to make a maiden attempt at preaching. Will he discqver more adroitness in the pulpit than in the tavern? That is the question sitting on the upturned faces of the large audience. The sermon is a great success in the best sense. This fact pleases '' good bishop Benson," who, having been a faithful friend of the inexperienced student, now gives him five guineas to help him onward, which, and an allowauce from another benefactOL' for university expenses, amply replenish Whitefield's pocket. He has now fairly started on his evangelistic labours ; and immediately after that Gloucester sermon we see him in London, first inspiring polite congregations with feelings of semi-con~ernpt for his youth, and tl1cn with delightful astonishment at his powers. One encouraging fact is drawn from Whitefield's experience-ho1Ycvcr dead to all that is attractive the populace may seem to be, they arc never sunk too low for the gospel to recover them. There were seasons when danger was threatened by the mob; but, notwithstanding, the preacher was exceedingly popular, and at times even became the iJol ol' the people. In Bristol, where he preached in 1737, while waiting to embark for Georgia, the excitement and eagerness to hear snrpasse<l anyU1ing of the kind before known in England. llis entrance iuto the city was a public ovation. Crowds of people, mounted and on_ foo_t, met the evangelist a mile from his destination, and conducted hun Ill triumph into the western metropolis. All denominations thronged the

~hureh where he offi~i~tccl, and ~-athcred in thousa!1ds when he prcnchecl m the open all". 1 his was smgulat· and pleasing ; but even more singular was the young man's resolve to visit a foreirrn and semil"ivilised land. He was turning his eyes towards the wild~ of Georuia while many were asking the pertinent question, "Have we not Indi~n~ enough in England ? •· The germ of that desire to found an orphan house at Savannah, and to convert the rovino- tribes was sown in tlrn "\_Vhitefi~l~'s breast by_ the zeal and devotion of Wesleys. Through life, solicitude for his orphans added fuel to his enthusiasm ; and Whitefield reaped one advantage from his many crossino-s of the Atlm_1tic. Those voyages were seasons of necessary relaxation from heaner duties. By the time that he was twenty-three Whitefield was the most popular preacher of his day. In a relio-ious, or even in a literarv sense i~ was_ almo_st a dea~ age. It ~as the harvest time of scepticism'. 'the kmg hunself, with sympatlnes more German than English, and "·ithout a taste either for literature or for art, contemned both· and his able minister, Sir Robert Walpole, followed in the royal wake.' W"ith an excusable curiosity we look back over a century and a-half, alHl on that England in which Whitefield first saw the light. Measured hy its population the country exter.ded to a quarter of its present dimensions. Yast districts in northern shires, now enlivened by huge manufacturing towns, were then pastoral solitudes ; or had their quietness unly broken by what "l\"ould now be spoken of as considerable villages. The Exe was about as important as the Mersey, and Taunton ranked higher than Manchester. As the second city of the empire, Bristol ,ms celebrated for the narrow-mindedness and the slave-trading proclivities of its citizens. The already famous town of Bath WflS sufficiently mean in appearance to hare shocked modern taste ; but, being exrensirely patronised by the affluent and the gay, beggars also '' came like fowl to the barn-door." A primitive simplicity reigned over country-places, for the bustle of preparing for summer excursions dis- ;irranged not the plans of city housewives. The beach was avoided rather than enjoyed, the roll of the tides being as yet unappreciated music. So wretched were the roads and all locomotive contrivances, tbat everJbody loved staying- at home; and they were more pitied than envied whom business called forth into districts which now are annually ,·isited by thousands of admiring tourists. The condition of morals and of education, even among the upper and middle classes, was deplorably low. Ignorance was so un_iversal that meu condoned their deficiencies, because others were as ignorant as themsehes. If this was so with the men, the case of the women was even more pitiable ; for such women as were cultured find intelligent were loudly laughed out of countenance. Schools for the people_ were scarce inauo-urated • and Addison was askino-, 0 "What a figure 1s the young heir likely to' make who is a dunce by his father's and mother's side? " While the vulgar were depressed by lack of knowledge, ~he world of the upper ten thousand presented a spectacle no more sa_t1sfactory. "\Yithout employment, and wanting the mental culture wlnch would have enabled her to relish reading, the high-born maiden found life almost a burden, and quite a blank. With nothing to occupy her time

besides fashionable trifles, she railed a"~inst O the Protestant Succession because, aFl she imagined, J acobitism carried a well-bred ring. Sh~ tastefully dressed her hair, wore hoops of the prescribed eircumference, and, wone than all, too often substituted a coveted excitement by copious draughts of intoxicants. Such. was ~ondon when first _partially aroused from its torpor by the awakenmg voice of the Methodists. The citizens contemned Whitefield on account of his ~onth: then the rush to the churches became a phenomenon of the times. Before break of day, people with lanterns groped their way along the cold streets, in order to secure seats or standing-room in the church wherein the darin" innovator was enaa<Ted to preach. What should be done? The popula~e threatened to snc~u~nb to enthusiasm ! On the other hand, the polite preaehers, whose action and elocution were of the approved style, bitterly complained and loudly demanded justice. The common people crol'l"ded the ehurches wherein Whitefield preached; they thumbed the books, trod on the cushions, soiled the hassocks, and kicked the paint! Could these things be tolerated in the capital of civilised England? An organised outcry was soon raised against the eloquent ernngelist -the mere innkeeper's son who presumed to attract large congregations, when so many well-bred divines, by their finest efforts conld produce no perceptible impression. When squires and clergy unite to cry down an obnoxious character, smaller beings are sure lo staucl ready to echo the words of derision. In the case of Whitefield friends drew off; new enemies stood forward, while the old ones stormed furiously. Even many straitlaced Christians added to the itinernnt's perplexity. By \lay of proving the last assertion, we may follow Whitefield into the North. Stout exponent as he was of ernngclical doctriucs, he disliked parties; and, therefore, declined joining the Erskines when they seceded from the Church of Scotland. Whitefield's visit to the sister kingdom in 17 41 is an entertaining picture of the tcnarity with which our northern cousins held their opinions relating to church government. Eyeing their visitor as a dark vessel, they yet demanded that he should preach only for them until such time as he received sufficient li~ht to yield to Presbyterian principles. In their charity they deemed it a strange circumstance, that a man should not at once renounce prelacy on crossing the Tweed; especially when having been reared in Egypt, he had enjoyed opportunities of observing the nnscripturalness of all systems outside the kirk. Was it not reasonable that he should preach for them only when they were the Lord's people? Hardly so: for difficulties arose in Whitefield'e mind, because " the devil's people" also needed warning and instruction. It waR evident that the Englishman had become an object of suspicion. They tried to argue down his principles. They waxed warm in debating what their fathers before them had waxed warm in debating-the divine origin of Prcsbyterianism. You may safely reckon that some of those determincJ. disputants will soon becom_e open opponents, who will class Whit_efieldism with many other isms of a heterodox hue; and they _will denounce their visitor as an irregular worker unworthy of tolcrat10n ! But, meanwhile, is Presbyterian ism of divine origin? Whitefield \s out of his element amid the clatter and din of argument, and, layrng bis

hand npon his breast, he meekly answers, "I do not find it here." "But I find it HERE ! " thunders a bystander, thumping a Bible to o·ive emphasis to his words. Many tears did those unyielding Scotch~cn dra\\" from the eyes of the humble Whitefield. But, the most considerable of Whitefield's conquests were won in the very heart of the enemy's country; and we are enabled to realise the cbaracte1: of that territor.v by learning something of the condition of London m those days. The real condition of the lower orders cannot be accurately described; and were it possible to suppl,v the outline, our '1'ork would mere resemble a moral distortion than a delineation of real life. Shrouded ~rom the observation of the rich and gay by a thick pall of squa_lor and !g1~orance, certain metropolitan districts were impregn_able_ citadels of ~ICe and crime. In damp, narrow lanes by the waterside, m the n0tor10u;; rookeries of St. Giles's and Clerkenwell, hordes of _benighted and vicious creatures lived to tutor one another in wrongdom~, and to prey on their thrifty and honest neighbours. When drawn from their haunts by the attraction of an execution, or a royal pageant, the mob presented an awful spectacle of moral defect.ion, such as e,cn London could not match at the present day. A favourite recreation ground of the common people at that time was the area of Moorfields. At Whitsuntide, and on other holidays, there ,ms there provided a liberal supply of amusements suited to the vulgar taste. Various ingenious games, athletic exercises, and portable theatres combined to make one monster attraction. Thither thousands, ernn tens of thousands resorted. But what were the sights and sounds of that Moorfields' fair, that Babel of ribald jests, rude laughter, and revolting blasphemy? The moralist might have avoided the spot as a very valley of despair: the evangelist might have turned aside, resolved not to cast pearls before swine. To carry the gospel message into such a company might show moral courage: the action might be recklesR bravado; and, whichever it was, there appeared no promise of a very handsome harvest. Bnt never hindered by personal inconvenience, or by thought of danger, Whitefield decided on making the daring venture. It was a treacherous, threatening ocean of depravity, but the gospel barque promised to rescue a few of the perishing myriads. What a -vulgar, degrading procedure must that action have appea1:ed in the eyes of the polite, well-bred preachers of the town, when at six a.m., ?n t~e ·whit-Monday of 17 42, the fragile-looking preacher strode fortl~, B1bl_e m hand, into the domain of the Lord of Misrule. By nature he 1s shrinking and nervous, especially when physical danger is ~hreatened, and some even say he is a coward. What, then ! have h1~ senses flown, that he will !!O there and by mounting a table make himself a target for the jeers of merry-andrews and the missiles of p~inted clown~! N ~t so, indeed! The evangelist's heart is swelling ~VJth_ compas_s1on, l~1s face ofows his eyes beam with an enthusiasm kmdhng w1thm, while bis clear t~umpet-like voice sends the text reverberating around Moorfields: "As MOSES LIFTED UP THE SERPENT IN THE WILDEitNESS, EVEN SO MUST THE SON OF MAN BE LIFTED UP." K ow watch and listen ; for a more interesting episode than some hard disputed battle is occurring in the history of England. The stoutest li ring Knight of the Cross has unfurled the royal standard of the

gospel; and, while with burning words he attacks the powers of darkness, he exhorts the dissolute throng no longer to submit to the thraldom of sin. That blaspheming, joking crowd of pleasure-seekers yield the homage of respect to the princely nature before them. They bend in obedience before an unseen p.ower. Are they under a spell, or is some beneficent angel working among them that they listen so intently and even weep? However achieved, Whitefield's triumph is complete. He has won a double victory; he has subdued himself-his repugnance to mix with that demoralised rabble; and he has conquered the undisciplined wills of ten thousand London roughs ! But, as yet, the contest is only begun ; for a service before breakfast is a small item in the day's work of Whitefield. It is now mid-day. The crowd has swelled since morning. Divers sluggards and cut-purses, whose nocturnal revels precluded their hearing a sermon at six a.m., are now astir to infase greater variety into the throng. It is a general holiday. The sky is clear; the air is balmy, and Moorfields' Whitsun-fair progresses merrily. The stalls are all gaiety; the wild beasts have breakfasted and invite inspection; the drinking booths are filled; swin"s and donkey-riding are in full play, while gipsy actors and merryandrews are beginning to warm in their antics. Is it prudent or rational to carry religion into this arena of wickedness? Then what infatuation can have seized yonder evangelist who is again mounting that table-pulpit ? This time he must anticipate a rougher reception than that of early morning. Yes, even so; for see, a rotten egg soils his gown, and the leg of a cat is a no more welcome missile. But the preacher is unaltered. His features glow as before, and again, his eyes beam with an inextinguishable enthusiasm. The crowd gathers thickly around, and the soft mid-day air carries the text throughout this camp of the enemy of souls : "GnEAT IS DIANA OF THE EPHESIANS.'' The sermon, as before, seems to command an involuntary attention. The comparative silence, the expressions of anxiety, and the many tearfnl eyes among ten thousand upturned faces tell what a power is present. Again· is Whitefield master of the field ; and this is his second Whitsuntide victory ! In the evening the conflict with evil is renewed. The crowd is even denser than at mid-day ; and, besides, the enemy is stung to vindictiveness by these oft-repeated attacks. The text again rings througbout the field. There is a charm in that eloquence which tor the time not unsuccessfully competes with the tinseled pleasures of the fair. Hundreds, and hundreds more, hastily forsake their sports and run towards the preaching-table. Rage and disappointment of gain prompt many ishowmen to oppose, and also to commit many acts of impiety. Nevertheless, the tide of c0nquest is irresistible, and a large company date their conversion from that never-to-be-forgotten Whitsuntide at Moorfields. Such was the man who sacrificed wealth, position, social enjoyments, and the things which most people are eagerly seeking, so that he might the more effectively preach the gospel. After the erection of the Tabernacle in Finsbury, wherein Whitefield officiated, when in London, the powerful attraction of his eloquence drew into the sanctuary many persons of position and title. Therefore the question arises, wherein

consisted the preacher's extraordinary power ? His sermons, which have been preserved are not productions such as would be likely to fascinate persons of taste and culture. The language is not stron« and the treatment of each theme is common-place. Surely these cann~t be Whitefield's discourses as he delivered them. At any rate, no puerile compositions could have won compliments from Lord Chesterfield, or have commanded the reluctant approbation of Bolingbroke and Hume. Besides mere elocutionary art, there must have been something more in this remarkable man than is reflected in his published pieces ; and occasional glimpses of what we suspect was the real truth strengthen this opinion. One day, he was addressing a company of seamen, when readily adapting himself to the place and to the circumstances, he broke out in a strain of language which not only riveted the attention of his rough audience, but brought them to their feet shouting with excitement, e.g.: "Well, by boys, we have a clear sky, and are making fine headway over a smooth sea, before a light breeze, and we shall soon lose sight of land. But, what means this sudden lo1rering of the heavens, and that dark cloud arising from beneath the 1restern horizon ? Hark! don't you hear distant thunder? Don't you see those flashes of lightning ? There is a storm gathering! Every mau to his duty ! How the waves arise and dash against the ship! The air is dark! The tempest rages ! Our masts are gone ! The ship is on her beam ends ! What next? '' So real did the scene :ippear, that forgetting where they were the men jumped from their benches, calling out, '' The long boat! Take to the long boat! " Similar episodes were frequently occurring during the preaching tours of Whitefield.

THE HEAVY BURDEN. L'~YA.~•s.. Pilgrim is first seen b_y him in his dream, as" clot.bed with rags, B standing: in a certain place, with his face from his own house, a book in bis hand, and- a great burden upon his back." "Clothed with rags," to signi(y be had no ri"hteousness of l1is own. "Standing in a certain place," to signify his determin~tion to seek some alteration in his condition, without knowing as yet what direction to take. "His face from his own ho~se," to signify h_e ha_d turned bis back upon his former pleasures and pursuits. "A book rn h!s liand," to signify he Lad been led, by reading that book, to see the fo!ly of In~ past life and the nece~sity of a change. And "a great burden upon l11s back, to signify a painful consciousness of guilt. The book in the hand. was t!1e occasion of the burden on the back, not the cause. It was the occasion of its discovery, and an awakened conscience was the cause of its being felt. "I looked and saw him open the book and read therein ; arnl as he read he we11t and trembled; and not being able longer to contain, he broke out with a lamentable cry, saying,' "'hat shall I do?' By the law is the knowledge ol' sin." Yes! and by the g:o~pel too. The book in the hand contained both, nnd Lot1 1 are needful to produce genuine convictions of g~ilt. The law r;vc:tls the burden of sin, and the gospel causes it to be felt. It 1s the burden of guilt, not

or punishment merely, tbat Pilgrim feek The burden of the fear.of punishment romes from the law ; the burden of the real aml full conscio1.1sness of guilt comes from the gospel. "They shall look upon him whom they have pierced, and mourn.'' Even the general goodness and forbearanrc or God, as revC'aled in the gospel, to:wards those who have long rebelled against him, mc.y suffice to make the conscience tender and agonisin" under the pressure ef its "t1ilt. There i:; first a book in the hand, and then ~ burden upon the back. "\Vhen the <'Ommandment came sin revived and I died." But the whole book in the hand was the occasion.of the whole burden upon the back; for the goodness of God, anrl not justice merely, leadeth to repentance. This burden Pil"rim carrirs with liim out of the City of Destr1;1ction. Had it been the fear of punishment merely.it would have fallen from him as soon as he was out of the city. It was a hea'l"ier and more inner burden, more real and cleaving closer to the soul; and, therefore, felt as much without those city-walls as within. It was the burden of sin on its own account; such as one of old felt when he exclaimed, " Mine ini11uities are gone over mine head; as an heavy burden they are too hean- for me;" such as is felt by those to whom the gracious invitation is gi,·en, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden ;" and such as precisely accords with the experience of a truly convinced sinner, whose sensation could not be more faithfully described than as stru,!!:gling and ready to sink under a burden too heavy for him to bear. This burden is not carried merely out of the City of Destruction, but some way on the pilgrimage itself. In the nnrrati,e of his conversion in "Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners," Bunyan tells us he carried this heavy burden two years. Guided by his own experience, therefore, he makes his Pilgrim take the burden upon his shoulders some wny on his pilgrimage. To get rid of it, in fact, wns the first object or hi~ pilgrimage. With t.his, therefore, he leaves the City of Destruction. \\'ith this he contends with Obstinacy nnd Pliable; and, but for the burden still upon him, would haYe yielded to both. With this he falls into the Slough of Despond. nnd struggles out on the other side. ·with this, by the ndvice of )lr. W orlclly-Wiseman, he is induced to go towards ~lr. Legality's house for help. 'Yith t.his, b_Y the advice of Evangelist, he goes up to tbe \Vicket-gnte, and passes through. "'ith this he goes forward to the Interpreter's house, and gains admission, and receives much instruction. ,vith this he. leaves the Interpreter's house and climbs a steep hill, at the top of which he obtains a sight of the Cross, and there in nn instant his burden falls. Bunyan thus teaches us from his own experience that a sincere penitent is on the wny from hell to heaven. That the burden is still upon him, is no proof that he is not in the right way. \Vhile for his encouragement, he may know he is not for from the· kingdom of hean•n; for his warning he must remember, that he has not yet gone beyond the point from which he could not turn back without the pos,ibility of being renewed again to repentan<:c. All is uncertain on this sitlc the cross ; on the other si1lc nil is secure.

IJ1m:rnn t-hus describes, in his "Grac_e Abounding," this_ part of his experience: ' JII_v neighbours "'.<'re ~mazed at th!s my great conversion from prodigious profaneness to _something hkc a moral hfe, and truly so they well might; for this m~- convers10n was as great ns for Tom of Bedlam to become a sober man. K ow, therefore, they bei::an to praise, to commend, and to speak well of me, both to my face and behmd my back. Now I was, as they said become aodly now I was become a right honest man. But oh, when I understood these" wer~ their 'Word~ and opinio\JS of _me, it please~ me mighty well. For though as yet I wns nothing but a poar pamted hypocrite, yet I loved to be talked of as one that wns truly godly. I was proud of my godliness, and indeed I did all I did either to be seen of, or to be well spoken of, by men; and thus I continued for about a twelvemontb or more." It is generally agreed that this part ofBunyan·s experience is_ d~pict~d i1~ Mr. ViT orldly-Wiseman and Mr. Legality. The brevity of the de5cr1pt10n m his allegory does not affect the resemblance, because its chi<'f excellence consists in graphic touches of characteristic states and feelings. Is it. then, a full description of Bunyan's own experience, or indeed of the experience of any Christian in relation• to his temptation to self-righteousness, to hnYe been addressed by an entire stranger of great worldly wisdom, and ndvisecl by him to go to the house of another individual equally unknown before, whose name was Legality, and to trust to him for the removal of his painful sense of guilt? Was this worldly wisdom so unknown to Bunyan before, and this Legality, that he needed to have them revealed to him by another? ViT as be listening to the advise of another, or to the suggestions of his own mind? Was Mr. Worldly-,Visemap without him, or within him? Was Mr. Legality's house without him, or within? Did these suggestioHs of living in respectability with his wife and children in the village of Morality come from without or from within? From within, doubtless. All was from within. Here, in himself, were the suggestions of worldly wisdom, here the inclinations to self-righteousness, and here the flashes of fire from the overhanging rock. This is so evident that it is marvellous that any other interpretation should have been so generally received. The village of Morality can hardly be supposed by any to be a literal village, or the hill bard by that flashed out fire to be a literal hill. Why, then, should Mr. Worldly-Wiseman and Mr. Legality, and his son, named Civility, be literal personages? Why real persons dwelling in a fictitious village and amidst fictitious fires? Let the whole be viewed as a well-known part of every Christian's experience, and it becomes appropriate and entire. The period at which Mr. Worldly-Wiseman and Mr. Legaltiy come into notice harmonises with the single experimental detail. Had they been sepan1te characters they might have come within the Pilgrim's obs~rvation_nt any time. It is while his burden is upon him, while yet clrenc~1ed m the mire of the Slough of Despond, and before he comes up to the Wicket-gate, that they waylay him. It is just when, if at any time, they would h~ve gained ascendancy over him. Let it be observed, too, that Mr. Worldly-Wiseman and :Mr. Lea:i.lity have a fixed residence in that place, and as such were well-known to Eva~gelist, as afterwards appears. Bunyan, it may be said,. put these c:lrnracters in that part of the way in which his Pilgrim was most hable to be tempted by them. True, it may be replied, and, therefore, the more likely to be personifications merely of the characte1· and force of thoBe temptations within him. They relate to him and to him only, ond are to be interwoven entirely with his own experience, and not in the least dC'gree simultaneously with that of any other.

articles.title: A Hew Interpretation of PILGRL'li'S Progress. ~29
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
A HEW INTERPRETATION OF PILGRL'li'S PROGRESS. ~29 THE WICKET-GATE. w·uERE the law leaves us, there the gospel finds us. Welcome, thrice welcome ·is evangelicnl, after more.I, teachin" to the weary and heavy laden soul. While Pilgrim is pausing and trembling before Mount Sinai, Evanuelist auain appears to him. The book is still in his hand ; he turns from th~ law t~ the gospel, from the Old Testament to the New, from Moses to Christ, from Sinai to Calvary. "rhis points him again to the Wicket-gate, to faith in Christ, as the only entrance to the cel_estial road. By its guidance he is auain in the riuht way, and comes up to the Wicket-gate. Over it is written, "Knock and it shall be opened unto you." This done, the gate is opened and he enters in. Close by the gate is the Castle of Beelzebub, from which arrows are shot at those that seek to enter in. The teaching here is that every effort is made by Satan to keep the soul from Christ. Any gate but this. The gate of Ritualism, of Rationalism, of self-righteousness, if you please; of the profession of Christ, of the example of -Christ, if you please, but not of faith in Christ. It is the discovery of the way of salvation by faith in Christ that is the Wicket-gate, rather than faith titself. It is a faith that removes not the burden, but shows how it may be iremc;,ved. Faith in Christ, as the only way of del:7erance from sin, is one thing ; faith in him for that deliverance is another. The one, however, is so likely to lead to the other that the great enemy of souls directs his whole artillery against it. The gospel creed is the gate against which his arrows fly thick and fast; that gate of the Lord into which the righteous shall enter. Never mind, say some, what a man's creed is if his life be right, and his heart be right ; but a man's creed we hold to be of the first importance, and so does Satan, too, or he would not direct bis chief' opposition ngainst it. No man's life is right if his heart is not right, and no man's hllart is right if his head is not right, and no man's head is right if his faith i8 not right, and no man's faith is right if his creed is not right, and no man's creed is right if it is not e. pure gospel creed. If God himself has devised and revealed a way in which he will be reconciled to sinful men, and has provided that way at the greatest cost which even he could possibly discharge, surely it is needful that we should discover that way, and it must be utterly ruinous to confide in any other. " '!'his is life eternal to know thee, the only true God, nnd Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent." "Yea, doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus the Lord." There may be much religion without n clenr knowledge of the plan of salvation, but it will be accompanied with difficnlties and dissatisfoction at every step; the more earnest, the more perplexed and bewildering it will become, and there will be no remedy but by retracing the whole steps back to a child-like disposition to know what the gospel really is. The knowledge of Christ as the way, the truth, and the life, the way of panlon through his blood, and justification through bis righteousness, is the Wicket-crate at the first entrance upon the way to heaven. On you may go, far along" the path, without annoyance from the wicked one, if you have entered upon it by any other way, as he knows well enough you are sme to return or perish by the way. Therefore, it is that his castle is built here, and his batteries are all turned towards this spot. The keeper of this crate is Goodwill. There is goodwill to those who pass through it, not assu1~nce. Goodwill cannot remove the Pilgrim's load, but it cheers him with the thoucrht that he is on the right way for its removal. Prayer is needful us wcll~~s knowledge to pass the Wicket-gate. Hence the inscription over it: "Knock, and it shall be opened unto you." It cannot be opened at the outside, but only from within. Prayer, which no walls cnn hinder, gets within, and prevails upon the keeper to unbar the gitte. Simple as the gospel way of salvation is, such is its contrariety to the pride of human renson, and the love of self-ricrhteousness; that the book in the han<l will not suffice without teaching from above to reveal it clearly, as with the light of heaven, to the soul.

And he will make it plain." Ti:e_y w~o ~nock by J?rayer a~ the h?use of God will meet with the interpreting spmt "!'1thm. The mst.1:uct10n ,~luch weary a?d heavy laden souls require. and which may be found m the faithful and enlightened ministry of the word is, fally . an~ c)early symb_olised iu the visions with their explanations with v ..11ch Pilgrim 1s favoured m the Interpreter's house. The examination of these· emblematical reJ?resentations would lead us too far from our present design. They are seven m number. The fi~st shows that all must be given up fo1· Christ ; the second, that the corrupt1011s of the heart must be discovered and remo'l'ed ; the third, that there is need of patience before receivino- the full reward; the fourth, that grace in the renewed heart is stronger than "sin ; the fifth. that a crown of glory will be given to those who are faithful unto d~ath; the sixth, how awful would be the consequences of apostacy from the f~1th ; and the se~enth, th:it the day of judgment must be continually kept in view. To some this delay m the Interpreter's house may seem needless, who may be surprised to find so much doctrinal knowledge required before such a view can be obtained of the cross of Christ that will give instant and full relief" from the burden of sin, and so it might appear to Pilarim himself who, during these instructions showed some signs of impatience to "be gone I and many there :ire, doubtless, who with far less instruction rush forward to the cross and obtain, some measure of relief. It must be remembered, however, that Bunyan is laying the foundation of Christian experience of his own type and order, and that the design of the whole allegory is to bring out the strongest points of Christian experience in their strongest light. Only the Pilgl"im who thus l,egins his pilgrimage with some knowledge of what he has to undergo, can thus brave its dangers, thus surmount its difficulties, and thus receive its full' reward. l\fany do not so feel the burden of sin, nor carPy it so long, nor need "uch instruction before they take a believing view of the cross; nor has their· faith been so severely tried because they have not such faith to try; but with less fears they have less hopes, with less sorrows less joys, with less labou1· less re,t, and with less agonising conflict a less glorious crown.

articles.title: The Sight of the Cross
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
THE SIGHT OF THE CROSS. THE instruction in the Interpreter's house has prepared him for this. It was. there he had received a full knowledge of the Cross, as the method devised and provided by Infinite wisdom and love, for magnifying the justice as well as the ~'Tace of God in the pardon of sin. He has now got the eye of faith, and all Le now needs is to have the Cross in sio-ht. Assured thnt it is the only thing that can relieve him of his burden, a~d confident in the wisdom and justice and love of its provision for that purpose, he hastens towards it. He runs up a hill with his burden still upon him, nlready feeling lighter from the nenr prospect of its removal. "I will run in the way of thy commandments when thou shalt enlarge my heart." At the top of this hill he gets a Sight of tht• Cross, and instantly his bur<len falls, nnd tumbles into a sepulchre at the foot of the Cross, and is gone from him for ever. That which nowhere else could he removed by force, here falls of itself nn<l is seen no more. He could not get rid of it in the City of Destruction, for he could not unbind it, and others could not loosen it from him. Neither the fear of hell nor the hope of heaven could enable him to throw it from him. Mr. ,vorl<lly-\Viseman could say, "Get rid of thy burden,'' but that was all he could do. Evangelist could not touch it. He did not my," Get rid of thy burden," but he directed him to,

one who could remove it for him. Goodwill, the keeper at the Wicket-gate would gl11dly have removed it if he could. The book in his hand could not tak~ it away; nor th~ ministry of the word in the Interpreter's house ; no, nor the Spirit of God himself, the Interpreter; but at the first sight of the Cross, it is gone, and gone for ever! Such is the experience of all who have ever got rid of the burden of sin. Such a burden there is upon every man in his natural state whether be feels it or no~, ~or is_ there relief for any fr?m that burden except in au enlightened and behevJng view of the Cross of Christ. It must be removed hPre, or remain for_ ever. lt _is :r:iot Christ merely, but (?hri_st on th~ Cross that takes away ~in. It 1s not Christ m the manger, nor Chnst m the wilderness nor Christ in the temple, nor Christ in the house, nor Christ by the way~ide, nor Christ in Gethsemane, nor Christ at Pilate's bar, but Christ on the Cross that takes away sin. " It is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.'' " Behold the Lamb of God that taketh away the sin of the world." "The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin." While his teachin"', 0 example, and ordin11nces cleanse from no sin, his blood cleanseth from all sin. The effect of a believing view of the Cross upon Bunyan's Pilr.rim is illustrated by the appearance of three shining ones, "the first of who~ said, • Thy sins be forgiven thee;' the second stripped him of his rags and clothed him with change of raiment; the third set a mark on his forehead, and gave him a roll with a seal upon it." These show that a fult atonement fo1· sin, a justifying righteousness, nnd peace of conscience, are the immediate results of a believing view of the Cross of Christ. They who bring no burden to the Cross, neither see its design nor feel its power. If they see not substitution there, see not atonement, see not righteousness for imputation, they see not the glory of the.cross. It is a matter of real commutation. If we have no sins to give to Christ, he has no righteousness to_ give to us. If we bring our burden to his Cross, he gives us his peace in return. "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.'' The faith which thus justifies, having nothing further to do for justification, becomes the principle to commence and carry on to perfection the sanctification of the justified, the whole of which is a life of faith in the Son of God, who loved us and gave himself for us. It is here that the great chanp;e of re11:eneration, or conversion, takes place; and it is remarkable that so little should have been said in this allegory of thnt which is almost the entire theme of "The Holy ,var." It is here spoken of simply as the witness of pardon and justification in the soul, according to the apostolic words, "In whom after that ye believed, ye were sealed with that Holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance until the redemption of the purchased possession." ( To be co11ti11ued.)

HROUGH the goodness and mercy of God, the Committee nre enabled to T present the Fifth Annual Report of the Metropolitan Tabernacle Colportacre Association with no less reason than heretofore for the belief thnt the labou~s of the last twelve months have not been in vain. The necc8sity for some effort to supply sound religious literature, in the place of the worthless and injurious trash which is now so extensively circulated, was never more apparent. The police records of the past year have added largely to our knowledrre respecting the number of instances of mental poisoning, occasioned by tl~e pemsal of sens11tional novels, and descriptions of crime and Yice, which have been sold by thousands in all parts of the country.

GOOD RESULTING FROM THE SALE OF BOOKS. ] . I sold the little book, entitled "The Blood of Jesus," to a woman on the lnd of llfarch, and when I called again, in April, she said, "What a fine book that is I got the other day of you. I have two daughters, and they have read it and got much good from it: they were about to become members of a chapel, but had many <louLts, Lut that book has removed all their doubts."

2. !',- friend said to ,me, at Bratto,n, :• That book I bought of you I cannot keep at home, it he.a be~n I don t know where '-1t wa.a "John Ploughman.' Another said," We have been longing for you, we wanted our books." Another friend said to me, " You never seem to come but what you a.re in a hurry; we wish you could stay longer." 3.. A very deaf person, ,who is a real believer, loves to see my return every month, to. bnng her Mr: Spurgeon s _se~ons, which she says she could not get on at all otherwise. Sometimes I hM·e seen the countenance beam with a smile of joy as I have entered the roo°:"· I called to see a d:ar old sa.i~t, at C ........ , about eighty-two, and as we were ta.lkmg together of the tnals and tnumphs of God's people, I said to him, "Do you ever get an attack from the enemy now 1». your state of weakness and age 1'' " Stop stop a bit," said the old man, "don't I though 1 sins of forty, fifty, sixty years ago ar; brought here on this bed before me!" Then said I, "you are not out of guuhot yet." "N~• no," sa)d the old man. After I had prayed with him, as I arose from my knees he lifted up his hands and said, "There, that is another manifestation of God's love t() my ~oul, your coming to-night ; and the Lord bless you, my brother, and strengthen you m your work."

articles.title: <Wes-air and Cottage Meetings Held
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text: <WES-AIR AND COTTAGE MEETINGS HELD. 1. In the Open-Air Meeting I have had much cause for rejoicing, and do, and will rejoice· and praise the Lord. I state to the praise and glory of the eternal God that hundreds have heard the gospel through this means when no other would have r<,ached them. Many open-air services have been held during this month, in different places ; and God has influenced many working men, who toil hard six days a week to earn their daily bread, to go with me-men that feared no man's frown, but sought to bring honour and glory to our dear Lord Jesus in trying to persuade men and women to flee from the wrath to come. On Sunday I went to Penny-lane with several brethren, and I believe some sisters in the Lord, and preached the gospel to the people, many listening. The Lord was powerfully present, and the people want us to go again as soon as we can ; in fact, I have so many invitations from men and women to go to places where there are dog fanciers, pigeon flyers, and gamblers, that I really don't know which to go to first. 2. I am glad to say that the Lord is doing great things for me here; my meetings this month have been greatly blessed, the meeting at H - - especially. One woman who came to hear me, the Lord touched her heart, and for several .Jays she was almost out of her mind, her burden was RO great. I went and saw her, and talked to her, and after several days of hard wrestling she found peace. There were also three others under very deep conviction. 3. The Lord is working amongst us here ; we are having special meetings all this week, and God is pouring out hiA Spirit. On Tuesday, after the meeting at the chapel, five young people came across to my ho1;se, and we had a blesfed meeting together; all five broke out in prayer for mercy ; and after last night's meeting six came, and it would have done your heart good to have heard the cry-Lord, save me, I cannot live like this ; Lord, make me happy. My prayer-meetings 11re crowded, and souls are crying-out for peace.

INCIDENTS OF THE WORK BY THE ROADSIDE. 1. I left B-- for my journey to-day, and as I was going through the forest where there were a number of men at work, grubbing, &c., I met with the manager who is a Christian man, and we walked up the hill togtther, and at the top we met_a company of men "ho were about to uegin work at that spot. The manager aa1d to the~, "Let us sit down on tile bank ten minutes and rest, you will work the better for 1t after and Mr. - - will ·read a chapter to us." They sat down and I stood up and read 'a chapter, and spoke a few words to them and prayed with and for them, and invited them to a service which I was i:oing to hold 11.t B - - in the evening. The men thanked me for stopping, and I went un my way rejoicing for the opportu~ity which had be<n given. I wrnt a little farther and called at a cottage, ar.d entered mto convenaiio n with the woman, talking about the Lord Jesus. 8he began to mourn becau~e ~he Lad no learning; l,ut, said 1, "learning has nothing to do with the salvation

-of the eoul." I rea.d Ieaia.h xxxv., showing that the work must be of grace. The tears rolled down her face, a.nd she said someone had told her she could not go to heaveR .becauee she had not been confirmed. I told her that confirmation had nothing to do with the matter at all. "Well," sh~ said, "I'm glad you've come," I wae glad too, and hope to eee her again some day. 2. About two months back I came across a gipsy and his wife, and both of them bee1an to re.ii against the dissenters, when I addressed a few words to them a.bout Jesus, but by speaking gently and quietly I gained their deep attention, while the Lord opened my mouth about his dear Son. I believe it was the first time they had heard the message .of God's love. The seed of truth was scattered upon the soil of their hearts, but . whether it will produce permanent good by leading them to the Redeemer is beyond my ken. 3. articles.text:
AN ADDRESS BY C. H. SPURGEON, DELIVERED AT THE CONFERENCE OF :mNISTERS AND STUDENTS EDUCATED AT THE PASTORS' COLLEGE, ON" TUESDAY, APltIL 16TH, 1872.

I OW that the time has come for me to address you, rny bclo,,cJ brethren, may God himself speak through me to yon ! The subject which I have selected for this address is FAITH. As believers in Jesus we are all of us of the pedigree of faith. Two lines of clescent claim the corcnant heritage. There is the line of nature, human efforts and worl-8, headed by Ishmael, the son of Hagar. We own no kindred then·. We know that the hig-hcst position to which the child of the flesh <:an attain will only end in "Cast out the bondwoman and her son, for the son of the .bondwoman shall not be heir with my son, crcn with Isaac." We, brethren, are children of the promise, born not after th<: flesh, nor according to the energy of nature, but by the power of God. W c trace our new birth not to blood, or the will of the flesh, or the will ol' man, but to God alone. We owe our conversion neither to Lhe rcasoniug of the logician, nor to the eloquence of the orator, neither to our natural betterness, nor to our personal efforts: we arc as Isaac was, the children of God's power according to the promise. Now, to us the covenant Lclongs, for it has been decided-and the apostle has declared the decision in the name of God-" that to Abraham and !1is seed were the promises made. He saith not, and to seeds, as of many ; bnt as of one, and to thy seed, which is Christ." "And if ye be Christ's, then arc ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promisc."-Gal. iii. IG, 2'.J.

articles.title: 24.G Faith
articles.notes: also indexed as: Faith
articles.text:
24.G FAITH.

We are altogether saved by faith. The brightest day which dawned upon,~s was the day in w_hich_we first" looked unto l~im and were lightened. It was all dark till faith beheld the Sun of Righteousness. The ~awn of faith wa~ to us the morning of li_fe ; b.v faith only we began to live. We ha,e smce then walked by faith. Whenever we have been tempted to step aside from the path of faiLh, we have been like the foolish Galatians, and we have smarted for our folly. I trust we have no~ ." suff~r~d so many things in vain."-Gal. iii. 4. We began in the Spmt, and if we have sought to be made perfect in the flesh we have soon_ disco,ered ourselves to. be sailing upon tbe wrong tack, and nearmg sunk_en rocks . . '' The JUSt shall live by faith," is a truth which has worked itself out m our experience, for often and often have we felt that in any other course death stares us in the face; and therefo~e, ,:• we throu_gh the Spirit wait for the hope of righteous~ess by fa1th .•-Gal. v. ;::,. Now, brethren, as our pedigree is of faith, and our claim to the privi_leges of _the coven~nt is of faith, and our life in its beginning and co_ntmuance is all of faith, so may I boldly say that our ministry is of faith too. We are heralds to the sons of men, not of the law of Sinai but of the love of Calvary. We come to them not with the command, " This do, and thou shalt live," but with the message, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved." Ours is the ministry of gracious faith, and is not after man, nor according to the law of a carnal commandment. We preach not man's merit but Christ crucified. The object of our preaching, as well as its doctrine, is faith; for we reckon that we have done noLhing for sinners until, by the power of the Holy Ghost, we bring them to faith ; and we only reckon that our preaching is useful to saints as we see them increase in faith. As faith is in our hand the power with which we sow, and as the seed we sow is received by us by faith and steeped in faith, so the harvest for whieh we look is to see faith springing up in the furrows of men's hearts to the praise and glory of God. Interwoven, therefore, with our entire spiritual life, and with all our ministerial -work, is the doctrine and grace of faith ; and, therefore, we must be very clear upon it-that is a small business, we must be very stron" in it,-that is the great matter. On that topic I will speak to you, praying earnestly that we may every one of us be strong in faith, giving glory to God, "being men full of faith and of the Holy Ghost." Our "\York especially requires faith. If we fail in faith we had better not hare undertaken it; and, unless we obtain faith commensurate with the serviee we shall soon grow weary of it. It is proven by all observation that suecess in the Lord's service is very generally in proportion to faith It certainly if> not in proporti~n to ability, nor doc~ it always run parallel with a kind of zeal; but it is invariably accordmg to the measure of faith, for this is a law of the kingdom without exception, "According to thy faith be it done unto thee." It is rssential, then, that we should hare faith to be useful, and that we should have great faith if ,re are to be greatly useful. For many other reasons besides usefulness-namely, evc:i for our being able to hold our own ngainst the enemies of the truth, and for ability to stand against the temptations

you in the habit of saying, firstly, secondly, and thirdly. I must plead guilty to the charge and_ follow the same method still, for I judge it to be no fault, but a practice helpful to the speakPr in the arranvement and recollection of his thoughts, and profitable to the hearer°in the remembrance of the sermon. We may risk being formal when to be formal is to be useful. Though not to be slavishly followed, the custom of announcing divisions in a discourse may be generally maintained, and we will rnaint.ain it, at any rate, to-day. I. I mean first to speak concerning faith under the head ot' this question,-WHEREIN AND UPON WHAT MATTERS HAVE WE, AS MINISTERS, FAITH, OR GREAT NEED OF IT? First, we havefaith in God. We believe "that God is, and that he is the rewarder of them that diligently seek him." We do not believe in the powers of nature operating of themselves apart from constant emanations of power from the Great and Mighty One, who is the sustainer as well as the creator of all things. Far be it from us to banish God from his own universe. Neither do we believe in a merely nominal deity as those do who make all things to be God, for we conceive pantheism to be only another form of atheism. We know the Lord as a distinct personal existence, a real God, infinitely more real than the things which are seen and handled, more real even than ourselves, for we are but shadows, he alone is the I AM, abiding the same for ever and ever. We believe in a God of purposes and plans, who has not left a blind fate to tyrannise over the world, much less an aimless chance to rock it to and fro. We are not fatalists, neither are we doubters of providence and predestination. We are believers in a God who orders all things according to the counsel of his own will. We do not conceive of the Lord as having gone away from the world and left it and the inhabitants thereof to themselves: we believe in him as continually presiding in all the affairs oflifc. We by faith perceive the hand of the Lord giving to every blade of grass its own drop of dew, and to every young raven its meat. We see the pre~ent power of God in the flight of every sparrow, and hear his goodness in the song of every lark. We believe that the earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof, and we go forth into it, not as into the domains of Satan where light comes not, nor into a chaos where rule is unknown, nor into a boiling sea where fate's resistless billows shipwreck mortals at their will; but we walk boldly on, having God within us and around us; living and moving and having our being in him, and so by faith we dwell in a temple of providence and grace wherein ernrything doth speak of his glory. We believe in a present God wherever we may be, and a working and operating Goel accomplishing his own purposes steadfastly and surely in all matters, places, and times; working out his designs as much in what seemeth evil as in that '1'hich is manifestly good; in all things driving on in his eternal chariot towards the goal which

2-18 FAITH.

infinite wisdom has chosen, never slackening his pace or drawinr, the rein, bnt for ever, according to the eternal stren!!th that is in him"' speeding forward without pause. We believe in this God as bein;. faithful to everything- that he has spoken, a Go:l that can neither Ii~ nor change. The God of Abraham is the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he is our God this dav. We do not believe in the ever-shiftiuovie":-, of the divine Being which differing philosophies are adopting: the \,od of the Hebrews is our God. Jehovah, Jah, the Mighty One, tl1e covenant God, is our God for ever and ever; he shall be our guide e,·en unto death. Whether we be fools or not thus to believe in God the world shall know one day, and whether it be more reasonable to believe in nature, or in po"ers that operate of themselves, or to believe in nothing, than it is to believe in a self-existent Being, we shall leave eternity to decide. Meanwhile, to us faith in God is not onl_y a necessity of rea,:on, but the fruit of a child-like instinct which tarries not to justify it;::clf by arguments, being born in m with our regenerate nature itself. X ext to this, our faith most e,unestly and intensely fixes itself upon the Chr-ist of God. We trust in Jesus; we believe all that inspired history saith of him; not making a myth of him, or his life, but taking it as a matter of fact that God dwelt in very deed among men in human flesh, and that an atonement was really and trnly offered b_v the incarnate God upon the cross of Calvary. Yet the Lord Jesus Christ to us is not alone a Saviour of the past. We be]ieve that he has "asceuded np on high, leading captivity captive," and that he "ever li,·eth to make intercession for us." I saw in the cathedral at Turin a verv remarkable sight, namely, the pretended gra\'cclothes of the Lord Jesus Christ, which are devoutly worshipped by crowds of Romanists. I could uot help obEerving- as I gazed upon these relics, that the ensigns of the death of Christ were all of him that the Romish church possesRed. They may well show the true cross, for they crucify him afresh; they mav well pray in his sepulchre, for he is not there, or in their church: and they may well claim his graveclothes, for they know only a dead Christ.. But, beloved brethren, our Christ is not dead, neither has he fallen asleep. he still walks among the golden candlesticks, and holds . the stars in his right hand. Our faith in J ei;o.s is most real. We believe in those dear wounds as we believe in nothinrr else· there is no fact so sure to us as that he wos 1,Jain, and lrns rede;med ~s to God by his blood. We believe in the brigbtnees of his glor_y ; for nothing seems to us so necessarily trne as that he who was obedient unto death should as his due reward be crowned with glory and honour. For this reason, nlso, we believe i_n a real Christ ,et to come a second time in like manner as he went up mto hea\'en; and, though we mav not enquire•minutely into times and searnns, yet we are looking for and basting nnto the coming of tlie Son of Man ; :.it which time we expect the manifestation of the sons of God, and the rising of their bodies from the tomb. Christ Jesus is no fiction to us:- " ,vhile ,Tews on thci1· own Jaw rely, And Gr~cks of wisdom boast, ,ve love tit' incarnate myster_y, And there we fix our trust."

beliern _in the Holy Ghost." Yet, my brethren, do you believe in the Hol_y Ghost? "Yes," say you unanimo11sly, spontaneously, and emphatically; "Yes," say I also: but, be not grieved if I ask JOU yet again if you verily and indeed believe in him; for there is a believing and a believing. There is a believing which I haYe concerning n man, fon,hich I may have but slender grounds, and upon which I would not risk a single penny of my substance: but it is another form of believing in a man when I feel that I could trust my very life with him, being assured that he would be true to me, and prove both :m able and willing helper. Have "l'l"C sueh a reliance upon the Holy Ghost ? Do "l'l"e believe that at, this moment he could clotlic us with power, ercn as he dicl the apostles at Pentecost? Do we believe that, under our preaching, by his energy a thousand might be born in a day? If "·e all ,o bcliern "l'l"e arc liappy to be in such an assembly, for the majority of Christim1s, if under one sermon e,·en a dozen persons were to cr_v out. "What must we do to be saved?" would exclaim exactly as the unbeliering- Jews did, "These men are ilrunken with new wine." They would condemn the whole transaction as the result of dangerous excitement; they coulrl never imagine it to he of the Lord. For this reason I mournfnllv conclude that there is not such a belief in the Holy Ghost in tl1c church as there ought to be; and yet, as certainly as we.hear the voice which saith, "Power belongeth unto God," as surely as TI"e hear I he divine voice of the Son, saying, "Ye believe in Goil, Lelievc also in me;" rn truly does the third person of the blessed Trinity elaim our loving: confidence, and woe unto ns if "l'l"e vex him by om· unbelief. When we have n. full faith in the Triune Goel, then shall we be "strong in tile Lord aucl in the power of his might." Farther than this, dear brethren, you and I beliere in /lte doctrines o/ the gospel. We hove I'.eceived the certainties of revealed truth. These are things which are verily believed among us. We do not bow down before men's theories of truth, nor do we admit that theology consists in " views" ar.d "opinions." "\Ve declare that there are certain vel'il ies .. essential, abiding-, eternal, from which it is ruinous to swerve. I am deeply grieved to hear so many ministers talk as if the faith were a variable quantity, n. matter of dail_y formation, a nose of wax to be constantly reshaped, n clond driven by the wind. So do not I believe' I ho.vc been charged with being a mere echo of the Purit.nns, hut I had rather be the echo of truth, than the voice of falsehooll. It may be want of intellect which prerents our departing from the good old way, but even this is better than waut of grace, which lies at the bottom of men's perpetual choppin~ and changing of their beliefs. Rest assnrctl that there is nothing new in theology except that which is false; and that the facts of theology are to-day what they "l'l"cre eighteen hundred years ago. But in these days, the self-styled "men of progress" who eon!- rnenced with preaching the gMpel degenerate as they adrnncc, and then·

divinity, like the snail, melts as it proceeds; I hope it ,viii never be so with any of us. I have likened the career of certain divinefl to the journey of a Roman wine cask from the vineyard to the city. It starts from the wine-pr!'ss as the pure juice of the grape, but at the first halting-place the drivers of the cart must needs quench thefr thirst and when they come to a f'.ountain they substitute water for what they 'have drank. I~ the next nlla~e there are_ nu~bers of lo_vers of wine who beg or buy a l_1ttle, a_nd the d1scr_eet carrier dilutes _a~am. The watering is repeated, t1ll, _on its_ e~trance mto Rome, the fl~1d 1s remarkably different from that_ wlnch origmally started from the vmeyard. There is a way of doctoring the gospel m much the s::ime manner. A little truth is given up, and then a little more, and mei:i. fill up the vacuum with opinions, inferences, speculations, and dreams, till their wine is mixed with water, and the water none of the best. Many preachers-and I speak it with sorrow-have built a tower of theological speculations, npon which they sit like Nero, fiddling the tune of their own philosophy while the world is burning with sin and misery. Tbev are playing with the toys of speculation while men's souls are being lost. Much of human wisdom is a mere coverlet for the absence of vital godliness. I went into railway carriages of the first class in Italy which were li.ned wi.th very pretty crochet-work, and I thought the voyagers highly honoured, since no doubt some delicate fingers had sumptuously furnished the cars for them. The crochet work was simply put on to cover the grease and dirt of the cloth. A great deal that is now preached of very pretty sentimentalism and religiousness is a mere crochet-work covering for detestable heresies long since disproved, which dared not appear again without a disguise for their hideousness. With words of human wisdom and speculations of their own invention men disguise falsehood and deceive many. Be it ours to give to the people what God gives to us. Be ye each of you as Micaiah, who declared: "As the Lord liveth, whatsoever the Lord saith unto me that will I speak." If it be folly to keep to what we find in Scripture, a!1d if it be madness to believe in .erbal inspiration, we purpose to remam fools to the end of the chapter, and hope to be among the foolish things which God has chosen. Brethren, our faith also, resting upon the doctrines of the gospel _and upon the God of the gospel, embraces the power of prayer. We believe in the prevalence of supplication. I am afraid this is going _out of fashion in the so-called Christian world. The theory of some 1s that prayer is useful to ourselves, but that it cannot be operative upon God; and much is said about the impossibility of the divine purposes being changed, and the utter unlikelihood of a finite being affocting God by his cries. We also hold that the purposes of God arc not changed, hut ,rhat if prayer be a part of his purpose, and what if h_e ordains that his people should pray when he intends to give them blessmg-s ? Prayer is one of the necessary wheels of the mnchinery of providence. The offering of prayer is as operative in the affairs of the world and the produc!.ion of e,,ents, as the rise of dynasties or the fall_ of nations. Wc lJelicve that God in Yery truth hearkens to the Yo1ces of men. For my own part, if any nnm should say to me now, "God does not hear prayer; such a notion is a piece of superstition," I should reply to

him, ''Nay, sir, but with you I have no argument at all. 1.'he whole question is a personal one which concerns my own character,-am I an honest man or no ? If I am a truth-speaking person, my testimony is worth receiving ; and I solemnly declare that the Lord has heard my prayers scores and hundreds of times, and that these answers have come so often antl so singularly that they could not have been coincidences." I should not ~rgue beyond this point,-" Unless you are prepared to make me a liar, you are as much bound to believe facts which I have witnessed, as I am to believe anything which you solemnly ass~rt." Brethren, we ought not always to profess our ability to prove scriptural truths to ungodl_v men, for many of them lie out of the region of their understanding. I should not try to prove to a blind man that the grass is green and the sky blue, because he can have no idea of the proposition which I am proving. Argument in such a case is folly on both sides. 'To us, at any rate, prayer is no vain thing. We go to our chambers alone, believing that we·are transacting high and real business when we pray. We do not bow Lhe knee merely because it is a duty, and a commendable spiritual exercise; but because we believe that into the ear of the eternal God we speak our wants, and that his ear is linked with a heart feeling for us and a hand working on our behalf. To us true prayer is true power. One other point, which I believe is essential to a minister's faith, is that we believe in our own commission to preac'!i the gospel. If anr brother here is not assured of his call to the ministry, let him wait till he is sure of it. He who doubts as to whether he is sent of God goes hesitatingly, but be who is certain of his call from above demands and commands an audience; he does not apologise for his existence, or for his uUerances, but he quits himself as a man, and speaks God's truth in the name of the Lord. He has a message to deliver which he must deliver, for woe is unto him unless he preaches the gospel. In the face of the Ritualists who boast that they alone have the apostolical succession, we declare that ours is the true commission, and that their claim is false. We are not afraid to submit our claims to the test which the Lord himself has appointed,-" By their fruits shall ye know them." We believe that God has anointed us to preach the gospel, and we do preach it, but who will testify that these priests even so much as know the gospel ? U nclcr our word the Spirit of God regenerates man, but he docs not so through these pretenders; for they do not even comprehend what regeneration is, but confound it with a ceremonial aspersion. Our gospel satisfies the heart, renews the nature, comforts the soul; but can these pretenders do so with their enchantments? If they be apostles, let them show us their signs. We claim to be the Lord's ministers, and our epistles of commendation are written upon many hearts. Now, having detailed the great points of faith, let me say, brethren, we believe, hence, on account of all this, that, notwithstanding tlw slenderness of our stores, the Great Shepherd of the s!teep will ymnt us an all-sufficiency with 1dtich to fee1l his people. Believing in God Allsufficient, we expect to sec om· loaves and fishes multiplied ; consequently, we do not lay by in store, but deal out at this present all thar. we have.
