Popery rose to ~cendancy by p_roscribing the Bible and d_isc~uraging sehools. Despotism prospers without senators and const1tut10nal advisers. But the dread of one monarch is the glory of another, and here, we are fond of claiming, that things arc ordered for the people's good. In England, circumstances favour the philanthropist. The English are lovers of liberty and progress. The pure religion of Christ is their heritage. The mcphitic atmosphere in which cruelty and tyranny thrive could not be breathed on our free shores. Why do we differ from our less fortunate neighbours ? Has not the spread of divine knowlege, partial as it is, repressed abuses in the State, and literally been to our senators, wisdom ~ Even a spread of mere secular knowledge raises the poor by teachmg them self-help and self-reliance; but the higher learning of the Bible blesses the soul. Ragged-schools have proved that Christian knowlege discourages crime by engendering in the minds of the young abhorrence of mean and dishonest courses. By teaching the juvenile out-cast to realise his value by the estimate of the cross, we lay the basis of moral restoration ; and every transgressor reclaimed for honour and userulness is a gain to the nation at large. In our crusade against ignorance and its attendant miseries, we are not moved by enthusiasm for-what at the least is but a daydream of ignorance itself-equality. Levelling may produce ruin; it can never benefit the masses. As things are at present constituted in moclern society, distinct classes are as necessary to complete the national fabric, as are the lesser and more imposing parts of architectural designs to the symmetrical proportions of noble builclings. He who raises Lhe poor from the depths of degradation, not only leaves untouched every social distinction, be becomes, in fact, a promoter of harmony among classes. Each Ragged-school teacher in an eminent <legree is a peace-maker in a troubled world. The word spoken in his class is good seed yielding fruit in the children and also at the home fireside. By each well-prepared lesson he distributes good first le~rned of Chrii;t. By eowing the germs of religion and moral rectitude among the neglected populace, we raise them in the rcs~ect of ~heir fellows, and beget in them also a becoming bearing to their supenors. Christianity teaches just notions of the relative positions of nch and poor, while it sympathises with the trials and privileges common to both. This is not all. Unless to prevent a revolutionary crises proper means are used-such as instructing betimes the rising generation of the poor-are not the opulent classes liable to become, what his_tory shows m; they have frequently been, the victims of the childre1;1 of 1g~ornncc? Arc tl1ey not liable, in some snch sudden and overwhelmmg CODJuncture as in the collapse of France, to foll a prey to those who, possessmg_ none of the learning which conduces to a life of rectitude, arc yet sufficiently cunning to seize opportunities of avenging themselves on those whose strange indifference has allowed ignorance to blight their lives? Is it not. a worthy work to promote harmony among our too widely separated classes? Are those foruidding moral gulfs, preventing the lowly from

approaching us, and across which we refuse to go to them, necessary for preserving a sombre background to our gentility 1 It would not appear so. It seems, rather, that class dangers, springing from ignorance, jealousies, and bickerings, are healed for ever by a liberal diffusion of Christian and secular knowledge through the agency of the teaphers of the poor. Thus, as we grieve over the vast amount of the squalid wretchedness of London, and ask whence does it spring, the answer is, from IGNORANCE. Ignorance of God, and of moral duties, is the heaviest calamity which can befall a mortal. In proportion as moral beings depart from God they Jose respect for themselves, and those who do not respect themselves are lost to honour and honesty. '' Knowledge is power," it is more, ~ is a revolutionary power in the best sense. Out of rough and unpromising human materials our teachers mould valuable members of society. The day has come for the exercise of true charity, which consists in discouraging mendicity, and in responding to the cry of the children who, running wild in the courts and alleys of our great city, involuntarily send forth their appeal from the streets. Our Ragged-school teachers in their daily toils, it is easy to believe,. would feel the crosses of th~ir life-work to be insupportable were they riot lightened by extraordinary encouragement. Some of the half-clad uncouth natures, who, till assisted by the mission agency, were subjected to evil influences on all sides, have received what in time of trial has conquered evil, ~nd asserted the supremacy of good. A newspaper boy once picked up a parcel containing £350, and dazzled by the vastness of the prize, and concealing his fortune from bit:1 associates, he made for Liverpool, intending to emigrate, and be a great person in a foreign clime. But, at Liverpool, conscience spoke, and the teaching of the class rose in condemnation until the Ind could not proceed. When he would have stepped on board the ship a voice within said, "THE MONEY IS NOT YOURS;" and so, returning to London, he gave the parcel to his mother, nn extremely poor but honest creature, who unhesitatingly returned the whole to its lawfnl owner. Now, how did that boy profit by raggedschool teaching in a temporal sense merely? Instead of three hundred and fifty, he received only twenty pounds ; yet, by being apprenticed with that amount, it lrnnt farther than any ill-gotten gain by introducing him to n good position for life. The owne1· of the money also· discovered that schools may return blessings into the bosoms of their promoters. It is not uncommon for truth to progress in the hearts of the children until they unwittingly set high Christian examples. A boy was heard rebuking some others for playing nt marbles on the Sahbath, and, unsuccessfuf in his appeals, he subsequently told his teacher that they refused to heed his words. " What did you do ? " was asked ; " I went home nnd prayed," he answered. A training which cnn produce scholars of this sample should supply the labour market with good material. This it evidently docs; for the emigrants from the London schools find cager employers on landing in Australia and other colonies. The kindly natures of many of the children, reared under circumstances entirely unpropitious, arc sometimes as grntil3·ing U8 affecting, and such frequently become a means of conversion to their

~foot- relatives. One little Mary, at the date of her aJm ission to a West-end school, presented a saddening spectacle. Spendino- their ttrnnings on vicious indulgence, her parents had allowed her to 1~am in nagged freedom, supplying her with little beyond what she herse! f prooored. But, quickly intelligent, Mary soon learned to read; and being influenced herself by Bible truth, began influencing others. Her home was a filthy den, and, in which, while half-sta1·~ed bv dav she had ,mly a little straw to lie upon at night. A change was· at hand, howffer. One afternoon, when the school was being closed, Mary enquired if t.he books were to be given out. ""\\"11y, do you wish for one to-night? " enquired the teacher. "~lother likes me to bring them home," replied the child; "For :.he J'e'<lds them to father, and he has left oft' drinking since she read to him ' Roger and his Home.' When she began to read he did not like it, and said, ' I have had enough of that; ' but she said, 'I must go •.' and read it several times. He told her again and again he did not !ike it, when she replied, 'You must like it.' Now we are very happy, and have a few things about us to make us comfortable." Thus good begets good. • One Sunday morning in winter, a lady while walking to church ~!oug a West-end thoroughfare, observed that a certain crossing was :kept by a young girl of a good expression or countenance, bot otherwise in a poor condition as regards clothes and cleanliness. Being of too consiclerate a nature to drop the customary penny :md walk on, the lady questioned the child, and found that 6be :resided in the notorious Church-lane, St. Giles's; but was one who ltad known better days. Shortly after, the lady enquired for the ~rl at tbe address given, where she lived with an old Irishwoman, their home being a loathsome cellar. The child's history, though a sad one, was interesting be~ause she had not fallen into gross vice. Her father, a journeyman carpenter, emigrated to Canada, where he lost hit5 wife, after -.:hich he himself returned to England and died. The orphan entered i.nto service, but thrown out of employment by the removal of Lhe t.imily, she was soon distressed for means of living. She necessarily ie~ her lodo-iog and accepted the offor of the Irishwoman, who out of kindness r:commended the girl to take to a broom. Of a sensitive .ll>1lnre, she did violence to her feelings by adopting this course, but in the main preserved her character. Being on the downwurd road, how- ~vr.r, the agency of the ragged-school came o~ly just in time t? res~uc herfrom lower degradation, and to place her Ill a respectable s1tnat1on. So.meliimes the case is reversed; and the unfortunate juvenile, overt::J.en by want, instead of being sought in his haunts by a kind gentl~man w philanthropic lady, will crave shelter and adrice at th~ hands of \hos!( he imagines will befriend him; e g., the city roiss10nary, tl!e :.1:acller, or even the pew-opener of a chureh. A boy, brought by l11s father out of Essex, and forsaken at the railway terminus on arrfring w London, was admitted to a Refuge after telling his story to the keeper of a chapel after service one Sunday night; and he, subsequently, >1ent. out as an emigrant. Another instance quite as remarkable was '.hat. of an Irish lad, \Yho ha,·iug accompanied his parents from Ireland ~i,i Wales lost them both by death at Cardiff. Being quite alone in the

world and ·nUerly destitute, he went to Bristol, where for a time he gained a precarious livelihood by selling newspapers in the street. When that employment failed he resolved on walkin(Y to London to seek better fortune. ~rrivin_g in the Capital without ;ny home to go to, or money to supply 1mmed1ate necessaries, he wandered about in a desponding conditiou, fiuding neither the employment nor the succour he had expected. Then, a happy thought occurred. In Bristol he had been instructed at a Ragged-school, and there he never receired au<Yht hut good treatment and wise counsel from the tcaehers. Possibly ";,imilar institutions existed in London. At any rate, he would look round and make special enquiries. To his great joy a sehool was actually discovered in a yard of Drury-Ian~, the superint.endent being a city missionary, to whom the starving and footsore lad told his story; and, according to his faith, found in him a friend and adviser. On being admitted into St. Giles's Refngc, his conduct was so exceptionally satisfactory that he became a communicant, and won the attaehmcnt of all the other inmates, who eal!td him Happy Jack. Ultimately he emigrated to South A.frie9,, from whieh place he sent home letter.,; filled with expressions of gratitude and details of abounuing prosperity. On one occasion he remitted £12 for a consignment of goods, with a further request that an apprentice should be selected from the institution -a lad with" a high forehead" betokening undeveloped talents for stitching and closing. This little life-story affords another illustration of the beneficial operation of school refuges. Cases of the above description might be multiplied. When the children are taught and fitted for respedable statiuns, the benefit. they themselves derive being the only return for the cost and trouble incurred, the teachers still have their rerrnrd; but, when the ragged-seholar progresses in good till he becomes in turn an effective teaehe1·, the moral triumph is doubly complete, as is Rhown in the following example. A certain intelligent lad was sufficiently unfortunate, uot only to have dissipnt.ed connections, but parents who were professed abettors of infidel sentiments. Having anivcd at the age of seventeen entirely uncared for as regards education, he coveted a little learning, but nerrnusly shrnnk from imading the precincts of the ragged-sehool. At home he had heard Christians spoken of contemptuously, "parsons" being especially denounced as impostors and hypocrites. Going to schonl called "unbending himself,"' and fur long he refused to stoop to the humiliation. At length scruples were overcome, and, after attending the classes for a time, he made surprising progress, reaching to the higher rules of arithmetic and even to the Latin grammar. Still improving rapidly, he applied for permission to teach in the Sunday-school, to the great surpri8e of his superiors, who explained the responsibility of such duties, and the mischievous results springing from indiseretion or unfitness on the part of those who undertake them. But, being thoroughly in earnest, and understanding the nature of the work, he went to his minister and told him he desired to identify himself with the chnr<:h of Clu·ist. Being a youth of rare promise, he subsequently entered a trainin"' college, whence he was taken by the Bishop or Sydney to preside°over a school in Australia. These are moral victories well repaying a little garment-soiling, or the inconvenience of going out

assurance that their scholars are happy in another state. Sometimes disease, aggravated by want and exposure, thins the class, and even worse calamities may conduce to the same end. One summer afternoon, some years ago, a number of scholars belono-- ing to a Westminster school were bitten by a mad dog, and five died ~f hydrophobia.. On~ _of the riclims was a little fellow of eight years, of a sweet d1spos1t10n, and possessed of good capacities. From his infant lips his mother learned the gospel, it having been his custom to repeat at borne the texts and hymns learned abroad. Lying in pain and weakness he was an example of Christian patience, and unconsciously became to beholders an affecting plea for ragged-schools. When not incapacitated by the nature of the complaint, he sang the verses which he had committed to memory in health. One day, when the end approached, both teacher and doctor stood by the bed, the latter observing to the disconsolate mother, "I fear your son cannot live mueh longer," " I am glad to hear it," directly cried the sufferer. "Why, my little man ? " enquired the surgeon ; " Because, sir, •I am going home," and, turning to his teacher, he continued, "Do not leave me yet, for I shall soon go home." Complying with the ragged scholar's request, the visitor sat until the neighbouring clocks chimed the midnight hour, when the spirii of the child was released to be numbered with the lambs of the fold above. How true is it that much of the good resulting from mission work in London will not be manifest until the day of universal reckoning. But, while these gratifying results of earnest labour abound on all hands, let it not be supposed that the way of our ragged-school teachers is not an up-hill path; nor that they arc never depressed by dark discourao-ement, 0 springing from unconquered evil in the pupils themselves, or fro m the depravity of abandoned pareuts. Our meaning may be illustrated by the experience of a number of the shoe-black brigade. The shoe-black society is an ofl'.-shoot of the "Union," and its hititory includes some strange insights into the byeways of London life. Many children have found this employment a door to comfort and respedability. One poor boy, when he entered the school, seemed to give much promise, and on joining the brigade, he prospered until he had money in the Lank. But this story of prosperity reached the ears of a drunken father, who, caring nothing for his son's welfare beyond coveting his money, forcibly withdrew him from school, sold his dothes, drove him into the street, and squandered the proceeds. In a destitute condition, the late seholar would not for shame seek renewed acquaintance with old friends nor ask help at their hands-which he might have done ,vithout risk of denial. On the contrary, utterly desperate, and not caring what he did, he fired a stack, was imprisoned for three yeari:,, and was probably thereby converted into a life-long criminal.

A singular chapter might be written on the trials of the Arabs of our streets-trials which happily do not often end in such disaster and ruin, as in the above instance. One shoe-black, on losing a mother, dearly beloved, shrank from the idea of having her buried by the parish. Insisting on paying for the funeral by instalments, he raised the final payment only a week before his own decease. Apparently dying of a broken heart, the expenses of his own funeral were subscribed hy his followscholars. Another boy became overjoyed at finding a lc,ng-lost mother : but was plunged into desponding grief at that mother's unconcern and complete indifference to his welfare. But, while speaking of the trials of ragged-school scholars, trials peculiar to thei1· position, or such as arc common to human nature, we must not overlook the hardships of labour "hich mere infants arc often compelled to undergo. To most persons such a scene as the followin;:- would constitute a new phase of human life. One day, a visitor entered a certain room where was found an olcl lady superintending the making up into shirts of a heap of material. The operatives were a number of little girls of five years and upwards, the eldest, who was invested with the authority of monitor, appearing to be not more than ten. Though silence was a rule of the establishment, it could only be nominally maintained, from the impossibiiity of controlling infant tongues. One would begin to cry because her next companion had made her lose her thimble. Another would show signs of distress on being taunted in a low voice by a neighbouring vixen, with the reminder that her father was transported. "And he wasn't transported," the daughter maintained in her eagerness to defend the family honour, "Because he had gone iu n. bootiful sip." Then the dispute wcnld wax more serious, and, being sufficiently loud to reach the ears of the crone in command, she, according to her humour, coaxed or beat her constituents into order. Blood from the tender finger3 of the workers smeared the seams they were sewing. Not unfrequently one would fall asleep, but the dame was not over hard in respecG of the sleeping ; for, at five years of age, sleep by day is almost as much a necessity as it is a luxury. 'l'he occupants of a room like this are borrowed children; and their mothers who g-o out to work are glad to be thus relieved, upon the consideration of thei1· offspring being supplied \\ith '' not half enough to eat.'' There is yet another class of children deserving compassion nnd assistance-the natives of a foreign land, who, brought hither by Lase deceivers as marketable commodities, endure a miserable existence. These nrc the Italian organ-boys of London, who, being kidnapped, (their experience warrants the use of the term), arc subjected to misery and hardship from day to day. The stories told of these unfortunates are often of a very harrowing description. Thus have we endeavoured, by illustration and otherwise, to girc a many-sided view of the work of ragged-schools. Enough has been said to show the vastness and importance of the work in which the teachers of the poor in London are engaged, as well as to demonstrate that abundant encouragement exists for perseverance in well-doing. These times call for large-hearted charity; hnt, our charity must be of a sterling kind, would we forward the good work of street philanthropy.

neglected child in the road to industry, comfort, and respectability; nnthinkingly to toss him a sixpence may only foster the indolence which u~ually ends in crime and misery. A gentleman, while passing over London-bridge. obsened a bov in one of the recesses, and, awaking liirn, found that he was a nati,c of Hampshire, who never knew his father, and t,hat he had been used to out-door labour. By sending him to a refuge, the ba&is of l hat prosperity which he was destined to enjoy in a foreicrn land, was laid; but, had the stranger given a donation and passed in, wl,o shall say where the lad's disasters would have ended ? What shall he done to extirpate mcndicity, and to secure for the poor the coins now thrown to beggars ? Nearly twenty years ago, the "Times" declared that, "in London, we have reduced the poor to the lowest scale of morals. It has come to this, that you will encounter more beggars of 011c sort or another, in a walk from Westminster Abbey to Oxfordt-trect than vou will in a tour from London to Switzerland." Unfortunately, th.is condition of affairs shows few signs of improvement; l.nt., street-al msgi.ers should remember that, by their misdirected kindness, they hinder the work of reformation, and frustrate the operations of the best friends of the destitute. Let the facts given i,:peak for themseh·es: and, if they excite sympathy for the work of reclamation going on in the London streets, our purpose will be answered.

URING a series of religious meetings held in the school-house of a D small village, a very little girl became much interested for the salvation of lier soul. Her father, a hater of holiness, who Ii ved next door to the place uf meetinµ-, and who had at one time soliciL~d the prayers of Christians for himself, strictly forbade her again entering the house of prayer. The poor little girl was much oppressed, and knew not ,vhat to do, but obeyed her father until the next meet in~ was nearly half through, then slipping out without his knowledge, and getti~g through a hole iu the baek-yard fence, she hastily ran to the meetmg. It was some time before her father missed her, but when he found her gone, he went immediately to the meeting, where she was on her knees with others for whum the people of God were praying. So enraged was he, that he went directly !orward, and took her in his arms, to carry_ her from the place. As he raised her from her knees, she looked np with a heavenly c;mile, and said, '' lt is too late now, pa; I have given my heart to the Saviour." . This was too much for the hardened sinner: he, too, sunk on his k11ee1, while God's children united in prayer; and very soon he found t.he Sa.\'iour for himself, though he had so earnestly attempted to shut him out from his daughter's heart.

BY VERNOX J. CHARLESWORTH.

[SECOND PAPER.]

A N unabridged biograpliy of the Lord Jesus is admitted to be an impossibility by the evangelist John, in that remarkable hyperbole with which his gospel concludes: "And there arc also many other things which Jesus did, the whieh, if they should be written every one, I suppose that el'en the world itrnlf could not contain the books that should be written." Happily, chronological completeness in the narrative is not required to establish our Lord's claims to be the Messiah. Much is left to a reverent spirit and a de.out imagination. The attempt to fill up every hiatus is unprofitable. Mr. Beecher succeeds as well as most writers in preserving- the thread of the divine history by discriminating study, and if he fails at times, the failure is due to the want of material. There is a progressive revelation in the ministry of Jesus as in the early histories and the prophetic writings of the Old Testament. "W c shall find him," says Mr. Beecher, "in the beginning, joining his ministry on to that of John: we shall next see him taking up the religious truths of the Old Testament which were common to him and to the people, but cleansing them of their grosser interpretations, and g:ving to them a spiritual meaning not before suspected : then we shall find a silent change of manner, the language and the bearing of one who knows himself to be divine; and, finally, toward the close of his work we shall see the full disclosure of the truth, his equality with the Father, his sacrificial relations to the J cws and to all the w0rld; and in connection with this last fact we shall hear the annunciation of that truth most repugnant to a Jcw-11 suffering Messiah." We must not infe1·, howel'er, from the progressiveness of the revelation, that the conseiousness of his Messiahship was a growth. We think that from early infaucy he realised his filial relationship to the eternal Father, although with but few exceptions, as far as we know, he conccaleJ the fact, and indulged hut few displays of his dil'inity. The question, "Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" and the assertion, "This is my beloved Sou." are separated by an intenal of, at least, nineteen years, he history of which is unwritten, and the conjectures which cover it are idle. "The whole life of Jesus was a trne and normal growth. His ministry did not come like an orb, round and shining, perfect and full, at the first ; it was a regular and symmetrical development. True, it differed from all othet· and ordinary human growths, in that no part of his teaching was false or crude. It was partial, but never erroneous. The first enunciations were as absolutely true as the last; but he unfolded rudimentary truths in an order and in forms suitable for their propagation upon the human undcrstan<ling." It was reserved as the prerogative of the promised Spirit, to lead even the disciples "into all truth." The Sariour's earliest teachings contained all the germs of the subsequent dcrclopmcut ;

hut the flower slumbere~ in the bulb, and the agency of the Holy Ghost was necessary for its perfect evolution. We thi_nk ou~ author sp_eaks unguardedly when he says, '' They u_tterly m1sconce1ve _the genms of Christ's work who suppose that he mmed at the estabhshment of an organised church. If Jesus came to _found a church never w~re actio!ls s~ at variance with purposes." It 1s true, as he says, "Clmst remamed m the full communion of the J ell"ish church to the last," but did he not promise to "build his church" upon himself, as the Christ ? The fuller revelation not only asserts that Christ broke down the middle wall of partition between ,J cw and Gentile, but that all believers are "baptised by one Spirit into one body." The church is a unity whether the fact is patent to the world_ or not, and to accomplish this spiritual unity, Christ died. '.' Clmst loved the church and gave himself for it, that he might present 1t unto himself a glorious church without spot or wrinkle or any such thing." It was never intended by God that this elect body should be compressed into a rigid uniformity by the "pompous claims of church hierarchies." The attempts to exhibit the unity of the church by external coercion have resulted in the deplorable schisms of Christendom. Unity in diversity is no less the law of the church than of nature. Christ's church, in the comprehensiveness of its embrace, is an organised body, by Yirtue of the union of every member with the living Head. Neither universal subscription to the articles of a formulated creed, nor agreement in the details of an ecclesiastical poiity, are necessary to the unity of the body of Christ. With us it is an axiom of primary importance that the church is an organised body, every member of which is vitalised by the in-dwelling Spirit, and that all should be admitted to the privileges of church-fellowship who are "born again." If the church is not an organised body it cannot be distinguished from the world, and Christian discipline is impossible. After the baptism of the Holy Ghost on the day of Pentecost, believers formed a body as compact as an ancient city enclosed by its massive walls: unhappily the line of demarcation is now as indistinct as that which divides a town from its surrounding st1bnrbs, This is to be depfored by all who are jealous for the honour of Christ and the purity of his church. In his last-recorded prayer the Saviour prayed for the manifested unity of the church as a proof of l1is divine mission. "I pray that they all may be one, that the world may beliern that thou hast sent me" (John xvii. 21). To 'Yhat extent the non-recognition of the claim of Christ is due to the s_clu~ms of Christendom, we do not hint a conjecture. That our ecclesiastical differences have delayed the answer to the Saviour's prayer there can be no doubt. In describin" our Lord's ·dsit to the marriarre festival at Cana, Mr. Beecher says, ,/"Nothing could well be a greater ;iolation of the spirit of his people, and less worthy of him, thnn the supposition that Jesus walked among the joyous guests with a cold disapproving eye, or ~hat he h~ld himself aloof, and was wrapped in his own meditations. H1s_whole hfe shows that his soul went out in sympathy with the human !1fe around him." This assertion, capable as it is of abundant illnstrat10n, should be a sufficient rebuke to those whose ideal of the di vine life is a selfish isolation from society, and the practice of rigid austerities. • Christ

never. ignores th?se true relationships which bind humanity together, nor withdraws his followers from any legitimate sphere or pursuit, as the condition. of the higher life. It is only the false in hnman character and society which he condemns. The precepts of the New Testament which enjoin that believers should not be "of the world," assume that they are "in it.'' "That the wine created by our Lord answered to the fermented wine of the Muntry would never have been doubted, if the exirrencies of a modern and most beneficent reformation had not created a"' stron()' but unwise disposition to do away with the undoubted example of our l,ord. . . . . The example of Christ, beyond all question, settles the doctrine that if abstinence from wine is practised it must be a voluntary act, a cheerful surrender of a thing not necessarily in itself harmful, ro·r the sake ofa true benevolence to others." Such concessions as these do more to disarm the opposition which temperance advocates have provoked, than the well-meant but unsuccessful attempts to prove that the wines sanctioned in Scripture were non-intoxicating. It must have been disappointing to the Jews, who were prepared by long ages of delay to recognise the Messiah in all the pomp and splendour befitting his lofty origin, to find that " he bcgau bis mission to others by going home to his mother. The household was his first temple; the opening of a wedded life engaged his first sympathy, and the promotion of social and domestic happiness was the inspiration of his first miracle. . . . . Through the household, as through a gate, Jesus entered upon his ministry of love. Ever since the Christian home has been the refuge of true religion. The religion of the synagogue, of the Temple, and of the church would have perished long ago but for the ministry of the household. It was fit that a ministry of love should begin at home. It was fit, too, that love should develop joy. Joyful love inspires self-denial, and keeps sorrow wholesome. Love civilises conscience, refines the passions, and restmins them. The bright and joyful opening of Christ's ministry has been generally lost sight of. The darkness of the last great tragedy has thrown back its shadow upon the morning hour of his life. His course was ronnued out, like a perfect day. It began with the calmness and dewiness of a morning, it came to its noon with fervour and labour, it ended in twilight and darkness, but rose again without cloud, unsetting- and immortal." The r.hapter on the first J udean ministry contains a very graphic desC'ription of the Temple and Lhe accessories of Jewish worship. It was on the occasion of our Lord's visit to Jerusalem, to attend the Feast of the Passover, that he asserted his authority, and purged the Temple of those who made it a noisy market for sale and barter, and a foul den of ~odless thieves. There must have been something superhuman in his hearing which carried with it an irresistible power, or the debased rabble would not have fled before the threatened castigation of a "whip of small cords." It was, doubtless, the assertion of the same divine influence which made the lawless band of ruffians "fall Laclrnnrcl to the ground" in Gethsemane. " It. was not in displeasure, but rather in eager expectancy, that the omcers put the question, 'What sign showcst thou unto us, seeing tl:ou doest such things?' That he ,rns not seized, ejected from the Temple, or even slain, shows that the rulers

horcd something from. this 11ew comer,_ who possessed such power of command. J csns replied, ' Destroy tins temple, and in three darn I ~_ill raise_it up.' . . . . It is not strange that he should identify tnmsclf with the Temple, for ,Jesus bore the same relation to the new dispensation '"'hich the Temple did to the old. What the visible altar ,md s~n?,tuary were _to_ ritual worship, that his heart was to spiritual worship. The Chr1st1an church has been very slow t.o learn this lesson for men still cling to the idea that sanctity of place is essential t~ di1ine ,rnrship. Xow, the worship which is exclusively associated with a p!acc is as essentially ri~u3:li~tic as tha~ which is _ex~ressed by the symbolism of art and the sublmnt1es of music. "Chnst 1s High Priest over the house of God," and no worship claims· the notice of the Father which ignores the all-sufficient sarerdotal functions of the Son. His not surprising that during the Passover a sincere and devout Pharisee should have sought an interview with our Lord for further instruction in this principle, which laid the axe to the root of Judaism. Not that he was too timid to come by day did Nicodemus approach our Lord under the cover of darkness. "The night was chosen simply because then ,Jesus was no longer amid an excited multitude." In his conversation our Lord seems to imply that he was spea)dng to a sincere man, but one by whom the divine life was confounded with the external accessories of the Jewish ritual. Nicodemus is the type of a large class who need to listen to the fundamental proposition of the gospel, uttered with all the emphasis of divinity, "Ye must be born again." Mr. Beecher gives a brief summary of his philosophy of religion in narrating this remarkable incident in the life of our Lord. He says, "M»n is born into the material world with all tho~e powers "·hich are required for his physical and eocial well-being, but within him lie dormant the germs of a divine nature. These can be developed only by the Spirit of God ; but when evolved they change the wl1ole nature, give to man a new horizon, new force, scope, and vision." How the writer can regard " a new birth" as the development of "germs" which have lain dormant, we are at a loss to conceive. "That which is born of the flesh is flesh," and though the development should be the result of latent forces acted upon by the Spirit of God, it is flesh and blood still, and flesh and blood, even at its best "cannot inherit the kingdom of God.'' Salvation is not the development of the good in human nature, but the impartation of the divine life. The sarcd man is a "new creature in Christ .Jesus," and ihe ministry which ignores this is a fruitless one, despite its perfect elaboration of a philosophical system. From this point in our Lord's history bis power was more frcquent.ly displayed, and the proofA of his divine mission were cumulative, or, as Mr. Beecher expresses it, by a I ouch of true poetry," He took one more step back tow.ird his foll original self. A portion of that might and majesty which had been rc;;trnincu by his mortal flesh was unfolding, and he was to work with a higher poll'er and upon a higher plane than before." The restraint of po1Ter during our Lord's ministry is enshrouded in mJstery, Lut we do not for a moment think that he was oblivious of his eternal antecedents, or uneomeious of his essential deity. was volnntary. It was not by the impulse of a morr.entary precuc:it_r, he confounded the doctors wheu Lut a boy of tw'"l ve years of age. The divinity of his perfect manhood was not a growth in any sense other than that in which the meridian sun is a growth. The orb of <lay i~ the same in the morning twilight :is \\'lien he floods the 'l'fOrld 1rith golden glory at noon. Few men have been such close students of hnman nature in its various phases as Mr. Beecher, and fewer still possess his graphic p0wc:r in the delineation of character. He can hold µp the faults nnd foibles of his fellow-men to the rebuke of a withering sarcasm, but he ahravs has a loving word, all aglow with sympathy, for humnn weakness aud sorrow. With a nicety of judgment he can point out the constituents of character, and throw them into prominence by indicat'ing their con. trasts. By a few touches he photographs into a speaking portraiture the diverse characters of Nicodemus and the woman ot' s~mariA. "Nicodemus was a man of rank aud consideration; the woman 11a!- of the lower order of an outcast people. He was cultivated, reflecti 1·c, and eminently moral; she was ignorant, unspiritnal, and umirtuous. Far apart as they were in all external proprieties, Loth cf them had been caught in the snare of selfishness. He had bnilt up a life for himself, and she for herself. He was selfish through his intellcetual and moral nature, and she through her senses and passions. Outwardly they were far apart; as a member of society she fell sadly Le low him; Lut in the sight of God both were alike sinful. It ll'as not needful to argne this with her; conscience already condemned her. But to ~icodemus it was necessary to say, "Ye must be born again." •Few writers and preachers can vie with )Ir. Beecher in the use of metaphor. His metaphors are not, however, mere fancies of the imagination thrown into the picture to heighten the effect of the subject. His theme shines through them like the golden thrends which constantly recur in the woof and warp of tapestry. In the w01 ks of some authors metaphors are so abundant that you suspect the purpose they are intended to serve is to increase the size of the book. This is not the case with Mr. Beecher. His metaphors arc the Leautiful setting of noble thoughts. One marl'els at the Yersatility of the genius which can elaborate them to express and illustrate almost every idea the mind conceives. By a single metaphor he sets forth the idea embodied in our Lord's saying _to the woman at the well-" Woman, believe me, the hour cometh when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at .Jerusalem, worship the Father." "No longer in this nest al(lnc, or in that, shall religion be looked for; but, escaping from its shell, l1eard iu all the earth, in notes the smnc in c\'ery language:, flying unrestrained and free, the whole heavens shall be its sphere, and Lhc whole earth its home." "'l.'he miracles of Christ cannot be taken ont of their life-connections and analvsed by themselves. They were to his teaching what gestures are to ai; orator, they go with his thoughts, and taken alone arc of no value. They were the glowing expressions of sympathy. As in the moods of love, the eye, the lip, the face have expressions that cannot be ~eparated from the emotions which produce them, w was it \\'ith Ohrist's works of mercy. 'l.'hey were not philosophical experiments

adds, "They are but a collection and better orderino- of maxims or aphorisms which existed in the Old Testament. F;rmerly, they lay scattered as pearls not detached from the parent shell, or as rough diamonds unground. Here they first appear in brilliant setting. They are no longer happy sayings, but sovereign principles... The traveller may to-day stand in Antwerp, near the old cathedral, hearing all the clatter of business, a thousand feet tramping close np to the walls and buttresses against which lean the booths, a thousand tongues rattling the language of traffic, when, as the hour strikes from above, a shower of notes seems to descend from the spire,-bell notes, fine, sweet, small as a bird's warble, the whole ail- fall of crisp tinklings, underlaid by the deep~r and sonorous tones of larg~ bells, but all of them in fit sequences pourmg forth a melody that seems unearthly, and the more so because in rnch contrast with the scenes of vulgar life beneath. In some such '\\"ay must these words have fallen. upon the multitude. . . . 'l'hey are the choicest truths of the old dispensation set to the spirit of the new. But not until, like bells, they were thus set in chimes and rung in the spirit and melody of the spiritual age, could we have dreamed bow noble they were." Of the second of the beatitudes, be says, "As frosts unlock the hard shells of seeds and help the germ to get free, so trouble develops in men the germs of force, patience, and ingenuity, and in noble natures 'works the peaceable fruits of righteousness.' A gentle schoolmaster it is to those who are 'exercised thereby.' Tears, like raindrops, have a thousand times fallen to the ground and come up in flowers." "The beatitudes constitute a beautiful sketch of the ideal state when the glowing- passions which in the day of Christ controlled even the religious leaders, and still so largely rule the world, shall be supplemented by the highest moral sentiments. The ostentatious wealth and arrogant pride of this sensuous life shall be replaced in the new life by a profound humility. The conceit and base content of a sordid prosperity shall give way to ingenuous spiritual aspiration. Men shall long for l!Ooclness more than the hungry do for food. They shall no longer live hy the force of their animal life, but by the serene sweetness of the moral sentiments. Meekness shall be stronger than force. The spirit of peacemaking shall take the place of irritation and quarrelsomene8s. But, as we can come to the mildness and serenity of spring only through the Llustering winds and boisterous <lays of March, so this new king-dom must enler through a periorl of resistance and of persecution; and all who, taking part in its early establishment, have to accept pcr- :-,ecution, rnll8t learn to find joy in it as the witness that they arc <:xalted lo a rnperior realm of experience, to the companionship of the noblest heroes of the prophetic oge, and fellowship with Uod." In Fpeaking of the parables, Mr. Ilccchcuays, '' it is highly probable that all of them were preceded and followed by expository matter, on

which the parables were wrought like the figures upon lace. . . . Men would remember an illustration when they would forget a principle." We have thus given a few of the metaphors from the closing chapters. They are equally numerous in the earlier portions of the book. As an example of Mr. Beecher's power in grasping tl;ie parabolic teaching of our Lord, we close with the paragraph in which he summarises the parable of the rich fool, as by common consent he is called. " Avarice, made good~natured by prosperity, counsels with itself and fills the future with visions of self-indulgence. Then from out the great realm above comes a voice pronouncing eternal bankruptcy to the presumptuous dreamer." In going through this book, we have been led again and again to compare the reader to a traveller passing along a well-known highway in company with a guide, who, knowing the road, has frequently commanded a halt to point out the more attractive features in the surrounding landscape. From advantageous standpoints we have had new views of familiar scenery. The discourse to which we have listened, though uninterrupted; has never wearied us, and if we have ventured to call in question certain conclusions of our guide, we have endeavoured to do so infidelity to our conscientious convictions and with a modesty which becomes us. We regret the interruption of the journey at this point, and feel impatient to resume it again. We counsel all who like vigour of thought, freshness of view, and beauty of illustration, to secure this book for themselTes. It will repay careful perusal and close study.

HE came about our house to wash; and we knew her as a hardy, S upright, .managing body. Her husband was a sailor, but had deserted her for some time, and her little daughter, aged nine years, was the only fruit of the diluted affection which existed between them. One day on entering our ,arlour, I found her sitting with my wife. "I've been at Edinburgh," said she, "and the doctors tell me that I am ill with cancer, and that I'll soon be in my grave." She then spoke about her child with tears; •• But," said she, "I must put my trust in God." . Missing her shortly after, I called along, and found her m bed. "I am just waiting on," she said, "but oh, he is putting me through the furnace, my sufferings are awful." After having a little worship together her daughter came in, when the mother burst into tears, crying "Poor thing, poor thing, but I just leave her in charge of my heavenly Father." The doctors here said that they could do nothing for her, and that she should just take what agreed with her, and keep herself as comfortable as possible. . . . .. . During frequent v1S1t11 I wa~ dehgh,te~ to observe the sp1_r1t~ahty_ of her mind, her acquaintance with the 8cr1plures, and her ch1ldhke faith and confidence in their Author. "Whatever my heavenly Fnthec says

is ri~ht.," she remarked," a good father knows what to do with his child." Once when I called, she said, "Read a few words in Song, second and sixteenth." I turned up the place and found, "My beloved ie mine and I am his." "Observe," she said, " its not my beloved shall be my mine, but my beloved £s mine ;" thus she was by faith in possession of the Christian's peace, by believing what Jesus says. Some of the neighbours came in, and we all worshipped together, crying for help for our suffering friend. Next time I saw her she was not able to speak, nor scarcely to hear. It is awfully solemn to sit beside the bed of one just passing into eternity. I sat and looked, and thought, and prayed. She was able to look at me, and such looks from a dying believer speak volumes; their sweet calm and quiet were evidences of patience and submission to her Father's will in this awful hour. Next time we worshipped together from the ninety-first Psalm. She 'l>as very death-like. She said, "I'm wearying to be at his feet now. Oh, what I've suffered; none knows but him how much I've suffered; but," she added, "he has given me patience." '' Yon will praise him for it,'' I said. "Oh, ay, I'm wearying now for his time, for that time, but it's no for anything in me, it's for his own Son's sake. Yes, it's all for Jesus' sake." I said, '' That's true." She continued, "My heavenly Father will be pleased to meet me. ay, ay, but it will be only for his Son's sake." I said, "His blood is precious and prevailing for the sinner." "Oh," she said, "it's dear, dear blood to Ille, and," after a pause, looking solemnly at me, " it's dear to him, too, it's costly blood." Next visit her weakness was extreme. "I think you'll get the new wine -in your Father's house to-night," I whispered. "Do you think it," said she, smiling; " Oh, I wish I would." • She shook hands with me, and said, "I hope God will not give yon so many sufferings as he has given me." "We need to be purified," I replied. "Oh, ay," she said, "all our dross taken away." On parting, she said, " Good bye, good bye. Oh that he would set me at his feet." She departed at two in the morning, commending her soul to Jeane, the Saviour, and her little girl to the Father of the fatherless. Dundee. J. C. S.

P ILGRIM is now on his way from Christ upon the Cross to Christ on the Thron_e·. Christ crucified i! for sinners, Christ glorified for saints. He ,suffered without the camp, before the whole world, but after his resurrection he showed him~elfto his_discip~es only; be~an~e in that capacity he belonged only.to them. Hal'lng got rid of bis burden, P1lgnm :rave three leaps for joy and went on his way singing. Of what now was he most in danger? To what temptations was he most exposed? \Vould they not be unsuspecting simplicity, and even presumption antl sloth? There is no need new, he might suppose, for much :anxiety and toil: my burden is gone and I may travel at my ease. These are the temptations that now lay in his way in the persons of Simple, Sloth, and Presumption, with fetters on theiJ• .. heels. They ,vere his own natural inclinations to these dispositions, and showe,l him what his condition would aiave been if be had yielded to them. Happily he passed quickly by them. There would lrnve been no occasion to place them as three strangers in bis way to receive a solemn warning from him, since they were precisely what would have occurred in his own experience, and woul<l need to be surmounte,l by him. Two other dispositions to which n Christian pilgrim would be exposed, immediately after his release from the burden of sin, would be Formality and Hypocrisy. Here now they come "tumbling over the wall on the left hand of the narrow way; nnd they make up apace to him." He enters into conversation with them, and thus ascertains their true character and his own distinction from them. The garment upon his shoulders, and the roll in his hand, are his comfort and defence. needed no soft repose. Faith is ever watchful, and po8se~ses nll rrraces within itself. While Pilgrim was in the Beautiful Palace, Faithful ha<l passed by. As he walked out with his friends to the gate, he asked the porter if he saw any Pilg1·im pass by. "Then said the porter, 'Yes.' I asked his name, ·and he told me it was Faithful." It was not night with Faithful as be .came up t~ the Palace named Beautiful, because be had not slept in the arbour, or lost his roll, and, therefore, be kept on bis way, and it was long before Pilgrim could overtake hi~. He bad ~o pass through the Valley of Humiliation witbout him, and hene~ hIS sh~rp conflict and fe~rs. \,Ya~chfulness, Discretion, Prudence, Piety, -and Chanty, which are all the frmts of faith, cannot do the work of faith itsalf. This is the experimental teaching, we apprehend, of this part of the allegory. As the duty of Watchful was al ways to remain at that lodge, and Discretion, Prudence, Piety, and Charity always remain in the Beautiful Palace, for there they were still when Christiana and her family went on their pilgrimage, it is ·strange that they should ever be regarded as separate Christians, and so many different Pilgrims to the heavenly city. "Can any be at a loss," says Dr. ·Cheever, "to understand the meaning of the house Beautiful, or that era in the life of the Pilgrim at which Christian had arrived ? We think e\"ery one will see drawn in these symbols, with great beauty and delightfulness of colouring, the institutions and ordinances of the visible church of Christ on ea.rlh ; the fellow- -ship and divinely blest communion, the mutual instruction and edification, the happiness, hopes, promises, foretastes, enjoyments, growth in grace, and pre- <paration for usefulness, peculiar to this sacred heavenly kingdom, belonging to the body of Christ, and growing out of a right use of its precious privileges." If the church militant were an institution in which one only is encouraged and strengthened to go on pilgrimage to the church triumphant, and the rest remain where they are, the analogy might be sustained. That Faithful did not enter the Beautiful Palace is explained by another expositor, by the facts that church fellowship is not essential to Christianity, that no compulsion should be used for this purpose, and that many'' belong te the church universal, but not to any locnl body of Christians." According to this interpretation, the Pilgrim who does not avail himself of the privileges of church ordinances, is more adv1mced in his pilgrimage, passes more cnlmly and securely through the Valley -0f Humiliation, and arrives at heaven sooner than the Pilgrim who does observe them. That all these graces may be revived in each individual Christinn by church fellowship mny be readily admitted; but that they are so many -different believers, or that nny one of itself suflices for an entire description of .a genuine believer, cannot be consistently maintained. The names of these fair and intelligent damsels, it may be observed, are not Discrete, but Dis- ·cretion itself; not Prudent. but Prudence itself; not Pious, but Piety itself; not Charitable, but Charity itself; and such we take them to be. The qunlity may be put for the essence, ns faithful for faith, and hopeful for hope ; but rarely, we see the essence put for the quality, as faith for the faithful, and hope for the hopeful. The personilication of the Grnces themselves is common to poetry and allegory. Charity is personified by Paul in the thirteenth chapter of the first Epistle to the Corinthians, which Bunyan here adopts and ~pp lies to its sister g1·aces. Personification, it should be rem em be red, lienotes the special presence and influence of that which is personified, beyond its ordinary presence and operation, and not separated from them. It is thus -employed by Bunyan to describe moral and spiritual states and emotions as -they become prominent, or have the rule, in Christian experience, without -denying their influence at other times. Hence Faithful passes by, while Pilgrim is ,vholly occupied, with the gentler graces, not that faith was separated from those graces, but only less distinctly reali~ed and eeen; and hence, as we shall afterwards see, Pilgrim's faith in the person of Faithful goes to heaven before he himself hns finished his life of faith upon the earth. His experience of the vanity of enrth had taken his faith to heaven, and fixed· it there. It is thus ·that the elements of both good and evil are strongly pourtrayed in their relation,

for t~e time being, and under a certain peculiarity of circumstances, to theexperience of the hero of the tale.

articles.title: The Valley of HU?lfiLIATION
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text: THE VALLEY OF HU?lfiLIATION. WE have now to follow Pilgrim through the Valley of Humiliation. The effect; of his supineness and lost evidences has not yet disappeared. The lo3t <Troundi has not yet been recovered. That he might not be too much discoura~ed he· bas been entertained in the palace called Beautiful, and bns been favour~d ;ith, a si11:ht ~ftbe De]e~tabl~ Mountains, Yet even this was a delay. After every decline m the drn&e hfe the lost strength has to be recruited as well as. lost duties to be performed. Nor is a season of indulgence for the recovery of lo~t strength the best preparation for the Valley of Humiliation. Haw Pilgrim evinced more determination and self-denial in climbing the Hill Diffi-- culty, lte might have been better prepared to pass through this valley, as may be seen in the case of Faithful. The hills and valleys of Christian experience· are so arranged that they become preparations for each other. "Lest I should be exalted through the abundance of the revelation3," says a former pilgrim . "there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me." There is a period, perhaps, in the experience of every Christian, in which, be has by some special effort to overcome the wicked one. This, according toan Apostle, is in the full vigour of his youth. "I write unto you, young men,. because ye have overcome the wicked one." It was so with the Lord himself,. and the servant is not above his master. The armour with which Pilgrim was invested, as he left the palace gate, was an intimation to him of approaching, danger. As sailors may be seen, while it is yet calm, to put on their rough clothing, to clear the deck, and reef the sails, and thus betoken to others thecoming storm, so Pilgrim is warned by the armour with which he is clad of a. severe conflict at hand. "Take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all to stand." He has not proceeded far in the dreary valley before he sees Apollyon coming to meet him,. who first endeavours to terrify him by his appearance, then to persuade him by calm reasoning, then to overwhelm him with a sense of guilt, then todestroy him with whole showers of fiery darts, and then by grappling with him to give him the finishing blow. In this last act Apollyon himself is wounded,. and spreading his dragon wings, flies away. "Resist the devil, a~d he will fl_ee from you.'' Yes, but what a resistance must be made before he will flee! Still, he does flee, and the severer the conflict, the brighter is the victor's crown. There is a race of Christians in our day to whom these sharp points of Chris\ian experience, these internal conflicts and triumphs, these belli~b depths and, heavenly heights, are utterly unknown; but there are some st1ll le:ft who are· familiar with them as the deep things of God. We would rather be of thelatter class than the former. Give us the deepest sorrows of the Christian with his highest joys rather than the even course which is insensible to_both.. Anything is better than indifference here. Let us have our whole being stirred up to its utmost depth~ upon a ~ubject that involves the anger or the friendship of God, and an eternity of happiness or woe.

articles.title: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
THE VALLEY OF THE SHADOW OF DEATH. F1toM one valley Pilgrim soon enters into another, or rather perhaps into a mountain-pass, known of old, from its bein" infested with enemies of every kind, as "the Valley of the Shadow of Death.""I•'rom contending with Satan he proceeds to contend with the fear of dying. As "death and him that had the powe1: of death '' had been conquered for him, so they must be conquered by l11m. Having conquered l1im that had the power of death, the sba~ow of death only remained; but the shadow of death is sometimes more terrible than the· reaiity. It is represente<l I,ere as dark, embedded with dec>p mire where there is no standing, full of pitfalls, resounding with dismal howlings, full of frightful,

apporitions, strewed with blood, bones, and ashes, and close by the mouth of hell. "Yet the dear path to thine abode Lies through this horrid land." Christinns pass through this valley when in hourly expectation of death from the hand of pe':'secution. In Banyan's time this was frequent, and hence the ea~ly and promme!1t place ~ssigned it in his allegory. Christians pass through this valley when swk and mgh unto death, when sufferin" from bereavement !111d when fr_om various other causes ~hey are oppressed with the fear of dying'. The Lord hunself pa~sed_ through this valley when, in Gethsemaae, he "offered up prayers and supphcat1ons with stron.,. cryin" and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was h~ard in° that he feared." It was here that he conquered the fear of dying, after which he showed no fear of death itself: Thus, if we conquer death wbile we live, it will not conquer us when we die. It is the fear of it. only that the true Christian has to overcome. It is not death but its shadow that he bas to encounter, and the sooner he passes through that in his pilgrimage the better.

articles.title: Faithful
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
FAITHFUL. As Pilgrim left the'Palace called Beautiful, he was informed by the port.er that Faithful had passed by, which led him to hasten forward in tbe hope of overtaking him. In the Valley of Humiliation Faithful was still before him. Toward the end of the Valley of the Shadow of Death, he thought be once beard bis voice, and soon as he came out of it he saw him, and called him to stay, but Faithful still went on. Pilgrim tben made a great effort to overtake him, and, was so pleased ,vith having accomplished this, that he even went beyond him. This caused him to stumble, and compelled him to wait until Faithful came to his assistance. A long conversation then too_k pince between them. They related to each other their adventures by the way. Faithful had hoped to have accompanied Pilgrim all the way from the City of Destruction, but Pilgrim had set out before him. He had escaped the Slough of Despond, but had met with one whose name wns )Vanton who had like to hove done him n mischief: At the foot of the Hill Difficulty he was met by Adam the First, wbo dwelt in the town of Deceit, nn<l who invited him to his house and told him he had three <laughters, whose numes were the Lust of the Flesh, the Lust of the Eyes, and the Pride of Life, and he might marry them nil if he would. At first he felt inclined to foll<nv him, and soon afterwards repented nnd turned away from him; but, for this half compliance, while he was nscen<ling the hill, one came nfter him, swi~ as the wind, an<l knocked him down, and would have made au end of him, if one with boles in his hands and in his side had not commanded him to forbear. )Vhen Faithful passed the lions they were asleep, and, having so much of the day before him, he passed by the Ilenutiful l\ilace without enterin" it. In the Valley of Humiliation, he met with one Discontent, who endenvgured to persuade him to turn hock, or he would displease nil his friends, Pride, A1-ro,,,mcy, 0 Self-conceit, )Vorldly-glory, with others. He also met with Shame, who tolc\ him that it was" a pitiful, low, sneaking, business for a man to mind religion, nnd that a tender conscience was an unmanly thing." Tbese were all that Faithful met with in that valley, for he "had sunshine," he srrys, "nil the rest of the wnythrough this, and also through the V nlley of the Shndow of Dl ath." Who is this Faithful? Of who!ll does Bunyan speak here?· Of his Pilgt·im, or of some other man? Of some other man, srry the whole round of expositors. "Christian" says one, "in a grent measure escaped the peculirrr temptations that assaulted Faithful, yet he sympathised with him ; nor did the latter deem the gloomy experiences of ~)s brother visionary_ or ima~in,a~ivc 1 th_ouf(h he_ had been exempted from them. Thus the experience of Ea1thful 1s mv1mably regarded as belonging to some other, a_nd not, therefore, as part o.f the one Pil,,rim's l'ro,,ress. lf it be the experience of some other, numernus other distinct persins must come upon the scene. ls ""anton a real person? fa

Adam the First a real person here f' Are his three dauo-hters, the Lust of the Flesh. the Lust of the Eyes, and the Pride of Life, real persons? Is the town of Deceit, in which they dwell, a real or imaginary town? Is Discontent a real person? Are his friends Pride, Arrogancy, Self-conceit, ,vcirlctlv-alory real persons? Is Shame a real person? Why not? If one, why not all? If Faithful be a real person, why not all the rest? If, on the other hand Faithful be a p~rs?nificat~on of faith, all t}1e other personifications naturally follow ; and tins 1s nothm~ more than m a professed alle()'ory might be expected. Let Faithf~l be tile one Pilgrim's own faith, and both the unity and harmony of the nar1·at1~e are preserved. He knew him, he said ; he was his townsman and near neighbour, and came from the place where he was born. • Pilgrim had left the City of Destruction under the influence of fem· more than of faith, which is sip;nified by J<'aithful tarryinir behind; and the whole experience of Faithful is his own reflections upon what his experience would have been if he had walked more by faith, and had been less guided by his own feelings. Had he been more influenced by faith he would have escaped the Slou()'h of Despond, as Faithful did. He would have felt less the burden of sin: but might have felt more the temptation to wantonness, as Faithful did. He would have passed further from the town of :Morality, but nearer to the town of Deceit, as Faithful did. He would :aot have needed a night's lodging in the Palace called Beautiful, but would have passed by it in mid-day, as Faithful did. He would not have been so fiercely attacked by Apollyon in t~e Valley of Humiliation, nor have bad so frightful a journey through the , alley of the ::ihadow of Death, but would have gone boldly and cheerfully through both, as Faithful did. He thus acknowledges what dangers he would have escaped, and what encouragements be would have had, if he had possessed stronger faith. He compares what he was, with what a life of faith should have been; not that the purest and strongest faith would have been without its temptations and trials, but be would have been more able to overcome them. It is not all at once that the Christian learns to walk by faith. He sometimes gets before faith, and sometimes faith gets before him. He is never more safe than when faith is close by his side. He is not without trials even then, but be has comfort and support under them. That period in which the Christian mal:es faith his principal guide is illustrated in this part of Bunyan's allegory. Apart from Faithful, the faith of Pilgrim is not spoken of at any time as in vicrorous exercise, except when it is translated to heaven, which gives it not le;s but greater power upon the earth. Had Pilgrim's strong faith been spoken of when he left the City of Destruction, or when he pa~sed the ,vicket-gate, or even when his burden fell before the Cross, for which real, rather than great, faith is required; or had faith been_ one of the _graces by which ~ilgrim was entertained in the Palace at the time that Faithful passed by, 1t must be ackuowled()'etl that it would have been highly detrimental to onr theory, but is it rn? K /:. Quite the reverse. Faith fol is not with Pilgrim when his own faith is weak· but Faithful is with him when his own faith is ~trong. The coincidence ,;.e conceive of the appearance and influence of Faithful with Pilgri1u's o-.~n faith proYe~ them to be one. T)1is ~ol~ness of allegory 1 m~reover, is such as Christian experience really requires for its strongest eluc1datwn, and is adopled by the great Apostle himself, as when be speaks of the old man and the new man ; when he says, " The goou that I would I do not ; but the evil wLicli I would not that I do·" when he says," I laboured more abundantly tlian they all: yet not' I but the' "race of God that was with me ; " nnd again, when Le rnys, •· I through the la"? am <lead to the law, that I might live un_to God. I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: ancl the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me." Paul am! ~unyon are alike enigmatical in descriuing a life of faith, and it would be clilhcult to prove that either in boldness of' imagery has exceeded the other. ( To be co11ti11ued.)

·"'ALL right" is as much John Bull's own worcl as "Go-a-heacl" is the especial . voice ?f ~ousin Jonathan. \Ve hear it every clay, and scarcely notice ,its cheer~ul s1gmficance; but th~ other mornin" the power of its negative fell very f?rc1b_ly upon us. Asleep m the cabin of the good ship "Orion," we were -dreaming m a happy manner when a very emphatic voice startlecl us into .thorough wakefulness by asserting most vigorously, "IT IS NOT ALL RIGHT." A sinking vessel, furious breakers, and bursting engines, like "battle, murder, and sudden death," all rushed before our mind. The hobgoblins which so much .alarmed Bunyan's Pilgrim were all before us. \Vhen a man bears witness in 'the dead of night with a sonorous voice that" it is not all right," he is clothed with the power of a Jonah, and arouses all who hear him, whether it be a trio an a eabin ora crowd in a city. We do not know a more sure and efficient method of chasing sleep from a landsman's eyes than by shouting in his ears, "it is not all right,'' at three o'clock in the morning, when he wakes up not in his own cosy bedroom; but in the little 1len wherein the steward has " cribbed, eabined, and confined him." After nil, there was more re,ison for fun than fear, ,for the prophetic voice proceeded from one of the companions of our voynge, who, so far from intending to warn us of some dread event, was himself hardly conscious of having spoken. Our friend was lying in the berth beneath us, and the boy corning in for the boots which it was his office to clean, not knowing that any living being was in the aforesaid berth had put his hand on our friend's leg, and leaned heavily thereon, while he groped on the floor for the the shoes: the sudden pressure made the sleeper spring up much to the amnzement of the boy, who very naturally cried out" All right, sir," but recci¥ed for answer a flat contradiction froru the half-awakened passenger," It is not all right.'' The explanation created a burst of laughter, but all chance of any more of '" Tired nature's sweet restorer" was gone for that senson. l\Iany a day al'tcr, the cry of "It's NOT all right"' lingered with us, and we thought of the large amount of truth which it contained. We entered the churches of a Popish city, and felt amid the mummeries and idolatries that "it wns not all right." ,ve thought of a church at home, which bas now become n Noah's ark wherein the unclean beasts nre herded by sevens, and the clean nnirnnls in twos only, and we reflected tlrnt "it was not all right." --we remembered three or four Presbyterian churches in which no eye unaided ·by n Scotch microscope can detect a difference, and we heard loud voices raging .against a hopeful union, aml we thought "it was not all right." ,ve considered the mournful fact thnt many English Nonconformists are removing all the old landmnrb, and seeking out novel inventions, and we lamented that "it was not all right.'' Then our mind passecl in review the hundreds of self-righteous persons, lovers of pleasure, and neglecters of the gospel, with whom "it is not nil right.'' We pictured the dying beds, the resurrection and the judgment, of men with whom "it is not nil right," and we felt that we hnd here a great text for a most jmpressive sermon; but, clear reader, we nre not going to inflict n discourse upon you, and, therefore, we drop our pen; only ndding one prayer thnt none .of us may have to exclnim nt the last,

articles.title: It's not All Right 99') ~~ J Jezebel
articles.notes: opening article of the August issue; no heading printed; title from volume index
articles.text:
R. PETER R\YNE has taken ,Jezebel as the subject of a poem." He is wise in bis generation, for the Sidonian queen was no ordinary woman, and he who was raised up to battle with her was that chief among men, "my lord Elijah."' 'l'he period in which these t,rn royal spirits appeared upon the stage was one of fierce conflict, in which the truth of God wrestled with the idolatries of the heathen, the spoil of battle being the Tl"hole nation of Israel, and the weapons of warfare the prophet's Yoicc on the one hand, and the sword of persecution on the other. It was a grand era, a time wherein the Lord revealed himself as "a man of war. ,Jehovah mighty in battle." As for its history, is it not written in the book of the wars of the Lord ? Mr. Bayne has not proYed himself too ambitions in his choice of a theme; he has worthily sung where most minstrels would ha re failed. If he has not girt himself with thunder, and ridden upon the whirlwind in such a manner as the subject demanded, throwing a fierce soul into the fury of the fray; he has, nevertheless, in flowing numbers, with a true poet's language, rehearsed the conflict, and instructed future generations in its teachings. It needed a Byron to sing a Jezebel: but, had he essayed the theme, his song would, in all probability, hare been such, that, like the painted enchantress herself. it hncl been better for the world had its voice never been heard. As for Elijah, the prophet of fire would require a poet of flame to Le his expositor. Till a thnmleruolc " "Tho Dav8 of ,lczcbel: '' an Hisloricnl Drnmn. By Peter Jla~·ne. Stmlrnn nml Co., 56, L,i<lgnl<' Hill. L,,ntlon. 1Ri2.

genius shall arise to speak in lightning and whirlwind, :Mr. Bayne's bright and benig-n star will be in the ascendant over Samaria and Carmel. The historical drama opens with a dialogue between Ahab and Jezebel, in which, with the irresistible weapons of a beautiful woman's tears, the queen subdues her husband to her will. She complains that her ideas of uni.ersal toleration for all religions had been insolently opposed by Jehornh's prophets, who had filled the public ways "with howlings against Baal and Ashtoreth," until the people "prompt to catch the flame of mad fanaticisms " were ready to revolt. She demanded that the prophets who resisted her liberal, broad-church, comprehensive policy should, at one blow, be utterly destroyed; for, a5 she said (and the present age is altogether of her mind),- " Tolerance Of those who will not tolerate is sin Against all toleration."

She was a bigot for liberality, an admirer of the music and statuary which adorned the divergent rites of the various religions, ardently desirous that all gods should be equally reverenced, and only fierce towards the God who so austerely demanded that he should reign alone. Her ideal of Church fellowship was the antitype of thar, which has the patronage of a certain learned dean, and a considerable and influential party both within and outside the National Church : she wished- " That every man of every nation round Who visited Mount Zion, there should find An altar to his country'R gocls, and thus With friendly gods above and friendly men Below, the broad green earth might smile in peace Up to a smiling, azure firmament.''

Obadiah enters while the queen is inveighing against the raving fanatics, and i;he fiercely puts it to him " think'st_ thou we cannot rt-ead these rebels down." The succeeding conversation appears to us to merit the highest praise, none but a true poet could so well have conceived, and so fitly have worded his conception. Obadiah. " They are most weak, 0 queen, if spear and sword And iron chariot are the only strength In which a man mav trust ; but if their God Be pleased to help them, all their enemies Shall be like stubble in the crackling flame, When win<IR scud rapid o'er the blackened groun<l.

Jezebel. Great swelling words, but with no jot of sense ! What armies can these prophets or their Jah Set in the tented field ? What fortresses Can lend them shelter? ,vm a javelin Not pin a traitor to the ground because He mouths a prayer to Jah?

Obadiah. What God will do, He only kuoweth. All unsearchable By mortal man the secrets of His reign. But what He can do He hath clearly shown By mighty signs and wonders. By a word, If such His will, He could the mountains fled"e With hosts of bannered angels, helmed with flame. The great sea is His slave, and, at His nod, Would bring its surges o'er the scarped hills. The solid earth obeys Him, opens wide Its rock-fanged mouth to close it upon those ~larked for its prey by Him. The moon by ni"ht 0 Pauses among the stars to write His praise In silver glitterings on the solemn clouds." There are many passages of equal power scattered all throuoh the poem, of which another sample may be taken from a scene wherein Elijah foretells the withholding of dew and rain. " There was a change That moment in the sky and on the earth, The sun drank up the clouds like cups of wine, And glared, red-eyed, above. The dewy drops Cn lily and on vine lhshed off in films Of thin white vapour, rushing to the sky. The wind moaned low and died. The air grew hot And touched the brow like fire."

Here and there the master's hand strikes what seems to onr ear a discordant note, or, to use another simile, the eagle wing wearies and flies too low, but there are great passages full of fine flights of imagination which will never be forgotten. The description of Elijah's mockery of the priests of Baal, the Snn-god, overflows with life, and strikes us as catching the very spirit of the Scripture narrative. 11 A fenrful glee was in his eye, a mirth Too stern, methought, for man of woman born ; His glnnce was vexing those robed prophets more Than the sun's fire; and then he gave it words. 'l\light he not spare one little spark, but one, Your fine l!Od riding there,' he cried, ' to light Your sncrifice? He surely has enough; He's burning you, if not your offering. Poor souls, I pity you!' They screamed for rage. ' A little louder,' smiled he, 'for perhnps In his wnrm chnriot he hns fallen asleep.' They lenped, they danced, they cut themselves with knives, Till the blood soaked their robe~ and poured in streams From their lanced foreheads. Then be laughed alond, Great shouts of laughter, till the echoes rang From crag to crag on Carmel. 'Keep it up, Another dance! ' he shrie:, ell ; 'another song! Leap rnthcr higher; never grudge some drops ·Of your dear blood, so precious in his sight. Y c know he is a god, my reverend friends;
