articles.text:
THE KING'S MOWINGS. 36!)

day? Should 'lfe not always live as if we knew our lnst hour to be at that the door? If a man in his right state were informed on a sudden, "You • will die to-night," he ought not to alter his mode of life.one atom; he should be so living that be had nothing more to do but to continue his course. It is remarked of Bengel, the great critic, that "he did not wish to die in spiritual parade, but in the ordinary way: like a person called out to the street door from the midst of businesE: so much so that he was occupie~ with the correction of his proof-sheets at his dying season, as at other times." To me it seems to be the very hio-hest kind of death to die in harness, concluding life 'lfithout suspendi~g service. Alas, many are nnready, and would sadly be put about if the midnight cry were suddenl.v heard. Oh, let us see that every thing is in order! Both for this world and the next nothing should be left to be hurried o,er in the last few hours. Christian man, is your will made ? Are your business affairs all straight ? They ought to be. everything- ought to be as near as you can keep it in perfect order, so that you are ready to go at any minute. Mr. George Whitefield used to live so in anticipation of death that he said, '' I never go to sleep at night with even a pair of gloves out of place." Oh, that 'Ire could be habitually ready and in order, especially in higher matters, walking before the Lord, as preparing to meet him ! Then, dear friends, this departure of many friends, while it admonishes us to be going, at the same time teaches us to do twice as much while we are here, seeing that our numbers are being thinned. A lJTave soldier in the day of battle, if he hears that a regiment has been exterminated by the enemy's shot and shell, says "Then those of us that survive must fight like tigers. There is no room for ns to play at fighting. If they have slain so many, we must be more desperately valiant." And so, to-day, if one is gone here and there, a useful worker from the Sabbath-schools, from the street preaching, then it is time our broken ranks were repaired. 0 you young men, I pray you, fill up the g-ap; and you young Tfomen who love the Saviour, if a Sabbath-school teacher is gone and you are teaching, teach better, or, if yon nre not teaching, come and fill the place. M.v dear brethren, I pray for recruits, I stand like a commander in the midst of my lit.tie army and see some of the best flmitten down, here one and there one, nnrl what can I do, but, as my Master bids me, lead you on, and say, "Brethren and sisters, step into their places ; fill the gaps in the ranks." Do not let death gain upon ns, but even as one goes into the golden city, let another cry " Here I am : I will fill up the place and seek to do the >l"Ork until the Master shall rall me also to my reward." As for us who are at work we must lnhonr more zealously than ever, we must pray more fervently than ever. When a certain great man suddenly died in the ministry, I remember in m.v yoUD" dnys an old preacher saying, '' I must preach better than ever I did ;ow that )fr. So-and-so is ~one." And you, Christian, whenever a saint is removed say, "I must live the better to make up to the church the loEs which it has sustained." One other thought, by way of admonition. If the Kin~ hns been takin~ his rnowings, then the King's eye is upon his clrnrch. He has not forgotten this field, for he has been mowing it. We have been pi:aying lately that he would vi~it us. He k1~ comC', he hns come!

ought to stimulate us in prayer. He ,vill hear us, his eye is upon us; this ou_ght to stimulate us to self-examination. Let us plll'ge out everything that will grie"l'e him. He is evidently watchino- us. Let us seek to Jive as in his presence that nothing may vex his Rpirit, and cause him to withdraw from us. Beloved, these are the words of admonition. III. And, now, a few more words by way of ANTICIPATION. I hardly know under what head tl) place them. What anticipations are there , that come out of the mowing? Why, these. There is to be an aftergrowth. After the King's mowings there came another upspringing of fresh grass, which belonged to the King's tenants. So we expect now that the King has been mowing, that we shall have a fresh crop of grass. Is there not a promise, " They shall grow as the grass, as willows by the watercourses " ? Fresh converts will come, and who will they be? Well, I look around, and I will not say with Samuel, as I look at some young man in the gallery, "Surely the Lord bath chosen him; " neither will I look down here and say, " Surely the Lord hath chosen him;" but I will bless God that I know he has chosen some, and that he means to make this fresh grass Rpring up to fill up the waste caused by the King's mowings. Do you know who I should like to come if I mirht have my preference? Well, where the daughter died, how glad I should be if the father came, or the brother came; and where the father died, how would I be rejoiced if the son shonld come; and where a good woman has been taken away, how glad would I be if her husband filled up the place. It seems to me as if it were natural to wish that those who loved them best should occupy their pnsition, and discharge their work for them. But if that cannot be, I Rt::md here to-night as a recruiting sergeant. My king in his wars has lost his men, and the regiment wants making up. Who will come ? I vut the colours in my hat to-night, but I will not stand here and tempt you with lies about the ease of the service, for it is hard service ; yet I assure you we have a blessed Leader, a glorious conflict, and a grand re,rnrd. Who will come ? Who will come to fill up the gaps in the ranks? Who will be baptiRed for the dead, to stand in theil' place of Christian senice, and take up the torch which they have dropped ? I will put the question round, and I hope that many a heart will say, "Would God the Lord would have me. 0 that he would blot out my sins and receive me!" He dclighteth in contrite hearts; he saveth sueh as be of a contrite spil'it. He will have whom he \Viii hav~, but the way to be enlisted is plain, "Oh," say you, "what must- I ~'IVe to be Christ's soldier!'" To be the queen's soldier you do not give any tl1ina; you receive a shilling. You take to be a soldier of the queen, :mri ~o to be Christ's sol<lier you must take Christ to be your all in all, liolding out your empty hand and receiving of his blood and rigliteousnesR to be ,our hope and your ealvation. Oh that his good Spil'it would !i\\"Cdtly incline your wills, that one after another were made willing in

the do.y of his power. 1\Iay he thus do, and our hearts will greatly rejoice. As I read the passage in Amos, which we have taken for oar trxt, I not.iced something about caterpillars. It is said that after the King's mowiags there came the caterpillars to eat up the aftergrowth. Oh, those caterpillars ! When the poor eastern husbandman sees the caterpillars, his heal't is ready to break for he knows they will eat np ever_v green thing. And I can see the caterpillars here to-night. There i;; the great green caterpillar that eats up all before him ; I wish I conld crush him. He is called the caterpillar of procrastination. Them arc many, many other worms and locusts which eat up mnch, but this w(>rm of procrastination is the worst, for just as the ~reen blade is beginning to spring up this caterpillar begins to eat. I can hear him gnawin~, "Wait, wait, wait; to-morrow, to-morrow; a little more sleep, a little more sleep, a little more sleep." And sothiscaterpillar devours our hope~. Lord, destroy the caterpillar, and grant that instead of the fathers may be the children, instead of the King's mowings may come up the aftergrass which shall be a rich reward to the husbandrnan and bring glory to the owner of the soil. We have reason to pray that the Lord would send the dew ancl the rain to bring forth the aftergrowth. "He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass.'' Now this congregation is like mown grass. God has mown it-a rich mowing has the King taken from us. Now, my brethren, we have the promise; let us plead it before the throne. All the preaching in the world cannot save a soul, nor all the effc.1rts of men; but God's Spirit can do everything, and, oh, that he would come down like rain upon the mown grass now. Then shall we see the handful of corn upon the top of the mountain multiply till its fruit shall shake like Lebano:i, and they of the city shall flourish lik0 grass of the earth. The Lord send it, the Lord send it now. If any would be saved, here is the way of salvation: "Delievo in the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved." 'l'o believe is to trust. What you have to trust in is this-that J esns is God, that he beeamc man, that he suffered in the sinner's place, and that whosoever Lelieves in him shall be forgi\'en because God has punished Christ ini,tead of believers. Christ bore God's wr&th instead of every sinner that ever did or e\'er shall believe in him, and if thou believest in him thou wast redeemed from among men. His substitution was for thee and it will save tl:ee; but if thou believest not thou hast no part nor lot in thii, matter. Oh, that thou wert brought to put thy trnst in J esm. This would be the pledge of thy sure salvation to-night an<l for evermore. God bless you for Christ's sake. Amen.

PrtEPARE to die whilst you are in health. It is an ill time to ealk the ship when nt sea, tumbling up o.nd down in a storm : this should have been looke<l to when she was in port. And as bad is it to bcg·in nn<l trim a soul for heaven when tossing on a Rick bed. Things that nre done in o. hurry are seldom done well. Those poor creatures, l /'e,\r, go in an ill dress into another world who begin to provide for it when they are dying . . . . but alas, they must go, though they ha\'e nor. time to put on proper clothes.-Gurnall.

W E sincerely ~i.sh this subject, so full of intere~t, and of profoundest meaning to every mm1ster and follower of Jesus Clmst, had fallen into other hands or had been :illotted to one w\th wider experience and richer heart. We scarcely hope, after wl!at has been written and ~poken upo!l the theme, to say anything beyond what 1s already known. But if we can give utterance to a word that may "licit the views, or remarks of our brethren, and thereby our own heart, and perhaps the heart of another, be refreshed :tnd stimulated, we shall feel repaid for our labour, and thankful that om· thoughts were guided in this direction. The word revival, when used in reference to reli<rion, has about it a certain amount of distaste, no doubt created by the excit;ment of those who possess zeal without discretion. Vre candidly confess that we share in the aversion felt by many earnest workers in the kingdom of our Lord to the Hpirit and mode of action of~- lar/!e portion of modem revivalism. We believe, however, that there is as much difference betwixt an organised or got-up revival and a aenuine work of the Holy Spirit, as there is in the contrr.st of midnight and noon. Re,,-irnls tl1cre ha'<"e been which have been created and sustained by a mere fleshly excitement, an imposing ceremony, a wild excitement, n fanatical oratory, or some other flash of human fireworks; but on the other band there have been "times ofrefreshinl!," seasons of divine visitation, and ~reat ~piritual birthdays in the Church of Christ, whe,n she has exclaimed, "Who hath begotten me these?" The slumbering Zion bas been aroused, quickened, re,·ived, and clothed in beautiful garments, and addressing herself joyously to her reclaiming work, she has with silver trumpet and high-sounding cymbal, together with the singers and players on instruments, kept)hcr jubilee. "'When the Lord turned again the captivity of Ziun we were like the~ that dream. Then was our mouth filled l\"ith laughter, and our tongue with singing, then said they among the heathen the Lord bath done great things for them." Revival implies a deadness, and if regarded in the light of a resurrection, a burial. But it also implies life, for that which does not exist cannot be rc'<"ived. It is not, therefore, a new creation, but a re-creation, or re-kindling, of the altar fires burning so dull and low. A revival is to the Church of Christ, what 8pring is to the world of nature. In spring we nre favoured with genial ~bowers, gentle breezes, and quiet, cheering sun-light. The landscape is flooded ,i-itb beauty, and the sombre hues of an unkindly winter give place to the richer tessclations of Rummer, when the whole is changed to emerald and diamond ; buds unfold their blossoms; birds chant their morning hymn; and by the gentle gales are wafted the odours of a thousand flowers from hill nnd dale. "For, lo, the winter is past ; the flowers appear on earth; nnd the voice of tl,e turi.le is !,card in our land. Tl1e fig-tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with tender grapes gi,·e a good smell." Thus, in the Church of Christ, when there is a multiplied power of divine life, the Holy Spirit being pleased to ~heel forth his benign and gracious influence, like the morning Lreeze or the showers that water the earth, the renewed fragrnncc of holy life is felt and acknowledged by all. Every heart bents high with joyous hope. Young men and maidens, old men and children, praise the Lord. Then fathers with grateful licarts tell of tl,e protligal's return, nnd the shepherd comes l,ounding into tl1e folcl, saying to l1is friends and his neighbours," rejoice with 111e for I Lave found tl1e Fheep which was lost.'' "'hnt mellings of heart and lirokrnne,;; of ,pirit, nncl comuinntion of effort mnrk s11C"l1 a sncred summer!

Then from hearts filled with joy, though bowed in humble adoration because of overwhelming favour, like the yellow corn bendin:r for very ripeness and fulness, there arises the anthem of praise, until the wilderness is made glad for them, and the desert rejoices and blossoms like the rose. But when shall these things be, or what shall be the sign of their coming ? The answer is at hand. " Thou shalt arise and have mercy upon Zion, for the time to favour her, yea, the set time is come, for thy servants take pleasure in her stones and favour the dust thereof." What then are the signs of a true revival? On the threshold of our investigation we are met with the words of Christ, reminding us that his kingdom cometh not with observation, but like all other great forces at work in the universe, acts softly and silently. This coming has been compared to the day-dawn; and what so gentle as the mornin" li..,ht risinomutely in the drowsy east, falling upon the sleeping flowers and kis;ino- the~ till they open their bright eyes for joy! Yet what more powerful th;n that selfsame noiseless dawn, driving back the darkness, chasing the mist beyond the distant hills, and setting wide open the gates of the day. Not with observation, yet are there signs, and guided by history and observation we cannot fail to trace the invariable omens and signals which appear before all great religious awakenings. 1rhe signs which we expect are; 1. Deep and extensive anxiety for the u:elfare of the church, and for the glon; of God in the salvation of man. As soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children. ·whatever may be the features of this anxiety, it will never lack sadness of heart on account of abounding wickedness, and an earnest overwhelming desire to see the aboundings of grace. There have been times when the church has relapsed into a state of carelessness; when she has ceased to be jealous of her Lord's honour, and become unconcerned with reference to the regeneration of the ungodly; when the channels are no longer flooded with the life-giving waters; when worldliness, backsliding of heart, and sin, have choked up ull the inlets of the streams which make glud the city of God, and her life has become like the little driblet creeping beneath the Yillage bridge, with no power to cleanse or wash away accumulations of pollution. In such times the world lying in sin gives the church of Christ no trouble. More anxiety has been caused to the holidny rum bier by u little cloud in a summer sky, thnu has been nwukened in the church by the floods of ungodliness which destroy the souls of men. ,ve surely cun huve no hope of a revival when this stolidity prevails. But, if the wickedness of the wicked lend to humiliation of spirit, confession of sin, and wrestling with God; if there be deep and extensive yearning of heart and vehement desire for souls, and the language of the lamenting prophet express the anguish of the church when he exclaimed, " Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep clay and night for the slain of the daughter of my people,'' then we see a sign of "R1.n·irnl." This is the standard lifted up in the breust of the aclvnncing flood. Such we believe to be attested hy all renewing or reviving seasons, from Paradise to Pentecost, and times following. We see it in the upper room where the disciples were met, waiting the sign und fulfilment of the promise; and, coming down the history of the ages, we find the like in connection with the " times of refreshing" experienced by the \Valdenses, the Lollarcls, and the Reformers, who struggled hard to keep the lamp of divine truth burning in a dark world. The like may be suid of the grent awakening in Gernurny under Luther and others; of Zwingle, in Switzerland; in Genevn under Culvin; in En..,land under Latimer and others; in Scotland under Knox and Henderson°; and, then again, in the astounding revival which attended the labours of ,vhitefie41 and \Vesley; or, that under Jono.thnn Edwards. One writer, referrino- to 'ibis latter movement, writes :-"Part of the previous night had been spent in prayer for the divine blessing. The soul of the preacher was oppressed with the burden of the Lord. The calm man of Goel announces l1is text. 'Their foot shnll slide in due time.' Sinners in the hands of nn nngry :n

~od i~ his alarming theme. His descriptions of' the doom and danger of the 1mpemtent are awful. 'Oh, i\fr. Edwards, l\fr. Edwards, is God not a God of mercy?' exclaimed one of the ministers, laying hold of his skirts. The result was what might be expected. Sinners were ccying for mercy on every hand. But who can tell what pangs and soul-travail went before the delivery of that message?" Do we not find the like at home? "Some three months ao-o "wi-ites one who has a dwelling-place in the heart of this assembly, having ie~ly risen from a sick bed, "ot~r heart felt hea1•y f?r the soul~ of dying men. Our ministry has never been without large results m conversion, but we were discontented and ill at ease, because to such multitudes the Lo1·d Jesus appeared to be without form or comeli_ness. Especially did it burd~n us to see so many of our regular hearers undecided. After so much preachmg were they, after all, to perish? ,vere they to find no savour in the Gospel but that of death unto death? These questions pricked us in our reins, and gave us no rest." Other ~igns in'l'ariably followed. Take one from the case of the same belo'l'ed friend. A brother wrote to him, sayin(J': "That fire wliich God has lit up in your soul for the conversion of sin~ers has become apparent to e'l'ery one. It has increased from a flame to a glowing heat; that fire has kindled a flame in others ; glory be to God for this. I am convinced that the Lord is about to work mightily among us. When I heard Mr. C.'s prayer last ~Ionday evening, tha~ prayer told out all that .I had 1:>een passing through. His troubled soul, his restless hours, and his cry m the niaht watches, were like mine. At one, two, and three in the mornina, 0 I h;ve been constrained to cry unto the Lord." Then followed a l:i.rge ingathering of the saved, the harvest of the firstfruits, the results following the signs. If the hyssop on the wall may stand beside the towei-ing cedar without being asked, What doest thou here? we may add, the like has been felt more than once by the writer. Cast down in spirit, and restless, because many who listened appeared to be unmoved by persuasion or appeal, he was led to mourn over unfruitfulness, and with weeping and supplication to seek the favour and smile of God. More especially did the burden lie heavy on account of the senior classes in the schools. Having spent nearly the whole of one night in wrestling for :i. blessing, he was surprised to find, a day or two after, that the like feelings had been pressing upon the whole school, and also some of the parents were found to be unusually anxious about theit· children. "I cannot rest," said one, "without a blessing. I have laboured so Ion"' without conversions." "Oh, sir," saltl another, "will you try and get hold of ~y dear boy. I am alarmed about his state before God.'' The very next Lord's day ( can you wonder when I tell you) we wept tea~s of joy a_t the teache)·s' prayer meeting, as we heard one after another breakmg out m sobs, while one dear friend, with strong cries and tears, continued to cry, "Lord, how loncr? How lono?" 0 Since then we have had the joy of receiving several intc;' fellowship. Many more incidents and facts could be p1·esented in proof of what we have stated, that a revival may be expected when there is deep and extenPive anxiety for Zion's prosperity and the glory of God. Deep yearning of heart and brokenness of Rpirit, and overwhelming desire to see ~en saved, like the cloud of sadness which p~ssed across the face o~ the ancient cup-bearer of Artaxerxes, are heralds of commg good ; as even the silent tongue, the harp resting on the willows, were prophetic of the coming joy, the bringing out of captivity, and restoration to former pri\'ileges. II. Produced by such anxiety there will be an extraordinary spirit of prayer. This we have implied in our foregoing remarks, but an?ther wor~ may not be without interest. We know by sad experience that at times the hfe of prayer is very feeble. The fo~m of prayer may ~o some extent be kep~ UJ;>, and the public praver-meetmgs well attooded, still the prayers are languid, formal, monotonous, n~d spiritless. ,vhat weary work it becomes to drag over the

'hour set apart for the purpose of pleading with God! But how different when praying men realise their need, and cannot rest until the blessing of God -descends ; who -truly say, '' For Zion's sake will I not hold my peace, and for ,Jerusalem's sake I will not rest, until the rio-hteousness 0 thereof go forth as brightness, and the salvation thereof as a lamp that burneth." Then prayer is no longer regarded as a weariness and a duty, but a privilege and a deli"l,t. Such prayers, like John the Baptist, announce the coming of the So;' of of God. Pentecost was preceded by a praycr-meetinrr.-" These all con tinned with one accord in prayer and supplication." And ~..gain, we read, when tlie 1:lisciples were gathered together to hear from Peter and John what had been done unto them at Jerusalem,-" And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together, and they were all filled ,vith the Holy Ghost." In all subsequent movements, we find the like testimony. Here is one, "A spirit of prayer which is really wonderful to behold has pos~essed the Lord's people." Take another, "The spirit of.prayer poured out upon the church has o-reatly surprised us," These are facts which speak eloquently. They require"'no comment. ,ve see in them God's own appointed sign. For these things will I be enquired of by the house of Israel to do it for them. "Prayer was appointed to convey The blessing God designs to give." Prayer is like unto the ladder on which the angels of God ascended and clesccnclcd, or the amber light on the distant hills, bright harbinger of the morning. If we would keep our pentecost we must hold our prayer-meetino-. Other signs suggest themselves, but our time is limited, and therefore only one more. III. When those who are engaged in the work of Christ are led to expect a revival, and feel constrained to seek the salvation of the ungodly and prosperity of Zion. "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him." Some seeds are placed in water to steep and swell, to be tested and set upon germination before sowing. The seed we sow has already germinated, if our tears lrnve fallen upon it. A tearful sowing ensures a joyous reaping. Such seed should always be thrown with a careful hand and an anxious henrt. '' I hnrclly cYer knew him (writes Cornelius ,vinter, referring to Whitefield), "go through a sermon without weeping more or less, and I truly believe his were the tears of sincerity. His voice was often interrupted by his affection, 11nd I have heard him say, 'you blome me for weeping, but how can I help it when you will not weep for yourselves?''' At times this mnn of God is said to h:n·e been so aroused, and so utterly overcome with emotion, that for n fow secomls you would expect he never would recover, and when he did so, nature would require some little time to compose herself. In the presence of such men some of us stand spee-:hless, but feel no surprise nt the marvellous results which followed their ministry. "'hat was their preaching but the lano-unrre of a burning, pa,sionate desire for the souls of men. They ago';.iz;d to see the unsaved brought to ,Jesus. Paul snill, when speaking to the Ephesians, "Remember that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with t~ars." " Oh, those te_ars," said an ungodly youth, to a pious mother, "You will break my henrt 1f you weep." And " Jes ns wept." "Did Chdst o'er sinners weep: And shnll our checks be dt·y?" Let all who labour and are lenders in Isruel take this to heart. 'Much of the matter rests with us. Not that we are forgetful of the various n:rcnr.ics God is pleased to employ; for like as the water oozing through some hidden fbsure of the mountain side, glides quietly on in tender rill, giving moisture to one little wild llower after another in its onward flow to the silvery sea ; and

his weary heritage. Yet we speak to the leaders, because surely on them must rest the heavier responsibility; for, are they not the watchmen who are expected to announce the signs which light up the sky? When those who labour in the kingdom of Christ are led bv the Spirit's gracious influence to expect and seek the salvation of the unirodly, we consider it is a i,-and "Siun of Revival.'' Are these not the men who turn the world upside down? When the_v move onward will there not be prog1;ess ? The signs indicated we believe to be what the church requires before she can have any hope of being a blessing- to the world ; her face must shine like that of Moses, or better still, must reflect the glory of her Lord. In the deep and extensive anxiety for the prosperity of Zion and for the glory of God, we see something of him who looked up to heaven and siuhed. By the praying church we may be led to remember, that Christ went up into the mountain to pr~y; in the anxious energy and effort fot" th~ salvation of the ungodly, we may see him who came to seek and save that which was lost. Such signs may not be much valued, nay, will not be recognised by the mere professor; but, to the man whose soul is all aglow with the divine fire, whose mind is on the wing and ready to hail the faintest trace of springtide in the church of the living God, such signs are like unto salvation. Despise not the faintest siun; for, as the modest flower, peeping out from behind the snows of winter, ~nnounces the approaching spring, so a single conversion, or one earnest heart, may be the beginning of a fruitful season, the first sign of revival. Then, "Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the briar shall come up the myrtle tree, and it shall be to the Lord for a name, for an everlasting sign." Wben the sleeping church, and the dead world shall have been silently transformed into the loveliness of life, the Lord shall indeed appear in his glory.

articles.text:
BY \'ERXOX J. CHARLES\VOTITH.

O1'1E time a_ go a ministerial conference was held in a provincial town and the S large attendance of the clergy excited the surprise a~d wonder of the si_mple rustics of the neighbourhood. Many uttered the question, "What does 1t all mean?" and very varied were the answers received. We have been favoured with two which are stamped with an originality quite their own. One sage rustic remarked that, " The parsons be out on strike." What the object of the strike might be; whether it was to secure an advance of pew rents, to oppose episcopal control, or to reduce the number of sermons per week, was of no concern to the bucolic mind. The answer was regarded as satisfactory by those who h_ad not coRsidered the chances of a clerical lock-out. Another wondrously wise individual was persuaded that " The parsons be met to change sermons;" and this solution of the problem was followed by the ready rejoinder, "Our parson gets the worst of it every time." However absurd these dialogues appear to our readers, they s11ggest the hvo-fold suspicion with which ordinary mortals regard the clergy, Yiz., that they are "ambitious of preferment for its gold" and preach other people's SQl'mons. That the clergy have done much to prov~ke and even justify these suspicions, few will deny. The antipat~y of the worlong classes to religion will retain its hold until their minds are disabused of these lieliefs. Our regret is that all ministers are made to suffer in this way, R8 it is Lelie"ed they are all tarrecl with the same brush. This is manifestly unjust and highly detrimental to the cause and progress of truth. Our business in

ithis paper is to _deal with th~ _question of vicarious preaching, not for the purpose of confir~nn_g the susp1c10n that many ministers preach what they never wrote, but to mclicn:te_ the extent and t~e pernicious influence of the pracLice, .and to call upon mm1sters to make as little use of written sermons as possible. We know that many men who can preach an effective written sermon are bewildered into the utterance of th~ merest ~waddle if they attempt an extemporan_eous addres~. When t~e habit of readrng has been acquired the preacher i,1 easily deluded mto the b~hef that be cannot_ d? without his manuscript; and ·so becomes tb~ slave of bis paper, but that this is a delusion many have proved. The most efficient prea~bers are those who think out their subject in the spirit of prayer, ~nd _allo_w thell" thoughts to clothe themselves in appropriate language under the i1!sp1ration of the hour. T~e man who talks to his people has the key to the1r hearts. Our own expenence has taught us which method of preaching is_ the most effective. '.l'b_e ethical essay, _polished in diction, may -charm the mtellectual few, but it 1s calculated to mduce sleepiness in the many; whereas the "cut and !thrust" sermon commands the attention of all, if only to parry the blows. Our immediate purpose is not to condemn the practice of reading, but to expose a class of delinquent preachers who, without acknowledging the obligation, piratically appropriate the labours of other men. There are several sources of supply which are resorted to without any quoJms of conscience by those who regard the Christian ministry in its professional aspect only. There are "Helps for the Pulpit" of every variety, and "Stems n.nd Twigs" of the tree of doctrine. There are "Homilists," "Analysts," and "Lanterns," for pulpits and preachers, and there are "Hints" and" Outlines" in rich profusion. This ready-made material would supply the ministers of our churches for the next century if the art of sermon-making were lost to-day. We do nat complain of the legitimate use of these helps uny more than we should complain of an artist for gaining suggestions from the etchings of the masters; but when they are employed to such an extent its to supersede the study of the Bible, and to check the inveutive faculty, we regard them as permcious in tl,e extreme. Sermous of remote or obscure uuthors havo been made to do duty iu modern pulpits. It was the custom of a noted minister in London to trl'nt his people occasionully to a sermon by tho Reformers or the Purittius; but its ho mudo no secret of the authorship his congregation were sn.tisfied. Not many ycurs since the fame of a new preacher wits hettrd in nll the churches. His sormous were regarded n.s mas~rpieces of pulpit elo<1uence, but his career wns l,ro11ght to Ltn. abrupt termination by the discovery that his pren.ching wn.s vic1trious, nnd that he was the living mouthpiece of divines who hn.d lived generntions buck. A minister may presume that the members of his congrcgn.tion, ore ignoraut of ordinary sermon liternture, and if ho be unscrupulous he will turn their ignorance to n.ccount. I lrnve before me a sermon which a learned D.D. of the Estn.blishment hn.s both preached aud published ns his own, though he hns:takcn it from n. volume by a Baptist minister. Probably tho doctor wns pleased with the effort of his obscme Baptist brother, and thought his sermon worthy of being rescued from the comparative obscurity of n. dissenting constituency, and, therefore, he delivered it to his own flock in the ordinary course of his miuistry. When he resolved to publish a volume he must either have forgotten the authorship of this particular sermon or ventured to run the risk of detection. In either case the doctor must bo held blamen.ble. American and foreign sermons are in great demand by some prenchers who do not scruple to preach them as their own. The chance of detection is slight, and the certain gain counterhalauces the risk. Doubtless, in one respect, the congregations are the gainers, for no mn.n would preach a stolen sermon inferior to his own. Three instances of gross plagiarism have come under our own notice. In the first, an Independent minister not ouly preached 1t scr1!1on from the "American Preacher," but sent it for publication to n. weekly religwus

paper. It went forth to the world bearing the name of its English fosterpareut. who must have fe8l·ed detection from the moment he saw it in print if he had any conscience. The publisher, being a personal friend of tb~ preacher, refused to expose the gross deception when bis attention was called to· it. In the second instance a. rector obtained his lest sermon from the same somce and preached it to his congregation. After bis death it was published. with his name on the title page, as an appropriate memento. In the third instance. a clerk in holy orders delivered a sermon taken from the same volume to an audience in South London, and afterwards published it, with several flattering testimonials from the local clergy. Is it unfair to assume that such instances might he multiplied? We think not. The occasional exchange of sermons by friends is a source of supply of which some a.ail themselves. ·we do not complain of this, provided due acknowledgement of the mutual obligation be made, but when this expedient is adopted, becanse men have not the industry to make all their own sermons we charge them with gross deception and forgery. An advertiser, who styles himself a" Beneficed Clergyman" offers to "lend his weekly sermons,'' which he describes as" original, earnest, evangelical," to· any' fellow cleric for "half-a-crown a-piece, or fow· for a post office order for ten shillings," but he adds an additional demand for "mutual confidence." This pronso suggests that the transaction will not bear the light, for if the businessbe legitimate why should he insist that it must be carried on with the utmost secrecy? The demand for re11dy-made sermons has created a corresponding supply, and a thrinng trade is carried on in these sacred wares. Circulars are issued soliciting subscriptions for single copies or a quarter's supply. Sermons, doctrinal, practical, and experimental are sent to order, also special sermons for anniversaries, and the successive festivals of the ecclesiastical year. Every variety of style is adopted to suit the elite of a west-end congregation or the unlettered ploughmen of a rural parish, and all the intermediate gradations of society, social and intellectual. In a circular before us we are offered sermons by " clergymen only of known ability and long parochial experience" at the· following rates:- £ H. d. "A Quarter's Sermons 0 15 6 Or if paicl at the commencement of the Quarter ... 0 13 6 A Specimen Sermon ... 0 1 Ci ~Iissionary Society, National School, Church Building, each... . .. ... ... 0 2 0 School Feast, Rifle Corps, Church Music, each 0 5 0 Yisitation Sermon ... l 1 0 Special Sermons as required."

A guarantee is given that" no duplicates will ever be sent into the immediate· neighbourhood of a subscriber," and it is strictly enjoined thut "no subscriber may lend any copy of a sermon, nor preach it out of his _own parish wit)1out the· consent of the eclitor." Thus the parties to the transaction mutually bmd euch other to prevent exposure of tbe deception. The se1mons are lithographed in imitation of a plain hand-writing which is easily read, and which prevents the occupants of the gallery from indulging the suspicion that their pastor is preaching a discouroe purchased for the occasion. We heard recently a Nonconformist minister make the followiug confession of one of the most daring expedients ever adopted. He said that, in his early days, he was a slave to his manuscript. On one occasion he found himself when some miles from home committed to an engagement to preach a special sermon. Kot IKiog provided with the usual sixteen pages 8vo. in deep mourning, and failiug in his efforts to find a substitute or guin a release from his engagement,

he entered a bookseller's shop and selected a sermon by a popular di vine which he purchased for a peuny, and delivered to an admiring congregation with as much of energy, if not of satisfaction 11nd comfort, as he would have done had it been his own. The trick was discovered, and, for several days afterwards, the study table of the delinquent parson literally groaned beneath the weight of the COJ?ies of the identical sermon sent anonymously through the post. There 1s no absolute guarantee of originality in an extemporaneous discourse, for we knew a minister who repeated from memory 11, sennon published by the Religious Tract Society in one of the largest chapels in London. The imposture being detected, the Secretary of the Local auxiliary duly supplied the members of the congregation with copies of the same sermon to the surprise of those who heard it. We blush to record these facts, but their exposure will do no harm, and possibly may induce some yonng aspirant to the ministry to confirm the resolution to eschew manuscripts altogether and preach with as few written notes as possible. Earnest preaching is the great want of the age. Polished diction and florid rhetoric, if destitute of the unction which comes from conscious sincerity and divine assistance, will fall powerless on the ears of the congregation. No wonder the weakness of the modern pulpit has proved an attractive theme for social gossip and newspaper articles. The charge of weakness is easily sustained, and it is our firm conviction the secret lies in the fact that much of the preaching is vicarious. The questionable expedients to escape detection stamp the efforts of these plagiaristic parsons with the brand of insincerity, and conscious insincerity is a barrier to their usefulness. God cannot hold fellowship with those whose ways e.re not clean in his sight, nor smile upon their efforts. Those who regard their pulpit reputation as the primary consideration are actuated by a false motive, and must signally fail, sooner or later.

articles.text: E remember a book bearing the title, "The l\Iodel Preacher,". at least we remember the title of it, and that is sufficient for our purpose; for we question greatly whether there ever lived but one "Model Preacher," nnd whether the process of modelling in connection with preachers be not; among the." many inventions" which man has found out since he lost his uprightness. Let every man called of God to preach the word be as his Maker has fashioned him. Neither Paul, nor Apollos, nor Cephas arc to be imitated by John; nor are John's ways, habits, aud modes of of utterance to be the basis for a condemnation of any one or all of the other three. As God gives to every seed its own body as it rises from the soil, so to each man will he grant his own appropriate development, if he will but be content to let his inner self reveal itscll' in its true form. The good and the evil in men of eminence are both of them mischievous when they become objects of servile imitation ; the good when slavishly copied is exaggerated into formality, and the evil becomes wholly intolerable. If each teacher of others went himself to the school of our one only Master, a. thousand errors might be arnided. With the previous paragraph before his mind's eye, the render may safely accompany us as we take a survey of the ministerial history of • Incidents and Anecdotes of RoY. Edward T. Taylor, for over Fortr Years Pastor of the Soamon's Bethel, Boston. lly Rev. Gilbert Haven and Hon. 'l'hom:is llussell. Lonclon: P.. D. Dickinson. CJ• ~-·

articles.text: a -greatly useful, but highly eccentric man-" Father Taylor " the Sailor Preacher of Boston, in the United States. Not Father Taylor of California, who is a considerably younger man, but Edward Taylor, of the Bethel,-the man whom Charles Dickens thus described in the wellknown passage in his "American Notes":- " The only preacher I heard in Boston was 1\Ir. Taylor, who addresses himself peculiarly to seamen, and who was once a mariner himself. I found his chapel down among the shipping, in one of the narrow, old, waterside streets with a gay blue flag waving freely from its roof. In the gallery opposite t~ the pulpit were a little choir of male and female singers, a violoncello and a ,•iolin. The preacher already sat in the pulpit, which was raised on pillars and ornamented behind him with painted drapery of a lively and somewhat theatrical appearance. He looked a weather-beaten, hard-featured man of about six or eight and fifty; with deep lines graven as it were into his face dark hair, and a stern, keen eye. Yet the general character of his countenanc; was pleasant and agreeable. " The service commenced with a hymn, to which succeeded an extemporary prayer. It had the fault of frequent repetition, incidental to all such prayers: but it was plain and comprehensive in its doctrines, and breathed a tone ot general sympathy and charity, which is not so commonly a characteristic of this form of address to the DE:ity as it might be. That done, he opened his discourse, taking for his text a passage from the Song of Solomon, laid upon the desk before the commencement of the service by some unknown member of the congregation: ' Who is that that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her belond '? "He handled this text in all kinds of ways, and twisted it into all manner of shapes; but always ingeniously, and with a rude eloquence, well adapted to the comprehension of his hearers. Indeed, if I be not mistaken, he studied their sympathies and understandings much more than the display of his own powers. His imagery was all drawn from the sea, and from the incidents of a seaman's life ; and was often remarkably good. He spoke to them of "that o-lorious man, Lord Nelson," and of Collingwood ; and drew nothing in, as the ~ayino- is, by the head and shoulders, but brought it to bear upon his purpose, natur~llv, and with a sharp mind to its effect. Sometimes, when much excited w-ith bis subject, he had an odd way-compounded of John Bunyan, and Balfour ofllurley-oftaking his great quarto Bible under his arm and pacing up and down the pu!pit with it; looking st~adilf down, meantime, into the midst of the congregat10n. Thus, when he applied his text to th_e first asse~bla~e of his hearer~, and pictured the wonder of the church at then· presumption m forminn- a conn-ren-ation among themselves, he st.opped short with his Bible under his arm in the manner I have described, and pursued his discourse after this manner:- " ',vho are these, who are they, who are these fellows? where do they come from ? "'here are they going to? Come from ! What's the answer? ' lenning out of the pulpit and pointing downward with his right hand: 'From below!' starting back an-ain and lookinn- at the sailors before him : 'From below, my brethren from ~nd~r the hatcht~ of sin, battened down above you by the evil one. That's where you come from! ' a walk up and down the pulpit: 'and where arc you p:oing?' stopping abruptly; 'wltere arc you going? Alof!; ! ' very softly, and pointing upward : 'Aloft!' louder: 'Aloft! ' lou_der ~till: 'That's where you arc going, with a fair wind, all taut and trim, stcermg direct for heaven in its glory, where there arc no storms or foul weather, and where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary arc at rest.' Another walk: • That's wl1erc you're going to, my friends. That's it. That's the place. That's tlw port. That's the haven. It's a blessed harbour-still water there, in all clian:,!<'S of the winds and tides; no driving ashore upon the rocks, or slipping your c:dJlcs and running out to sea, there: Peace, peace, peace, all

articles.text: peace! ' Another walk, and putting the Bible under his left arm : 'What ! these fellows are coming from the wilderness nre they ? Yes. From the dreary blighted wilderness of iniquity, whose only crop is Death. But do they lean upon anything-do they lean upon nothin7, these poor seamen ? ' Three raps upon the Bible: 'Ah, yes. Yes. They lean upon the arm of their beloved,' three more raps : 'upon the nrrn of their beloved,'-three more, and a walk: 'Pilot, guiding star, and compass al! in one, to all bands-here it is '-three more: 'Here it is. They can do their seaman's duty manfully, and be easy in their minds·in the utmost peril and danger, with this '-two more: 'They can come, even these poor fellows can come, from the wilderness leanin7 on the arm of their beloved, and go up-up-up,' raising his hand hi"'hcr and hiuher at every repetition of the word, so that be stood with it at last°stretche<l ibov~ his head, regarding them in a strange, rapt manner, and pressino- the book triumphantly to his breast, until he gradually subsided into some otl.1er portion of his discourse. "I have cited this, rather as an instance of the preacher's eccentricities than his merits, though, taken in connection with his look and manner, and the character of his audience, even this was striking. It is possible, however, that my favourable impression of him may have been greatly influenced and strengthened, firstly, by bis impressing upon his bearers that the true observance of religion was not inconsistent with a cheerful deportment and an exact discharge of the duties of their station, which, indeed, it scrupulously required of them ; and, secondly, by his cautioning them not to set up any monopoly in Paradise and its mercies. I never heard these two points so wisely touched (if indeed I have ever beard them touched at all), by any pre:icher of that kind before." We are not so enamoured of Charles Dickens as to consider his verdict upon a preacher to be of any very material consequence with reference to the man's real usefulness: but as a judge of vivacity of manner, and power of style no better critic could be found. He, above most men, knew what would win the attention and touch the heart. For the innermost music which belongs to the world of the regenerate he did not elo.im an appreciation; his judgment exercised itself in another court, where we regard its dicta with respect. This extract at once marks out .M.r. Taylor as eccentric, an:1 renders it all the more imperative that he should not be made 11 model. He was a man of his own order,-a glorious order too, but an order of one. He who should imitate him would not become a copy but a caricature. Mr. Taylor rommenced his preaching while a prisoner of war in the hands of the English, at Dartmoor, and his discourses as a. captive gave prophetic intimations of his future style. 'fhey were racy, and overflowed with mother wit. The sermon in which he mixed up George III., and the Prince of Darknes,i was such as none bnt an original preacher could have delivered. The text was "a poor a.nd wise child is better than an old and foolish king." "The youth beg-an, blundering and tangled, but with the root of the matter in him; which root suddenly burst forth into rich blossoms and fruit. As he poured forth the river of his speech, and described the old and foolish king, with burning words of sarcasm and illustration, they all trembled for themselves and their youthful preacher; for his Boston -Richmond blood was up. The king their fathers had fought, for eight weary yeurs, from whom they had wrested their independence, was then, though an idiot, 'old and foolish,' waging war against the sons of their fathers, and holding him and his associates fast in his

Seein!!' the peril in which his epithets were placing him, h~ cried out: 'You think I mean King Georg·e, I don't, I mean the Devil.' This hit was worse than all that preceded· it, and set him do,,n at once for being as adroit as he was bold, as capable of firin"' Parthian arrows as advancing shots. The officers could have found n~ fault with such a retreat, and the prisoners exulted in its tact and point. He was instantly ,otcd theil' chaplain ; and a note was sent to the Commandant petitioning for the privilege of having their own praying and preaching done by theil- fellow-captive. It was ()'ranted. Thus he began his life-work among his own brothers of th~ sea in the hold of a prison-,essel, himself a prisoner.'' ' When he obtained his liberty, and returned to his native land, he itinerated in the double capacity of pedlar and preacher,-a sort of :,.piritual Dr. Marigold, buying old rags, and extolling the robe of righteousness, selling tin wares and blowing the silver trumpet. In those days, one of his famous texts was, " Buy the truth and sell it not." His first regular recognised official holding-forth wns before a quarterly )Icthodist Conference, assembled to judge whether or no he should receive a license to preach. It has been reported that upon this occasion he had the coolness to select as his text the words, "By the life of Pharaoh, surely -ye are spies;" bat his biographer says that althou!!'h those words might have been worked into the sermon, the real text was a more humble but eqnally singular one, "I pray thee, let me live." H c adds, that the triers saw that his fervour and talents were more than :m offset for his defects: and, in answer to his prayet·, they "let him live." We do not see how they could have done otherwise, for no Conference wou.ld ham been strong enough to kill him. His tongue had been touched by a fire which no critics could quench; nnd had their verdict hccn a(l'ainst him the flame would but have burned the more fiercely. Afte~ itinerating for some few years, the man and his mission met, ond Father Ti!ylor took up his abode in Boston, as a minister of the !iiethodist Episcopal Church, specially set apart to labour among !lailors. His chapel, at first, held about five hundred hearers, and wa8 im!Ilediately fillerl to its utmost capacity. He began in I 82~ in full re,·irnl Yigour, frequently preaching four times a day. He was t)1cn ~-rmag, full of animal spirits, ardent, daring, and at the sam~ tm~e intensely desirous to do good. 1'o him it nev~r occurred to pohRh _his 1:;tyle, and prune awa_v its power; he spoke as his heart prompterl 1nm, and wrought as the Holy Spirit moved him. ~le did work enough for two mr:n, and had a double blessing upon 1t. In a vcrj' sho1:t time Boston felt his power, and its wealth and culture were nt l!1s feet as well as its poverty and roughness. A noble Bet_hel wn!:! ~mlt for l1im, a house of large dimensions, a fit sphere for l11s opernt10n1,. At the opening i;crviccs, he said, "America is the centre of the world and the centre of America is Ilosto11 and the centre of Boston ii, No;-th Square, and lhe centre of North Square is the Bethel." would entitle it to his best exertions. Mudlicot to Father Taylor ,rould have been the hub of the universe. As it was, "he made ' the Bethel' famous in all lands. He made that familiar name his own, so that, since Jacob, no one has arisen with whom that word was so closely identified as with Father Taylor. 'The Bethel' was no other seaman's chapel. It was his alone. He and it were almost synonymous terms. He was the Bethel, the Bethel was he. If a sailor in any part thought of one, he thought of the other. The blue and white flag that floated over it seemed to dance before the wandering eyes of mariners under every sky. The mighty man of God wbo preached beneath its folds equally presented himself to those floating souls at every port." It was not at all wonderful that sailors especially, and other classes of the community in proportion, should flock to hear Mr. Taylor, for he was a man of great human sympathies, manly, bold, honest, childlike and outspoken ; and, witha.1, n man on fire with love to Christ and perishing souls. His preaching never could be dull, the intense white heat of his nature prevented that. He "as in earnest beyond all measure, and commanded the attention of all around him for that very reason. No ideas of propriety, or notions of delicacy, hung about him like fetters ; he spoke to sailors, not to squeamish pomposities, and tn "the sons of Zebulon" he poured out his great heart in a homely eloquence, which was all on flame. One who heard him in 1B3r.,, said of him-" His eloquence was marvellous: his control O\'er the audience seemed almost absolute. Tears and smiles chased each other over our faces, like the rain and sunshine of an April day. Two eharllcteristics gave tone und power to his marvellous eloquence. He had one of the most brilliant imaginations that c\·er sparkled and lmrnccl. His sermon was all poetry, though it came in burst~ and jets of flame. It wns like the dance of the aurora, changing all the while from silver flame to purple, and bock again. llut the 8eeret of hi11 magnetic power was not here; it was in his o.crllowing sympathies, that leaped over all barriers, and had no regard for time or place. There was no wall of formality between him an<l his hearers, any more than if he were talking to each one of us in a prirnte room. He would single out a person in his audience, and talk to him individually, with the same freedom as if he met him in tlie ,trceL ' Ah I my jolly tar,' turning to n Eailor "ho happened at that moment to catch his eye, 'here you arc, in port again; Ood bless you! See ttJ your helm, and you will reach n fairer port by-anti-by. Hark! don't you henr the bells of heaven over the sea ? ''' The ludicrous was allowed comidcruble ploy in his discourses, nn<l ,re think rightly so. Many count the use of humour to be unlawful in the pulpit, but our belief is, that the exclusion of it is for worEe. '!'here is no more sin nor virtue in n laugh than in I\ cry. 'l'o the vure mind. none of the powers of our manhood are l'Olllmon or unclean. Humour can be consecmted, and should be. We grant that it is a power cliflicult to manage, but when it is under prcpcr l'Olltrol, it more than repays for oil the lnbour Epent upon it. Chill~rcn do sad damage with gunpowder, but what n force it is when n. wiEe man dircds it~ energy. .!\fr. 'l'nylor made men lnugl~ thnt they might \H'l'Jl. del~ghted to honour. Farthing candles rail at the sun for his spots, wlule they cannot be sure that· those spots are not excessive light• and may be 9.uite sure of an?ther thing, that, spots or no spots, ten tho~sand such glimmers as theirs are not worthy to be compared with the stray beams of the great orb of day. At the prayer-meetings Father Taylor was most at home and like a father in his family, cast off all restraint, and unveiled his inner'nature with child-like unguardedness. Here we have a string of strange odd bits, such us must have made the meetings all alive. His ejaculations were not always flattering. "Everyone has heard of the wealthy gentleman who, in the midst of a very warm meeting made a speech, telling the sailors bow much had been done for them: and how grateful they ought to be to the liberal merchants for all their goodness. As he sat down, with a feeling that the church would run itself for that year on this condescension, he was surprised by the enquiry, ' Is there any other old sinner from up in town who would like to say a word before we go on with the meeting.' A visitor "l"l"ho was telling at a meeting an appropriate anecdote, which had appeared in all the religious newspapers of the country, was startled by Father Taylor's singing out, 'Lord deliver us from stale bread!' And still another, who was slow and dry in speech, was encouraged by the prayer, ' Lubricate, Lord, lubricate.' One of his most remarkable displays of this kind was after an address by a visitor, who related the death of a very wicked man, a hardened sinner, who was blown up a few days before in one of his own powdermills at Wilmington. He came down all crushed and mangled, and gave his heart to God ; and now who would not say with the holy man of old, ' Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my last end be like his?' Father Taylor rose at one. 'I don't want any trash brought unto this altar. I hope none of my people calculate on serving the devil all their lives and cheating him with their dying breath. Don't look forward to honouring God by giving him the last snuff of an expiring candle. Perhaps you will never be blown up in a powder-mill.' 'That holy man,' he continued, ' that we heard of was Balaam, the meanest scoundrel mentioned in the Old Testament or the New. And now I hope we shall never hear anything more from Balaam, nor from his ass.' Upon another occasion a brother in the meeting was suffering from severe temptation, and after a full account of his exercises, was advised to take courage from his own experience : • For,' says Father Taylor, 'the devil was never known to chase a bag of chaff! Yon may be sure that there is pure wheat in your heart, or the Old Serpent would not be after you so hard.' As he was going away to Europe, lie gave the church a charge, and said, 'Brethren, you'll of course have some quarrel while I'm gone. N1pr, begin to quarrel with your sins. I give you full scope. Begin

now, and keep it up till I come back, or till you haven't one sin left.' When a Lrother from another church, who was afterwards aEsociated ,vith the Bethel meeting, and attended on Father Taylor through all his last hours, had spoken in meeting, Father Taylor introdneed him by saying, 'He's an old navigator; he has given the devil the slip a thousand times, and worked dead to the windward of him, with the leeboard of grace from the Lord Jesus Christ.'" His own prayers were at all times most original, and were more like the utterances of an Oriental, abounding in imagery, than a son of these colder western climes. Think of his prayt:r at the dedication of a new church, "If any man attempts to sow heresy in this pulpit, or to preach aught but Christ and him crucified, Lord drive him out of the house and sweep his tracks off the floor." The Sunday before he was to sail for Europe, in his prayer he was entreating the Lord to care well for his children during his absence, meaning the Church. All at once he stopped aud ejaculated, "What have I done? Distrust the Providence of heaven ! A God that gives a whale a ton of herrings for a breakfast, will he not care for my children ? " and then wenL on, closing his prayer in a more confiding strain. Father Taylor, .despite his willingness to pursue any and e,ery reform which promised benefit to the poor people among whom he laboured, did not make the ordinances of Christ subservient to Total Abstinence, but kept things in their right places. His opinion of those abominable mixtures styled" unfermented wines" by some people, but more properly called " Essence of Stomach-ache," was exactly our own. He called the stuff" raisin water," which errs as a title in the direction of being too complimentary. So deeply did he lay this to heart tl..mt one of his last addresses contained the following admonition :-" When I am laid in the grave, I want the ordinance of the Lord's supper administered in the very same way in which the Saviour was not too good to administer it. I want the emblems of the body broken and the blood shed just as they came from my Master's hanu.s; and, in my name, cast from this church any man who would come up to tbe altar with his dye-stuff." Upon Father Taylor the common plague of ministers fell with its usual force. Re was the victim of callers and gossips. He says himself that his "life was very much like that of a bear climbing a greased pole. He had his study and his Looks, and he was often among them ; but, by the time he had opened one his door-bell would ring, and he must go down, hear a long yarn, and then bow the interrupter out as gracefully as p~ssible, and then return to -~is books; . but Ly the time one is again fairly opened, the door-bell Jmgles agam, anJ u.own he O'0es scratching is head, and often not a little out of humour: and thus his life is spent in going from his study to the door, and from his door to his siudy." • "His work in one peculiar field is not generully known. Living at the North End, near by the lowest haunts of vice, he was often called to attend the sick-bed, the death-bed, and the funerals of the most wretched and abandoned of wome~. Protected by his eccentricity and his pmity alike from any shadow of suspicion, shielded from all danger by his utter ignorance of fear, he always obeyed such a summons. At

all hours of the day or night he visited the foulest haunts· of crime in this noble service; never with one harsh word for the fallen, never with any 11pology for their crime. A record of his prayers on such occasions would add ,ast treasures to the wealth of the Christian world. His warnings :-:gainst trusting to a death-bed repentance were reserved for vigorous and prosperous offenders ; but, when the sinner's life was ending in agony, he never forgot that the first convert of his Master's cross was a thief, and that his first promise of pardon was given to a harlot. He receil'ed many warnin~s, some anonymous, against venturing on 1mch errands. The only notice that he ever took of such warnings w~s to lay aside his cane, which was elsewhere his constant companion, but which he ne,·er took with him when he visited the cellars and garrets of North Street. This was simple courage in the Christian soldier• but it was also the wisest prudence." ' It grie,es one's heart to relate that after many years of glorious service Father Taylor gradually withered. He faded by degrees during ten long years, losing slowly all his powers. It was as the Lord would ha,e it, but, indeed, it seemed a sad wny of ending a glorious career. To drift about as a poor hulk, with the armament removed, and the light in the binnacle extinguished, was very grievous both to the old man and his friends, and we sympathise with the Rev. Mark Trafton when he said, "How I wish be could have gone down after one of his tremendous broadsides, shaking the ship from kelson to truck, every spar <Juivering, and her colours nailed to the mast ! or that a spark might have reached the magazine, blowing her in a moment to invisible atoms ! or that in one of his adventurous flights to the upper regions, in full career, putting spurs to lightning, in his own startlin/! phrase, he could have slipped in out of sight while we stood gazing after him, like the prophet of old." • So passed affay one whom Emerson called one of the two greatest poets of the United States. He was a Predobaptist,, an Arrninian, and a man of a thousand divergences from our line of things, which we believe to be more Scriptural than his, but, for all that, upon the coffin of a good man and true, with no grudging hand we cast a funeral wreath, and sav "Would God there were others who could fill his place!"

articles.text:
BY VERNON J. CHARLESWOI:.Til.

WHEN, in 1852, the Rev. Thomas Binney <leliverc<l a Lecture in E;i;:eter Hall before the Young :Men's Christian Association, an<l a year afterwards elaborated it into a book, a great deal cf criticis:n was provoked by the title he adopted-" ls it possible to make the best of both worlds?" The very question savours of selfishness, but the reverend essayist did not intend to encourage this Yicious weakness in the professors of Christianity. Mr. Binney premised, that "011 the theory of two worlds, many suppositions and possibilities are conceivable. It is supposed, for instance, that it is possible to make t!.e worst of both; to go through the present to future wrctchcdnc;;s; tw-ning this life into a preliminary hell. Then, again, it is supposed to be possible to make the worst of this by folly and sin ; to destroy and waste it; and yet, by God's mercy, to gain a favourable footing in the next: to "lay hold on eternal life," and to secure that it shall be spent after an improved model. It is supposed to be possiule to make the worst of this by heroic virtue; willingly to lose it, to spurn, and sacrifice, and throw it away, and count it as nothing in Joyal service of the true and the right; and, while doing this-making the 'l"l"Orst of the present world-to be securing and making the best of the next; the one being the price for the other, or being willingly and cheerfully given up for the sake of it. It is thought to be possible to make the best of this (or to appear to do so), to secure and multiply its varied satisfactions, to enjoy it in all its resources and extent, but to do this in such a way that the next life is the price of the pleasure, the futme being sacrificed to the present. All these alternatives arc supposed to lie possible. But the question with us is, whether there is not another supposition, another possibility; whether, in fact, it is absolutely necessary for either one world or the other to be sacrificed; or whether it may not be possible to make the best of both ? " Walter Powell is one of those who proved the existence of this last class, for ,vhilc maintaining a Christian character m its integrity, he achieved very considerable success as a "Thorough Business Man." To "get to live" is the divine order of our existence here: to " live to get," is a perversion which is attended with perilous consequences to our present ,vell-being and future prospects. In an artificial state of society, it is difficult to draw the line with sufficient distinctness which separates between the two classes. By an easy stride men pass from the first into the second class, before they arc themselves conscious of the fact. The spirit of emulation is one of the most prominent features of humanity, and one of the most potent factors of modern society. Few like to be out-distanced in the race for gold, the pursuit of' plcasnre, or the ambition for fame; and in these facts lie the perils with \\'hich the Christian profession is fraught. The dread to encounter tlte perils of • "Tho Thorough IluBiness Man. 3fomoirs of \V11ltnr Powell.'' By llonjami,, Gregory. London: Strahan & Co.

the ocean of life has constrained many to choose the monastic cell as a comenient harbour of refuge; this is fatal to the manly development of Christian character, which, like the oak, strengthens Ly contact with the fierce winds which test its stability. Christianity contemplates us as men " in the world," and commands us to "deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world." In submission to the discipline thus imposed, it defines for us the conditions of true success here, and the secret of the imperishable hopes which shall find their full realization in the world to come. We heard an earnest Christian say some time ago, in justification of the course he was pursuing, "Grace has not made a fool of me." This remark has the vigour of an epigram and the force of tr_utb. Born at Tottenham, in the year 1822, the subject of the memoir before us, while yet an infant, became an emigrant, with his parents, who sought to improYe their circumstances in Van Dieman's Land. "The bitter mortifications of moneyless gentility " were some of the lessons of his early childhood. " Having few play-mates or school-fellows, he grew into close commpanionship with nature. He became an intense watcher of the habits of insects and forest birds, spending hours in an admiring study of their various forms of life. He loved to wander amongst the stately gum-trees, rising like cathedral columns, straight and round, for a hundred or a hundred-and-fifty feet without a branch, and crowned with feathery foliage ; and the superb tree-ferns with stems twenty feet in height. . . . One of the earliest forms of selfhelp which the young Tasmanian developed was the manufacture of his own playthings. One day, while superintending the hardening of some clay marbles in the fire, Walter, then only five years old, watched his work too closely and one of the heated pellets flew out of the fire, and hit him in the wide-open eye, depriving it for this life of all power of vision." While still a boy, he was out shooting with his brother, and came into contact with the keeper, who, not knowing they had permission for a day's sport, shot their favourite dogs. By a merciful providence young Powell was saved from committing murder, for the gun which be leYelled at the keeper's head was happily unloaded. At the age of twelve he secured a situation as clerk in a merchant's office, and resolved to retriere the fortunes of his family by his all-conquering energy. He remained with his first employer three years, when he left to take another situation in the office of an auctioneer. "A young man of eighteen," says his biographer, "he has learnt self-help and self-reliance from the necessities of his position, self-respect and self-con~rol from the glaring miseries of those who wanted both ; he has acquired physical fearlessness amidst a normal state of danger, and from the enforced companionship of men who had little else to teach ; he is by tempe!ament high-spirited, and feels in his veins the blood of an Enghsh gentleman; be is lovable, attractive, musical. He h~s in him the makin"s of a noble character. One can scarcely fail to feel some interest in this frank, generous youth, whom filial love ~as chained to_ the desk ever since he was twelve years old. What _will become of him? Will he make the best of himself, the best of hfe, the best of both worlds ? Let us see."
