articles.text:
THE THOROUGH BUSINESS MAK.

"Walter Powell's conversion was attributed to the gracious influence of a Wesleyan minister, who visited him after a severe illness, during which his life trembled in the balance; and from the time of his admission he remained a consistent member of the Wesleyan Society till his death. The same energy which he manifested in his devotion to his business, characterized his efforts to attain 'the measure of the stature of the ~ulness of Christ.'_ ~e reduced everything to system, and was emphatically a 'Methodist. He kept a journal, in which he recorded his experience, and which, at his death, had reached to eleven folio volumes. The persistent self-scrutiny and rigid introspection which this suggests, would, in some, savour of a sickly pietism, but in our -hero bespoke t:ti.e reality of his determination to live a Christian life. Re records his failures with unflinching fidelity, and regards no attainment as a ground of boasting. With laudable consistency he adopted the various expedients of W esleyanism to foster and develop the di vine life in the soul. The class-meeting, the band-meeting, the love-feast, the covenant-service, and the prayer-leader's plan, furnished the means he found helpful to his soul's prosperity. Whether or not he would have succeeded equally well without the aid of so much machinery, we do not care to enquire; but think it possible that, with greater freedom from self-imposed restraints, he might have found ' a more excellent way.'" In 1845, Mr. Powell found it necessary to leave his employer, whose daughter he had married eight months before, in order to seek at Melbourne a sphere in which his energies would find ampler scope. After recording his deep sense of the goodness of God in his preservation, he adds, " Lord, grant that since Thou hast extended such mercy to the unworthy, I may live and work for thy glory." A year later we :find him taking office in a Sunday-school, and shortly after he records his appointment to other offices in connection with the society. To recruit his health, and open up accounts with manufacturers, Mr. Powell came to England with his wife, and on the voyage their second child was born. Having purchased a large stock of ironware, he returned to Melbourne, and found ready customers for his ware amongst the people who were flocking to the dig-gings. His success was as great as it '\"fas sudden, for he had, by his forethought, anticipated the necessities of the emigrants. His liberality kept pace with his prosperity. He was very regular in his attendance at the means of grace, although he was working at high pressure. '' This swift deluge of care, perplexity, and prosperity, utterly unforeseen, did not carry him off his feet. He still daily exercised himself unto godliness. This sudden summer of prosperity, after the long winter of anxiety, did not blight his kindly, generous sensibilities, but made them blossom as the rose." In 1856 Mr. Powell came to England a second lime, und in ten months made a complete tour of the manufacturing districts of England and Scotland, and enjoyed a seven weeks' trip to the United States. Returning to Melbourne, he found his business "quite snug," and soon after he took the two young men who managed it during his absence, into partnership. This arrangement gave him greater facilities than ever to labour for the good of others, for he " reduced his attendance on business to two hours daily."

articles.title: -100 the Thorough BusrnESS l\lAN
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
-100 THE THOROUGH BusrnESS l\lAN.

T~e business prin?iples o~ Mr. Powell, as _detailed by his biographer, furmsh not only an mtercstmg- chapter of biography but an instructive lecture to Christian men of business. "Sincerity was the root, consistency the stem, and benevolence the flower" of his character. "Business was to him not simply a department of duty; success meant enlarged facilities for spiritual and mental cultivation, the means of helpin~ the needy and deserving, and contributing to the material resources of the kingdom of God, and the speedier attainment of such an income as would justify his retiring from business, making way for younger men, and de,oting himself to the humble offices of Christian philanthropy. . . . . lie never attempted a compromise between the interests of this world and the next. No one could detect in him two interchangeable characters-a man of business and a religious man. The whole mass of his secular dealings and dut.ies was leavened by the spirit of Christianity." In writing to a young friend he says: "I think the right way is to give business our attention, to work at it with manly energy, to do all honestly, and in the fear of God, but resolutely to avoid corroding care, and the perpetual scheming how to make a a shilling out of ninepence ; to cheerfully ask God's blessing on one's business, shunning everything on which his blessing cannot be confidently asked ; and, withal, to let our business influence be for the good of others." Mr. Gregory enumerates the following as business characteristics possessed by the subject of the memoir: "Conscientiom; shrewdness, aFtuteness, firmness, energy and push ; laboriousness, concentration, intelligence ; foresight, insight, promptitude, and regularity; prudence, caution, judiciousness, and vigilance; frugality, fairness, contentment, and moderation." Nor, judging from the quotations in proof, do we think the biographer has overstepped the boundary of truth. He regards his subject as a paragon of commercial ,irtues, and writes accordingly. He very truly remarks, "There is no subject on which such a cloudiness and confusion of ideas, and Ruch a diversity and divergence of opinion, exists amongst sincere Christian people, as with reference to the just action and the true limits of those qualities which conjointly constitute business talent • Rnch as intelligence, foresight, sagacity, promptitude, and energy'. What is the fair field, and what the just commercial advantage of these gifts aud virtues ? That business is not merely a sphere for the action of truth and fairness, but is also a legitimate arena for the triumph of acuteness and forecast over muddle-headedness and thonghtlesmess ; of a brisk, prompt regula~·ity ov~r a sleepy, s~rnffling, mooning negligence, and a ltappy-go-luclcy 1mprov1denc~ ; . of m~ustry and concentration over indolence and inertness ;-all this 1s admitted: hut Tl"bat are the exact restrictions which the former qualities should impose on the latter? There'R the rub.'' During the last few years of his life Mr. Powell resided in Engla!ld, and while directing his Colonial interests, he acted as the J?anagmg partner of a London firm. His constant liberality kept _bi~ wealth 71·ell pruned, so that it never grew beyond manageable limits. He fixed a tenth as the minimum proportion of his income to devote to the cause of God, but during most years he gave more largely. On hiR 'Jf"J,han nephcm, and nieces he srcnt nearly £1,200 a year for many

years ; and gave, in benefactions to individuals durin11 the decade 1~50-60, on an average ~1,600 a year. To Mr. Ha;greaves, the d1sco~erer of the Austra!tan gold fields, he sent an anonymous clonattou. of £250. '.' This was accompanied by a graceful letter rcl?resent1~g the donatton as a scant offering of simple justice." He pa1cl tl,e difference between the rent of a small and ill-situated cottaoc and that of a good-sized house in a pleasant locality fur the minist~r who had been instrumental in his conversion. To a lady in New York cmbarr~ssed by difficulties, he sent £60 to pay her passage to Australta. These, and ~~ny other examples which might be quoted, show that he regarded g1vrng not only as a principle but a passion, the indulgence of which afforded him unmixed pleasure. He had discovered one, at least, of the lessons the Saviour sent his disciples to the lily to learn. The lily as it blushes in quiet beanty, and breathes out its life with its fragrance, does not grow and bloom for itself. "The flower shines uot for itself at all, Its joy is the joy it freely diffuses, Of beauty and balm it is prodigal, And it lives in the life it freely loses. No choice for the flower but glory or doom, To exhale or smother, to wither or bloom. To deny Is to die, To give Is to live."

Such an example of manly industry and Christian generosity illustrates the truth of the divinely uttered proverb-" A man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." What 'ire are, not what we appear to be: what we do, not what we sa_r : what we give, not what we hoard-these are the true tests of life. Bailey has given expression to the same truth, in language as true as it is chaste- " \Ye li1·c in deeds, not breaths,- In actions, not in figures on a din!. \Ve must count time by heart-throbs. Ile most li,·cs \Vbo thinks most, feels the noblest, acts the best." The world could ill afford to lose such a character as Walter Powell. Uc was "in the world,'' and made his mark as a "thorough business man ; " but, he was "not of it," for he realized a higher destiny, and li'l'ed to make his "calling and election sure," by singleness of purpose, purity of motive, and by methods of dealing with his fellow-men, which bore the impress of a Christian character. The church mi! it ant ('Ould not well spare him, for by the influence of his exam pie, autl the\ aid of his purse, he fostered and developed every noble scheme ,rhich sought to extend the Redeemer's kingdom. At the age of forty-ft ve he ended his mission, and fell asleep in the Lord. In one of his last letters he writes-" My crime is that I have tried to do too much. I have wrouaht in my business and in the church like a strong man, when I oug·ht rather to have nursed myself. I could not believe my doctors that I was killing myself, till one day head and hand refused to do any more." During his illness he gave utterance to his convictions and experiences, which proved the reality of his religion, :i.ml

expressed the joy and peace of his soul in the prospect of death. Grasping a friend by the hand, who sat by his bedside, he said-" I haYe not to g~ to heaven to be_ with Ch_ris~; he is here " (laying his hand upon 111s heart) ; "He is here-it is Christ in you-heaven within .. I l~:i,c_ him here.'' ". 0 m~mma," said he one morning, addressmg Ins wife, " such a glor10us mght ! Such a baptism of love ! Christ is in me, the hope of glory !" On another occasion he said, " It God spare me, I shall be very happy to work a little longer for Him; but if not, I shall depart and be with Christ, which is far better." There can be but little doubt, we think, that his constitution, never strong, was impaired by the wear and tear of brain and muscle, and that, humanly speaking, his end was hastened by his unceasin(l' devotion to his calling. His life, however, was not frittered away in folly nor squandered in sin. It was spent in the exercise of that godliness which " hath the promise of the life that now is, and that which is to come." We do not know a more healthy and bracing piece of biography than that which records the toils, the struggles, and the achievements of "Walter Powell, the Thorough Business Man." It should be in the hands of every trader, and it would prove of incalculable service to those who are setting out in life. Its perusal will bring to the front the three most potent motives of human industrywealth, pleasure, fame; and assist the reader to estimate them at their proper value. It is not money we should covet, and call it wealth; character is wealth, and the highest type of character is that which reaches nearest God's. It is not pleasure we should seek, and call it life; we live only as we realise the end of our being, and discharge our duty in the world. "'Tis not the laurel wreath or the name emblazoned on the scroll of fame, which compensates for years of hard toil, bnt the epitaph written by the recording angels, with a pencil dipped in sunlight,- 'He walked with God,' and the commendation of the Jndge of all the earth-'Well done, good and faithfnl servant, enter thou into the joy of thy Lord.'"

"JTwere har; been said a thousand times, I say it once again as though it the revelation of the pref!ent hour, that if we do not come as we are, 'hnngry and thirsty, our soul fainting in us,' profitless workers in our utter wearineBs, sinners in our sin, we i;hall never come at all. . . . Would a man be considered very kind and hospitable, who, knowing that some travellers were coming to his house, along rocky paths and across burning sands, should send a message to them while yet the_v are miles off, to say-' Do not come any nearer until you have washed and made you clean. Come; by all means come: I am not inhospitable: hut be sure you come with ointment on your head, all fragrant

with myrrh and spice, and clad in rich evening dress, ready for the banqnet.' . What would the pilgrims think of receiving such a message? They say m a moment-' He doesn't want us. This is a message to say we are not welcome. We mast seek some other gate than his.' My brethren, the case is ever so, as between us and God. He does not send a mocking message to frail, disabled men, in this dustv defilincr, wilderness world, sinful although they be, bv the offer of sal~·ation to them under utterly impossible conditions. He does not say ' Come to me for salvation, but be more than half-saved before you dome.' He comes to us with a whole salvation, with healinrr, cleansincr vivifvincr grace, which will grow in us, and develop us i~to perfcct;'ess. it i~ not the finger of direction, but the hand of help he gives us. We are not pointed to the Mount Zion which is high and far from us, and to which we could never climb. But he builds a sanctuary for us just where we are, and as we are, into which, the moment we feel ourselves in distress, we may enter, and i'n which, the more we desire and ask, the more we shall behold, receive, and have.''

" FAITH IS BETTER THAN DOUBT. we are never encouraged in the Scriptures, nor are we justified by any of the dictates of natural wisdom in cultivating, as an inner habit, an intellectual or moral scepticism. We are encouraged to ask questions of God and man, to read books, weigh evidence, reject fallacy, in one word, to' prove all things;' but all this with a view to the ending of hesitancy, to the settlement of faith, and the holding fast of ' that which is good.' So that to say we are encouraged to doubt, is only another way of saying we are encouraged to believe. The one is the mrans; the other the end. The means, as such, have no value apart from the end; even become injurious if the end be lost sight of, or missed, or too long delayed. To rest on the sure ground of ascertained truth, is to be in a state only second to that yet more perfect condition, which is described as 'dwelling in love.' But, to be in a state of perpetual equipoise-to be conducting an eternal examination into 'evidenees'-to be still vaunting what is called 'the spirit of enquiry'-to be ' ever learning, and yet never able to come to the knowledge of the truth '-is to spend a life not only of personal discomfort, where there is any sincerity, but really of little credit or honour to him whose life it is ; while, to glorify doubt as some do, and set up a cultivated sceptic as a kind of demi-god, a paragon of all the intellectual virtues, is, !o say the least, extremely foolish. What would be thought of a chemist, who should conduct an experiment, day after day, making a number of little variations in his method, but always withholding the deciding element from the crucible, or else persistently refusing to look at the result? Or, what would be thoucrht of a merchant, always reckoning up his figures, but never writi;g down the final sums ? Or, what of a captain who should sail _his ship in a circle ? Or, of a traveller always on the road, never reachrng home or inn ? But such is he who gets as for as being a bearer of the message, 'Art tho~1 he . that .should come?' but who neve_r reaches Christ's presence to dehver 1t ; or who, when he comes mto that presence, does not wait for Christ's answer, or else docs not receive, or perhaps understand it when it is given."

"INnwELLIXG or THE WoRD OF CHRIST.-' Let the ·word of Christ <;well in you richly.' • The exhortation is to let it dwell, to dwell 'richly.' There is plent.v of it lo fill the mind, to furnish and adorn, and light up c ver.v room in the large and \Yonderful house. Down to the deepest base of life it ''"ill go, where the passions lurk and slumber, and, flowing round them and through them, it will purge away what's hateful and unhallowed, leaYing onl.v wholesome forces, to do their part in the strengthening :rnd perfecting of the character. Into the rooms that lie more open to cnmmon day, and more level with the world, where many busy feet eome and go-where knowledge gathers her stores, and prudence holds her scales, and juclgmcnt records her decisions, and diligence plies her tasks, and acquisition counts her gains, and foresight watches the npening future; into all these rooms this living Word will enter, and ,,t her ingress the darkening shadow melts, and the _wrinkles of a ;;atheriug care arc smoothed, and sinuous and slippery things cease their blandishments and pass out more quickly than they entered, and injustice and unkindness, ashamed, hide their heads. Up higher yet the Word will flow, where imagination lights her lamp, and invention ~tir·s he;.· fires, and desire bends the knee, looking upward, and hope sils watching with nothing between her and the stars. This living Word fills alike the deepest and the loftiest rooms. Inspired by him whose \\"ord it is, it gives the old salutation of the first gospel messengers, 'Peace be to this house,' and, like them, it there abides. 'Let the Word of Christ dwell in you.'"

"Go among the mountains, and you will sec that it is the living si,ring that flows away. .And where it flows the grasS'. is green, and the fowers bloom, and the cattle drink, and the children linger to dip the foot, mid hear the sweet song of the little rill. Yet the spring itself is ir: no way exhausted by all this. Exhausted? It :pever will be. It is fed by the drawing snn, by the condensing mountains, by the bountiful ciouds, by the great and wide sea. When the sea ~s e~pty, and the hea,ens are dry, the little fountains of the earth will yield no more. Well up without stint, ye springs sent into the valleys, which run r,monrr the hills! Give drink to every beast of the field, let even the wild :.5scs quench their thirst! Go murmuring in_to rills_ of laughter, :,.nd rollincr into rivers of song, and never be afraid or give one back- ,rnrd look! You have the sun abo1·c you and the hills around you, and the oTcat oceans of the earth behind you, all holding themselves bound :,nd ~-eady to serve you, if you continue to se_rve others by 1our fl?w. Christians, let your inner life, fed and nounshed by the md_welhng word of Christ, have not ostentatious, or self-confident, or noisy, but yc:t natural, continuous outflow and expression." "You cannot carry ihe Bible from Genesis to Revelation in yo~r ;c.cmory every day, and all day long. No man can do that. Nor 1s tlicre need. We do not need all the Bible every day. The world needs it all. Individually we need it as we need corn in the ~ranary; 11s we need clothes in the wardrobe; as in a journey we need the hostel, or wanidc house to rest in, when we come to it; as we need the boat to U•J:·e us over the broad ri,·er which we can neither ford nor swim; as we

perhaps those chapters will be betLer unto us than thousands of ()'old and silver, and we shall read them through our tears." ,..,

[PART II.]

HE experience of the Mission has shown that there are numbers of T thieves in London who only want an opportunity and they would gladly turn to honourable courses. One declared he would live on bread and water if he were able to obtain it honestly, and when taken to a reformatory he proved his sincerity. Many reformed thieves, as~isted io emigrate to America, have led useful lives; but without such an agency as the City Mission they could not have amended. Indeed those who earnestly desire to reform find in this agency a last resource. A poor lad called on a Westminster missionary, and in craving assistance, explained that he had already used all available means to help himself. He had sought out members of his own family-mother, sister, and brother-but they refused him countenance, and wonld not even see him. '' I have been three days without food rather than steal," he mid; " I have been thrice taken off the street insensible, and placed in the hospital through want. I cannot describe what my sufferings have been. I wish to be honest. Do something for me for my soul's sake." This boy, after passing a season in a reformatory, prospered in America; and when writing home described himself as " one saYed from ruin." The following example of grateful reformation also comes from Westminster, n locality notorious for the shelter it has afforded to professional thieves. In a low lodging-house a lad was met with who begun thieving at nine years of age; and thus early he also tasted prison discipline. The father being a disreputable character, sons and daughters were trained in ci·ime or shame. This boy's earliest recollections were of ill usage ; for unless he procured money or money's worth, he was refused even the shelter of his miRerable home and turned into the skeet. On this account he forsook the parental roof and slept in the lodging-house. where he was first spoken to by the missionary and taken into a reformatory. News of his son's amendment reached the worthless father, who called on the missionary and said he wished to take his son nway to '\"\'Ork; but well knowing the bad character of his parent, the lnd refused to see him till otherwise advised, and then what he uttered

might have been the complaint of hundrPds of other Westminster youths : " You know that I haYc been obliged to steal for my livincr for months, and during that time you had neYer looked after me; but now that you ham heard I hare got into this institution to try nnd do better yon want me out ::ig-ain. When I was at work you took my wages on Saturday night., "·cnt to a public house and sat down, and did not learn nntil you had spent nil ; and then <luring the week I might get lodgings how I could. Ko! I am admitted here. I want some education, and if the missionary ~viii allow me to remain I will not leave. You want me to go back to my crimes and get transported. J will remain." On hearing this speech the man stormed and swore, but to no purpose. The boy, after landing- in America, found himself in a brighter world, and soon obbiined a desirable situation. His letters sent home abountled with expressions of gratitude; for words, be said, could not express the affection felt for the London City Mission ; and he prayed daily for the agent who had been instrumental in reclaiming him from the dominion of sin. Were Christians more active, such triumphs might oftener be ac-hie,·cd; for the society whose agents thus bear the burden and heat of the day merits the support of the universal church. There are numbers of publichouses specially used by thieves, where they meet as in a common home. A separate room is occupied, where, undisturbed, they hold what are called "Secret jaws" or private meetings. •Sometimes they aRsemble in small companies at houses comparatively respectable, but, in such cases, Mr. Landlord is carefully kept in ignoranre of his customers' profession. A publichouse missionary has been known to take part in a thieves "jaw," and one such adventure will be worth recording. Early one e,·ening, while passi11g along the street,, he met a youthful thief, and entering into con,·ersation, learned that several fellows were going '' to have a little jaw together" at a house specified. Such an opportunity of rarrying the gospel to lost characters was by no means novel ; for this kind of work had frequently been done before ; but tlw present promised lo be a more than ordinarily choice occasion. Something stirring or exciting was in the wind, and was about to J1c discussed, so tbnt perh:ips more eagerly than usual, the evangelist walked straight to the pince of meeting, which happened to be an apartment in a l0w beer-shop. Entering the bar, now neurly deserted, he passed tl1rough a forbidciing looking JJUEf;agc, leading to the_ taproom: but, the landlord, fearful of cYil consequences, and perhaps 111-pleaserl at the bold intrusion, <·:died out peremptorily, "Don't go there!" Though well comprehenc.led, this warning was not heeded, and with ~11 object to attain, tlie intruder proceeded immediately to place himself m the midst, of a company of ordinary and cxtrnordinary thieves, or a:- they would haYe called themselve~, sneaks and magsmen. It nppeaml that some special grieranec brought them together, it being just about. tl1e ti111e when public iudignation prernilcd on account of the atrocilie~ connected with garotte robberies, and because of the increase of" ~arotting in general. On that same day, a sc·vere article graced the• ··Times" approving a more tlrnn t1l'1rnlly heavy sentence pnssecl 011 ,:,'.rt.nin of the thieves' fraternity. When the missionary entered.

LONDON THIEVES.

suddenly ancl unhidclen, a start of surprise or apprehension '\'.as observable, and some to whom he was unknown desired he would retreat, in rather disre~pectful tones; while others, seeing no fear, gave a friendly nod of recognition. It was a critical conjuncture, needirn::: much discretion. '' Pretty fellows, indeed, to hold a secret meeting," cried the missionary, "I could not come down the :Marylebone-road without hearinµ- about yon." There was a brief silence. Who could have turned trnitor? How could their movements be thus blazer] abroad? But none spake until t!ic speaker again continued: '· "\Yell, you know I am safe; and I have eome to <lo you a good turn-the Liest that one man can do another." Prejudice was now overcome, and the cou rersation proceeded, the grievance of Lhe hour being freely discussed, wliile 011 the beer-stained table lay the current number of the " Times" containiu~ the obnoxious article. Was not England deeply disgraced by judges, who, in the name of justice were obviously oppressing unfortunates, and treating men as thocgh they were savages? Of course, in company like this, the wisest policy is to avoiJ giving opinions, and, if possible, it is well ingeniously to direct the conversation into another channel. The missionary, therefore, told his auditors of a certain French gaol, where there lived a smith, whose daily business consisted in rivetting fetters on the limbs of prisoners. They were surei,v unfortunate creatures whoentered that priwn, for once there, there was no escaping the shackle~. But there were others, such as those before him, who wore fetters of their own forging, and were so lending themseh·rs to the senice of' sin that misery would follow. ·• Seven hundred years before Jesus Christ was born," continued the speaker, "a prophet wrote of him as the great fetter-breaker, that he should proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound." These things and the exhortation to repent and believe were listened to in silent attention, till the conversation touched on the harcl experience of thieves who abandon evil courses and strive to lil'e respectably. In showing his appreciation of the work of the missipnary, one present named a late comrade who became a real convert under his friend's instrumentality; and this afforded an opportunity to the visitor or recounting the events of "Rattling Bill's" conversion and of his triumphant death. After thus spending an'honr in a meeting arranged to aliuse the authorities, and to devise means of protection in lawles8- ncss, some of the men followed the missionary to the street for furlhcr conYersution, and three afterwards called at his house for Christian aclvice. Thns the gospel may profitably be taken into the lowest dens. The Jarker their surroundings the greater the need of reformation. But adventures in public-houses among- dishonest characters are not always propitious; for though most publicans rccei,·e the missionary with courtesy, some wil I treat him very roughly. One agent, ou beingappointed to tavern visiting ir. an East-end district, like his eompcers under similar eircumstnncef., trembled at undertaking the task. When he commenced the round he ,ms well rr,ceived in a number of places, and probably IJegan to regard former fears as phantoms, until walkinginto a certain bar, Mr. LandlorJ, on aecepting a copy of the" SuuLlay

at Home" dipped it in beer and threw it in his face. This was soon compensated for, however. Two or three hours afterwards there came encouragement. The city missionary, more than any other toiler should accustom himself to forget what is unpleasant, and gratefully t~ -w_elc?me what is genial. But even public-houses are not alrrays forb1ddmg, for some landlords close on the Sabbath, and will allow nothing improper to run riot on their premises, their procedure arising from Christian feeling. What is perhaps a little more common is to find the Christian wife of an unbelieving husband gratefully welcoming- the missionary's message, and sending his tracts to relatives abroad. But what has this to do with thieves ? Nothi~ more than this : places good, bad, and indifferent, are frequented by thie,es ; and there the missionary must follow them. Speaking of tracts, how varied are the adventures of those little messengers among loose characters in public-houses. Once, in a crowded bar, an old man who refused one, directly after, as if repenting, held out his hand, and then converted the paper into a pipe-light. " That's not the best use to make of a nice little tract," quietly said the missionary; "Now I want no talk, so just be off," said the man in reply. But the on-lookers were not satisfied. "What behaviour," one called out, " Is it not time you were beginning to think of your soul ?" The offender knew be was wrong, but rather excited sympathy by confessing, " I am downright hungry, and I know none of you fellows will give me a penny." "How do you know that?" replied the missionary; "there's a penny ; go and buy a loaf, and may the Lord bless you." But the agency of the London City Mission extends much farther than merely seeking the dishonest and the depraved in their homes and chosen haunts: it follows sinners even to the bar of justice; to the ante-rooms of police-courts. Alas, those who invade these dismal precincts for Christian purposes, have many stories to relate of the ruin following on the wake of transgression. In the ante-rooms of a court like that at Bow-street, the missionary finds a miserable company congregated, each awaiting his turn to appear before the magistrate. The scenes in such a place are heartrendin 0o- to a Christian . mind. From one direction • come noisy and profane words, and from another, what, under the circumstances, arc dismal jokes. All here do not belong to the degraded cla~s. Had one looked round the ante-room at Bow-street, on a certam morning some time ago, he would have seen in one corner a crouching figure, with shame and remorse written on her countenance. H~ could ha,e told by a glance that her present trouble was a first acquamtancc with the magistrate; for the clouded brow reflected h~nest sha~e. One thoughtless act of indiscretion brought her there. Gomg out w1!h some companions she drank too freely, to find herself when sober m charge of the police. Now, in answer to what is.said to her, she p~omises to reform her ways, to relinquish drink, and lead a new hfe. Beside this unfortunate culprit is another offender of a far. prouder r;pirit. She reads the Bible, and knows quite as much about it as the parson can tell her: even a cautious body may be overcome_; b~t once bitten twice shy; that demon drunkenness caught her rn his meshes, but not again will she be a ninny and listen to the tempter.

Among such companions the professional thief will also bear a word of exhortation. There, too, stand the trained beggar, the begging-letter writer, and the would-be suicide, all awaiting punishment, or at least rebuke, at the hands of the representatives of law and order. Besides these, behold that pseudo-gentleman, who, with folded arms, consequentially strides up and down the inner court, conversing with a comrade in misfortune. His features express rather forcibly that only by inadvertence did he get into a place like this. Those abominable policemen interfered, as he, merely for diversion's sake, reeled brawling homeward at three in the morning, and thinking to do both the neighbourhood and him a kindness they lodged him in a cell of the court, and by their pains aroused his indignation. It is a morally dark and unattractive place; for here, says the visitor, are met, "The married and the single; the fallen, and the female of generally pretty good repute; the servant and the mechanic ; persons occupying respectable positions, and others in the lowest scale of society; the shrewd sceptic, and the dull thick-headed animal kind of being; the bigoted Romanist and the reckless Protestant ; the swearer, the thief, the murderer, the embryo gambler, who spends his Sabbath in 'pitch and toss,' instead of going to school, or to public worship ; the mother with the innocent babe in her arms, and the woman who has lost all sense of shame. Here they come week after week in ceaseless succession, to pay the penalty of their folly or their crimes, and to each a word in season has to be spoken." The constituency of the police-court is largely composed of women. There is seen the unyielding countenance of the crone, hardened in sin; and there also appears the wretched unfortunate, summoned by some shameless profligate for a petty robbery. These are commonly willing listeners to a friend, who having attended the death-beds of many such, can point to their untimely graves. Then, yonder, is an old one-armed man, with a gaudily coloured picture of the battle in which while fighting for his country he became maimed for life; but as begging is illegal, he has presently to answer for the offence. All classes of offenders crowd the police-courts. . Side by side stand the fallen woman and the "respectable" wife, who scared and trembling can scarce tell how the fit of intoxication originated whid1 brought her to this disagreeable place. Many other sin-deluded creatures are herevisible; for the syren they have followed leads to destruction ! 011 one seat is a specimen of the saddest spectacles which even policecourts can present-a young man with a countenance expressive of anxious pain, who, just after starting in trade, has too soon anived at ruin. He might have prospered, but he walked with the /oolish; and to support expenbive gaieties forged a draft, which brought him within the grasp of the law, and now he awaits committal for trial. Not far away is another forger, whose appearance bespeaks the man of education and of social position. "Ah," he saJs, " I know all about it." Yes, he knew better; but mere knowledge could not shield him from "drink and bad company." The above is a slight picture of what may be daily witnessed in a London police-court. Oue prisoner will turn an indifferent ear to what is spoken, because lost to a sense of shame; another in a freak of drunkenness has lost character-his all.

These hwe to find shelter in districts where the inhabitauts arc huddled together _without regard to decency; and, therefore, ,ve may remember that samtar., reformers are the proper pioneers of city missionaries. Crin:e must be ramp~nt where life's. highest enj~yment is gin-drinking, :rnd its sweetest music tarcrn brawhng. Were 1t not for our itinerant missionaries, who would direct these sin-blinded people to present peace and an eternal refuge ? It is surely a work partaking of the spirit of Christ to seek the criminal in his haunt., and to transform contaminators of others into exemplary citizens. Such is the work of tLe City Mission; but so widespread is its influence for good among thieves, that a dilfieulty of selection natural!, arises. A critical time with a thief, and especially with a young member of the, fraternity, on being- discharged from prison, is the first few days of liberty. Without friends, or prospect of honest employment, he is sure to find sympathy among old comµanions, who clustering around, will reintroduce him to their abandoned ways. One youth of this class had tire fortune to meet with a missionary before he could :be again in- Ycigled l,y 1·icio11s comrades. His position was as low and deplorable as .Jn_'I" to which human beings can descend. Being without money, and l"iith a wardrobe only extending to a scanty suit, he in the course of conversation, expressed a longing to escape from the thraldorn of sin w-hich had sunk him into degradation; yet he saw no alternative but that of returning to thieving until offered refuge in a reformator.l". Here he staid about half a year, and only left it through a sin!!l.llar aC:venture. His family were comparatively well-to-do, but had lost sight of him aboct four years previously, and enquiries and 8earcbes in ,•arious directions had Leen alike in vain. One day, "\Then out walking, the lad met his sister, and she manilested no les8 surprise than emotion at the sudden appearance of the prodigal. One strange part of the story was that, when this sinner, after volu11larily forsaking the parental roof, would have returned, he could not recover the address. 'l'hus he had been "lost; " but now '' the gladdened father received him as one risen from the dead." Leaving the reformatory, th<:! late convict laboured for the support of his parents; and all hearts concerned overflowed with gratitude for the blessing conferred upon them by the mission. When such are led baek to ho11esty, they regard themselrcs as repetitions of the Prodigal Son ; and happy indec,d are the results spriuging from their reclamation._ lnstcad uf coutaminating others, a youth becomes an example of mdustry a?-tl rectitude; instead of preying on others, he assists those who reqmre a~~isl ance. M ul tiforrn are the benign fruits of Christianity. • The ernn_'.!clist among the thieves is frequently cheered by hearing of' -~·uod F.pring:iug from tract distribution ; for thonsands of' tracls arc

Kpeaking in places where the voice cannot follow : and when one dr~pped by the wayside brings forth a holy harvest, there is reason to beheve others also bear fruits unseen. The followincr has been often told, b~t ~he facts are sufficiently striking to bear rcp~ating. A missionary once observed a man standinrr in the street in that hulking manner which betrays the idler wh~ cares not for honest labour. " Have you no work, my friend," he asked: " I am out of work," replied the man. This answer appeared to be an evasion oC the truth, a?d while expressing a belief that he was living disreputably, tl~e evangelist solemnly asked whether such-a course was a happy one. The man confessed he was not easy, out would gladly become respectable. " To tell the truth I am not happy," he "'·ent on drawing from his pocket a dirty little pamphlet, "That makes me, unhappy." The cause of disquietude was a tract gil"en by an unknown itinerant some time before, and the word had ma<le a sure ludgment, This man, being originally a thief, had become so familiar to the police that he dared not practice in the profession ; all he now did was to sneak out at night and train boys for pickpockets. Ko less than fire hundred youths, he considered, had passed through his curriculum. '' But I can never keep the young 'nns long," he said, '' for as soon as I have made them clever at the business, if they are not taken by the police, they leave me and start for themselves ; so that I 'flm obliged to look out for new hands." This character, who must have cost the public annually the entire cost of twenty missionaries, was taken into a reformatory, where the care bestowed on him excited his gratitude, and he soon gave evidence of having experienced a change of life. So much for the influence of oue tract ! The action of the missionaries among thieves is the divinest form of charity, and is often a lasting blessing. Some young persons at the crisis of taking the first step in a do1mward course are stopped; others who have just committed their first indiseretion are helped to regain a respectuble standing. An affecting incident under the last head was once witnessed at the Central Criminal Court, where II poor girl was going through her trial for stealing. Knowing it to be a first theft aud a yielding to sudden temptation, the missionary stood by the prisoner at the police-court examination, where she begged him to write to her father and crnve his forgiveness. Exposed in open court upon a disgraceful charge, the culprit indeed seemed to be friendless and despised ; but one friend would not forsake her in the ordeal of facing judge and jury. The missionary went to the prosecutor, and persuaded him not to press the case too hardly; and when the question was asked, "Docs any one appear on behalf of the prisoner ? " the same advocate stepped forwnrcl :rnd said, "I do." This action produced surprise in court, if not someLhing better; for the judge passed an encomium on a philanthropic society whose agents showed this sleepless nssiduity. As before observed, profcssioual beggars are thieves also. What shall be done with our swarms of mendicants whose numbers arc annually augmenting ?-is a question which social reformers 1rould be thankful to have satisfactorily answered. It is time the public relinquished

indiscriminate almsgiving; for nothing is more certain than that the majorit.y-and all but a very small minority-of persons pi·actisino• ~treet begging are impostors. A charitably disposed gentleman on~ morning offered a comfortable meal to an apparently famishing I\Tetch 1,ho craved money for a breakfast. The conditions were easv and reasonable. A heap of manure being in process of removal from the road to the garden, the supplicant was required to take a few loads to their destination, and earn relief like an independent man. Not liking directly to refuse, the fellow seized a load, but presently retaliated for the i!1sult offered by overturning the barrow and its contents, prior to runmng a\Tay ! These shameless impostors crowd the rookeries of London and other large towns, emerging thence into country lanes and villages to drain those sources of charit_y which should flow for worthier objects. The more clearly to show what kind of thing is sanctioned by indiscriminate almsgiving, a passage from the life-experience of an inmate of Sherborne 1,orkhouse may be given. When young, George Atkins Brine attended the charity school of Sherborne, and at the guardians' expense was apprenticed to a butcher; but early discovering that restlessness, or repugnance to regular labour, characteristic of vagrants in general, he relinquished industrial pursuits and adopted a roving life. Dorchester gaol he called his town house, and so well were the prisoners treated that George ·would occasionally break a window, or maim a street lamp to secure the hospitality of the prison. He always retained a partiality for his native air ; and the master of Sherborne poorhouse stood high in his favour. The freedom of a vagabond life soon came io be highly relished; for he attended fairs and races, and as much as possible associated with the higher classes on the ground. What is surprising in the instance of such a character is the fact of his being endowed with good mental gifts, and a tolerably liberal education. He made a leading figure in a Blue Book on vagrancy, presented to Parliament in 1848. Even now, though in bis sixty-third year, he is rather unsettled ; for the late master of Sherborne Union having found another sphere, George, at the date of writing the subjoined letter, was anticipating one more ramble. The document, it may be explained, was prepared at the request of the Secretary of the Charity Organisation Society:- J uly 3, 1871. "Honoured Sir,-Apolocrising for not having replied to your courteous note earlier, I beg to answer so~e of Mr. R. T.'s inqufries respecting me. In the first place, Mr. R. T. desires to know what induced me to adopt such a mode of ii,·elihood; 2ndly, how I have supported myself in my wanderings; 3rdly, the casual wards I have visited, and my opinion of them ; and 4thly, the gaols in which I have been incarcerated, with the cause of these incarcerations. ~ ow in reply to the first question, I left 8herborne to seek employment at my trade (that of a butcher), and not succeeding for a time, I soon discovered that more money could be got without work than with it. \Vhat knowledge 1 lacked was soon instilled into my mind by professional vagrants. 2ndly. How I have supported myself during my wanderings. Now, I mean to make a clean breast of it, I will candidly declare that I have stuck at nothing. I have worked (but very little) at my trade; I have been a cattle drover; I La1·c been ~alesman with three dilforent Cheap Jacks; I have been a pot

hawker; I have been II vendor of pens, paper, razors (Peter Pinclar's), spectacles, laces, etc. ; I have been a distributor of religious tracts ; I have been in tl)e employ (for two years together) of manslaughtering qui,,ck doctors-four different ones (I am more ashamed of this than any other of my follies, for the majority of them are not robbers only, hut homicides). I have sold cards at all the principal races in England. I also attended for many years all the principal prize-fights. I have been a "shallow cove" (i.e., a member of the land navy); also a" bighflyer" (i.e., a begging letter impostor); a" lurker,'' one who is· 40 different trades, and master of none. My favourite "lurk" was butcher, tallow chandler, or currier; and, to crown all, I have been a preacher! This game pays well in remote village streets on Sunday evenings, provided you are well stocked with tracts; but I was not fit for it; my risibility is too easily tickled; and once when I was invited to "hold forth" in a small chapel, I was in no little danger of grinning in the pulpit at my own roguery. This was at Rothbury, Northumberland. I must also tell you, in short, I have been a rogue, impostor, and vagabond of each and every denomination. I say this because it is true, and because I am now heartily ashamed of it. "3rdly. Mr. R. T. wants to know my opinion of the casual wards I have visited. Now I have visited but very few-I think I could swear that I never was in twenty different ones during the 22 years I was rambling-but I am fully con,inced that they all tend to foster vagrancy. Even such places as Oxford, Cambri,lge, Bath, Rochester, Norwich, and Hastings, do more harm than good; for out of every ten tramps there are nine impostors, or professional tr11mps. You may think this saying is too much, but I am sure it is the truth. If there was no relief to be had, there would be no vagrants. The difficulty lies in distin)!;uishing between the honest working man and the rogue. Now, the distributors of Watts's Charity in Rochester seem to pride themselves upon their own sagacity on thts point. I have been a recipient of Watts's no less than eight times, so I leave you to guess whether they relieved a deserving customer in me or otherwise. In Norwich, at St. Andrew's Hall, it is the same. I once gave my ticket, which I had obtained there, to a poor blacksmith who bad been refused one. The reason he hnd been refused was because !he was not so consummate a liar ns I was. This is truth. If he had been a trading lio.r be would ho.ve gotten bis bread, cheese, beer, and bed, valued at eightpence. Again, Mr. R. T. and his colleagues will never den! effectually with vagrancy unless they begin nt the right end. 'Let them, or the Legislature, suppress two-thirds of the common "padding kens," or low lodging-houses. These arc the great receptacles of vice in its its most repulsive aspect. Too often unacquainted even with the rudiments ,)f knowledge, and reared from infancy in criminal courses, the subjects of the society retain only dim not.ions of right and wrong, anrl frequently no conception at all of Christianity. articles.title: Christ, Obedience, The Test of Love to 421 Clergy and Laity

articles.text:
HERE are three main ways in which the relations between minister T and people may be adjusted. Th_e fi_rst is to red?-~e the ~inister into a condition of utter dependence, subJect1on, and servility to Ins flock, bv taking him from the position of a leader and turning him into a mere f~g. A picture in the Royal Academy's exhibition of a season or two ago not unaptly represented the nominal leadership, but real slavery, wherein many a holy man is well nigh tortured to death. A guide was portra-ed in the act of conducting •a party of soldiers over a trackless swamp. He is a little in advance, picking his steps with evident painfulness and precision, while the band of armed men press on close behind with bayonets pointed in dangerous proximity to his bending, jaded person. He is a guide, he looks like a fugitive. The next is to make the minister a master, a lord of God's heritage, by investing him with sacerdotal supremacy, enthroning him in an authority absolute, uncontrollable, and unapproachable, and reducing the peop~e o~ his r;harge into a blindly submissive flock of followers. The tlurd IS. to reaard both the minister aud the church as respectively possessmg in~lienable rights, which are not of themselves antagonistic, and may be exercised in their different spheres with perfect harmony, and without

speed the good boat by an even course over the waters. In th~ bustle and hurry of church activity, or in the apathy and obstruc_trnn of church stagnation, it is impossible always to maintain this theoretical balance of power. The "come" and "go," the" o-ive" and "take," the ceaseless action and reaction of countless influ~nces ever stirring in church life, are sure to tilt for a while the authority of the pastor or the church into undue preponderance. The vast variety, too, of the circumstances of the churches, the diversity of the gifts and temperaments of the pastors, preclude the possibility of laying down any hard and fast law with regard to their individual functions. Love is the only divinely given bond to bind ever.v man in his appointed place, and all in one harmonious whole. Nevertheless, it cannot be disguised, and must never be overlooked, that the very absence of precisely defined rules has allowed such scope to the designing and amLitious, that the powers safely entrusted by the people to tbe sincere and honest have been turned by the unscrupulous into whips of scorpions; and the liberties and prerogatives frankly and cheerfully accorded to the rueek hare grown, through the manipulations of the tyrannical, into iron bands. The successors of presbyters have sunk into prelates, and the successors of pastors have degenerated into popes. The fact of such a de,clopmeut, or rather degeneracy, having been possible, doubtless points to an inherent fault in the churches themselves. No such steps :is these could ever be taken did there exist in the churches a strong con- ·sciousness of freedom, an intelligent view of their rights, duties, and responsibilities. No error could be thrust upon them did they themselves uphold the truth. No strange ritual could be instituted among them did they maintain the primitive simplicity of worship. No doubtful practices could be started in their midst did they cherish in their hearts and lives the wholesome precepts of Christ and his apostles. But here is the very pith of the difficulty. The vast crowd of church members do not independently investigate the evidences, principles, doctrines, and facts of our faith. Many, and these often the most amiable and beautiful in their lives, are led rather by a Christian instinct, than by an enlighted Christian intelligence. Could the ayernge members be well instructed, thoroughly grounded in the great leading truths of our common Christianity, so strong a breakwater would hereby oe formed that the waves of clerical aggression might beat against it in vain. But when church members CP,nnot give a reason for "the hope that is in them," even " the lame" can make them an easy prey. Yet the real strength of the pastor resides in the vigour of the people. Wherever the pastors have gained head against the people, wherever they have succeeded in centralising the power in their own hands to the silencing or weakening of the voice of the people, wherever they have o-rown through combination into the conviction and practice that they ;onstitute the church, at that point poison has touched the body,

In sharp contrast with this elevation of a class to the detriment of the whole, the unwearicd tenderness of apostles and ·apostolic men towards the individual members of churches rises before us. Throughout the Ne,, Testament there arc deEcriptions scattered here and there, which, could the reality underlying- them be n'acl:ed and fully brought, into view, would appear in many respects to the easy going ecclesiastics of the present day, novel and extraordinary. The very names and epithets, fresh gathered from the social, political, or, in one or two instance~, from the religious world around,. which the first pastors appropriated to themselve~, denote a depth and intensity of self-abnegation and de,otedness to the kingdom of Christ and to the meanest of his followers, that would startle and scandalise the common-place piety of the day. When the apostle took up the epithet oov'A.01:, slave-which is rather euphemistically rendered servant in our version-and applied it to bis relation, position, and service in the churches as well as in reference to Christ, we seem to forget that it was in those days, as in our o,rn, a word steeped in the dark dye of degradation, connected with all that is most despicable, low, and benighted in our race. The word inr 11pfr 11 ,, 11iinislP-r, is certainly a step above doulos, but still connected with <lrudgery, sel'l'ility, and the most menial offices, hardly ever rising-, except in princely and imperial households, to a degree of moderate respectability. It by no means blunts the edge of these epithets to say that in princely households servants reflected some beams of their master's dignity, and consequently Paul must have been invested before the eyes of others with highest honour as the minister of Christ. Alas ! Christ was then a prince unacknowledged, despised, unknown; the worid had executed him; and bis minister was accounted the offscouring of all things. Yet the apostle aud bis follow -workers took kindly, cheerily, loyally to the usage they received, and to the names that best of all del'cribed their services. Now here in their writings is there found a single hint, except in condemnation, of that arrogant ambition which soon afterwards sprouted forth, and bore such fatal fruit among the churches of the East and West. Even when they assume the titles bestowed upon them by the Lord, they wear them in a spirit 80 meek that they seem jealous lest a single.spark of pride should he ,isible in the exercise of their authority. As " Pastors," they take heed to feed I he flock; as " Overseers" or ''Bishops" they abstain from the very appearance of being lords over God's h;ri tage ; as "Am hassadors," they beseech; as "Fa_thers," they carry their spiritual children in their imns. How easil:y the thorough ecclesiastic could find in these epilhets, even in the mildest of them, a pretext for the most unbounded pretensions_. is seen by a single example. Chryrnstom is discoursing- with great fervour in his treatise De Sacerdotis, concerning love to Christ as the noblest of all passions that can animate the human breast, when in a moment he glances off with the proud prelatic words-after saying that he who has the oversight of souls must be like Saul among the Hebrews- " Not only must I seelc lttre for the measure of head and shoulders, but as great as the difference is between rational men and irral'ional animals, so

articles.title: Cleugy and Laity

CLEUGY AND LAITY.

_qreat let !ho diskmce be between the I'aslor and the people of his clmr_r;e, not fo say even greater." Bnt another m::gic word is needed, and the only equipment needed oy the 8hepherd is a sla[f; the clearest mark of a bishop is a mitre; the most conspicuom; fe.ather in the ambassador's character is his thirst for homage due exclusively to his master; and the infallible sign of the spiritual father is his strenuous endeavour to keep all the Christian world in a state of spiritual babyhood. Of these encroachments on the liberties of the people, the words clergy and laity, remai~ in our tongue to this day, as unmistakeable proofs. The;- are both den ved from a Greek source, cler_r;y from i:J... 11por: a lot or inheritance, and laity, from >..nor; the people. Throughout Christendom the ministers of religion •styled themselves the heritage of God-his peculiar treasure. With equal modesty and hardihood they termed all others laity, and in process of time, ingenious minds, finding that lcw.,-, people, was too respectable an origin for this word, they added insult to injury by inventing a new paternity for it in laas, a stone. Concerningthe influence of tl1ese words, we are not disposed to ~et on foot any new theory, like that of the philosopher, who attributed all the diseases, to which human flesh is heir, to the universal use of salt. Yet the trite observations that the world is ruled by names, and I suppose the Church too, receives a singular illustration in the history of the words in question, for the men who wielded them succeeded in turning the Church upside down. Even in our own day the spell and glamour of dergy and laity are not quite broken, but hold fragments of their :rncient mystic force over some who lay claim to an eminent share of the intelligence and religion of the community. At present the general question is one of most Tital importance to all sections of the church of Christ. Fo1· it is impossible to close the eyes to the strong tendency setting in in several quarters to isolate ministers of the gospel more and more from the people, and to invest them with at least some of the characteristics of a distinct class or caste. By such means it is easy to perceive important ends would be secured. The official might be trained into a better official, and 11 closer solidarity between individuals of the same profession might awaken and sui;tain a more enthusiastic esprit de corps, their interests might be more sedulously advanced and proter:tcd, and in some respects a more imposingarray might he presented, and a stronger influence might Le brought to bear upon the external phases of i;ociety. But these are not such unalloyed good things as to hinder one from looking their decidedly pernicious consequences straight in the face. For the ground cannot be widened between ministe1· and people without the people tr,king less interest in his work, and giving him less sympathy and help. Isolation from the people produces in the pastor ignorance of their mental nnd spiritual condition, their habits of thought and life, and takes out of hi~ hand one of the main keys wherewith the door is to Le opened for his appeals to their reason and conscience. The attitutle of separate classe,; to one another is ever that of rule or subjection-division destroyf; equality. But the relation of Christian to Chri~tian in church fellowship, and especially of the Christian minister to his people, is founded nn Lrotherhood, and everylh1ng that makes him less a brother renders him less fit to he a minister. Finally, it if; impossible to sever from such a

class the semblance and some of the traits of sacerdotalism. Their natural development is more of the priest, less of the pastor. Happily, our churches are well constituted to resist and repel all pretensions of this kind, should they ernr approach our borders. The church members are not helpless before the majesty of an Act of Parliament or a j udgrnent of the Privy Council : they have a sharp and effective remedy always at hand. So strong, so omnipotent, are they in their control over their own affairs that it almost seems that excess of jealousy regarding their individual rights makes them shy of combining to secure the common objects of the denomination. Were this extreme narrowness of spirit abandoned, and ministers and delegates entrusted by the churches with distinct powers, then the manifold empty and irresponsible discussions of Association and Union meetings might give place to grave and fruitful deliberations, which wonld tend to call forth to a greater extent, the latent resources of the churches for the practical advancement of the kingdom of Christ. While thus far concessions might be wisely made to the exigencies of the time, no one need unfasten his hold of these four truths which ever stand as immutable supports of the rights of the disciple and the liberties of the church :-First, that no vi"carious function is committed to the minister which is not equally allowed to the humblest disciple ; secondly, that no mystic secrets are entrusted to him which are not open to all the faithful; thirdly, that no superior sanctity belongs to him, which is not also attainable by ail; and, fourthly, that there is no divine favour exclusively shown to him which is not the portion of all those who truly seek God's face. DEMOS.

articles.text: S we stood looking upon the famous Laocoon at the Vatican, a A friend uttered the singular remark, "Look at that eloquent great toe." We did look, and confessed the eloquence of anguish which it indicated. The unhappy father, perishing with his two sons by the " blue venom " amid the crushing folds of the monstrous serpent, labours in his anguish to tear off the hideous coils, In his agony every member of his bodr participates ; ~ot alone is t~e countenance full of misery,-every Yem, nerve, and smew reyeal his death-pangs. The man's ::wony burns in every limb. PosEessed by other and hapJ?ier influences, our soul's paisson _should manifest itself in our entire bemg. We ought to be so filled with the love of God lhat the minor actions of our life should reveal its power. Preaching ;ith a yiew to God's glory and the salvation of sinners, our action should evidence our fenour; each several utterance should thrill with emotion. Or, if we be unable to ascend the platform, our prayers, our words, our walks, our recreations, should all be Yocal for Jesus. In our life-statuary there must be '' that eloquent great toe:" When the bush in Horeb was a-glow with Deity, each separate twig was a-Llaze with the m,·stic fire ; so should our whole being burn with zeal. Spirit, soul, bod)~-all should participate in the celestial ardour. ·would to God we were all thus! C. H. S.

42G OBEDIEXCE THE TRUE TEST OF LOVE TO CHRIST.

go into your closets and think of it yoursel'l"es. It is a solemn trnth: There is much in all Christians to render their love to Christ suspected. UL And wi:iat am I doing? Am I exciting undue fears in your souls? No, I am not; at least I would not, and for that reason I have distinguished between the being a~d gro7;Vth of love. And I _have wished that not only we might J..71ow we lo"<"e Clmst a little, but that we might know we love him so much that our little lo,-e was com_paratively strong-yea, tha~ we had full proof, without a doubt. that we loved hun beyond every other obJect in the world. Come let us hear his voice. Christ looks on you, ye timid souls, you, who durst not' die and start from the sound of death when it is uttered in your ears-Christ look~ to you, ye timorous creatures, who durst not draw near to a throne of grace and he pities your condition, and says to you, "If you would put your love t; me out of doubt, keep my commandments "-keeJJ my commandments. Do not ask if there is any other way; this is the King's high-road, the straightforward way-shall I take the liberty to say to-night the common-sense way, " If ye lo,e me keep my commandments"? I call it the King's high-road because in this way all who enjoy Christianity live; but let us hint at particulars. If you will put your love to Christ out of doubt, you must keep bis commandments universally: one cause of doubt, is that we keep them but partially. My brethren, in what light do you view yourselves when you look at Christ's commandments? Are you a sort of a gentleman, to whom Jesus Christ proposes his law as a matter of complimentary invitation, and you take the liberty to r~ject some of it, as if you had as much right to reject his invitations as he has to give them? But you should not do so, it is a wicked spirit that makes us pick CJu;st's commandments, keep this, and leave that, remember this, forget that. Some people will go to hear God's Word, but not to the ordinance of baptism ; some to that of baptism, not to the Lord's Supper; some to all these but give nothing to the poor, though they can afford it ; others to all of them we have mentioned, and yet not to the doctrine of humilitv -a command of Christ,_ when they have done all to say,'' We are unprofitable servants.'' Keep Christ's commandments universally, and then you will have proof of your lo,·e to him. I will tell you why we are all inclined to keep some of Christ's commands. We are all of us inclined to keep some of Christ's commandments by constitution. Now, if I only obey what suits my constitution and make, it proYes nothing, but if I keep all his commandments, and those that go against my constitution and habits, why then I give proof that I act, not upon selfish but on Christian principles, not upon my own ideas, but upon those of Jesus Christ. For instance, one person loves retirement, and to be alone, it is with him a constitutional turn. Jesus Christ commands Ch1;stians to be in their closets, to pray, and to search the Word; that man retires, reads and -prays, but must I say all this alone prov_e_s nothing? Tl~e.t same person is disposed to be mean and covetous :-but now, ~t that perso_n wln~e ol,serl'ing the other commandment, observes also those which go ~gamst Ins disposition, if be becomes bountiful, benevolent, open-he~rt~d, "a libernl man who denseth liberal thiug;;," I call that man a stro~gChnst111n, for he acts not upon his own ideas, but upon those of Jesus Cl!r!st; he_ th~reby_ pro~es that he has imbibed the "Ospel, and that the spmt of 1t lives 111 Ins soul. What right have I, wretch that I am, to pick and choose which of ChrisL's laws I will keep'? I dare not treat my friends ~o; I dare not treu,t my 1_111rent~ so; I dare not treat my master so; what nght have I to tr~at Clmst so. Am I not bound to obser"<"e all his commands, by the same ties that I am bound to observe one? And therefore Christ says, If you would put your love to me out of' doubt, keep my commandments universally. Secondly, if you would put your love to me out of doubt, keep my commandments constantly. Some keep Christ's commandments in t~e m~etrng-hous_e, and in good company. Ah I but ont of the meeting-house, with friends, und 111 other company, and alone too-whose men are yon then? Can you frorr~ your soul say, J am most sincerely Jesu~ Christ's. \\'hen I am alone I thmk of

h_im; my meditations of him are sweet. 1 pray to him, though it be but ~Jaculatmg, as J turn the corner of the street, as I am going about my business, e.s I am lying in my bed, when I am coucerned in the things of the world ; often in a day my soul a.spires to him, and by one word-but that one word keeps the way open between me and my only Friend-I say," Lord, be merciful to me. Lord, quicken me. Lord, lift up the light of thv countenance upon me. Lord, keep me from evil." Am I in the clouds while I speak thus? The Christian's heart will reply, No; you are in my -.;ery experience. \Vhy, then, you are men that are in the high-road to obtain, by a holy, universal life of love, a full testimouy that you love Christ sincerely. Brethren, I conclude. Lastly, if you would put your love to Jesus out of doubt, keep his commandments when you lose by keeping them. Do not let us keep Ch1ist's command only when we gain reputation by it, but let us keep his commandments in those articles in which we are sure to lose, I wiJl give you e.n instance or two. If you enter into the modern virtue of charity, and put your hand into your pocket, and give nobly to u cha.1itable plate, by that you will gain reputation ; all will applaud you (supposing all along that you are well able to do so); but if that he your rule of action, and you only serve Christ where you gain approbation from men, belie-.;e me your lorn to Christ will be accounted precarious and suspicious. Certain duties are out of fashion, and there are certain virtues that the bulk of men, even formal, decent Pharisees, agree to run down. Now, if you can go into the practice of these virtues, and agree with all your heart to give up as well as to acquire for Christ';; sake, undoubtedly you have the mtl.l"k of genuine Christianity, thnt love to Christ which rises out of an uttnchment to him, and leads you into conrses where your own interest could not possibly guide you. Let us depart-and let us bear upon our minds this word. \Ye are goingwhither? some of us to leisme, some of us to business ; some of us to prosper; some of ns to decay; some of us to health and prosperity, friendship, ,ioy, and long life ; others of us to poverty, sickness, long und wasting illuess uml puin; and in the end, death. And to us all does not the Prince of Peace say, ·• If ye love me, keep my commandments"? I know some of yon are going to affliction: "If you love me, be submissive to me aud patieut under your ailiictions." Others of you are going into prosperity and joy: '' If ye love me, do not be elated with these, they are but momentary and worldly things." Love me, your Lord and Redeemer, a.hove all. "If ye love me, keep my commandments." If ye love me, love me to the last moment, for even then I command you" to commit the keeping of your sonl to me in well-doing, as unto a faithful Creator." A.nd we ministers of Christ, shnll we not pay a special attention to this word of our Saviour? What obligations are we under to love him? What obligations are we under to adore him? and, being under theso obligations, he.ve not we in onr least infirmity, stronger arguments to doubt of our attachment to Christ than our fellow Christians? Lord, forbid it that our love to thee should be doubtful. Let our Jove to everything in the world be doubtful, but not this; let us love him, and love him so as to _keep his c?mmandments; so as_ to keep all his commandments, and those particularly which respect the leacluug and manifestation of his doctrine; those doctrines particularly which nre the most contemned, and the most out of fashion. Happy men! to whom Christ will at last say, "You are they who have followed me in the regenerntion, You have continued with me in my temptation, and now I appoint you ton kingdom," May God bless this subject to us all!

articles.text:
TALKATIVE. 'lITH~LE Pilgrim and Faithful were convers(ng upon the good things of the ft' kmgdom, a man whose name was Talkative suddenly accompanied them. " There was room enough for them all to walk." This is very suo-"'estive. It is seldom that the Christian is so entirely governed by faith th:'t°there is no room to profess more than he feels. He walks by faith, but faith does not always take up the whole road. Sometimes his path is so narrow that there is r~om_ for faith ~nly, at oth~r tim~s there is room for another to join them. As P1lgrrm and Faithful were m a wide path, and were conversino- 0 freely with each other, "Faithful, as he chanced to look on one side, saw a man whose name was Talkative, walking at a distance, beside them ; for in this place there was room enough for them all to walk. He was a tall man, and somethino- more comely at a distance than at hand." "Faithful as he chanced to look on o~e side saw a man whose name was Talkative." It is the province of faith to look either far backward ·upon Christ on the cross, 01· far forward upon Christ on the throne, but never to look on one side. It is this which makes room for Talkative. Faithful could talk well, but here was on_e that far surpassed him. He could talk fluently upou all subjects, sacred and profane. He was sound in doctrine, and could give a hundred texts in support of his opinions. " What a brave companion have we got!" whispered Faithful to Pilgrim. Ah! said Pilgrim with a smile, you do not know him. I know him well; he comes from our town, his name is Talkative, and he belongs to those who '' say and do not." He is a saint abroad and a devil at home. Well, "I am bound to believe you,'' said Faithful, "and I see that saying and doing are two things." Try him, said Pilgrim, put some heartsearching questions to him, and keep him to the point, and he will soon withdraw from you. The trial was made, and the result was as Pilgrim foretold. Think it not strange that a Christian should know more of Talkative than his faith, because, as it is here said, they come from the same town, but "faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen." It is by faith that the Christian tries the spirits whether they are of God. If Faithful were a fellow pilgrim who had gone from the same town he could not have been so entirely ignorant of Talkative. Faith may be ignorant of him, but there is no Christian to whom he is unknown. The character of Talkative is invariably regarded as independent of both Faithful and Christian. They are considered, in fact, as three separate persons. In our Yiew the whole three are contained in one. The name of Christian includes the other two; and in giving that name to his Pilgrim, Bunyan intended that all others should be included in that one. None of the others are comprehensive of an entire character, but are attributes only, and as such are here applied. Talkative, therefore, is not an entire character like !O that of Ch~istiun, but a part of Christian's own experience, and naturally resultmg from the imperfection of his faith. "I believe," said one of old, "and therefore speak." "We also believe,'' says an apostle, "and therefore speak." There are time~, however, in the experience of believers when they speak more tha? they behev~, when they should think more and talk less, when from mere habit they speak m word only, not in power. The profession of faith, on the whole,.comes better from the life than from the lips. Do preachers of the gospel behevc from the heart all they say? Do they never preach the faith of others instead of !heir own? Is their own faith in the whole sermon? Is there no room for Talkative to come between them? Is it not when their faith looks on one side that they see o. man whose name is Talkative close by them, and others see him too? Bunyan, no doubt, knew what it was to give utterance in the pulpit to more than he

really felt, ond after the most profitable conversation to fear that he had led ·others to s1;1pi;>ose that he was better than he really was. He needed not, ,and no Christion needs, to go far to find out who this Talkative is. The use which Bunyan would have us make of the interview with Talkative is admirable. '.' Let u~;• he _says, "ass_ure o_urselves t_hat at the ~ay of doom men shall be Judged accordmg to their fruits. It will not be said then, Did you believe? ~ut wer_e you ?oers, or. talkers ~nly? •· T_his ~hows that Bunyan's _aim, in the mstruction which he gives to his own faith, 1s to teach'' that faith without -works is dead."
