They were soon billeted around amon)': the c1t1zens, nnd the followm" 0 day a public meetin" was called in the church or town-hall, and a co~mitte~ api,ointed of leading citizens. The agent thc1: addressed the assembly, statmg the benevolent objects of the Society, and somtthing of the history of the children. The sight of their worn races ·was a mo,t pathetic enforcement of Lis arguments. People who were childless cam,· forward to adopt children; others, who had not intended to 1akc anv into their families, were induced to apply for them; and many who really 'wanted tl:c, children's labour pressed forward to obtain it."

Very effective in producing the best results was the system of firs~ educating and then removing .agrant children into spheres where their labour was valuable. It is said that the agency might eYen be extended until it superseded all the orphanages iu New York, for eligible situations can readilv be found for five thousand children annuallr. The demand for strong active boys is virtually unlimited, thougli in the 1irst instance the farmers were not entirely free from misgivings. One asked, " ' ·won't the boys run away ? ' ' Did you ever see a cow run away from a hay-stack ? ' was Mr. Tracy's rejoinder. 'Treat him \\'el: and he'll be sure to stav.' And the bland and benevolent mmmcr in which he would reply to an irritated employer, who came bad;: to report that the 'New York boy' had knocked over the milk-pail, and. pelted the best cow, ond let the cattle in the corn, and left titc yonngturkeys in the rain, &c., &c., was delightful to behold. ' l\Iy dear friend, can you expect boys to be perfect at once ? Diu'nt yon ever, pelt the cattle when yon were a boy :''" In the course of all these endeavours among the roughs of New York the experiment wns tried of providing free news-rooms for the working-classes-rooms where light refreshments could be hod, but no intoxiconts. This did not at once succeed; for though comfortable well-supplied apartments were seeured, the institution had to be regarded as n failure, nnd was therefore closed. Subsequently, the scheme was revived, and the superintendence was intrusted to a man who had been o celebrated prize-fighter and notorious profligate. It may not often be well for such characters to fill places of publicity nnd trnst; but this man's converson was so sincere that his may be spoken of as an exceptional case. Under his core the free news rooms were blessed with much success, and hundreds of perBons of the classes intended to be benefited, found good by corn iug into contact witli the converted pugilist. Eventually. the superintendent was compelled by circumstances to relinquish his situation, and the rooms were closed, though others of a similar character were opened in different parts of the city. Another important branch of work undertaken consisted in offering help and encouragement to such friendless and homeless girls as Imel not wilfully strayed from virtue, and were under eighteen years of age.

.\ kind of lodging-house was opened, the accommodation of -which the inmates 1:1aid for, or _received gratuitously according to their condition. The sub1ects especially sought were the unfortunate and destitute rather than the vicious, though some who were actually fallen found their way into the institution. . "The plan seemed at once to reach its objects: the doors opened on a forlorn procession of unfortunates. Girls broke out of houses of vice where they had been entrapped, leaving eYery article of dress, except what they wore, behind t_hem; the police brought wretched young wanderers, who had slept on the station floors; the daughters of decent country people, who had come to the town for amusement or employment, and, losing or wasting their means, had walked the_ streets all the night long-, applied for shelter; orphans, selling flowc_rs, or pedlm~ ~bout the theatres;_ the children of drunkards; the unhappy daug:l1tcrs of fan~1hes where quarrelh?g and abuse _were the rule; girls who ~a~ run away ; ;;Iris who ~ad been driven away; girls who sought ii respite in mterrnls of nc<',-nll this most unfortunate thron" began to beset the doors of the Girls' Lodging House." " Having reached the classes intended to be benefited, and in re"ard to admission, having drawn the line where prudence dictated, another grateful harvest of good results was reaped. The gospel knowledge imparted was supplemented by instructions in housewifery and other useful arts. Then, as they became competent, or as situations opened for their reception, these girls, in many instances picked up from the streets, were mnde comparatively happy for life, and became a blessing instead of a curse to their generation. Occasionally some real romance enters into the history of these young creatures ; for an old scholar has reappeared as a lady staying with her husband at a leading hotel ; and naturally she would call at the institution and tell her exr,erience since leaving the friends by whom she was first put in the way of prosperity. In ten years many thousands of girls passed through the lodginghouse, not a few of whom must have been benefited. "Among this number there are many cosily sitting by their own heart~-.stones; others are filling positions of usefulness and trust in families and stores ; some have been adopted in distant towns, where they fill a daughter's place; and some have gone to return no more. A large number we cannot trace. During this period, 1.hree thousand one hundred and one have found employment and gone to situations, or returned to friends. Fifteen thousand four hundred and twenty-nine garments have been cut and made, and distributed among the poor, 01· used as outfits in sending companies west." Some worthy success was also achieved in a quarter of t~e city _where the youthful population were except;onally bad, the boys m part1~ular, becoming a terror to peace-loving people, and known to the poh?e as street-rats. Notorious robberies, and even murders, were comrr:11tted hy characters known as "the nineteenth street gang." In_ this department the work of the evangelist was uphill indeed, 11:nd m1~h_t _have been relinquishe<l in despair, on account of the apparent 1mposs1b1hty of producing any good impressions. Yet fo!th aud persev:eranc~ w_ere rewarned, when boys, who seemed incorrigible up to the time of ~omg W esrward, were led to see the error of their ways, to repent and to reform.

which threaten large empires, when the vicious and ignorant are allowed to multiply and to attract whatever is impure and criminal, the Americans are as ready as ourselves to support any agency which Christian philanthropists may propose for lessening sin and misery. It is well it is so; for in the United States there are five millions of persons over ten years of age who are unable to write, and of this demoralized and demoralizingcrowd New York has an undue proportion. "The demagogues of this city would never have won their amazing power but for those sixt_\· thousand persons who never read or write," says l\I r. Brace; " I:-, is this class and their associates who made these politicians what. they are." Americans who are working heartily in that noblest of callings-the carrying of the gospel to the very poor, are setting- an example which we, on this side of the Atlantic are glad to hear about, and by which we hope to profit. Such a record as the one written by Mr. Brace, as well as the Reports issued by our own Raggcd-school,Union should teach the kind-hearted among us in what true charity consists. Such reports loudly condemn street almsgiving. Experience has shown that charity may commit mistakes. While hoping that she is relieving the necessitous she may really only be encouraging the idle and vicious. Indiscriminate almsgiving becomes a national moral curse, for it overlooks the poor, who will not parade their poverty, and it encourages the unprincipled, who by cunning and deception gain liberal incomes, and too often live comparatively luxurious lives. Let us be discreet even in our philanthropy. We work in vain if we do not foster self-respect and independence in the poor, by teaching them to help themselves in the true spirit of Christianity.

A WELSH SASSIWK. 4GJ mcnt to hold a large solemn reli11ious meetincr. " One denomination uf English. Dissen~e~s" writes a loeal journat with a touch of quiet humour, "111 a spmt of emulation of Welsh zeal and enthusiasm hold their love-feasts. But the love-feast was as an exotic amon; cool English minds, and has never claimed national importance.?' Several reasons conspir_e to render sueh gatherings in England somewhat unpop~la~· ;• and 1f we have been spoiled by the facilities v.-hich our large bu-ildmgs afford, we have few or those attractions of scenery, association, and passionate love of lan"uage 0 which so powerfully affect our We~sh lleighbours. Whether that decadence of the language, the suggest10n of which arouses passionate indignation on their part, which is going on, will greatly affect the disposition to hold Lhese peculiarly Welsh meetings cannot be determined; but the Cahinistie Methodists, with other bodies, are still Yery tenacious of their timehonoured practice. If, then, they were \l'Ont to take long pilgrimages to the place of meeting, which they reached weary and footsorn, the convenience of railway locornot.ion will rather aid than retard their populari~y. Anyhow, the concourse this year was noble and imposing. "'l'he 01·!.lerliness of the great crowds," says an independent ,Yitness, "was striking, and when it is considered that the principal element in these crowds is that of the commonality, composed of labouring person& from the quarrying aud agricultural districts, the absence of unseemly conduct, and the uecorum observed do infinite credit to Wales, and speak highly of the religious tone whieh pervades the countr}' and ,vhich goes so far to purify the moral 11tmosphere, and to present light criminal calendars and empty Welsh prisons." This enlogium is not in any way exaggerated, as anyone will believe who has obsened with grntilication the almost general religious observance of the Sabbath-day in the country from which we are this month writing. And as tht' Calvinistic Methodists have had !L considerable share in producing this grand result, and ha,e a history ]Jregnant with lessous, we purpose devoting a couple of chapters to their work. The Association meeting at Carnarvon was confined to the North Wales branch of this denomin1ttion. It was in the northem portion of the Principality, as we shall see further on, that the :Methodist revival had wonderful success. The general conference of ministers and deacons deals with matters of detail in the working of the synod and the churches composing the same. The ministers' fund for granting proper assistance, to aged and disabled preuchcrs and the widows and orphun children of ministers' received a promise from one gentleman of £2000 on condition that £8000 were collected in the next four years ; and although it will be a struggle to raise the required amount, the feeling in the connexion is very decided. Welshmen have goou grounds upon which to plead their poverty, but perhaps the rule ot' systematic giving requires a much more he11rty and general acceptance in their churches. It was stated by one layman that it was only now that some churches were beginning to understand the principle of maintaining the ministry, aud hitherto justice had not been clone to their ministers, and that was a blot upon the connexion. The Welsh Calvinistic Methodists share too much in the failing of some of our Baptist churches-strangely inverting the divine order, and practically

holding that it is more blessed to receive from the ministry than to rrivc to the ministry that which is its due. It was the conviction of a Y a1~kec wit that "what the world wanted was less talk and more do :" more of the silence which is golden might bring into the treasury of the Lord more of the money of the same value. It was stated that the funds of the ho:m~ mission were very low, although the great work of forming new m1ss10n churches on the border demanded liberal aid. Mr. Charles, of Bala. "The eyes of the Lord arc upon the righteous, an,l his ears arc open unto their cn·."- PsALM xxxiv. 15. • UCH th_a.t is beautiful in poetry is not tnie. Things arc often conceived as M they might be, and under poetic inspiration men have been tempted intt> writing their conceptions as though they really existed in fact. Have you not been charmed into admiration of the poet's genius as you read, spell bound, the easy flowing verse? And, anon, has not your admiration cooled into disappointment as the question struggled for utterance, "But is it true?" A proposition is not true because it wears the beautiful ga.rh of poetry. Were the poetry of some of the greatest poets narrowed down to the limits of sober truth, thP ponderous volumes on our shelvea would assume different dimensions; and what we had thought, or fondly hoped, to be golden ore, would p,roveworthles~ as clay, or, at best, but glittei'ing tinsel. It is to be lamented that trnth is too often trimmed to suit a rippling rhythm, and that enor is adorned with truthlike beauty to complete a stanza. Now, this may apply to human poetry, but to divine, never. You may search the Bible through and through for its poetry, and though ea.eh page eclipses in its beauty and grandeur the loftiest reaches of the most gifted poet, yon will never find the shadow of an error distorted into a seeming trnth, nor truth exaggerated into undue proportion. The drnpery in which inspired writers presented truth does not constitute the chief charm of divine song. Holy men of old, under the spell of inspiration, saw divine tmths in the halo of divin,· light, and in their true proportions; hence, the sublimest language in which their souls struggled for expression proved au imperfect instrument, nnd, flt best, but inadequately set forth what they SllW and felt. It is thus with the verse of poetry which furnishes our theme for meditation : "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears are open unto their cry." Here we have a profound truth set in un exquisite gem of poetry: not henuty nt the expense of truth, hut benuty and tmth combined hy the jewelled clasp of poetry. Ha.cl not a divinely-inspired penman recorded such a truth by such rnPtuphors. we should have shrank from the t1tsk ourselves ns, flt least, ver.v de.ring; bnt since it came by n divine inbreuthing, we grutefully receive the truth, nn1l admire tho wisdom which pla.nned the mode of its admission. That Goel, being n Spirit, has an eye or un ea.r correspondent with those organs, us possessed by man, we do not for n. moment contend; but the figures enable us to ren.lise those truths which an unslumhering, cver-w11tchful eyP. nod un ever-open, listening enr suggest. If God's eye is ever-wakeful, tre.ckingour every step, watching our every net, and searching the inmost recesses of 0111· hoa.rts, rending all our motives; if his enr is ever turned to earth, cn.trhing om· every word, 1111d listening even to the thoughts of our henrts ns th<'y throh. instinct with life, then his knowledge of us is intimnte. his interest in us unfailing, his anxiety for us intense, his love perfect, nnd his provision for 0111· wauts will be adequate. Oh, let ns rejoice nud be glnd that" The eyes of tlw Lord arn upon the righteous, nnd his enrs nre ope1;1 unto their c1_-y ;" nnd thnr " This God is our God for ever 11nd ever. He will he our gmde ev<:'n untn death." It encournges and consoles us to know that,- " There is nn eyo that never sleeps Bonen.th tho wing of night: There is Rn el\r which never shuts \\'hen sink tho beams of light." " The ricrhteous "-not those who claim crcntme perfection, an inl,crcn t righteous~ess, for in this sense" there is none righteous;" but those who hy

sight and sound are among the most wonderful with which God has endowed us, a!1d_wl_1at we see ~nd hear we may be_ said_to know .. It is impossible for the eye, d1sc1plmed to seemg, and the ear to hstenmg, to fo.11 of receiving and communicating knowledge to the mind. It is the man ,vhose eye the light touches, but fails to penetrate; whose ear the wa'l"e of sound strikes, but fails to impress, who is destitute of knowledge. He may touch, and taste, and smell, but oh! how little does he know, can he know, while those a,·enues of the soul, the eye and the ear, are closed! But human knowledge has its limitations. No man can observe everything, nor hear all the records of knowledge, though he spend the lifetime of a ::\Iethnselah as an attentive obserTer and a patient listener. Yea, the more a man sees and hears, the more is he impressed with a sense of the vastness of that unexplored region beyond which eye bath not seen nor ear heard. It is true the prophet exclaims, "Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased," a declaration which accurately describes the restless striving after knowledge of the present day; but when men have grnwn blind and deaf with age, wheu the pen is still because the hand which held it is paralysed in death, when all the libraries of the world are brought to completion, as tired thought folds the wing e.nd owns her goal is reached, the sages of a thousand generations shall own in chorus, what they severally held to be true: "Now WE K:S-O\V ONLY IS PART." But, to God's knowledge we can affix no such limit. Nothing escapes his notice. He tracks the path of the rolling planet, the burning comet, and the flashing meteor. He sees the eagle as he cleaves the sky, the insect as it floats in the beams of the summer sun, the fish as it steers through the trackless deep, and the beast as he prowls through the pathless wood; he trucks the ways and wanderings of his creature in every part of the world, e.nd observes the workings of nature's secret and mysterious laws; yea, all that happens, from his throne in the centre, to the utmost limits of the universe is seen by God, and comes within the range of bis knowledge. Oh! believer in Jesus, if this be true in the comprehensive sense, how true must it be in all that concerns ~-ou, seeing that the text narrows down the sphere of observation-" The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry." Nothing, my brother, affects your character- nothing comes within the range of your experience-nothing enters within the circle of your half-defined desires even, which evades the knowledge, or escapes the notice of '' your Father who is in heaven." "The Lord is a God of knowledge." That dark doud which overhung your sky, refusing a passage through its sable folds of one recreant beam from moon or star, and which seemed to shut you up to n ~loomy individuality while you felt alone in the world; yes, that dark cloud did not intercept the vision of JehovRh, nor prevent your faintest utterRnce from reaching bis ears. He knows the sorrows of your Jot, the difficulties of your path, and the struggles of your heart. He knows that questionable transaction in which you engag-ed, und that secret sin in which you indulged. He knows, what men can never k11ow, the thoughts of the heart and the motives which inspire your conduct. Yon may be misunderstood, maligned, persecuted, but God's judgment iti just; for, "men judgeth from outward appenrance, but God looketh at the heart." Let this truth impress our hearts and influence our lives. It som1<ls a warning note to all who are not walking in fellowship with God, and whispers heavenly peace to those who do his will. II. The fa.et that " the eyes of the Lord a.re upon the righteous, and his ears are ope.n unto their cry," proclaims the unceasing interest which the LorJ ever feels in ~he w_ay and welfare of his people. Have you not felt, my brother, as the psalmist did, when e. sense of loneliness overcame him, and he uttered that bitter we.ii, '' No man ce.reth for my soul"? Oh, let me tell you, God cares, and your individual wants press e.s really upon him as though vou were the only living being in the universe. Do not plead your poverty, your insignificance, your worthlessness even: tell me, are you "righteous"? Then the heart of Jehovah beats with an undying interest in your present and eternal welfare. You can say with the psalmist," I am poor and needy, yet the Lord thinketh upon me." Another and a deeper truth is present in our text-God is anxious for bis people. Anxiety is somethinp; more th11n knowledge or interest. A crowd may be interested in the search for a lost child, but only one heart knows a mother's anxiety. The Lord is anxious for us. His knowledge ripens into interest, and his intei-est issues in anxiety; not o.n anxiety which distresses the heart, but which gets while it gives happiness. The record of God"s dee.lings with his people, in all ages of the world, is the record of a Fathei>s auxiety. l) Christian ! while you are anxious for your own welfare, anxious for the issue of your thorny path, there is one heart which is anxious for you, Call yourself an orphan no more (John xiv.); never cherish the thought that you are a.lone in the world, 11nd must fight single-handed the battle of life. While it is true "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears 11re open unto their cry,'' it must be tnre that the Lord is o.nxious about you. Anxious when yon are rich, lest upon the mountain top of prosperity you should forget yom dependence upon him, and assert your self-sufficiency. Anxious when the chilling wind of poverty strips you of your comforts, and leaves you friendless in the gloomy vttle, lest you should lose your hope and sink into despair. Anxious when in health, lest the pleasures of the present world should absorb your affections and we11n you from the better home above. Anxious when in sickness, lest you should faint under the affliction and forget to utter tho language of submission: "Father, not my will but thiue be done." Anxious when the hour of trittl comes upon you, and your feet 11re well nigh gone, lest yon should stumble and foll. YEs, ANXIOUS EVRR ! If God is anxious for us, we should be anxious for one nnother. There is too much of self in our religion. The gospel binds us together in the bond of a holy brotherhood, and bids us bear one unother's burdens. IV. Another truth which meets us in the t11xt is. Goifs love is ul upon his people. He would never acquaint himself with us, interest himself in us, 11nll maintain a constant anxiety for us, did he not love us with 11n unbounded love. If we ask the secret of that eye which w11tches us uncensingly in our going out and our coming in, in our rising up 11nd our lying down ; if we ask the secret of that ear which listens to our every cry, the answer must be'' 1.on:." "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry,'' is only LOVE spelled out l11rge. proved deaf to earth's discord while it listened to the music of the skies long long ago, had not his love been set upon us. It must have been a touching sigh~ to w~tness the ~gP-d father. of the parable pacing the roof day by day, hi 8 eye scanning the horizon, and his ear bent, to catch the earliest glimpse and to he~r_the first footfall of the returni,!g prodigal; and the secret of that paternal sohc1tude was love. He loved Ins boy, though he had grievously wrouged him, and had well nigh broken his heart with grief. This is but a faint picture of the love of God. Oh, how iutently does he watch us as we tread life's path-way; how e.uxiously does he listen to every breathing of the soul after him! This love is from eve,·la.~ting. Ere mau, the crowning work of creation· came forth from his Maker's hands, ere sin had sullied this fair world the iove of God was set upon the objects of his choice. You cannot point to' a moment, through all the ages of a past eternity, and say then love began. "I have lo,·ed thee with an everlasting love" forecloses our task, and bids us wonder and adore. -~nd this l?ve ~hall_ never cease. For when countless cycles of ages have run their round, it will still be true, "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righleous and his ears are open unto their cry." Yea, as this love inspires a counsei which shall never cease, commands a wisdom which shall never fail, wields a power which never can be overcome, it shall assimilate all its o~jects to itself, and find its satisfaction in their everlasting bliss. While the redeemed will gaze adoringly on the glories of their Lord, and chant, in ceaseless strains, his loftiest pnise, he himself shall see in the white-robed group, ·and hear in their thrilling hallelujahs "the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied." • Nor does this apply only to the living. And when the universal church is redeemed and gathered home, oh! !1ow true will be our text then! "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open unto their cry!" When the road is rough e.nd thorny, and the pilgrim's feet begin to tire, his pe.ce shall be quickened with the gracious promise, "As thy day is, so she.II thy strength be." When the day of prosperity issues in the night of affliction, with not a single star to shed its benignant smile through the murky gloom, fear shall be banished and hope inspired by the sweet assure.nee," Fear not, for I am with thee.'' And when Death comes, as ~ome he may, and friends bid you a sad farewell this side the ve.lley whose shadows gather blackness, and leave you to meet its gloom alone, the Shephercl shall meet you there; and as you feel the clasp of his loving hand, the joyons strains of the psalmist shall tremble from your lips, and make the valley ring with the echo of yonr song, "Yea, though I walk through the valley or the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art witu me; tr,y rod and thy staff they comfort me." But what of the sinner? "The eyes of the Lord a.re in every place beholding the \)vil and the good." Oh, sinner, it is no consolation to yon to tell you the.t the eye of the Lord is upon you. But, it iA trne, you c1rnnot escape it. Yon may choose the dead of night to commit your sin, you may boast that you are undetected in your crime, but that eye! Ah! yon cannot e$ce.pe it. articles.text: HOPEFUL. No sooner has Pilgrim witnessed the translation of Faithful to heaven than Hopeful becomes his co~pa~ion. As Faithful was the Pilgrim's own faith, so we take Hopeful to be the P1lgr1m's own hope. Hopeful was true hope as Faithful was true faith. "Why," it may be asked, "should a Christian's faith be removed to heaven,_an_d hope remain, since of hope we read that' it is laid up in heaven;' and that 1t 1s ' an anchor of the soul, both sure and steadfast, and which entereth into tbatwitbin the veil'"? The reason is obvious. Hope is the fruit of faith, and as Bunyan here says," rises out of its ashes," and cannot therefore precede it. Both are fixed above, as it is said, "that your faith and hope might be in God," but, as a matter of experience, it is faith in Christ in heaven that gives us hope in him in our pilgrimage on the earth. All true faith centres, first, in thP death of Christ for salvation, and then in his intercession for preservation. Salvation comes by the one; salvation to the uttermost comes by the other. There is a period in the history of every true Christian, in which his faith is transferred from the Lamb that was slain on earth to the slain Lamb in the midst of the throAe. It is then that bis faith goes before him into heaven, and the hope that springs from that faith accompanies and animates him to the end of his pilg-rimage. his hy faith that we are risen together with Christ, and are seated with him in heavenly places. Hope does not give this representative privilege, but is founded upon it. Hope, therefore, is strong on earth, in proportion as faith takes firm hold on Christ in heaven. We "are saved by hope." Hope is our salvation from all the temptations and dangers that beset our path. It accompanied Pilgrim every step of bis future cour~e. It followed him reluctantly into By-path meadow, and was the first to sound a retreat. It w11s imprisoned with l,im in Doubting Castle, and preserved him from the selfdestruction to which he was nearly driven by Giant Despair. It kept him from sink in" in the separatin" flood. This is all in full accordance with Sc1·iptu1·e teachi~"- "If we hold° fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto th~ Pnd." "\Ve desire that ever) one of you do show the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end.'' "Be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ."

Other characters are soon afterwards introduced, ~~ Mr. Hold-the-world, Mr. Money-love, Mr. Save-all, and Mr. Gripe-man. I hen we ha.ve Demas whose great grandfather was Geha.zi, and his father Judas. Now are _all .t~ese separate ?haracters? Are they to be literally interpreted, as so mnny rnd1v1dual_ persons r Is Demas, for instance, or his father Judas, or his g_randfather Gehaz1, or all thr~e together, to be taken in a literal, or in a figurative sense!' h the town of Fair-speech, or the market town of Love-gain, or the county of Coveting, to be literally interpreted? If the men are real persons why_ ~h~uld not the towns in which they live be real places? Or are they (which 1s much the same thing), figurative descriptions of so many different PElrsons and places? How strange that they should have been regarded as different persons professing to be pilgrims, but a.II agreei1;1g to make the best of this world as well as of that which is to come. View them as different forms of the one sin of worldly-mindedness to which even the best of men are liable, and all becomes forcible and clear. As the effect of the enmity of the. world upon Christian experience was exhibited in Vanity Fair so the effect of the friendship of the world is represented here. The several characters introduced afforded an admirable opportunity of bringing out all the subtle pleas and considerations that a.re usually adduced to justify worldly conformity in those who profess not to be of this world and to have their only treasure in heaven. After a deep experience in persecution or affiiction of the vanity of the world, during which faith has been fixed entirely upon heavenly things, and hope hR.S been selected as the only guide, there must be no half-heartedness in the things of God, no more conferring with flesh and blood, no more men-pleasing, no more regard to wor<lly ell8e and pleasures. Temptations to these indulgences may retarn, and many specious considerations on the ground of prudence e.nd even of religion itself mny be pleaded in their favour, but they must be firmly with- ~tood even unto death. This is the.t pa.rt or Uhristian experience which is here fully portrayed ; and mu.y he referred to that period of Bunyan's own experience wben, after being released from prison, he became exceedingly popular on account of his preaching, and writings, and his s1:1fferings for conscience sake ; and opportunities for promoting bis worl<lly interest8 were placed within his rench, such as he had not known before. It was then that he overtook Mr. By-ends nnd hnd n long conversation with him and bis numerous companions. The questions which Mr. Hold-the-world put to Mr. Money-love, and to Pilgrim himself, are precisely those which, at this time, must o~en have been sugl?ested and solved in Bunyan's own experience. The suhject is doubtless considerably expanded for the benefit of others, and especially of Christian ministers, who, by yielding to such temptations, have lost much usefulness on earth and much glory in hea.ven.

behnlf, but none knew but himself the dreadful alternations of hope and fear in his own brei.st. The merchant, whose whole fortune is risked in a sinrrle undertaking, is tortured with continual interchanges of confidence and desp~ir. "X ow they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.'' Think of the object which the Chri~tian pilgrim has in view, and the awful alternative of missing the prize, and the reasons of his deep and minrrled emotions must be obvious to all. They are changes of feelings, or experie~ice, strictly so called ; and not of moral principles, or of doctrinal views. In proportion to his desire to seize the prize, will be his eagernei.s in its pursuit~ and in proportion to his strivmg, will he the agonizing intermission of hope and fear. It is the magnitude of the object which he has in view that demands rnch anxieties and cares. These are the deep things of God, and are known to those only who are of Goel. The majestic 1·iver, with its foaruinu0 cataract, and its resistless flow, now silently reflecting in its deep bosom tbe glories of the peaceful heavens, and now breaking the silencP. with the voice of many waters, as the voice of a great thunder, is not to be judged by the murmuring rill. "The world knoweth us not, because it knew him not."-Him, who, "for the joy that was set before him, endured th.i cross and despised the shame." ,ve have now to behold Bunyan's Pilgrim under the cruel anrl crushin..,. 0 influence of Giant Despair. This is preceded by the pleasantest part of his past pilgrimage. He has walked and slept. in company with Hopeful, by the banks of a river surrounded by green trees, with all manner of fruits, and for several days and nights. The way then becomes rough. In By-path Meadow, a smooth path seems to lay parallel with the rough road before them. Here they pause, and by the advice of Pilgrim, they enter upon it. They have not gone far, before they meet with Vain-Confidence, who falls into a deep pit and is dashed to pieces, just before them. Who was this Vain-Confidence? It was Pilgrim's own vain confidence, without doubt, which had led him astray. He had "asked him whither that way led?" He said," To the Celestial Gate.'' "Look," said Christian, "did I not tell you so ? By this you may see we are right." Now that Vain-Confidence is dashed to pieces, and Hopeful says, " Where are we now?" Pilgrim is silent, as mistrusting that he had led hi1u out of the way. He had been guided by vain confidence rather than by hope. Night suddenly comes on, and amidst rain, anrl thunder, and lightning, Pilgrim and Hopeful endeavour to retrace their steps. At length they fall to sleep from very weariness, and in this state are discovered in the morning by Giant Despair, on whose grounds they had trespassed, and are taken by him into Doubting Cas~le. Here they are put into a dark and filthy dungeon, from Wednesday mornmg till Saturday night, without food and without anyone to visit them. The next morning, by the advice of his wife Diffidence, Giant Des~air goes ii:ito the dunrreon and with a cudgel beats them unmerc1fully. 'lhe next mght he reco~m;nds them to put an encl to their own existence, as the best way of putting an end to their miseries; from w_hich Pilg1:im i~ prnven1ecl b~ the intluence of Hopeful. The Giant, soon after _retururng, ls enrng_ed to lrnd they have not taken his advice. The next morning he takes them rnto the cnstleyard to see the bones and skulls of many ~ho L~d there died, and the1!_ lea_ds them back to their dungeon. The next night, after they had prayed, 11lgnm recollects that Le had a key in his bosom, called Promise, ~hat woulcl open any lock in Doubt.ing-Castle. "Tlum," saicl I-Iop,~ful. ''. that _is good news, good Lrother; pluck it out of thy bosom and try. With th•~ he soon opens the <lun7eon door, and the door of the castle-yard, and the iron gate; and they run back to the stile in By-path Mea<low, ,md are glad to fiucl themselves, once more, in the King's highway. It is adn,itted by all interpreters that Giant Despair and hi~ wife Diffidence are not characters Hpart from Pilgrim's own experience. They woul?, doubtle~s, ha\'e given then:i a separate existence if _they _coulc.l._ '~heir ~hcor_y demanded it of them and nothinrr but the absurdity of carryrng 1t out Ill t.l11s iu~tance prel'ented them. Dr. Cheever says: "The personilicution of Despuir

thm.k, b~ "perfec_t story or allegory," in itself considered. A perfect story may ?e mcluded m the allegory, but the allegory itself is not the story. We ta~~ 1t to -be ~ perfect a_llegory, or! in other words, an allegorical representation o_t hteral real)t1e~. It 1s not fict10n, properly so called. Fiction is a c\escrip- ~10n o~ what Is hter~lly false, allegory of what is literally true. The allegory itself 1s not to be literally taken, and yet this, we humhly conceive, has been repeatedly done in the interpretution of this book. The confusion to which it l,eads is evident in the instance before u8. Hopeful is a real person, Giant Despair is not. Why the one and not the other? If Giant Despair be the personification of Despair, why should not Hopeful be the personification of hope? Why should despair and hope, the two conflictinu 0 principles in the mind of Pilgrim, be so differently portrayed that one should be his own experience, and the other the experience of some other person, the one within him, the other without, the one his own despair, the other another's hope? Carry out your literal theory to the full, we say, if that be your rule of interpretation. Let a "perfect allegory " be the rule, and no inconsistency occurs. Christian is the only person on this occasion ; and his is the only name that could not be a mere personification. By-path Meadow, Vain- Cunfidence, Giant Despair, the wife Diffidence, Hopeful, Doubting-Castle, the foul Dungeon, are all contained in the one individual experienl'e. The influence of Hopeful is evidently the part which his hope would take, when tempted first to vain confidence, nnd then to despair; and without which he certainly has no hope of his own. Hopeful wns more inclined than Pilgrim to turn aside to view the silver mine at the invitation of Demas, while Pilgrim was more inclined than Hopeful to choose the path in By-path meadow. Tl,e one was in sight, and the other not. Hope that is seen is not hope. Hopeful was no grent scholar, but was scholar enough to read the inscription upon a pillar by the road side, "Remember Lot's wile,'' because thnt spoke eloquently of the necessity of fleeing for refuge to the hope set before us. Hopeful was silent during the days and nights they were lying down in green pastures and beside the still waters; because, "if a man hope for that which he sees not, then doth he patiently wait for it." Of By-path meadow, Hopeful says to Pil"rim, " I was afraid of it at the very first, and therefo1·e gave you that gentle caution. I would have spoken plainer, but that yon are older than I." Of course, every man is older than his own hope, but not necessarily older than the hope of another. Hopeful takes the lend back, as Pilgrim hue\ done when t.hey went astray. Hopeful is Pilgrim's only companion in Doubting Castle, prevents him from destroying himself, and encourages him to hope against hope, so that he wn~ literally snved by I-lope. 'When the key of promise Wll8 discovered in Pilgrim's bosom, Hopeful recognised it at once as the wny of delivernnce ; for hope gives the key of promise its aduptution nnd power. 'l'hus Hopeful takes the very part which every Christian's hope would take in similar circum~tances, and is therefore his own hope, and needs not be that of another.

articles.text: OMEN are out of place when they usurp the position of men. The gentle tenderness of the female nature is a choice je11el, and anything which impairs its radiance is a loss and not a gain. We have seen female evangelists who evidently ought to have been men, and we have been impressed b~· them, but not with admiration. Their rnnnners have made us thankful that we were not yoked with them in wedlock, nnd their mode of conversation has made us feel that, whoever might be saved by their ministry, one woman at least was spoiled by it. On the other hand. it hns been our felicity to know some of the loYeliest, most earnest, and most practical of female workers, and to feel that, take them for all in all, in their own spheres, no men could rintl them. Working- for J csns, guietly and unostentatiously, with determination and self-denial, such sisters in Christ are queenly in their modesty, and all the more powerful because they court retirement. That zeal which wonld brazen the face of modesty, can very well be dispensed with ; but the loving fo!'l'Olll' which can calmly pursue its own suitable path of usefulness, the church cnn by no means dispense with. We have been greatly struck with the omnipotence of wonrnn·~ influence when sanctified b_y grnce, while reading- the life of Sarah Martin, the prison visitor of Great Yarmouth. It has been a means of o-race to us to peruse it. There are no thrilling incidents, or sensationat'situations, or amusing anecdotes; the story glides softly along, and never startles the reader; but HOLINESS TO THE LORD is written upon each page and a sacred influence pours forth from every line. We feel sure th~t we are doinl! the Tract Society and our readers a service by giving a short resume of the story, very much of which "ill consist of extracts from the memoir itself. ~arah Martin was the child of a small tradesman in the village of Ca1stor, near Yarmouth. She was born in 1791. Her parents dying, she c~me under the c:1re of a godly grandmother, whose holy example exercised a powerful mfluence over her. She commenced life on her own account as a dressmaker, and, to her serious injury, became a prey to the pernicious habit of novel-reading, and to religious doubts, most of_ ,~hich were ~uggested by a deistical old man resident in the village. Drvme grace did not leave her to her own devices, but at the age of nineteen she was convinced of sin, and led to put her trust in the Saviour. Her own words will best describe her deep emotion while her first love was burning towards her Redeemer with abounding ardour : '' Having obtained peace, I looked upward, with adoring wonder and grateful astonishment, to my precious God and Redeemer, and at his mighty power, which had actually cast down and overthrown all my deeply-rooted and bitter prejudices, had beaten down all the tyranny of Satan, and had made me alive from the dead. And now, in the glorious liberty wherewith Christ had made me free, I wished to give proof of my love, and desired the Lord to open privileges to me of serving my fellow-creatures, that happily I might, with the Bible in my hand, point others to those fountains of joy, whence my own so largely flowed." .A woman of this spirit could not long remain out of her place. Sarah commenced teaching in the Sabbath S?hool, and ere_long the L?rd gaye her a gracious token of his approval, m the comers10n of one ht~lc girl in her class. Of her call to Sabbath-school work she gave full evidence, working prayerfully and perseveringly. Soon the Master caped her to other Eervice. "A wider field of usefulness presented itself. She found admission to the workhouse, where the poor had no chaplain, the sick no comforter and the children no instructor. In the ho8pital of the workho~se a young woman was ill. Sarah Martin was al101,ed to visit her· and at her death, at the request of a number of afflicted and aged wo~en in the ward, she was permitted to continue her visits, to read the Scriptures, and pray wi~h. them. In t~e. course of time the inmates of all the sick wards solicited her to visit them also, which she did, to their great satisfactio~ and her _own joy. "Not content with instructing and consolmg the sick and age~, she yearned over the poor neglected children in this abode of the destitute, and devoted one day in the week-Monday-to these ?ff-casts. At first they were taught in a confined 3:nd :unfurnished ~lceprng garret •.. A~er sometime a school-room was bml t m the yard, out the teachern "ere selected from the workbousc inmates.

. "The master of th~ house saw the value of her plans, and sought to aid them;_ but the chief difficulty lay in the impossibility of selecting from the mmates of the honse a suitable person to instruct the children regularly. There were no funds supplied by the authorities to procure a competent teacher; and the governor selected to fill the post a poor old man who, by dr_unkenness, had reduced himself to poverty. John Stagg had one quahty, however, that rendered him of great service to Miss Martin. Though not a religious man, be entered fully into her 'views, was attentive to her wishes, to the utmost amount of his abilitv sought to carry out her plans, and gave her a hearty reception on the occasion of her weekly visit. To the poor teacher, as well as the children, the instructions of this devoted woman were made nsefnl. After a few years, he became a decidedly religious man, and was wont to give thanks to God that be bad ever entered the workhouse schoolroom. " For several months before his death be suffered much from asthma; and when the difficulty of breathing prevented sleep, and compelled him to sit up much during the night, he would not de_sert the children in the day, being no longer the mere mechanical teacher, but the affectionate master, and the friend to the souls of the children. His natural temper was impatient; and, at an earlier period, he had been anxious about the children; but when confined to bis bed, and his separation from them entirely effected by the hand· of God, and lire was closing, he resigned his precious chaxge to the love of God, and with every earthly care removed, he found rest. On his death-bed he said to Sarah Martin, ' I feel myself to be a guilty sinner, but I cast myself entirely on the mercy of God, in his dear Son.' " The successor was an old sailor, a man of bad character, and known to be a thief. He was the only person in the house able to teach the children to read. Here was a new difficulty. She feared his temper and disposition would mar all that already baa been accomplished. But she gave herself to prayer, and God heard her. This man also became a penitent believer in the Lord Jesus Christ. I-I is changed life presented a strong contrast to'what he had been. 'In this school-room God taught me,' she heard him say, 'what I never knew before-that I nm a sinner, and that I have mercy in my Saviour.' " In due time, the social irriprovements of the period visited even the workhouse, proper school-rooms were erected, suitable teachers appointed, and the work of education thoroughly carried on. Meanwhile, Sarah had ascended in her service of the Lord by dcscenuing a stage lower, to seek and to save that which was lost. She, like Elizabeth Fry, became the heroine of the jail; and there achieved great things for her Lord. Yarmouth Jail was, we· suppose, neither Letter nor worse than other such places at the period. They were all bad, and tho\1gh we co~1ld _not have said that any were better, for that would be degradmg the adJectire, yet certainly some were worse than the rest. Schools of sin, harbo1~rs of idleness, dens of iniquity, they all were ; proLably no other English Institution so much fostered crime as imprisonment in the comlllon jail, unless it were that of public legal strangulation. In those common jails the innocent unjustly immured were speedily corrupted, the

the language of a Report on their state, published in 1821 :-' In thirt~, gaols, constructed for the confinement of 2,985, there "·ere, at one time in the last year, no fewer than 5,837 prisoners, and the whole number imprisoned in those gaols during- that period amounted to 26,703. There are still prisons where idleness and its attendant crils are yet unrestrained; where the sexes are not separated; where ali distinctions of crime are confounded; where few can enter, if uncorrupted, witl1out pollution, and, if guilty, without incurring deeper stains of criminality. There are yet prisons which receive not the visits of a Christian minister, which the light of knowledge never enters, and where the truths and consolations of the Gospel are never heard. There are yet prisons, where, for the security of the prisoners, measures are resorted to, as revolting to the feelings, as they are repugnant to the spirit and letter of English law.'" "Such a gaol was that of Great Yarmouth. The celebrated John Howard visited it in 1776; and in his 'State of Prisons in England and Wales,' thus describes its condition:-' Besides the gaoler's house, in which are rooms for master's-side debtors, there are for felons a day• room and comt-yard, both too close; and two lodging-rooms for such as pay for them ; t.wo dungeons, or night rooms, down a ladder of ten Fteps-one for men, the other for women. Allowance, a penny loaf a day [thirteen ounces in weight,] four chaldrons of coal a year [for the. prison in general.] They send out a begging basket three times a week. No table. Clauses of Act against spirituous liquors not hung up.'" At the time Sarah Martin commenced her work in the gaol, the doors were simply locked upon the unfortunate and guilty inmates, who, without restriction, spent their time in gambling, swearing, fighting, in talking o~er their various exploits, and in planning fresh crimes when released from prison. The only care of the cold-hearted keepers was the safe custody of their prisoners, who in turn stood behind the bars rattling a begging-box, to invoke the charity of the 1_mssers~by. ,isitors, as bad as the criminals they came to see, were admitted mthont any difficulty, who joined in the orgies of the place. Sunday and week-dav were alike. There was no Divine worship, nor any respect paid to ·the moral or spiritual need of the horde of wretched bei~gs crammed too-ether within its awful precincts. It was an abode of vice and misery~ whether looked at from a religious or sanatory point of view. There were underground cells, even down to the Y:ar 1836, quite dark, and deficient in proper ventilation; and an ancient apai:tmc~t, called 'the Hold,' had iron rings fixed to a great beam, to which, 111 more rigorous times, the prisoners were chained. 'The prisoners,' says the Government Inspector, 'describe the heat of these cells in summer as almost suffocating ; hut they prefe~· them for their warmth in winter. Their situation is such as to defy mspection, and they are altogether unfit for the confinement of an.f human being.' The whole place was 'filthy, confined, unhealthy, and its occupants were infested with ,;ermin and skin disease.'"

I had, ho~cver, access to One whose care wag over me, in whom I had perfect confidence that I should be preserved from evil, whose laws impelled me to forget all else in the important work; nor did I hope in vain. And then how eacrerly did I resort to the BiblP, and feed on such assurances as these : ' There ~hall no evil befal thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling' (Ps. xci. 10). The promises of that beautiful Psalm suited my case, and the support was equal to my requirements.'" It was not a work which self-love would ha,e chosen, but the love of Christ impelled her to it, and sustained her in it. Her mind wa;; delicately formed, and full of elevated and e\'en poetical thought, and yet she voluntal'ily dedicated herself to unremunerated toil among the most brutal portion of the community. She visited the prisoners, prayed with them, read to them, instructed them, and even preached to them ; aud when they left the prison she aided them in commencing life. From the first she acquired a marvellous power over the prisoners, because she evidently loved them, and sought only their welfare. Her prayers, readings, instructions, and advice were received thankfully, or if refused, were declined with a respect which one woudcl's at in men and women so depraved by vice. Sarah Martin knew how to manage people; she had tact and common sense, as well as zeal. Hence she soon hit upon the blots in penal discipline; and though no Prison Conference had then been held, she discovered nearly all that modern philanthropists have at length brought to light. Had the government made her general inspector of j11ils, they could scarcely hare made a better appointment. "After three years' perseverance in this, as she terms it, 'happy and quiet course,' perceiriug that idleness in the prison on the week clays was a fruitful source of vice, she sought to devise plans to employ, first, the female prisoners, and afterwards the men. Having but small means, she showed her ingenuity in doing much with little. Her economical wisdom was equul to her zeal; her common sense shone forth as conspicuously as her piety; for lack of this humbler quality many fervent people make shipwreck of hopeful enterprises. '" In 1823, 11 gentleman gave her ten shillings, and another, in the same week, a pound, for prison charity. It then occurred to her that she could profitably expend it in materials for baby clothes. She did so. Then she borrowed patterns, cut out, the materials, fixed the prices for making the -various articles, and ascertained the cost of a set, so that they might be sold at a profit. The plan was a great success. By this means many of the women were taught to sew, and had a little money to recei l'e at the expiration of the term of their confinement. We ha~e seen her care for the morals and the temporal welfare of her poor pupils, but Sarah Martin's great aim was their spiritual good, and upon this she spent her main exertions. We are glad that several outlines of t~e sermons which ~be preached to the prisoners are given in the memoir before us, for it enables us to appreciate her teaching. Here is one of them:- " Let t~e wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts : and let him-return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and tG our God, for he will abundantly pardon."-lsaiah iv. 7.

"To presume on the mercy of God for forgiveness at the last, whilst we yet go on in sin, is most daring and dangerous, inasmuch as God is a God of justice. In Christ Jesus alone has he revealed himself as a God of mercy, and invited sinners to himself, whilst no encouragement is given to the sinner who goes on in his wickedness, for unrepented and unforsaken sin cannot but end in eternal ruin. That the awakened soul, just brought to a sense of his 01,n guilt and ruin by a sight of the holiness of the divine law, may not de,pair, he is directed by the Word of God to the gracious and glorious scheme of redemption, by which the justice and mercy of Jehovah, our lawgiver, are magnified in the redemption of transgressors. This bltissed passage is most sweet and welcome to the troubled soul under the burden of sin. By it such are invited to Jesus, and the consolations of the Almighty brought to their happy experience. May the sword of the Spirit, God's all-powerful Word, separate every false hope from our souls, cut us off from our errors and refuges of lies, that in our extremity we may be enabled to embrace the remedy, to flee to the gospel of God's mercy in Christ Jesus, and remain in spirit at the feet of Jesus, not only to hear the voice of pardon and of peace, but to receive instruction as to our future course, that we may hear and believe, love and obey him. To this effectual end may the Holy Spirit direct our attention as we proceed. I. The text points out a character: 'The wicked,' and 'his way ; ' ' the unrighteous,' aud ' his thoughts.' II. .A gracious invitation: ' Let him forsake it, let him return unto the Lord.' III. The blessed promise of good : ' The Lord will have mercy upon him-our God ,,ill abundantly pardon.'" There is nothing sensational iu all this, and yet it is an average specimen of her outline add~esses. Her known love to all th? as~cmbled sinners no doubt gave mterest and power to sermons whwh tram any other lips would have been ~hought ex?eedingly commonplace. .A visitor in the town thus descnbes a service conducted by Sarah Martin. A LETTER ADDRESSED TO THE EDITOR OF "THE SWORD AND THE 'fROWEJ,," AND READ BEFORE TUE BAPTIST UNION, IX THE FREE TRADE HALL, MANCHESTER.

D EAR SIR,-Have I been dreaming or not ? If I have not, I have a serious case of moral obliquity among Baptists which I wish to bring before the brethren comprising the Baptist Union of Great Britain ancl Ireland. Be it understood that I am a Baptist myself, but shall be almost ashamed to confess it unless my present statement should turn out to be mere imagination. Sir, I have been, either really, or in fancy, to a country very much like our own, a bright and happy land as like to England as one rose is to another. I thought I was in my own native country till a strange discovery undeceived me. Having occasion to do business with n. worthy tradesman of the Episcopalian denomination, who was withal a most intelligent man, I ,ery naturally enquired as to the po~ition and prospects of the Baptists in the district. He answered me with n. degree of warmth and severity which somewhat surprised me, for he was a man of ,ery gentle mould and genial disposition. "Why sir," said he, "I suppose they must be prospering, for I have this morning paid £7 14s. 6d. for tithe to their preacher in this parish. I haYe never even seen the reverend gentleman in the pulpit, for I am satisfied with my own minister. He is, I have no doubt, a very respectable man, but he is certainly none the better for living in part at the expense of those who do not belie,·e in his teaching. Is it not monstrous that in a country which calls itself free, I, who am a law-abiding Episcopalian, paying all my dues to the powers that be, should sec another sect set in high places and called the National Church, and should myself be called a Dissenter because I do not hoppen to agree with the immersion of adults, and other Baptist pcculi11ritics :'" I sympathized with the good mau with that fellow feeling which makes us wondrous kind ; and although I suid but little to him, I felt so ashamed of the "·hole businc&s that I resolved to call upon the Baptist pastor, and tell him a little of my mind. I was exceedingly pleased to find him living in the best house in the villogc, except the squire's, and I was pleosed to notice a neat croquet lawn where a young assistant minister was occupied in a very engnging manner with some young ladies. Having introduced myself as a Baptist, I was cordiolly received and proceeded at once to my point. The dialogue ran somewhat in this fashion:- " So, my dear friend, you have turned the tables upon the Episcopalians, and have taken the good things of the State out of their hands." "Indeed, no. We have always possessed our present property. T_hc Episeopalians are a modern sect, who sprung up some few centnnes acro. W c are the old Catholic and Apostolic church, practising the o~dinnnces as they were delivered unto us. All other churches nre guilty of schiam, for it is as clear as anything in history that the

Do you concerre the ongrnal Baptist churches to have had this privilege and to ha,e exercised it?" "Well, that i~ a len~thy question which our divines have long ago settled most sat1sfactonly, but I am sorry to say that Episcopalians, and other sects, are agitating the question ; and those known as Political Episcopalians are peculiarly pestilent. My own opinion is, that they are a set of robbers, and want to take away from our church what was bequeathed to her by pious ancestors." " Is it true that the Episcopalians have tried to take away property left to you by wills which you can produce ? " " Well, not exactly that. We say that there were pious ancestors all over the country, one in every parish, who left a tenth part of all property to the Baptist Church ; but the date is so far back that the documents are lost." , I thought I saw his eye twinkle roguishly as he said this, and as I was convinced that he was not such an idiot as to believe what be was saying, I did not dispute with him. I am afraid we grew a little warm over the point, for I was a good deal nettled to meet with a Baptist who could so disgrace the honourable name of our denomination. To make a long story short, I found that a few years ago these Baptists compelled the Episcopalians to pay for the baptising gowns of their ministers, and the water in their baptisteries, and that they were ,ery reluctant to part with the precious privilege of presenting robbery to God as a burnt-offering. However, in this matter public sentiment proved too strong for them, and they have been deprived of their church rates. Yet I found that to this day their leading ministers, including Maclaren, the Right Reverend Father in God, the Lord Minister of Manchester; Mursell, the Lord Minister of Leicester; Landels, the Lord Minister of London; Chown, Lord Minister of Bradford, and others, occupy seats in one of Lhe great courts of legislature, always vote against every measure of progress, and by their very presence insult every Episcopalian, Wesleyan, and Independent in the land. It oozed out that many of the pulpits of this lordly community were put up to auclion to the highest bidder, or were given by certain Lord Deacons and others to their sons, and called livings. The ministers themseh'es I found all subscribed to the Baptist Confession of Faith, but there were nerertheless three sorts of them, as different from each other as rattlesnakes, lambs, and owls can be from one another. I could not understand how they could all honestly profess one creed, and yet hold scarcely anything in common except ~heir tithes: but there can be no doubt that '' they are all honourable inen." . Everywhere I met with their influence, in the almshouse and in the grammar-school, in the soup-kitchen and in the clothing-club; and I found ~hem everyw~ere fighting for Baptist ascendency. An attempt at Nat10nal Educat10n had become a cause of universal dissatisfaction, mainly t]1rough their unexpected and unmanly use of a certain clause of the Act. Looking proudly down upon all other Christians as schismaties, these Baptists try to prove their apostolic succession by an utter disregard of apostolic love of the brethren. Sir, ought these things so to be ? Why should a Baptist oppress an Episcopalian? Why should the Episcopalian be blamed if he feels the oppression keenly and struggles to escape from it? Is there any justice in the state of things which I have represented to you ? The golden rule that we should do to others as we would that they should do to us, appears to have been entirely ignored. Episcopalians in that country have to support their own ministers, and do so with no little difficulty, because few of the great and noble cast in their lot with them; why should they be called upon to sustain those of a body with which they do not agree, which enjoys, moreover, the patronage of the highest in the land? They ought before the eye of the law to be equal to Baptists or any other religionists. I feel ashamed of Baptists who can occupy such a position of unrighteous vantage. Ask the Baptist Union if they are nQt also ashamed ? Ask the Episcopalians of England if they are not indignant that such gross injustice should be endured by brethren of their own faith and order? Perhaps, however, dear Sir, it is all a dream. WILLIAM PLOUGHMAN,

We extract from the Christian Age the following narration by the Rev. Wm. C. Wilkinson, which. is headed, "A Curious Incident in Mr. Spurgeon's Preaching":- " During the spring of 1862, while in London, I met at breakfast one Sunday morninrr in my lodgingJ·a number of gentlemen with whom I had formed the travelle~·'s trnnsient ·acquaintunce as their fellow-guest for the prC\-ious week. He evidently had a story of lus own to tell, nnd 11.t length he told it. Said he:

Such an episode, then, in Mr. Spurgeon's preaching must have occurred. :But it must have been extremely exceptional ; perhaps it was entirely unique. 1 have myself been a somewhat frequent auditor of his, and certainly I never witnessed anything at all resembling the incident which I have narrated. Possibly, Mr. Spurgeon having his attention casually directed to that young man, a sudden and irresistible impulse suggested the hazardous experiment of a personal appeal to him in so public a manner, by way of arresting his conscience with an unexpected and unusual impression. Pe~sons are to be me~ with who saw us slide down the rails of our pulpit sta1rs, and o~hers will swear that they were present at the same time, and yet nothmg ever occurred to give even a colouring of truth to that shameless falsehood. The present piece of imagination is less gross but is equallJ: fabulous. We have been personal, ,er_v personal, and me~n to be so shll.. We do not wish to be " relieved of the imputation of actual personality ; " we plead guilty to it, and only wish we had been more chargeable therewith. But it so happens that we are qnite incapable of noticing people's garments. When we have been told of some fatly',; excessive finery, we have betr:i.yed our total oblivion of the fact, and if a gentleman were dressed in the loudest fashion ll"e should never discover it unless it were pointed out. Our preaching and its effect absorb us ; we watch faces with eagerness to see if onr hearers feel our words, but whether men wear brown or black clothes, we should never notice, for we are gifted with what we ma,· designate an almost absolute incapacity for sartorial obserrntion. 11 e cannot imagine how a description of coats and waistcoats could point a morn! or adorn a tale. and we do not believe that we ever wandered in that direction; if we ·aid so, the description must have belonged to some personage in a narrative we were detailing, and could noL haYe been drawn from anyone before us; though it is very possible th ... t it may have corresponded exactly with the dress of some one in the assemblyin so large a congregation it would be remarkable if it did not. When persons in the congregation are inattentive or ill-beharetl (which, by the way, has hardly occurred a half-dozen times in twenty years), we have given them some gentle hints which they could not help appropriating, and which we have no doubt they will never forget, but even these have had no reference to their garments. The whole matter is a misunderstanding. There could not have been the slightest trnth in the stntement, for the reason named, which is a marked peculiarity of om mind. Why do not people tell the scores of real instances in which we have painted men to the life, and made them feel thnt the Lord spoke to them by us? Infinitely more singular than this incident are the caseR which have come under our own knowledge, but vil1ich we care not to tell, for few would believe them. We aim at speaking personally and pointedly to all onr hearers, and they arc the best judges whdhcr we ncccomplish it, and also as to whether we use language at which any man ought to be offended. Very seldom does a week occur without our receiving letters from persons unknown to us, thanking us for adl'ising or comforting them in our sermons, the parties evidently being under the impression that some friend had communicated their cases to U5, Lhough, indeed, we knew nothing whatever of them. Frequently we have had apologetic notes acknowledging the justice of the rebuke, and correcting us in some minor details of a description supposed to refer to a special sinner; whereas we were unaware of the writer's existence. W c have ceased to regard these incidents as curious, for we remember that the 'i\·ord of God is "a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." c. n. s.

Deists of the eighteenth century mould are a comparatively rare genus now-a- days, and pure Atheism is not fashionable because men who wish to appear before others as persons with mind; will not lightly embrace the philosophy of fools. Even those weak natures who may have strayed into the uninviting paths of that modified Atheism which is known as Pantheism, will not be comforted by remembering the aphorism of Mr. Disraeli,-" Nothing can be more monstrous than to represent a creator as unconscious of creating." That horrible and he~rtlessly cruel lie, which, having an origin in the regions of darkness, gamed strength, and stalked abroad in the last century, is becoming in a measure obsolete. Atheism is such an unscientific, boorish sort of belief, that even an artisan with any pretentious to culture and power of mind, will hesitate before avowing among his shopmates that he is only a mere Atheist. The profession carries a degradation with it, with which few who have any self-respect care to become associated. It is, in fact, saying, I am nothing, because I have not the sense to be anything. Thus, in a valuable work,* recently published, we read: "Naked Atheism is a repulsive creed. It is a heart-withering negation. It touches no sympathy; it stimulates no play of intellect; under the deadly chill of its unlighted vacancy, imagination cannot breathe. There is nothing about it refined, or subtle, or profound. It is the barest and hardest form of infidelity, and has been professed by the coarsest minds. It demands no effort to comprehend its one uni versa! negation, and it taxes no skill to expound it. It is an arid and barren, a cold and dreary hypothesis, which no genius, not even that of Lucretius can make attractive. The old illustration is conclusive as to its absurdity. It would be immensely less monstrous to maintain that the Iliad, in its full perfection, might have been the product of the 'fortuitous concourse' of the letters of the Greek alphabet, than that this infinitely wonderful and glorious universe is the result of the 'fortuitous concourse of atoms.' Stark Atheism, therefore, however it may have flourished in the heartless and hopeless France of a hundred years ago, was never likely to take root in the soil of European scepticism as the alternative of Christianity. In England it has had very few votaries." It appears, then, that in these days even infidelity must not walk abroad clothed in too coarse a habit, unless it would rather disgust than attract votaries.
