to enounce its absurdities in obscure by-ways, or in repelling "halls of science," but to retain its hold of the more respectable classes, modern unbelief must change both its name and tactics. The contemptible dwarfs who find pleaaure in enticing people, more ignorant than themselves, into mere Atheism, will never rise into anything higher than dwarfs-small creatures who account themselves rewarded when complimented 'on their height by auditors who cannot see. The street evangelists of London pass much of their time in the society of infidels of all shades and temners; and even the most intelli()'ent of those who vehemently oppose "Christianity, are found offering i~ its stead only a repulsive substitute. Many cavillers against the Gospel are not wanting in mental power, though such as rail at. religion will often also exemplify the meanest attributes of humanity. The creeds of the unbelieving undoubtedly sanction a low standard of morals. When Christianity is reviled aud discarded, most of the things which help to make man noble and attractive are sacrificed at the same time, and thus an incidental testimony is borne to the value of truth. .A man, for instance, who yields to a debasing Socialism, will necessarily bring his notions of morality down to the same level. One such has been known to abuse a City Missionary for teaching nothing better than Christianity, and then to show his own superiority, by absconding to the Continent and leaving his family to shift for themselves! Oftentimes, all will go well with a working-man until home is invaded by immoral opinions, and their entrance is the forerunner of social ruin. Wives mar be found, to whom the surrendering of all religious principle on the· part of husbands, bas meant ill-usage and neglect, and frequently the workhouse for themselves and their children. A strikiug instance of the manner in which Atheism aud its work can bring people to the darkness and misery of dire poverty, occurred some years ago in London. A missionary who was visiting in the neighbourhood of Saffron-hill, came to a certain dilapidated house with a broken door ; knocking, he entered in response to a weakly spoken "Come in," to find a man and woman living in a condition of shocking wretchedness. Indeed, the spectacle was so utterly horrible that the visitor involuntarily shuddered and sickened at what he saw, familiar as he was with strangely repulsive sights. The man, as an invalid, wonld have been confined to his bed had he possessed one, but wn.nting that convenience, he lay on a little straw, beneath a coarse wrapper, with a brick for a pillow I The remainder of the furniture consisted of an old chair and a saucepan. There was no fire, ancl the woman in attendance being subject to fits, sat in speechless misery, as if resigned to her fate. It might have been supposed that such a scene was the result of uncommon profligacy, or that ruin had come from the imprudent and false steps which are taken through ignorance. It was not so, however. The man who lay like a beast in that pestiferous hovel was a gifted author I While in health he had worked for an infidel publisher. He had written poems against Christianity, besides publishing a book to disprove the doctrine of the soul's immortality. A more singular example of the blighting nature of immoral opinions is rarely discovered.

"\fhen found, such things are worth recording, if only to serve as warnin!.'"s to otherg, At first the sufferer was not disposed to be communicative to the friend who had so unexpectedly invaded a hidden corner in the great cit.,, where a fellow mortal seemingly lay within a few davs of death: Yet the two probably understood each other. Perhaps •the outcast detected the expression of sympathy on the Christian's countenance; for, as he looked up from his bed of straw, and cast his heavy eyes around the room, he said, " THIS rs THJ.; WRECK OF INFIDELITY.!" A ~reek indec>d ! His situation was truly <lrendful; for poverty and s1ekncss were far from being the only evils borne. The woman in a_ttcndanee, wh~n maddened by the fits to which she was subject. raged hke a hungry tigress, and would spring at her charge with glarinO' eves, biting and scratching with the strength of insanity! Then wh~n "the fit passed away she became kind and docile. Of this strange couple the evangeli~t ~ndeavoure11 to make friends. The man was highly intelligent, and with a culturecl mind prejudiced aQ"ain~t the gospel, it was necessary to begin with the e-yidences of Chr:stianity. He listened attentively to the relation of the advent of Christ, and exclaimed, "Well, that is remarkable." He was then more fully referred to the prophecies pointing to the Messiah, and he said, " Tliey are quite overwhelming. I do not believe any man can contradict them." He was spoken to about the Saviour's sufferings, and it was observed that tears ran down the poor Infidel's cheeks. He was touched in the heart. His faith in Atheism vanished, th0112:h the question of miracles seemed still to be associated with some difficulty. "Suppose I read the narrative of the Jew who received siirht?" said his friend. "Do, sir, I should like to hear•it." The man listened to the passage and then said, "That must be t.rue ; it carries conviction on the face of it.'' He then heard tbe account of the raising of Lazarus, and on learning how "Jesus wept," he interrupted, "Ah, that was compassion like a God. I cannot help admiring- the character of Christ." The poor fellow became more. deeply impressed and was greatlv affected. "I believe now there is a God,'' he cried, "though I ha,e for a long time doubted; but I will never write a'.!ainst Christianit, a()'ain if I recover. I see such a loveliness in the Christian Eyst~m,"since I ham been afflicted, that I beg-in to love it. Infidelity now appears a cold and heartless thing." "Yes," answers the other, "it leaves a man to die like a brute; not so the gospel of Jesus." "Ko! That bloornR with immortality." Still the man rernained for some time in gloom and doubt. He admired prayer, though_ he could not use it ; for after such a course as his, it looked like mockmg God. He ,roulcl have giren worlds to appropriate as his own a hymn which was read:- "Let the sweet hope thnt thou nrt mine," &c.

IIe was now frequently found in tears, and on his friend's leaving, he ,;i·ou Id say, "When will you come again ? " He also confessed, "My_ trn~t in Infidelity is gone. You have no conception of the agony my mmd 1s in. Virtue without Christ is folly." A dnrk array of terrors pasrnd through his wul, whic:h gradually rnbsidcd os he became enabled to

make the coveted gift of prayer his own, and to rejoice in faith. His health was providentially restored. He separated from the woman with whom he had lived in adultery, and returned to his wife and home. Afte~L so_ singular_ and painful an experience he could well testify, "Infi.d~hoy 1s an acbmg void, a blank, a blot, a dark and fearful chasm in which hope sinks, and all that renders life desirable is swallowed up ; but religion lights up the gloom, and dispels the dark clouds which hang over human destiny." ~hen n1~n reject the Scriptural doctrine of a personal reigning- De1t,v, supermtending all things, whither do they arrive? Certainly not m a land free from difficulties. To make nature our God, as does the pseudo-scientific Pantheism, fashionable now-a-days, is in truth to manufacture difficulties. "Every difficulty," says a lecture in the valuable book, before quoted, " which belongs to the thought of God's existence belongs to this also. This force must be self-originated, must have been from everlasting, must be creative, omnipresent, providential, equal to all plans, purposes, contrivances, inspirations, which ha\"C been, or ever will be, in this daidalean and infinite universe; must be the source of all intelligence, though itself unintelligent; of all sympathy, although itself incapable of sympathy ; must have formed the eye, though it cannot see; and the ear, though it cannot hear; must hare blossomed and developed into personal intelligences, although personal intelligence is a property which cannot be attributed to it ; must unquestionably be omniscient as ,veil as omnipresent, or it could not, in its infinite comertibility, anticipate all needs, meet all demands, answer in absolute and unh-ersal harmony to every faculty, capability, and tendency, of all things that are and all things that become. Now is it reasonable to object to the doctrine of a personal Deity because of its inconceivability and its stupendous difficulties, and yet to beliern in such a primal, essential, immaterial, creative, infinite, blind, and unintelligent force as this? Surely no contradiction could be greater. 'l'l:c conception of God ns from everlasting is stupendous. But an infinite Protean Force from everlastinir, destitute of intelligence and will, yet continually operative as the life, soul, wisdom, and providence of all things, is nothing less than contradictory and absurd." But unbelief is more than a mere opinion. The iufidelity which is spreading its meshes to entan!:(le all classes is a very blighting thing. It would not be difficult to collect evidence illustrative of the degrading tenrlency of Atheism, Secularism, 8ocialism, and other follies of human invention. These anti-Christian systems have made many a once promising life become barreu of good, and have besides, carried unhappiness and even despair into homes where domestic enjoyment once reigned supreme. Near Leather-lane there once lived a young married couplL·, the characteristics of the husband being devotion to Deism and love of drink. This man was conversed with and exhorted to abandon his evil ways. He perceived the state of degradation to which he had fallen, and the superior attractions of Christianity, In tones of pain he said to his Christian adviser, " I wish you could convert me." "That is not my province,'' was the answer "I may by the blcEsing of God comincc you ; it is the 1n·ovincc of the Holy Spirit to crnvcrt men.'' The man 3:!

was then asked if he were happy. Such a question might have been !-poken ironically ; but t~rribly serious was the Deist in replying, " I am not happy. I am dm·en almost to despair. My principles have made me a drnnkard, a bad husband, and all that is wretched and miserable. I ITish I had had a friend to talk to before. I shall be miserabl~ when :,ou are gone." Such was this ~an when first found by a true friend. What made matters worse was havmg broken his arm in a drunken braw 1. . Then there was no wife to attend him; for beaten and other_wis~ ill-used, she ran ~way _s0~e time before: All this evil, directly and indirectly, came to its v1ct11n as the frmt of Infidel opinions. Loose morals were soon the parents of loose morality, until drunkenness and its train of woe destroyed every prospect of peace and domestic enjoyment. Happier days were in store, however. The wife was spoken to about returning to her hearth, and under the circumstances, she was delighted to do so. The couple were advised to read the Bible for direction, to attend the public worship of their Maker, ancl so lead a happy life. Judge Christianity by its frnits when it effects such moral and social transformations as these. " What a good thing it was you visited me," said the convert as he set out with the missionary to the house of God one Sabbath moming; '' If I had not seen you i should have been drunk all the week. I should have smothered my feelings and senses with drink and have made myself worse and worse." People thus reclaimed are sufficiently grateful ; yet there are people in the ',,orld who will actually laugh at a man for being a ninny because he <exchanges squalor and wretchedness for plenty in the cupboard and peace in his conscience. It was so in this instance. The man's convivial companions would have jeered him out of these new ways, and out of newly-found trearnres, but they did not succeed. A light heart, a cheerful young wife, a happy home, and bright hopes for eternity, were things of too sterling a value to be surrendered to those whose approval is after all no more to be regarded than their mirth, which is as the crackling of thorns under a pot.. Even some of the most common-place instances teach the importance of persevering in a good cause. Near King's Cross once lived a man, who, though often warned ,md exhorted, refused to listen to the gospel messa"e. "I am a Deist, and a Deist I mean to live and die," he said -when ~poken with concerning religion. Soon, howC'\>'er, he was seized v,ith illnese, and when his philosophy gave way, nnd he fe_lt all the foundationr, he hacl buildcd upon to be sliding from beneath l11s feet, he could obtain no comfort. Despair took hold of him. He cried, "It is all over I fear; " "I have no hope now either for body or rnul.' • "What?" was the reply, "have you no anchor_ to_cast now the stor!n is come!'" "No I" "You do not find your pnnc1ples support you m the honr of affliction ? " "Ko! " This once unlikely character became c:om pletely chang-ed. Deistical books were superseded by the Scriptures : and in due time he departed this life in Christian triumph. . While learning to wage a relentless war with sin, earnest evangel~sts :ilso learn from the example of the Great Teacher to act a forbearmg part towards the sinner. Were they, on the contrary, to r~gard the abuse, the rebuff.~, and minor insults to which they are sometunes subjected, as anything more than the opposition of the common enemy

~~ey would have to !·elinquish their work in their despair. Our street 1tmerant~ mus~ patiently combat the obstinate cavilling resistance of an oftent1mes mtellectually weak infidelity. In a northern district of London was found one of the i o-noran t species, who for Jon~ years resisted all entreaties to lead ~ more becoming life, and did so in no polite mood. On one occasion he turned his _visitor into the street, and told him not to Yenture there again. But an mfluence was at work such as the Deist little suspected to exist, or to he of such surpassing potency. Disease overtook him, and he felt that unbelief afforded uo resting-place for his soul to lean upon. In dismny he sent for the friend so lately despised. A great change occurred, and the home of this lately violent bbsphemer presented a scene surprising even to those who were accustomed to strange experiences. The man's mind was humbled; his face was suffnscrl with tears; and as he stretched out his thin wenk arms, he cried, " Do you think there is mercy for such a wretch as I have been ? " "Yes," was the answer, "if you give up your unbelief." The sufferer's very soul appeared to be wrung- with agony. ":My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me! " he cried in piteous tones, " Oh, why did I ever doubt ? Ah, ah! that was a bad srhool I went to to learn these opinions." But even in so uninviting a place, and at so unseasonable a time, there is present a Saviour ready to save to the uttermost. How eagerly tlo subjects like this prostrate Deist learn that the gates of heaven are never closed against those who believe and trust in Christ; and that none but the wilfully impenitent are, or can be, shut out. This is indeed a balm with which the messengers of mercy heal the bleeding hearts of despairing prodigals. " Shall I pray for you? " asked the visitor. " Do! " said the dying man with great eagerness; " Pray that I may have faith in Christ." That prayer was not in vain ; for when, a short time afterwards, while the last earthly struggk was taking place, the penitent was asked, "Tell me, can you trust your soul 1\'ith the Lord Jesus Christ?" he answered, "1 can, I can, I am not afrnid to die. God bless you for all your kindness." Numbers, doubtless, retain their insane philosophy to the end of their days; n-,vcrtheles~, many instances occur wherein salf-conceitcd abusive infidels are changed into humble-minded and teachable believers. The blessings they receive come to them at first unsought; but they have only to be tasted to become appreciated according to their proper value. Many "·ill have reason to bless God eternally for the agency which rescued them from swift destruction, whither they were blindly hastening. The gratitude of people whom the gospel thus encounters anti conquers in the streets is very utfccting. A few hours before dying a mau has presented a shilling to the funds of the City Mission as an acknowlcdgment of benefit receired. At one of the local meetings a young man once attended, who, on being questioned, said, '' I have wallml four miles, and would walk twenty to sec a City Missionary." He ancl his mother were found out while living in London, anti while lhcy cam! not for the gospel. Some memorable wortls had been left with themwords which fasteued themselves on their souls-" There are but two places to go lo, and the end of these things is death." fall in his high service; may-as has been known to be the case-be visiting ~he ~oor i1:1 the ~or1~ing, a~d lie dead in his coffin at night ! O~r aun Ill tl11s article 1s to illustrate Christian work among a particular class, and also to prove that among all the various systems of unbelief, not one is found to yield satisfaction in life, nor to bear the sear_ching test of d~ath. Some wil~ affect to tr_eat the last enemy with sem1-~,m1ternpt; ~v11l seem_ to be_res1gned to then· doom of" everlastinir sleep. Some will even Jest with death ; but with the stoutest and greatest of infidels, t~e _sub_terfuge is a very pitiable affair. Could philos?pby ensure tranquillity m _th.e prospect of death, surely a philosopher like Hume should have enJoyed a full share of felicity· but what a shocking spectacle was presented to the world, when, standi~g-, as it were, on the very edge of the grave, the historian found nothing nobler wherewith to employ himself than the pastime of joking about "Charon and his boat." What John Foster wrote concerning the death of Hume would apply to a thousand others who have adopted Burne's belief: "We behold him at last carried off, and we seem to hear, the following moment, from the darkness in which he vanishes, the shriek of surprise and terror, and the overpowering accents of the messenger of vengeance ! " Invariably, we may ·say, in the case of infidels, remorse or terror takes the place of bravado, when symptoms of decaying strength set in. A hard-working and successful missionary in an enst-end district found himself greatly plagued by a conceited and obstinate Atheist whose natural temper was no more attractive than his creed. The man announced his disbelief in God, and spoke of the Bible in a manner repelling enough to make the ears of listeners to tingle, and their blood to rnn cold, as indeed one confessed who heard for himself: "You speak about a soul," he would say, "Man has no soul, no more than my old tom-cat; and then vou will talk about after death comes judgment, when we must render an account of the deeds done in the body before a righteous and just God. Why, after death, I shall turn to a cabbage, a dog, or some such thing, I cannot tell_ what I sh~ll be, nor do I care, either. It does not trouble me!" The mfidcl contmued in this temper until reduced by bodily weakness, P.nd tl1ere came a season of terror and misgivin". Through one awful night he lay restless and wearv, talking of~his Gtely rejected friend. Never before in his life-exper'ience probably, had he so longingly watched for the morning light, when the gospel could once more be listened to nnd ~ccepted. Happily, he did not repent too late. He yielded to th~ gent!~ mflu~nce -of rdigion. The blasphemy of unbelief was exchanged for praise. Wilful disregard of God was superseded by faith in a living Saviour. . The evil fruits of rcrseverance in infidelity spring up on nll sides. Atheism deadens men's finer instincts by removing them from God •. ~t deadens the heart until it becomes hard and still harder, so that it 1s scarcely surprising if, occai;ionally, this and kindred systems sometimes lead even to tragic results. In Saint Pancrae once resided a man nnd nis wife, hoth of whom harboured the most degrading sentiments which curse humanity. What made their sin more flagrant was the fact of t !ieir knowing better; for the man had been respectably reared by a

to produce good impressions on characters like these, hopes of benefUing them are never relinquished until the men or the women are beyond the reach of human ageacy. This was a very deplorable case. One morning the Atheist cut his wife's throat, and then destroyed himself ! A catastrophe doubtless springing from unholy principles, and an awful illustration of the words, " He that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.'' . With such facts to enlighten, and with such exam pies of infatuation to perplex us, we might again ask, what attractions are found in unbelief, and what difficulties are removed by embracing any one of its many systems ? Deism, as half obsolete, retains few attractions and may be summarily dismissed. Atheism, or believing in results without a cause, is too gross a folly to be accepted by any beside gro.elling, ignorant minds. But is not a pseudo-scientific Pantheism more reasonable ? Is there not at least a kind of fascination, a halo of mystery, about the idea of "God in everything" ? Happily, there is no need in this place to reply to such follies. None of our readers are in any danger of sacrificing their high moral attributes, those endowments which exalt man infinitely above all other creatures of God on earth ; and the chief rnlue of which consists in the ability they afford us of taking advantage of the unspeakable privilege of drawing near to Him who is the source of all goodness and of all joy. "God in everything," may be a fascinating faith to such as wish in their hearts that there were no God at all. It may suit the " intellectual" and the "cultured" men who have become engrossed in scientific pursuits until they lose sight of the Author of science. These "advanced" sages may go their way ; ancl the only favour we ask from them is that of being allowed to go ours, since the truest philosophers find it far "easier to believe in a personal God than in such an impersonal divinity 11s this Protean force."

T preachmg of Mr. Thomas Walsh are extracted from "The Lives of Early Methodist Preachers ; " they st,rike us as being so exactly descriptive of what a true minister of Christ should be, that we commend them to the earnest perusal of all who endeavour to preach the gospel. Young men especially may f!ather much from the quaint but suggesti,e paragraphs. 0 that all of us were such men as Thomas Walsh, except his Arminianism : - " The language of his whole conduct was, in truth, what on a certain occasion he breathed out in the following words :-' 0, how does my soul thirst for the salvation of men! How does my heart bleed with desire, that the fulness of the Gentiles were brought in, and that all Israel might be saved!' This concern for the kingdom of Christ, and the conversion of mankind, made him superior to whatsoever hardships and difficulties attended his labours. He watched every opportunity; and was, 'instant in season, out of season,' continually, at a11 times and places, seeking how he might Lest accomplish the end for which alone he desired to live. The intenseness of his desire, and his application to this 'one thing,' kept him continually on the "·ing, spending and being spent in this behalf: regarding neither reproach, pain, loss, imprisonments, nor death itself. 'I have,' as he said on a certain occasion, 'bnt one lif'e ; and it is a hard case if I cannot readily lose that for His sake, who gave His life a ransom for mine. My soul bleeds for the world which lieth in the wicked one.' He seemed to have continually Lefore his eyes that whieh the Son of God suffered out of love for man. It was the spring whence proceeded his ardent zeal for the glory of his Lord in the ical ration of the purchase of His blood; for he judged that the best testimony he could give of his love to Jesus was to suffer wmething for His sake. It '\\as his desire to give life for life; 1md to requite Him, even, if needful, by death itself. It was owing to this, likewise, that he embraced every possible opportunity of crying aloud, in the most conspicuous places of public resort, and of enforcing the voice of Wisdom, saying-, 'How long, ye simple ones, will ye lorn simplicity? and scorners delight in scorning, and fools hate knowledge l Turn ye at My reproof: behold, I will pour out My Spirit upon you, I will make known My words unto you.' Mountains, market-places, highways, meadows, rooms, prisons, and r,hips, were the frequent theatres of his publishing the Gospel of pe~ce. And herein there appeared in him something next to marvellous, be1~g a liYing tire, continually burning in the love of God and man ; still mounting upwards, and kindling all about him. He seemed as prone 1.o fervour and activity, as Eome arc to coldness and indo_lencc. He was never weary of well-doing, nor ever spoke slightly, and mth an indifferent affection, of the great God, and of the things of religion in

g~neral; but with__a seriousness and reverence becoming one who, by faith_, saw the Inv1s1ble, and looked to be shortly with Him . . His w~rm heart (Luke xxiv. 32) and fervent courage feared no danger 11;1 the discharge of his duty; bein~ well assured, that walking uprigbt~y, be walked surely. He dreaded not the faces of men, but, where occasion offered, boldly reproved what he saw amiss in everyone. Wherev~r there appeared any probability of his doing good, he was never bmdered therefrom by the prospect of personal danger. He , could truly say- ' To leave my calling'! disdain; Behind I will not stay, Though shame, and loss, and bonds, and pain, .And death obstruct my way. ' Secure from dan11:er, and from dread, Nor earth nor hell shall move, Since over me Thy hand bath spread The banner of Thy love.' In one place, having preached to a vast number of Romanists and others, and a prospect appearing of doing much good among them, he intended to go thither again. But a• report prevailed, that ir he attempted it, a certain great man woald either have him stoned, or sent to jail. 'On this occasion I reflected,' says he, 'what God had done in former times for those who put their trust in him, and he gave me strength according to my day. I found my faith in Him greatly strengthened, and resolved simply to rely on His protection; not doubting but that He would stand by me. So I went thither, and preached in the name of the Lord. ' The fear of man prevented the poor people giving me entrance into their houses, as before; RO I stood on a chair in the street, and thanked God for the pril-ilege. They received the word without disturbance, and with joy. On my return, I prayed at two houses in the way, and the power or God was greutly in the midst of us. Praised be God and the Lamb for ever! 'The Jo,·e of Chl"ist doth rnc constrain To seek the wnud'ring sons of' men ; ,vith crie~, entrenties, tcnrs, to save And snatch them from th' infernal wave. 'My life, my blood, I here present, If for Thy truth they mny be spent! Fulfil Thy sovereign counsel, Lord, Thy will be done, 'l'hy name adored.' His whole conversation was like fire; warming, refreshing, and comfortino- all that were about him, and begctting- in their souls a measure of the"' same zealous concern for the glory of God, and the salvation of sinners which burned in his own breast. It was not possible to be much ,~ith him, and not to hear discourses which bred a detestation of sin and a Jove of holiness. 'To what purpose is it to live, and not to liv~ to some good purpose?' . . . . . ' 11.nd other sentences to like purpose. I ,ml! remember one instance of the good effect of this, which a person mentioned to me since his death. ' I shall ne,er forget,' says he. 'a ~-ord which M:r. Walsh, taking me by the hand one day, spoke to· me in my shop : ' 'Tis worse tbn death my God to love, and not my God alone.' It was like a nail in a sure place, and left a useful impression upon the person's mind ever after. The gravity and earnestness with which he deli.cred these little mementoes to his friends, carried them by God's help, to the heart, and left them there. So that I hav~ heard several of his sayings, in this way, called to remembrance since his decease, by his acquaintances. A certain person meeting a brother, one day, who seemed to do what he was about negligentl.v, 'Brother,' said he, ' for whom do you do it?' The brother ans"llered, that he did it 'for the love of God.' 'Certainly,' replied he, 'if you do it for the love of God, you are highly to blame. To be slack in serving men is not commendable, but to serve God negligently is intolerable.' This was far from being the case with Mr. Walsh. He did whatsoever he did for God with all his might, spending his fu]I force upon every holy action, even as though he should merit hea ,en thereby; and yet, at the same time, heartily despising himself as an unprofitable servant. The state of his own heart had much influence on the particular subjects of his sermons; as is surely the case with all to whom preaching is not a mere business of course, but an affair of the weightiest importance. He knew that the words of an unfeeling heart are but empty sounds; and tbat although they may please for the present, they rarely profit the hearers. It was on this account that, attending constantly to the motions of his own soul, he hardly ever preached asermon without conveying the like Eens'.ltions to others which he felt in his own soul, whether for deep contrition of spirit, holy mourning, or spi!itual joy. 'When,' says he, 'I am in heaviness, l am led to speak chiefly of trials; when lively and fervent, I am led to speak of the comforts of belierers; and when I am hungering and thirsting after righteousness, I press upon others to cleanse themselves from all filthiness of flesh and spirit, and to perfect holiness. And hence I learn,-lst, How nec:<lful it is for a preacher to be in a right spirit himself, whenever he speaks to others ;-and 2ndl,r, I see the w_isdo_m of qod, in so ordering my experience that every soul may receive its port10n of the milk or the word in due season.' All his sermons might be truly said to be his own, from God. He stole not the word from his neighbour, (J er. xxiii. 30,) nor catched at trivial incidents to furnish him with an hour's discourse. His heart was a treasury well furniRhed, insomuch that he was never at a loss for something in season. Even when ·he has been so necessarily taken up with other parts of his calling as not to have the least time for preparing- to preach, the pourings out of his soul evinced themselves to waiting hearts to be of God. There was nothing whinino-, 0 light or trivial in his ,discourses; nothing put on; nothing that could dxcite an air of levity, much 1¥s

laughter; but rather, and which ,vas commonly the case, groans, and tears, and cries. His sermons bad in them such a depth of Di ,inc truth, confirmed by the word of God, with such a "reatness and majesty, as begot in the hearers an awe and reverence, ;hich removed far away all petulancy and thoughtless irreverence of spirit; and produced, _m many, a solemnity and attention of soul becoming those who hear discourses for life or death eternal : to all of which his grave and mortifi_ed countenance contributed not a little. In short, his whole behaviour in the pnlpit was such as became a messenger of God, put in trust with the ministry of reconciliation. His discourses were of a general nature, suiled to give a portion tu everyone, as their need required; milk for babes, and for stronger men stronger meat; though still they had this one main tendency with regard to all,-to excite people's hearts to the pure love of God. And, although he preached 'faith in Christ,' as the only way of obtaining all the good things of grace and glory, yet he did it in such a manner as effectually to guard against the abuse of libertines, who turn the freeness of the grace of God into an occasion of wantonness; who, while they promise liberty to themselves and others, are, at the same time, senants of corruption. Persons of this character could not, in the least, serve themselves from his discourses; in every one of which he so preached faith in Christ, as to 'establish the law' in its true sense; so as to secure all the interests of genuine holiness, both in heart and life. . When he first began to preach, his chief talent seemed to be for quickening such as were dead in trespasses and sins; to terrify careless sinners with the dread of God's judgments and lead them to flee from the wrath to come. He judged that there was nothing more likely to pull down the strongholds of Satan, than to lay the axe at the root of sin; and in all his sermons, he ever used to discover its filthy and detestable nature, pressing upon the conscience an entire purgation from dead ,works. And he did it in such a manner as often pierced the very joints nnd marrow of his bearers. But it was not as a Boanerges, a son of thunder, only, that he excelled. His own happy experience of the forgiving, healing, ancl comforting virtue of the blood of Jesus, together with bis mighty acquaintance with the promises of life in Him, fitted him for aclministeriog comfort, and much encouragement, to the weary and heavy-laden with sin. To such he was, in truth, 'a son of consolation;' his lips dropped sweetness to them, as the honey-comb, while they poured forth abundantly ' Thoughts immaculate and pure, Balsamic truths, nnd healing sentiments!'

O God, how many a bleeding wound hast Thou made him nn instrument of healincr, 0 by pouring into the hcart8 of the disconsolate ' the wine and oil ' of the Gospel, in a rich profusion of those precious golden promises, which, being ratified to us by the holy blood of Thy dear Son, are yea and amen in Him, to Thine eternal glory ! . He had not, it must be acknowledged, at least he made but little use of, the &rt of preaching: not, indeed, that he was ignorant of such rules

as orators lay down for ordering and conducting of public discourses. His knowledge both of logic and rhetoric was far from being inconsiderable. He both read, and in some good degree digested, the principles of both. But the eagerness with which he undertook and proceeded in his work; and the rapid flow of his soul, did not suffer him to attend with exactness to niceties in composition or delivery ; nay, e,en prevented that moderation in delivering his discourses which ~rould ha,e been more easy to himself and to his audience, many of whom were often in pain for him ; though afterwards, when the repeated ad,•ice of his friends, and the necessity of his constitution, obliged him to a more slow and deliberate manner, some ascribed it to (what they called) his 'want of power.' How common is it to imagine, that the presence and power of the Spirit of God depends upou the loudness of the preacher';; voice, the swiftness of his expression, and the like; in other words, upon the strength of a man's lungs, and the assurance of his gesture and utterance !-a sentiment most strange to the truly wise. As though noise and animal activity should be dignified with the names of spirit and power; and the want of them ascribed to dryness, deadness, and formality ! Strictly Epeaking, indeed, there is no necessary Divine power in any man's manner of speaking, whether loud or low, swiftly or softly. 'It is the Spirit that quickeneth,' as He pleaseth; and it may be questioned whether effects that have been sometimes produced by a loud, vehement, and o,erbearing manner of speaking, were not in great measure merely animal or mechanical, if not sometimes of Satan himself, to cast an odium upon the work of God. There mny be often a strong wind, an earthquake, and fire; but the Lord is in the 'still, small voice.' His word, it is true, is a sword and a hammer, which wounds and breaks human hearts in pieces; and by how much any one's manner of speaking contributes towards the so doing, so far it is to be commended. But, considered independently of this, the loudness of a man's voice is in reality no better than the blowing of a trumpet, or the sound of a drum. 'Kot by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit, saith the Lord of Hosts.' His sermons were seldom less than an hour Jong; and yet had in ihem such an a"reeable variety, judicious explanation of Scripture, and affecting energy, that they were rarely, if ever, tedious? unless to such as wanted a savour for the things of God. Often might one see, on these occasions, 'Attentive crowrls the heavenly words admire, Han" on his lips, and catch the sacred fire; In c~owding ranks on every side arise, Demanding life, impatient of the skies.'

He was always, at the conclusion, in a bath of sweat. And, the nlaee of preaching Leing often at some distance from his lodging, his ;uddcn ly growing cold ngain was one reason of the frequency of t~e fon:rs which he had from time to time during his whole life of public labour. He often resolved, Lefore he began to preach, to restrain the rapidity of his spirit; but in Yain ; the sword, being too keen fo~· the ~c-abbar<l. The fenour of his soul broke through all rcsulut1ons,

rejoicing to spend and to be spent for the Lord Jesus; but wasting, at _the same time, and cutting away the very springs of his animal life, which although, at the time, he had no apprehension of, yet he felt immediately afterwards. . With regard to the manner of his preparing for sermons, he seemed to keep between the two extremes, of an enthusiastic disregard to, or neglect of, all actual previous preparation on the one hand, and a merely dry scholastic composition of exact materials on the other. To have no regard to the matter and manner of his discourses beforehand, under the pretence of dependence upon heaven for immediate influence and utterance, he judged to be a cloak for a lazy, lounging, indolence of spirit, on account of which, nonsense has been too often dignified with the sacred names of inspiration and power. And yet, on the other hand, he judged it nearly, if not alike culpable, to seek after and trust to mere dry human skill, in fixing upon heads, and taking such measures, as to preach often only one's self, independent, as it were, of the quickening, enlightening presence of the Holy Ghost, without which all preaching and all hearing are equally vain. He prayed aud studied, and studied and prayed again, going always (unless necessity prevented) from his closet, and off his knees, into the pulpit. But when he came there he gave himself up wholly into the bands of God, to be actuated and used by him in all respects as might be most for his glory. And it was glorious and wonderful to see the good effects which were produced at those times by the words of Gc,d flowing from his lips, and entering into the heart, without the ornaments of studied eloquence, but in thei1, native majesty and simplicity. One might easily gather from his way of preaching, how sensible he was of a mistake in many preachers, who content themselves with having spoken things which cannot be reasonaLly gainsayeu. Whereas, if there be nothing more than clearness of demonstration in a sermon, it may, indeed, be so far said of the preacher, 'Thou prenchest well.' But what then? Who is edified to salvation ? Who arc quickened in thdr pursuit of God and heaven ? Who hates his sins, or who loves God the more for vour discourse?' Now, where these arc not to be found, may not a "sinner as well be hearkening to a mathematician demonstrating Euclid's elements as to a preacher only proving a point of Christianity? It was far from satisfying him that his sermons had in them sufficient demonstration ; for still retaining in mind that the true encl of preaching is to bring souls to Jesus, and build them up in God; he rated his sermons accordingly: and, for the more effectual promotion of this, he studied to be well acquainted with all the motionH and sentiments of the human heart, pointing his discomscs there continually; laying hold, as it were, of its inmost thoughts, and with the sinner's own weapons sln}·ing the enemies of his salvation. He applied to the conscience at every turn; and, after having at any time demonstrated a peculiarly interesting truth, of a gcncrnl nature, he ahrnvs took care to make it a personal thing, by questioning the heart of everyone concerning their part therein. IIc frequently intr?- duccd, by way of comparison, many of the incidental octurrcnccs 111

life, things respecting callings, families, .and a thousand little matters, by which the great concerns of the soul and another world entered more deeply and sensibly into the minds of the common people. I have heard a woman of knmrn integrity say that, intending one evening to have his judgment, after preaching, on several particulars which were a wei"ht 0 to her mind, he so anticipated all objections, and answered them in his sermon, that she needed no further enquiry, being entirely satisfied. It was ,ery usual with him in his sermons to propose and answer di,-ers cases of conscience; which was often an inexpressible satisfaction to many. In describing vices, he did not so much dwell upon the vice itself abstractedly, as he showed the persons to themselves, who were guilty thereof; and represented the unavoidable danger of such as lived and died therein. It was not so much 'pride, envy, anger, lust, drunkenness, swearing,' and the like, which he painted in their deformed and detestable nature (though he did this also;) but his drift at such times was, to describe the proud, the envious, the angry, and the lustfol man; to alarm the drunkard, and the swearer, &c., as with the voice of thunder, to escape for their li,es. The most guilty person can sit and hear the vice described, with composure enough; bnt the conscience of a sinner cannot so easily escape when the preacher, speaking as it were to one person, charges it home by crying, ' Thou art the man.' It was in this way that his sermons were, by the grace of God, effectual to the awakening and converting of so many. His whole life being one series of holy living and mental improvement, preserved his heart like an ever fresh and overflowing fountain, which on every occasion poured fourth its fruitful streams of holy doctrine and persuasive exhortation. It was easy enough to discern that he felt the things be delivered. He gave himself wholly to this one thing ; and, which was the crowning glory of all, was himself a pattern of the truths he taught. Indeed this was, from first to last, his main concern, that while he ministered to the want of others, he might 11ot sustain loss in his own soul, nor have to take up that sad complaint, ' They made me the keeper of the vineyards ; but mine own vineyard have I not kept.' (Canticles i. G.) It is a fearful case for a preacher to be only like a channel in a garden, through whi_c~ the wa~er runs _to cool and moisten the herbs and flowers, but retarnrng nothmg for its 01rn use; if not like the spoils of beavers, sheep, and silkworms,_designed to clothe others but made the occasion of their own nakedness, 1f not the cause of their' death. This, indeed, is never the intention of God concerning- His servants; but men bring it upon t~em:5e!ves, tl11:ough the abuse of His favours. Alas! how wretched a thmg 1t 1s to bmld an ark for others, and to be at last ourselves castaways.'' Prayer for min-islers is the best way of showing our love to them, and of making us love them more. Do not ,'lJ_Jeak against them to man, but plead for tltem to Goel. Dissatz"sfied hearer, try this remedy, and if it Jails, try it agai,1.

The writer traces back some of its features to ,valkerism, which berran with l\lr. ·walker a fellow of Trinity College, Dublin, some thirty years b;fore. To these were ;dded the chief doctrines of Edward Irving respecting the church as the body of Christ; the '(lresence of the Holy Ghost in the church ; justification in virtue of union with Christ in resurrection ; the coming of the Lord a second time, and the rapture of the church. The last was handled by De Burgh at the time with much earnestness. De Burgh was a clergyman of the Church of Enrrlancl, and in his latter years Professor of Hebrew in Trinity Collerre, Dubli~. These doctrines were adopted by a body of Christians calling tbe~selvcs "Brethren,"' afterwards styled "Plymouth Brethren," Plymouth having: become their chief centre in England. As a body, they adopted the main principles am] doctrines of ,valker, Irving, and De Burgh, in respect to the abo'l"e subjects, and so continue to this day. But, singular to say, when Irving and De Burgh brought up those doctrines to the front, and when much enthusiasm was manifested about them, both in England and in Europe, between the years I 820 and 1830, these very men began to let go the foundations of Christianity itself, and speculated on the nature and person and experiences of our Lord, and on eternal j udgment, to the extent of involving the faith itself. X ot very long after, some of the chief teachers amongst the Plymouth Brethren, puffed up likewise by having: got hold of those exalterl doctrines without a corresponding 'thorn in the flesh' to preserve humility, fell into the same snare of the enemy, and a di'l"ision ensued. l\fr. Newton, of Plymouth, in seeking to combat some of the errors of Ining: fell himself into error; and Mr. Darby, in seeking to combat the errors of Newton, fell himself into error again. It is with this last gentleman and the party or section of the Plymouth Brethren which he has attracted to himself that we are now dealing. Mr. Darby has written a commentary on the whole Bible, and tracts innumerable, and has wade three translations of the New Testament into the three principal languages of Europe, German, French and English. In short, he hns been most assiduous and indefatigable in his writings, his tenchings, and his labours. Such at least is the drift of the preface. But nny one acquainted with tl)e subject of the collalion of MSS., must know that nil these nssertions are simply learned flourishes and gasconadin:i:, for it would tnh the labour of a life to collate for oneself and determine thus the text of the N cw Testament so as to give the product any weight whatever. And l\Ir. Darby hns a qunntity of ot~er things on. hand._ However it is with the tr:rnslation of known texts, of which no quest10n exists, that we now have to do, nlHI • The following ob.S<'rvations nud criticisms will bo found to tnko in scvl'rnl pnrts ,,f Scripture, nnd will Le, with the I.ord's blessing, both useful n~c\ i~teresting to thnsl' ,~hn wish to investig1tlo nnd eenrch into tho lrno force of the rn~p1rrd words of the N,w 1'1·stnmcnt on soino most important subject~.

The Ernngelist wants to point to the persistency and continuity with which they persecuted the Lord, not merely the fact that they did so, hence he uses the imperfect tenses for tlrnt purpose. Again in Mark Mr. Darby has, 'And in private he explained all things to his disciples.' It should be, 'But in prin1te he was in the habit of explaining (epeluen) all thinrrs to his disciples, (Mark iv. 34.) The Evangelist is careful to show that the Lo~-d not merely on a certain occasion explained things to his disciples, but was in the habit of doing so, and consequently uses the imperfect tense. And, at the burial, it is not merely that Mary Magdalen and i\Iary the mother of Joses 'saw' where he was 'put,' but were obsening 'where he is laid,' (etheoro11n pou tetheitali) (Mark x,-. 4i). The Evangelist using the present and imperfect tenses and employing a striking verb not merely to tell the fact that they saw a transaction most deRr to their hearts, but were observing and contemplating it whilst it was happening. And in Luke, when the seventy disciples were sent out and returned, saying that the demons are suqject to us 'through thy name.' 'And he said nnto them, I beheld Satan as lightning falling out of heaven,' (Mr. D.) It should be, 'I was beholding (etheorotm) Satan as liohtnino- fall (pesonta) from hea,·en,' (Luke x. 18). The Evangelist, by using th; impe,fecl, connects these two matters together. That is, whilst the devils were being subjected to them through his name during their mission, the Lord was beholding Satan, as lightning, fall from hea,en, and thus the chain and connection of the passage i, preserved. Jesus was beholding him as if already fallen. 'then, at the Cros~, where the force of the imp~1j'ect should be strictly preser.,.ed, they are all turned into historic past tenses ; e.g., the people and rulers 'sneere<l,'-the soldiers 'made game of him,' and the malefactor' spoke ir.sultingly to him.' (Mr. D.) It should be the people and rulers' kept sneering' or deriding. The soldiers kept or continued mocking him. 'And the malefactor kept railing at him.' The verbs are exemuliterizon, enepaizon, and eblasphemei-all imperfects. giving vividness and continuity to the sad scene. They are not merely historic aorists or past tenses, as if the Evangelist were telling us facts and leaving them there, but vivid pictures of things going on, presented to the min<l, (Luke xxiii. 35, 36, 39). And in the touching conversation on the way to Emmaus, the disciples say, not merely that we 'had hoped,' but 'we were l10pi1w' 0 (elpizornen) that it is 'he who should have redeemed Israel,' (Luke xxiv. 21 ). Thus emphasis is laid on the continuity of their expectations up to ihe time of his death at Jerusalem, not merely the fact that they had such expectations. Again, in John, a beautiful passn/!e is lost by disregarding the verb. The Lord himself chancres the verb twice in the same sentence, which in itself were sufficient to ~all attention to it: 'Judge not according. to sight hut judge righteou:5 judgmen~,' (l\Ir. I_).) should ?e,' Ju?ge not h~bitually (1)1·inete) ccordin" 0 to sirrht, but Judoe for once (k1·znate) righteous Judg-ment, (,Tohn vii. 24). The present imp~ralirn ~arking the habit, the aorist the d_efinite :,d. and so two different tenses m the same sentence. Mark this d,fkr~nce, the force of which is lost by rendering both in the same wny. Of ( our~e our language being analytic it is to be <lone by a periphrasis, but in a ~ynthetic lan,,.ua_ge, like the Greek, by changing a letter only. One more example, and w~ pass on to the Epistles. But it is an example of putting the :10rist for the imperfect to the loss of the whole passage. Mr. Darby here misses the idea. Jn Luke v. when the ships were stnnding by the lake of Gennesaret, 'but the fishermen ha\'in)l' come down from thence were wa~hingtlieir nets, and gettin" into one of the ships, &c., &c., he asked them to ch·aw ,,ut n little from tbe land . . . draw out into the cleep, &c.' (Mr. D.). It ,liould be,' they had wa~hed (epbmun) theh· nets,' ond then the Lord gett!ng into one of the ,hips a~ke<l to'' launch out again into the deep," (epanagage111). Tl1e point oftl,e pasrnge here i, in tl,e force of the verhs. The fishc("n)en hacl :iln·ady waFhed their nets, not' were washin~' 1hc1r.-the work was lm1sbnlvcl J efus my,, 'Launch out again into the deep,' &c. Then Peter E:iys, '"' e

have toiled all the nia-ht and have taken nothino- nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.' Their faith is sharply te~ted. If it we;e merelv that they were in the act of washing their nets, and the Lord said, ' draw ou't iato the deep water,' (Mr. D.) there would be in it little to remark, but the word comes after they had washed their nets and finished off. Jesus said ' launch back again into the deep.' and they do so. Here a beautiful passal7: loses its main instructive force by disregard of the verbs. " To give one or two illustrations from the Epistles, there is in Peter a remarkable passage elucidated by attention to the verb, a passage also on which there has been no little controversy. It refers to the Lord in life and death, as follows: • Who, when he was reviled, reviled not auain ; when suffering, threatened not; but gave [himself] over into the ha~ds of him who judges righteously: who himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.' (Mr. Darby.) It should be, 'Who, when reviled, used not to revile ; when suffering, used not to threaten; but was in the habit of committing himself to the care of him who judgeth ri~hteously: who himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, etc.' (1 Peter Ii. 23, 24.) The last not continuous but a single act. The apostle here uses four verbs; the first three are in the imperfect tense, referrin)! to the habit of the life of Him who left us an example, that we should ' follow His steps.' The last verb is in the aorist tense, referring to the definite single act of the sacrifice on the cross ; the apostle himself changing the tense purposely in the same sentence. Thus the exquisite beauty and accuracy of this lovely Scripture is in measure lost by disregarding the verb, and nothing gained over the authorised version. The other passage to which we refer in the Epistles is one to the Church of Ephesus, where the apostle says, according to Mr. Darby, 'In whom ye also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.' It should be, • In whom ye also are, being builded together to be ( smwikodomeisthe eis) a settled cl wellingplace of God in the Spirit.' (Ephes. ii. 21.) The verb is the present indicative passive, 'are being builded together, etc.' and so Alford ; but Mr. Darby puts it for the past, are built together,' by the antiqunted method of putting one tense for another, even the very opposite, to which ,Viner refers. But there was an object in thus changing it, for it is the standing text of Darbyism to prove that the church on earth is perfect, even 'as perfect ns the Holy Ghost himself,' to use the language of one of their school (Mr. Patterson), which is very evil indeed! Be this as it may, the real lnnguage of the text states the opposite. It looks at the church as a whole in process of formntion, and going on unto completion nt the day of glory, and Ephesus a structure ( oilwdo111e) forminp; unto that great cm!, but not as a thing already built or completed. To change and put the past tense here for the present is interpretation, not trnnslntiou; yet on this fob~ tramlntion is built almost the entire edifice of Da1·byism. III. ,vc come now to the gravest part of the subject, viz., where vital passages are interpreted, not translated, and supported by the aid of fal~c renderings of Scripture. We shall begin with the fundamental subject of justificntion by faith. There is in the N cw Testament a number of passnges bearing upon thi., point, and it now recei,·es 11 meaning in this 'New Transl11tion' which it never before received from the time the New Testament was written. For instance, where it is said that in the gospel 'the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith,' it is rendered in the' New Translation,'' The righteousness of God is revealed on the principle of faith,' etc. Now, it is quite true 11s doctrine that God does justify on the principle of faith, and that sinners are justified on the principle of faith, but that is not the meaning of the term 'by faith,' or • from faith' ( ek pisteos ). This rendering therefore refers it back to God, viz., thnt God is dealinrr with men on a principle; but the term • by faith' refers to the man himself, and it means, from faith, as the suqjcctive origin or source whence a man is justified, not merely that a man is justified on prin?,i.1~le. Therefore having been justified on the principle of faith, we have peace toward God, etc,-Rom. v. i. 5. What then shall we say, that they of the nations who did not follow after righteousness, have attained righteousness, but the righteousness that is on the principle of faith. But Israel pursuing after righteousness has not attained to that law. Wherefore? Because it was not on the principle of faith, but as of works.-Rom. ix. 30-32. 6. We also have believed on Christ Jesus, that we might be justified on the principle of the faith of Christ and not of works of law; because on the principle of works of law no flesh shall be jllstified.-Gal. ii. 16. 7. Know then that they that are on the principle of faith, these are Abraham's sons. And the Scripture foreseeing that God would justify the nations on the principle of faith, announced beforehand the glad tidings to Abraham, etc. etc. So that they who are on the principle of faith are blessed with believing Abraham.-Gal. iii. 7 -9. 8. Ye see that a man is justified on the principle of works, and not on the principle of faith only."-James ii. 24. Such are Mr. Darby's renderin,!!s of all these verses in which the common version reads 'by faith,' 'ex fide,' Lat. ; 'ek pisteos,' Greek._ . The above list will show that all these passages, treatmg on a most vital subject, are perverted and changed. They are applied to God-God dealing with man on a principle. There Mr. Darby informs us that a man is 'justified on the principle c,f works and not on the principle of faith only.'! . . . We wonder where l\Ir. Darby learnt this meanmg of the Gre~k words. ,v1th Irving the cloctrine of justification which ia a?optecl ~y parby1sm be_gan-thnt it is in virtue of the new man in union with Christ m resurrect10n. And whether the above renderings be meant to carry out this view or not.we cannot say. Jlowcver, on no subject have 1\lr. Darby ond !1is fo~l~wers wntten_ rn?rc prnfusely than on that of justification; and as their writmgs ore II p1ccmg

together of the thoughts of other thinkers nothing is explained or defined. In (net, not one of them from Mr. Darby downward ~eems to understand the subJect, nor to have thought out the subject. ·when men write on such a text as 'Christ is the end of the law for ric,hteousness to everyone that believe~h,' and deliberately illustrate it by saying 'That the end of the law for a culp~1t guilty o~ death is the rope,' it is plain they understand not the subject on which they wnte ; and their mode of treating it is as oper: to objection as the one they combat. Indeed, Mr. Darby himself in answer to The Record uses the following remarkable words. After having, as he thinks, exh:iusted the subject in expounding it, he says: "This is not properly justification, but it is the justification we have got, seeinir how we have obtained the justification."-Letler to the Record, p. 49; Morrish: London. TIIE DELECTABLE MOUNTAINS. THAT was a noble, hardy, stalwart., brnYe, and manly race of Christians that flourished amidst the storlTl<l of the Puritan nge. They m.re men of gre11t stature. We are in our sight as grasshopper~, and so we shouhl have been in theirs. Outward trials deepen inward experience. The changes without nnd within are upon the same mngnificent scale. High pressure gives more ~reed. The streno-th of "race is in proportion to the resistnnce to be oYercome. The more it i; necd;d, the more it is sought; and the more it is sought, the more it is obtained. Cnn the race of Christians tlegcnemte? Certainly, it can; not in birth, but in organic vigour, in intensity of purpose, and in daring exploits. Its constitution ·is affected by n bracing or a relaxing climate. \\'here storms are more frcrp1cnt, the air is more pure.

We have to do here with a Christian of the Bunyan type, of the Puritan type, of the Martyr type, of the Apostolic type. What would be the· reflections of a Christian of such a type upon his recent escape from Doubting c~~le an_d the perilous _grasp of_ Giant Despair? They would be neither very exh1laratmg nor very d1sheartenmg. There would be a strange mixture of joy aud grief, of hopes and fears. "It shall come to pass in that day, that the light ~hall not be_ clear nor dark: but it shall be known to the Lord, not d~y, nor m~ht; but 1t shall come to pass, that at evening time it shall be light." Accordmgly, we find the reflections of Bunyan's Pila-rim at this time to be strangely intermingled with light and shade. The Delectable Mountains are not what they would have been to him, if he had not recently gone astray; and, yet, from their contrast with the dark duno-eon 0 of Doubtinu0 Castle there was an inwardly repre~sed joy which he would not otherwise h ave felt. He needed the Delectable Mountaius, both for humiliation and for exultation. It was Emmanuel's !_and, and abounded with gardens, and orchards, and vineyards, and fountams of water. There were shepherds on these mountains, feeding their flocks, that Pilgrim might see in those flocks a contrast with those that wander from the fold. The names of the shepherds were Knowledge, Experience, ·watchful, and Sincere. Had Pilgrim placed himself under the guidance of these, he would not have gone nstray. These what? These angels ? these men ? these fellow Christians? No ! These inward principles of the new heart and right spirit! Had he possessed more knowledge, more experience, more watchfulness, more sincerity, he would not have gone so far astray. What would the Knowledge, and Experience, and "'atchfulness, and Sincerity, of others have availed him under such circumstances? "Precious names ! " says one, '' "What is a pilgrim without know\edge? What is head-know ledge without heart-experience? And watchfulness and sincerity ought to attend us every step! ,vhen these graces are in us ancl abound, they make delectable mountains indeed.'' Dr. Cheever, on the other hand, even here, seems to adhere to the external theory. "Here were shepherds of Christ," he says, "appointed to feed and keep his flock on these mountains, precious, holy men, named Knowledge, Experience, Watchful, and Sincere, who took the pil{J'rims by the hand, instructed them by their conversation, and lecl them ab~ut to show them the wonders of these mountains, just as the good Interpreter had shown them the rarities in his house_." One pilgrii:n ~nly, we maintain, was in the good Interpreter's house, and 1t was to one pilgr1_m only, and the good hope which even in Doubting Castle had not forsaken him,. th~t the Shepherds were giving instruction. These shepherds, too, were w1~lun the one pilgrim, and allegorically represent the graces that were brought mto exercise by reflecting upon his recent fall. From these sh_epherds he has much more to learn. They showed him from the top of a hill, called Error, the bones of many who had fallen from thence, and bad ~een dashed to pie?es by the fall. From the top of another bill, called Caut10n, they showed _111111 t)1e very stile that led to By-path meadow. They opened a doo1: by the side of n Lill and showed him the by-way to hell, by which hypocntes go even from the' fold of Emmanuel upon the Delectable Mountains. They showed him next through a telescope the gate of the Celestial City, but he could not see that ~o clearly, nor hope even, as they had seen the door of the by-way to hell. If it bad not been Pilgrim's own hope, and that just after he had escaped from Giant Despair, the Celestial City must have been more clearly seen. I~ Hopeful had been a distinct character, he must surely have seen_ tb_e ,gnte ol the Celestial City more clearly than the door to hell. It was Pilgrim s_hope, obscured by the remembrance of his recent folly, that could scarcely d_1scern the Celestial Gate. He would have enjoyed these Delectable l\fountmn~ far more if he had recovered from the effects of Doubting Castle. "0 t~rnt thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a nver, and thv. rio-ht,,ourness e as the waYes of the sea."

articles.text: IGNORANCE AND MANY OTHERS. 'THE effects of Gia!1t Despair in his Castle, and of the shepherds upon the Del~ct~hle_ Mount~ms, are still str~ugly commingled in the experience of Bunyan s P1lgrun. This leads to a variety of reflections and much internal conflict. Numerous characters, illustrative of what he micrht have been if he had followed out the suggestions of his own mind, pas~ before him. ' Here is Ignorance, "a brisk lad from the country of Conceit, with whom Pilcrrim has no sympathy, and puts him aside for a time. Here is Turn-away fro~ the town -of Apostacy, at the very sight of whom Pilgrim trembles. He mirrht have been such an one if left to himself, but nothing could now be furtlier from his ,thoughts. "Will ye also go away? Lord, to whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life." Here is Little-faith, from the town of Sincere. He was once attacked by three sturdy rogues, whose names were Faint-heart, :Mistrust, .and Guilt, who felled him to the ground, and took from his pocket a bag of silver, and then fearing lest one Great-grace should come to his assistance they ran away. His jewels they could not find, nor his certificate of admittance at the Celestial gate, so that with a little odd money left, and by ber,rrin" from -others, with much difficulty and maiiy privations be held on his ';a/ Pilgrim here sees what he had known in part, and what his whole course might .have been. "I myself," he says," have been engaged as this Little-faith was, and I found it a terrible thing. These three villains set upon me, and I beginning like a Christian to resist, they gave but a call, and in came their master. I would (as the saying iD) have given my life for a penny, but that, as God would have it, I was clothed with armour of proof. Ay, and though I was yet so harnessed, I found it bard work to quit myself like a man; no man can tell what in that combat attends us, but he that bath been in the battle himself." This Little-faith was evidently Pilgrim himself. "I myself," he says, "have been engaged as this Little-faith," and so he might ba'l'e said of Faithful and Hopeful and others. He himself was either all of them, or he might have been. Here next is Flatterer, who, under the pretext of showing him the right path, leads him into a net, from which a shining one rescues him, and with a whip of small cords chastises him. Hopeful, too, goes astmy, and is chastised with him, which is doubly painful to him. Bunyan, at times, was much exposed to tlattery, and had felt the need of severe chastisement on account of it. How often ministers foll into this snare, and, if men of GOll, they need no other chastisement than of their own consciences on account of it. Here is Atheist. Nay, does it not sometimes rush into notice on the very verge of heaven? The very awfulness of the thought may give it, at such 11 time, a momentary existence. As with Bunyan's Pilgrim, it quickly comes and •1uickly goes. articles.title: The Enchanted Ground
articles.notes: not listed in volume index; split at printed heading
articles.text:
THE ENCHANTED GROUND. Tms was not what the name might seem to imply. It was not an enchantment; to be indulged, but to be resisted. One of the shepherds bid the pilgrims beware of the Enchanted Ground; not because it was either rouah or beset with active foes, but because it presented a strong temptation to drowsiness. Its whole danger consisted in encouragement to inactivity and sleep. That part of Christian life which answers to this description is a season of uninterrupted enjoyment of religious privileges. It is such a season as the- Christian, when severely tried, earnestly longs for, and seems to him in the distance to be enchanted ground, but which is often found to be really Jess favourable to spiritual progress than to spiritual sloth. The effect of the· Enchanted Ground was happily resisted in the case of Bunyan's Pilrrrim 0 by renewing his acquaint:mce with the fundamental truths of the gospel. It was. a favourable opportunity for heart-searching enquiry into his views and experience of all the essential articles of his faith, such as could not be expected when climbing- with weary footsteps rugged hills, or contending with evil spirits in dark valleys. One part of the journey through the Enchanted Ground was occupied in conversation with Hopeful, another part in conversation with Ignorance, and another part in renewed conversation with Hopeful. This, which is generally adduced as an example of the converaation by which Christians should warm each others' hearts and stimulate each others' prog-ressin the divine life, is here considered to be illustrative of seasons for retired self-coutemplation. The whole may be easily referred to one and the same mind. Pilurim's hope becomes drowsy on the Enchanted Ground, because hope that i~ seen is not hope. Hope had reproved Pilgrim in Doubting Castle, but now Pilarim reproves Hope upon the Enchanted Ground. To keep Hope awake, Piln-rim enquires into all the particulars of its experience, whif'.h are in fact the pa~ticulars of his own experience as related in "Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners." Pilgrim gives no account of his own experience in return, which might reasonably have been expected, if mutual profit had been the chief aim, and it had been designed to be an example of _those that fear the Lord speaking often one to another. The questions are precisely such as every Christian would put to himself in closely investigating the ground of his own hope. How needful is it often to do this, and especially at the end of his pil!!rimaae when near to the solemn realities of the future! It is not to others me~ely, bu't to himself, he should be ready to give a reason of t~e hope t~at is in him with meekness and fear. This will enable him to say with one of old, "I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him agaiust that day." . The conversation of Pilgrim with Ignorance brings out the _ground of his hope with greater clearness, and distinguishes it from everythmg that _could possibly be mistaken for it. The teaching of Hopeful becomes the ~ee~hmg of Pilgrim himself. The conversation is then renewed between P1lgr1m and Hopeful upon matters _of duty and c~necien~e, in ~hi?h there is an entire unanimity both of sentiment and feelmg. 1. hus Pilgrim kept Hope awake-

God? It is found in the gospel only. Is there enchantment in a peace of conscience which passeth all understanding? It is found in the gospel only. Is there enchantment in the sure prospect of eternal rest in heaven? It is found in the gospel only. The enchantment of the gospel is well known to every true believer. He may be pleased with the beauties of nature and of art, with the refinements of literature and the discoveries of science, and he may not be insensible to the charms of virtue and of social bliss, but the full gospel to him is the only enchanted ground. It is to him what Paradise was to our first parents, and what heaven will be to the redeemed. " I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her saints shall shout aloud for joy." articles.notes: no display heading in the extracted text; title from volume index
articles.text:
GOD'S EYE A.i.'l'D MEN'S EYES.

LL persons who read will have heard of the unfortunate prisoner whose A greatest cross in captivity was the thought that, sleeping and waking day and night, there gazed upon him, through a hole in his cell door, a human eye ! The man in such a plight would deserve pity. Any one of us who would rejoice in attracting the admiring gaze of thousands, would tremble at the very thought of being watched by one ! And we should feel well nigh an- _nihilated if the world, by common consent, pointed at us the finger of scorn. Yet, One is ever marking our thoughts and. actions; and compared with this Omniscient Eye-to borrow one of Foster's similes-" the gaze of all created intclliJ?ences is infinitely less than the unconscious look of a new-born infant!" John 'Wesley once stood out very nobly in disregarding tbe eyes of men so long as he stood acquitted in the sight of God. Among his many persecutions arc to be numbered the falling back of former friends, including his wife. 'l'hese turned against him, and published many spiteful things, even defaming his character in a shocking manner. Brother Charles hastened off in alarm and indignation to enquire what defence Brother John would set up. There was no time to lose ! The eyes of the world were upon him, and God's enemies and bis own would be glad to make capital out of so contemptible a business! What was Charles's surprise to find that John was resolved on doing simply nothing I The great preacher was calm and comfortable in miud, being entirely free from any concern for the future. Why should he be perplexed when he had entrusted God with his all-even with his reputation? None are so safe as those whose characters are in God's keeping. Such often consider that they dishonour God by setting up puny defences of their own .against the cavils of the wick_ed. They think 1J1ore of that one eye of God which is ever looking on them, than of the eyes of men.

M IDDLESBROUGH, or as its people proudly call it, lronopolis, is in some respects the most remarkable town in the country. Its origin was largel_y the r~sult o_f the i~veD;,tion of the locomotive, and i'8 development has run side by side with the mst1tution of the Cleveland iron trade, of which it forms the centre. It has so rapidly assumed the p~oportions of a large town, th~t upon the spot where forty years ago stood a single farmhouse, tbere now exists a populat10n of nearly 50,000 persons. This population contains representatives from almost every part of Great Britain, and even from the Continent. The spiritual condition of thousands of these people is deplorable; they neither know the Gospel, nor do they care to know it, and if they did, there is not accommodation for half of them in the places of worship. Of far too many all that can be said is, they work, they drink, they die! Amidst this dense darkness several Christian churches are endeavouring to hold forth the light of life ; amongst their number is the Baptist Church at present worshipping in Park Road School-chapel, of which Mr. W. H. Priter, a student of the Tabernacle College, is the pastor. The Church was formed some sixteen years since, and in late years was presided over by the late Rev. ,v. Bontems, under whom land was purchased and schools erected at a cost of £2,000, £800 remaining as debt. In February, 1870, Mr. Priter accepted the unanimous invitation of the Church, then numbering eighty members, to become its pru!tor. God has been pleased graciously to smile upon the union, so that amidst much difficulty and many discouragements the work of the Lord has gradually progressed. In order to provide for the numerous hearers, the Sunday evening service was removed to the Oxford Music Hall, where many were savingly converted to God. Sunday afternoon addresses to working men have also been delivered in the theatre. In addition to the ordinary tract distribution, the idea suggested itself that a selfsupporting paper might be published and gratuitously distributed among the homes of the people. Thus the "Christian Pionee1·" was established, with a monthly circulation of 5,000; the total number sent out has now reached 120,000, having cost nearly £120, the cost being met by the advertisini department. By this mean~ many have learned the story of redeeming love. 'l'he proclamation of the Gospel bas not been without success, and the church membership has increased to 200. Among the more recent additions have been severo.l young people from the Sabbath School. Would that our Chw·ches were more frequently refreshed and strengthened in this way ! As God's blessing increased, the absolute necessity for a larger place of meeting became more apparent. Difficulty and dangers abounded-a. heavy debt, no wealthy people, but a faithful God. To go forward seemed impossible, but in the strength of the Eternal, the determination was made, and the work commenced. A bazaar was held which realised £200; subscriptions were solicited and promised, and in March 1872, the found11tion stone was laid by Mr. Thomas Vaughan, the mayor of the town, who h11s nobly given £150 towards the erection. The new chapel is designed to sea.t 1,030 persons, and will cost, exclusive of land and schools, £2,700. Towards this, about £1,400 have been raised, and every effort is being made to obtain the greater part of the remaining sum by the time of the opening, which will be early in the spring. Assistance would be most gratefully received. Meanwhile, the attempt is being made to form new interests in the many destitute parts a.round. At South Bo.nk, a pl11cc that might rival any hcnthcn villac,e a work has been commenced with the aid of a Christian gentleman, which promises soon to result in the formation of a Bn.ptist Church. At North Ormesby, open-air seryices ~ave been ~aintained duri1_1g the ~ummer, ~ml 11 room has been taken m which to contmue the meetmgs dum1g the winter.

But while so much energy is absorded in the erection of the new chapel, evangilization cannot be prosecuted with the vigour which the pressing needs of the district demand, and which we hope will soon. be thrown into it. In the North of England our denomination is very weak, but being growinaly confident in the greatness of its principles, and the intensely practical hearing of its distinctive ordinance, we fear not but that amid the toiling tens of thousands of this important frovince there is "a future for the Baptists••; and merging the denominationa into the Christian, we firmly believe that in the midst of the great workshop of England, he who disdained not to wear the workman's garb, shall one day be the centre of the affections of all, and the gentle leader who shall guide many followers in the ways of peace. We insert this to show that the College men are fully at work, and to excite our friends to help both this particular work, and the College, which in a hundred places is doing like work.
